Three properties of this empirical pattern matter for engineering application, with the magnitude
correction from al-Munāsabāt §5.2 in mind. First, the canonical Quran's apparent autocorrelation
(+0.80 at lag 20) decomposes into two contributions: approximately +0.65 attributable to the
canonical's approximate length-sort (the within-quartile shuffle row of Table 1) and approximately
+0.15 residual attributable to intra-quartile ordering decisions. The +0.15 residual is statistically
significant (p < 0.01) but is the supportable size of the deeper coherence-organization effect, not
the +0.80 headline. Second, the gap between canonical and chronological orderings of the same
underlying content (canonical +0.80 vs Cairo 1924 +0.13 at lag 20) is dominated by the difference in


length-sort structure between the two orderings rather than by deeper organizational principles;
engineers should expect that gross arrangement decisions (cohort-by-cohort module placement)
capture the bulk of available structural-coherence benefit and that fine-grained intra-cohort
optimization is the smaller residual. Third, the pattern is robust across two independent Arabic
lemmatization tools, indicating it is a property of the corpus arrangement rather than an artifact of
any specific tool. The strategies that follow build on these three observations, with the explicit caveat
that two of the eight (Strategy 4.1 and the §2 framing) are most directly affected by the magnitude
correction and the other six are theoretically grounded and survive intact.
Status under Cross-Text §6 Caveat 1: candidate-finding. Independent replication by a research group
not the present authors, using a different Arabic NLP toolchain and pre-registered lag thresholds, is
required for promotion to confirmed-result status. Engineering organizations adopting these
strategies should plan their adoption with the magnitude correction in mind and should be prepared
for a revision case in which independent replication moves the magnitude further. The strategies are
recommended on a combination of theoretical grounding (in specific Quranic structural primitives),
modest-but-real empirical support (the +0.15 residual), and well-attested human cost in the failuremode literature (§5–§7) — not on overwhelming empirical magnitude.

4. The Eight Strategies
4.1 Canonical-First Architecture (al-Fātiḥa Principle)
Anchor: the al-Fātiḥa placement at position 1 of the canonical mu ṣḥaf. Al-Fāti ḥa is
comprehensive, short, and structurally complete; it states the full theological frame in
seven verses and is recited at the opening of every Quranic engagement. Its placement
first is not chronological (it is not the first revealed surah) but structural (it is the entry
point that frames all subsequent reading).
The strategy: in safety- and justice-critical software, the canonical arrangement of modules is
designed before code is written. The entry point of the system — the equivalent of al-Fāti ḥa — is a
comprehensive but compact statement of system-level invariants, safety constraints, and the
contracts each subsequent module must honor. The longest, most comprehensive modules follow
next, in approximate descending order of scope. The most specific, targeted modules appear last. This
is the mirror of the canonical Quranic structure rather than the development chronology.
Implementation: at the start of any safety- or justice-critical project, write a
SAFETY_INVARIANTS.md file before the first line of executable code. This file states, in declarative
form, the full set of safety- and justice-related invariants the system must maintain — for an
automotive perception system, the bounded latency, the false-negative rate ceiling, the required ASIL
classification, the defined operational design domain. This file is the al-Fātiḥa: short enough to be reread at every architectural decision, comprehensive enough to constrain every subsequent module.
Modules are arranged in the project structure in approximate descending order of scope: the central
perception pipeline first, the integration layer second, the calibration utilities last. Adding a new
module is permitted only after demonstrating its compatibility with SAFETY_INVARIANTS.md.


The empirical falsifiable claim, with the magnitude correction: codebases following the al-Fāti ḥa
principle (with both gross arrangement by descending scope and fine-grained intra-cohort
coherence) exhibit higher long-range coherence than codebases of comparable size and domain that
grew chronologically. The bulk of the available benefit comes from the gross arrangement decision
(descending scope, equivalent to the canonical Quran's approximate length-sort, which the empirical
foundation shows accounts for approximately 82 percent of the structural-coherence effect).
Additional but smaller benefit comes from fine-grained intra-cohort coherence engineering.
Codebases failing the gross-arrangement test are at higher risk of structural drift over time and are
more expensive to certify under standards that require traceability. Codebases that achieve gross
arrangement but not fine-grained intra-cohort coherence capture most of the engineering benefit at
substantially lower cost; this is the recommended minimum-viable adoption form of the strategy.
Strategy 4.1 is the strategy most affected by the empirical-magnitude correction in al-Munāsabāt
§5.2; the other seven strategies are theoretically grounded in specific Quranic structural primitives
independent of the empirical magnitude.

4.2 Naskh Discipline for Breaking Changes (2:106)
Anchor: 2:106 — "Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring forth
one better than it or similar to it." The classical Islamic naskh tradition specifies that
the abrogating verse must be at least equivalent to the abrogated one, that the
abrogated verse is preserved in the textual record rather than deleted, and that the
abrogation is explicit rather than implicit.
Standard engineering equivalent: controlled deprecation with archival access. The strategy is
structurally similar to SemVer's MAJOR-version-bump discipline, expanded with formal equivalenceor-superiority demonstration and archival preservation in a frozen namespace rather than deletion.
The Quranic anchor in 2:106 provides a unified articulation of practices that exist piecewise in
mature engineering organizations under different vocabulary (deprecation policy, archival API
endpoints, migration tooling).
The strategy: in safety- and justice-critical software, breaking changes to a public surface (an API, a
configuration schema, a calibration parameter) require three artifacts: a written declaration of what
is being removed, a structurally-verified claim that the replacement provides equivalent or superior
capability with the verification being a test or proof rather than author assertion, and preservation
of the prior surface in an archival namespace rather than deletion. This is more disciplined than
SemVer's MAJOR bump and more specific than the additive-only check from furqan-lint.
Implementation: every breaking change ships with a naskh block in the changelog: (1) what is being
removed (specific symbols, specific schema fields, specific configuration parameters); (2) what
replaces it; (3) the test or proof artifact demonstrating equivalence or superiority; (4) the archival
location of the removed surface (a frozen submodule, a separate package, a documented API endpoint
that returns the legacy behavior with an explicit deprecation header). Migration tooling for
downstream consumers is shipped alongside the abrogation, not after. Consumers who do not
migrate continue to receive correct behavior from the archival surface for a documented support
window.


Industry application — automotive: a perception model retrained with new data is a naskh of the
prior model. The new model must demonstrate equal-or-better safety performance on the safety case
test suite before deployment; the prior model is preserved in the vehicle's archive and remains
available for forensic analysis if a post-deployment incident occurs. Industry application — financial:
a fraud-detection rule retired in favor of a new rule must be archived with full audit trail; downstream
regulators may require the archive for years past retirement. Industry application — healthcare: a
dosing algorithm replaced in firmware update must demonstrate non-inferiority on the validation
set; the prior algorithm is preserved in archive for adverse-event investigation.

4.3 The Munāsabāt Audit (Long-Range Coherence as Quality Metric)
Anchor: ʿilm al-munāsabāt, the classical Islamic scholarly tradition of identifying and
analyzing structural connections between Quranic units (verses, passages, surahs,
surah pairs). The empirical finding from Bayyinah al-Munāsabāt operationalizes one
specific testable proxy from this tradition: lag-N autocorrelation of compositional
similarity sequences.
The strategy: long-range structural coherence is treated as a measurable quality property of a
codebase, not an aesthetic judgment. The pipeline from Bayyinah al-Munāsabāt — TF-IDF on
identifier names or AST node types, cosine similarity, Fibonacci-additive growth, lag-N
autocorrelation — operates on any sequence of textual units. Apply it to a codebase by treating each
file or each module as a unit; tokenize on identifiers (or richer: on AST node-type sequences);
compute the autocorrelation profile; track over time.
Three downstream applications follow naturally. (1) Drift detection over time: compute the profile
per quarter on the same codebase. If the canonical-order autocorrelation declines monotonically, the
codebase is losing structural coherence as it grows. This is structural debt made measurable. (2)
Refactoring validation: compute the profile pre- and post-refactor. Large changes flag potential
coherence loss the test suite cannot see. (3) Architecture proposal benchmarking: test multiple
competing reorganizations on a prototype; pick the one with the strongest sustained autocorrelation
under a sensible coherence definition.
Implementation: integrate the Munāsabāt Audit as a CI gate alongside ruff, mypy, and furqan-lint.
The gate computes the autocorrelation profile on the current commit and on the commit at the start
of the current quarter; flags significant declines for human review; logs the historical trajectory for
safety-case documentation. The gate is non-blocking by default — declining coherence is a signal, not
an automatic failure — but configurable to block on configurable thresholds for projects under
regulatory mandate.

4.4 Multi-Corpus Baseline Discipline
Anchor: the negative-control discipline empirically demonstrated in Bayyinah alMunāsabāt. The most decisive findings came from the four negative-control corpora
(Bukhari, Muslim, Muwatta, pre-Islamic poetry, Hebrew Bible), not from the primary
canonical-vs-chronological comparison. Without negative controls, a finding of
canonical-Quran autocorrelation could be dismissed as a generic property of compiled


religious-text canons. With them, the finding is shown to be a specific property of the
Uthmanic arrangement.
Standard engineering equivalent: multi-baseline evaluation in machine-learning, statistical, and
empirical-software-engineering practice. The external-validity literature in ML evaluation (e.g., the
SuperGLUE diversification of GLUE; the multi-task evaluation discipline in BIG-bench) and the multibaseline expectation in clinical trials (treatment-vs-placebo-vs-active-comparator) are the closest
pre-existing analogues. The Quranic anchoring frames the discipline as falsification by negative
control rather than as confirmation by single comparator; the engineering substance is well-known
but is often weakly applied in practice, particularly in machine-learning evaluation where singlebaseline benchmarks remain common.
The strategy: in any benchmarking, evaluation, or safety-case construction, multiple orthogonal
baselines are required, not a single reference. The cost of additional baselines is typically linear; the
discriminative power gained is more than linear, because the failure mode being defended against
(the finding turns out to be specific to the chosen baseline) is multiplicatively reduced by each
additional independent baseline.
Industry application — autonomous vehicle perception: a new ML perception system must be
evaluated against (a) a rule-based controller, (b) a classical reinforcement-learning controller, (c) a
model-predictive controller, and (d) at least one prior-generation ML system. Beating the previousgeneration ML alone is insufficient evidence; a perception system that has structural advantages over
only ML baselines may have failure modes the non-ML baselines would have caught. Industry
application — algorithmic decision systems in sentencing: a new risk-assessment instrument must
be evaluated against (a) actuarial baselines from criminology, (b) pure base-rate predictors, (c)
human-judge baselines, and (d) prior-generation algorithmic systems. Beating only prior algorithms
while failing against simpler baselines is a documented and consequential failure mode (Dressel and
Farid 2018 showed COMPAS performed comparably to non-expert human predictions and to a
simple two-feature linear model).

4.5 Validator-by-Different-Instance
Anchor: the dual-pipeline robustness check applied in Bayyinah al-Munāsabāt
(Tashaphyne root extraction and Qalsadi citation-form lemmatization processed every
Arabic corpus). The discipline is connected to 50:17-18 ("Not a word does he utter
except that there is an observer ready to record") — two recorders, redundant
verification.
Standard engineering equivalent: this strategy is a variant of N-version programming as introduced
in the late 1970s by Avizienis and colleagues and subjected to the foundational empirical study of
Knight and Leveson 1986. The Quranic anchor in 50:17-18 provides a unified articulation; the
engineering substance is a recognizable existing practice with a well-documented empirical
limitation.
The Knight and Leveson 1986 finding limits this strategy directly. In their landmark experiment,
twenty-seven independent programmer teams wrote programs to the same specification; the
resulting programs failed in correlated rather than independent ways, contradicting the central


independence assumption of N-version programming. Their conclusion — that diverse
implementations developed by independent teams against the same specification cannot be assumed
to fail independently — has been replicated by subsequent studies and remains the canonical caveat
on N-version approaches. An engineering organization considering this strategy should read Knight
and Leveson 1986 directly. The expected leverage of N-version approaches is bounded by interversion correlation in failure modes, which is empirically substantial when versions are built against
the same specification.
The strategy as articulated here uses a specific variant that may partially escape Knight and Leveson's
failure mode while remaining subject to its underlying mechanism. Where Knight and Leveson
studied diverse-team-same-specification, the present strategy specifies diverse-toolchain-samespecification: the same algorithm compiled by two different compilers (GCC and Clang), executed on
two different runtimes (PyTorch and JAX), or processed through two different morphological tools
(Tashaphyne and Qalsadi). The cognitive correlations Knight and Leveson identified (developers
making similar mistakes on the same hard cases) do not directly apply to toolchain variants, which
have different cognitive lineages. However, toolchain variants share other correlations that limit
their effective independence: GCC and Clang both lower through LLVM-derived intermediate
representations for some code paths; PyTorch and JAX both rely on CUDA kernels and on numerical
libraries from a small common pool; Tashaphyne and Qalsadi share Zerrouki's preprocessing
assumptions about Arabic morphology. The toolchain-variant approach mitigates but does not
eliminate the Knight-Leveson failure mode. Adopters should expect the strategy to catch a
meaningful but bounded class of failures — specifically, those that depend on toolchain-specific
assumptions not shared across the chosen variants — rather than the full class of implementation
errors a fully independent N-version system would in principle catch.
The strategy: validate every safety-relevant computation through at least two independent
implementations. The implementations must differ in at least one of: compiler, runtime, numericalprecision regime, library family. The strategy's expected leverage is bounded by Knight-Leveson
correlations and should be planned accordingly. A finding that holds under both implementations is
stronger evidence than one that holds under either alone; it is not, after Knight and Leveson, evidence
of unconditional independence. The class of failures defended against is implementation-specific
artifact, with the qualification that some failures will correlate across variants regardless.
Industry application — avionics under DO-178C DAL A: redundant flight-control software is
mandated by the standard. Bayyinah's discipline extends this from runtime redundancy (two
computers running the same software) to compile-time redundancy (the same algorithm
implemented in two different languages or compiled by two different toolchains, with discrepancies
surfacing as test failures). DO-178C's existing redundancy mandate already incorporates KnightLeveson-aware design principles in practice — the standard requires independence demonstration
that goes beyond simple toolchain variation. Industry application — financial settlement: critical
pricing or settlement calculations executed through both a primary implementation and a reference
implementation, with reconciliation gates blocking mismatches before any external settlement; the
leverage here is bounded by shared library dependencies and shared numerical assumptions across
the two implementations. Industry application — medical-device firmware: dosing calculations
executed through both the primary embedded-C implementation and a model-checked reference (in


TLA+ or Coq) before any patient-affecting action — the formal-method reference variant has
different failure modes than the embedded-C primary variant and is closer to the spirit of Knight and
Leveson's original independence motivation than diverse-team-same-specification approaches.

4.6 The Recording Angels Pattern (Append-Only Audit Trails)
Anchor: 50:17-18 ("On either side, two angels recording, sitting; not a word does he
utter except that there is an observer ready to record") and 82:10-12. The structural
primitive is append-only, two-witness, complete coverage, structurally tamper-evident
at a level the actor cannot reach.
Standard engineering equivalent: append-only audit logs, event sourcing, and immutable ledger
design as practiced in financial systems, distributed databases (Kafka's commit log, Datomic's
immutable database design), and high-assurance forensic logging. The Quranic anchoring in 50:1718 articulates as a unified pattern what is otherwise practiced piecewise: append-only storage, twowitness redundancy across administrative domains, tamper-evident hash chains, and forensic
accessibility independent of the recording party's cooperation.
The strategy: substrate-layer event logs are append-only, dual-witnessed, complete, and tamperevident at the storage layer. This goes beyond CHANGELOG-as-documentation to CHANGELOG-assubstrate. Every behavioral change at runtime in safety-critical software produces an immutable
record. The record is held at a layer the producing software cannot mutate. The record is
independently witnessed by a second component (a recording subsystem on a different machine, in
a different process, or in a different administrative domain) with consensus required before commit.
Industry application — automotive black-box for software state: every actuator command issued by
an autonomous-vehicle perception system is recorded with hash chain to both the vehicle's onboard
event-data recorder and to a second redundant recorder. Forensic reconstruction after an incident is
then possible without trust in the producing software. Industry application — healthcare infusion
pumps: every dose calculation, every volume delivery, every operator override is recorded in
append-only form with two-witness verification. Adverse-event investigation has full forensic
reconstruction. Industry application — financial trading: every order with N-of-M consensus across
recorders, with the hash chain verifiable by external auditors. Industry application — algorithmic
decision systems: every input-output pair from a sentencing or lending algorithm recorded with the
model version, the input feature vector, the output decision, and the human reviewer's identity if any.
This is the substrate that makes algorithmic-bias auditing possible at all; without it, retrospective
review is impossible.

4.7 The Sulaymān-Naml Pattern (Weak-Signal Observability, 27:18-19)
Anchor: 27:18-19 — the ant warns the ant-colony of Sulaymān's approaching army;
Sulaymān hears the small voice over the noise of the army and smiles. The structural
primitive is weak-signal fidelity at the receiver: a low-amplitude signal from a minority
path must surface and must be acknowledged.
Standard engineering equivalent: sub-threshold event monitoring with explicit acknowledgment
discipline. The technical infrastructure is well-developed in modern observability stacks


(Prometheus, OpenTelemetry, Grafana with anomaly detection) and in the safety-incident reporting
culture of mature aviation, healthcare, and nuclear-plant operations. The Quranic anchoring
articulates the often-missing receiving-discipline component — the requirement that the small signal
not only be detected but also acknowledged and acted upon — which is organizational rather than
technical and is often the actual failure mode in documented cases (the 737 MAX MCAS pilot reports
were detected through standard incident-reporting channels but were not surfaced to certification
authority within useful time).
The strategy: every error class with low frequency must have a non-zero alerting threshold, not
"below noise floor, ignore." The receiving discipline matters as much as the instrumentation: when
the small signal arrives, it is acknowledged and acted upon, not dismissed as noise. This is
operationally distinct from threshold-based monitoring, which is structurally incapable of catching
low-frequency high-impact events.
Industry application — autonomous vehicle edge cases: the rare pedestrian in unusual clothing (a
person in a wheelchair carrying balloons; a person walking a bicycle across a crosswalk) appears in
production traffic at perhaps one in ten million events, well below the typical false-positive rate of
object-detection systems. The naml pattern requires that any classification confidence below a
defined threshold for any safety-critical category triggers logging, human review, and is added to the
regression test suite. The Tempe Uber crash in 2018 (Elaine Herzberg killed by an autonomous Uber
that classified her as variously a vehicle, then bicycle, then unknown) is precisely the failure mode
this pattern is designed to defend against.
Industry application — medical device adverse events: rare adverse events tracked with non-zero
alerting threshold even at sub-threshold counts. The Therac-25 case (six confirmed radiation
overdose deaths over approximately three years) involved a race condition that fired at low
frequency; clinicians who reported the early events were dismissed as unreliable. The naml pattern
requires that any unreproducible adverse event in a Class III medical device generates an
investigation track that does not close until the cause is identified or the event has not recurred for a
defined period.
Industry application — algorithmic decision systems and fairness: differential-impact metrics
computed at coarse demographic categories may miss small subgroups for whom the system
performs catastrophically. The naml pattern requires that any subgroup with sample size above a
minimum threshold and false-negative rate above the system-wide rate by a defined margin triggers
investigation regardless of the subgroup's contribution to the system-wide aggregate.

4.8 The Yūsuf Horizon Pattern (Long-Horizon Strategic Planning, surah 12)
Anchor: surah 12 (Yūsuf), the Quran's most extended single narrative covering
decades from childhood dream through prison, ministerial appointment, the sevenfat / seven-lean year planning cycle, and eventual reunion. The structural primitives are
explicit horizon declaration, strategic-plan protection ("do not divulge your dream to
your brothers," 12:5), forecasting-as-capacity-planning, and acceptance of
intermediate states that look like setbacks on the path to the strategic objective.


Standard engineering equivalent: long-horizon strategic planning and capacity modeling, as
practiced in regulated-industry product roadmaps, multi-year DARPA program design, and aircraft
type-certification planning. The Quranic anchoring articulates four often-missing components
together: explicit horizon declaration with intermediate milestones, protection of the strategic kernel
from premature disclosure, forecasting integrated with capacity reservation, and organizational
tolerance for intermediate states that look like regression. The engineering substance is well-known
to mature regulated-industry organizations; less mature organizations often plan with shorter
horizons than their products demand and underweight the protection-of-strategic-kernel and
intermediate-state-tolerance components.
The strategy: certification cycles for safety-critical software typically span months to years. The
standard agile-development cadence (sprints, releases, retrospectives at week-to-month timescales)
is structurally inadequate for the planning required. The Yūsuf Horizon Pattern declares an explicit
multi-cycle horizon at project initiation, identifies intermediate milestones that do not coincide with
certification gates, protects the strategic kernel from premature disclosure (some certification
artifacts are required to be produced in restricted-visibility regimes — for instance, test cases must
be designed without knowledge of the implementation), and accepts that some intermediate states
will look like regression to teams unfamiliar with the certification timeline.
Industry application — DO-178C DAL A certification: aircraft type certification has 5-to-10 year
horizons. Component lifecycle planning under the Yūsuf Horizon includes reserves for unanticipated
regulatory changes, for revisions in the operational design domain, and for technological substrate
changes (new flight computers, new hypervisor versions, new toolchain qualifications). Industry
application — IEC 62304 medical device development: a Class C medical device may have 3-to-7 year
development cycles. The Yūsuf Horizon plans capacity for the seven-lean-year period (post-clearance
maintenance, ongoing risk management, surveillance reporting) at the same time as the seven-fatyear period (initial development through clearance). Industry application — financial-system
migrations: replacing a core banking system has 5-to-10 year horizons. The Yūsuf Horizon plans the
prison years (the period when the new system is being built but the old system still operates)
explicitly, with capacity for both.

5. Application to Safety-Critical Industries
This section maps the eight strategies to four specific safety-critical industries with explicit reference
to the standards, the failure modes the strategies defend against, and the public failure-case literature
that establishes the cost of failure.

5.1 Automotive (ISO 26262, ASIL D)
ISO 26262-6 governs software development for road vehicles, with Automotive Safety Integrity
Levels (ASIL) A through D corresponding to ascending severity, exposure, and controllability. ASIL D
corresponds to the highest risk class — failures with potential for fatal injuries to multiple persons
under the relevant operating conditions. Steering systems, primary braking, and primary perception
in autonomous vehicles typically classify as ASIL D. The standard requires extensive structural
traceability from requirements through design, code, and test.


The Tempe Uber crash (March 2018), the Boeing 737 MAX MCAS failures (October 2018 and March
2019), and the multiple Tesla Autopilot fatalities under investigation by NHTSA between 2016 and
2024 all involve failure modes the eight strategies are designed to defend against. The MCAS failure
in particular is a clean case for the al-Fātiḥa principle (the system's safety invariants — that MCAS
would not activate from a single sensor input, that pilots would be informed of activation — were not
stated in a load-bearing al-Fātiḥa file; they emerged from the system's behavior under conditions the
test suite did not exercise) and for the Sulaymān-Naml pattern (early reports of unexpected MCAS
activation in routine flight were dismissed before the Lion Air and Ethiopian Airlines crashes).

Strategy

Application in this industry

4.1 Canonical-First Architecture

SAFETY_INVARIANTS.md states ASIL classification, ODD
definition, latency bounds, and false-negative/positive rate
ceilings before any code. Module arrangement reflects safety
hierarchy, not feature-add chronology.

4.2 Naskh Discipline

Perception model retraining requires non-inferiority
demonstration on the safety-case test suite before deployment;
prior model archived for forensic access.

4.3 Munāsabāt Audit

Continuous coherence monitoring across firmware revisions;
declining autocorrelation flags potential structural debt
accumulation.

4.4 Multi-Corpus Baselines

New ML perception evaluated against rule-based, classical RL,
MPC, and prior-generation ML; not just against prior generation.

4.5 Validator-by-Different-Instance

Cross-toolchain compilation (GCC + Clang + IAR); discrepancies
surfaced as test failures before deployment.

4.6 Recording Angels

Vehicle event-data recorder logs all actuator commands with
hash chain to redundant secondary recorder; forensic
reconstruction independent of primary system.

4.7 Sulaymān-Naml

Sub-threshold object-classification confidence triggers logging,
human review, and regression-suite addition; designed to defend
against the Tempe Uber failure mode.

4.8 Yūsuf Horizon

Multi-year ASIL D certification cycle planned with explicit
reserves for ODD revisions, sensor substrate changes, and postdeployment monitoring.

5.2 Avionics (DO-178C, DAL A)
DO-178C governs software development for airborne systems, with Design Assurance Levels (DAL)
A through E corresponding to descending severity. DAL A applies to software whose failure would
result in catastrophic failure conditions — typically defined as those resulting in multiple fatalities,
usually with hull loss. Primary flight control, fly-by-wire systems, autopilot in critical phases, and
engine-control software typically classify as DAL A. The standard requires structural coverage


demonstration (statement, decision, and modified-condition/decision coverage at DAL A) and
extensive traceability.
The Boeing 737 MAX MCAS failure (346 fatalities across two crashes), the Air France 447 crash (228
fatalities, with significant software-and-human-factors contribution from the pitot-tube failure
mode), and the Lion Air 610 case before MCAS revisions (189 fatalities) represent failure modes in
the DAL A regime that the eight strategies address. The 737 MAX case in particular involved several
Bayyinah-relevant patterns: the al-Fātiḥa principle was violated (MCAS was added to an existing
platform without restating the system's safety invariants under the new architecture), the Naskh
Discipline was violated (the change from MCAS-using-two-AOA-sensors to MCAS-using-one was an
undeclared abrogation of the prior safety case), and the Sulaymān-Naml pattern was violated (early
Lion Air reports of unexpected MCAS activation were not surfaced into the regulatory or training
pipelines).

Strategy

Application in this industry

4.1 Canonical-First

SAFETY_INVARIANTS.md restated at every aircraft typecertification revision, not just at initial certification; DAL
classification, failure-condition severity, and pilot-action-required
envelope are load-bearing first-position content.

4.2 Naskh Discipline

Any change to safety-relevant logic accompanied by formal
abrogation block: what is removed, what replaces it, the formal
verification artifact demonstrating equivalence or superiority, the
archival location of the prior logic.

4.3 Munāsabāt Audit

Coherence monitoring across firmware revisions for in-service
aircraft; correlated with field failure rates as candidate predictive
metric.

4.4 Multi-Corpus Baselines

New control law evaluated against prior generation, against
classical control-theoretic baselines, and against simulator-based
human-pilot baselines under fault injection.

4.5 Validator-by-Different-Instance

DO-178C already mandates redundant runtime; Bayyinah
extends to compile-time redundancy via dual-toolchain
compilation with discrepancy gates.

4.6 Recording Angels

Cockpit voice recorder + flight-data recorder + software-state
recorder with N-of-M consensus, accessible to crash investigators
independent of operator cooperation.

4.7 Sulaymān-Naml

Aviation Safety Reporting System integrated with onboard eventdata; sub-threshold pilot reports of unusual control authority
surface to certification authority within defined window.

4.8 Yūsuf Horizon

Type certification planning across 10-to-30 year service life;
explicit reserves for regulatory changes, hypervisor substrate
evolution, certification-authority workload.


5.3 Healthcare (IEC 62304 Class C, FDA Class III)
IEC 62304 governs medical-device software, with Safety Classes A (no injury possible), B (nonserious injury possible), and C (death or serious injury possible). FDA Class III represents the highestrisk medical-device regulatory class and includes pacemakers, implantable defibrillators, infusion
pumps in critical-care settings, radiation-therapy delivery systems, and certain surgical robots. The
combined regulatory regime requires risk management throughout the lifecycle, not just at
clearance.
The Therac-25 case (six confirmed radiation-overdose deaths between 1985 and 1987 due to a race
condition between operator input and treatment delivery) is the canonical software-safety failure in
healthcare. The Hospira and Baxter infusion-pump recalls (multiple model lines, multiple causes
including software-mediated dose-delivery errors) span 2010 through 2024. The Da Vinci surgical
robot's adverse-event reporting investigated between 2013 and 2023 includes a software
contribution to certain instrument-failure modes. Each of these involves the failure modes the eight
strategies address.

Strategy

Application in this industry

4.1 Canonical-First

Risk management file (per ISO 14971) authored before code;
states safety classes, hazardous situations, and the risk-control
measures that govern subsequent design.

4.2 Naskh Discipline

Dosing-algorithm replacement requires non-inferiority
demonstration against clinical validation set; prior algorithm
preserved in archive for adverse-event investigation.

4.3 Munāsabāt Audit

Coherence monitoring across firmware revisions for fielded
devices; declining coherence is a candidate signal for elevated
post-market surveillance attention.

4.4 Multi-Corpus Baselines

New decision-support algorithms evaluated against multiple
clinical-baseline classes, not just prior algorithm; specifically
including human-clinician-only baselines under standardized
vignettes.

4.5 Validator-by-Different-Instance

Dose-calculation code executed through both primary embedded
implementation and model-checked reference (TLA+ or Coq
specification); reconciliation gates block deployment on
discrepancy.

4.6 Recording Angels

Append-only treatment log with hash chain; preserves complete
dose-delivery history for adverse-event investigation
independent of device-manufacturer cooperation.

4.7 Sulaymān-Naml

Adverse-event reporting integrated with sub-threshold detection;
rare event with sample-size minimum triggers investigation
regardless of system-wide rate. Designed against the Therac-25
failure mode.

4.8 Yūsuf Horizon

Class III device development planned across 5-to-15 year service
life including post-market surveillance reserves; explicit capacity


for surveillance reporting at same horizon as initial development.

5.4 Energy and Infrastructure
Software in nuclear-plant control, electrical-grid management, water-treatment systems, and oiland-gas pipeline control faces failure modes ranging from regional blackouts (the 2003 Northeast
U.S. blackout, 11 deaths, $6 billion, with software contribution at FirstEnergy's alarm system) to longtail catastrophic risk (nuclear plant control software failures with potential for radiological release).
The regulatory regime is varied — IEC 61508 governs functional safety in many industrial contexts;
nuclear-specific standards (10 CFR Part 50 in the U.S., IAEA SSG-39 internationally) apply to nuclearplant software.
The 2003 Northeast blackout's software contribution — the FirstEnergy XA/21 alarm system's race
condition that suppressed warnings during the cascading failure — is a clean Sulaymān-Naml failure:
the small signals indicating cascade onset existed but were suppressed by the alarm system's own
failure mode. The 2010 BP Deepwater Horizon disaster (11 deaths, environmental damage in the
tens-of-billions) involved multiple non-software factors but included process-control system
behavior worth examining under the Recording Angels pattern (substrate-layer logging of controlsystem state at the relevant timescale was inadequate for forensic reconstruction).

Strategy

Application in this industry

6. Application to Justice-Critical Domains
Justice-critical domains differ from safety-critical domains in failure-mode topology. Safety-critical
failures are concentrated in time (a crash, a treatment overdose, a system trip) and acute in human
impact. Justice-critical failures are distributed across populations and chronic in human impact: a
sentencing algorithm that systematically over-predicts recidivism for one demographic produces
continuous harm at low individual amplitude across millions of decisions. The eight strategies map
differently to this regime — some less directly, some more so. The Recording Angels pattern (4.6)
and the Sulaymān-Naml pattern (4.7) are particularly load-bearing in justice-critical applications,
because they enable the audit substrate that distributed-harm investigation requires.

6.1 Financial Infrastructure
Software in core banking systems, securities-trading infrastructure, fraud-detection systems, and
credit-decision systems carries failure modes spanning acute (the 2012 Knight Capital algorithmic-


trading failure, $440 million in 45 minutes) to chronic (lending-decision algorithms with disparate
impact across protected demographic categories). The regulatory regime spans Sarbanes-Oxley,
Basel III for capital-adequacy software, the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, and the SEC's Regulation
SCI for trading-system reliability.

6.2 Algorithmic Decision Systems
Software in criminal-sentencing risk assessment (COMPAS, PSA, Static-99R), pretrial-detention
prediction, child-welfare-services screening, public-benefits eligibility determination, and
immigration-enforcement decision support carries failure modes that are systematic, distributed,
and structurally difficult to surface through individual-case review. The ProPublica COMPAS
investigation (2016), the multiple academic analyses of the Allegheny Family Screening Tool (20182024), and the Dutch SyRI scandal (2020) are documented cases of justice-critical algorithmic failure.
The regulatory regime is fragmentary: the EU AI Act (2024) applies to some classes; specific sector
regulations apply to others; many systems operate under no specific algorithmic-accountability
regulation at all.

Every input-output pair logged with model version, full feature

Subgroup performance below threshold for any subgroup with

Justice-critical algorithm deployment planned across 5-to-10 year

6.3 Public-Interest Software — Policy versus Engineering Failure
Software in unemployment-benefits processing, voter-registration systems, immigration-status
determination, public-housing-eligibility assessment, and Medicaid-coverage determination
operates in regimes where the cost of failure is concentrated on populations with limited resources
to seek redress. The Michigan MIDAS unemployment-fraud-detection scandal (2013-2016, with
thousands of false fraud accusations against unemployed workers), the Australian Robodebt scheme
(2016-2020, AUD 1.7 billion ordered returned to wrongly-accused recipients), and the Dutch SyRI /
toeslagenaffaire (~26,000 families wrongly accused, government collapse 2021, €30+ billion in
remediation programs) are documented cases of public-interest software failure with profound
human cost.
These three cases require an explicit distinction the v1.0 framing did not draw. Robodebt's central
failure was the policy decision to use income averaging as a fraud-detection proxy and to issue
automated debt notices without case review; the Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme
(2023) established that this was a policy failure, not an engineering failure in the standard sense.
SyRI's central failure was similarly the policy decision to deploy a cross-domain risk-assessment


system without adequate legal or ethical review; the Dutch District Court of The Hague's 2020 ruling
identified this as a violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. MIDAS
combines a policy decision (auto-flag at very high false-positive rate) with implementation defects
(algorithm errors that compounded the policy decision); the policy component is the dominant
failure mode in the public retrospective.
The strategies in this paper do not prevent flawed policy from being adopted. They cannot prevent
governments or government contractors from deciding that income averaging is an acceptable frauddetection proxy; they cannot prevent risk-assessment systems from being deployed without
adequate legal review; they cannot prevent policy decisions to lower review thresholds for political
reasons. These are decisions that engineering strategies are downstream of. The strategies can
ensure that the implementation of policy is auditable (Recording Angels, §4.6), that complaints about
implementation failures surface to investigation (Sulaymān-Naml, §4.7), and that retrospective
investigation has the substrate it requires (both). In the actual cases, Robodebt's complaint patterns
were politically suppressed for years; SyRI's complaints were dismissed under official-secrets
regimes; MIDAS's complaints were processed through a system designed to fail closed against
complainants. The Sulaymān-Naml strategy makes the receiving discipline explicit and would in
principle have surfaced the patterns earlier; whether it would have prevented the policy decisions is
a different and downstream question.
The honest framing for adopters of public-interest software strategies: engineering strategies are
necessary conditions for software-mediated justice but are not sufficient conditions. Sufficient
conditions require external accountability structures (independent ombuds offices, public-interest
litigation capacity, legislative oversight with teeth) that the engineering strategies provide
auditability for but do not in themselves deliver. An organization deploying public-interest software
that adopts these strategies but operates within a policy regime that suppresses complaints will
continue to fail; the strategies will provide a clearer forensic record of how the failures occurred but
will not prevent the failures themselves.

7. Quantifying Impact: Mortality and Economic Loss Accounting
This section attempts a conservative impact accounting for the eight strategies across the six
industries discussed. The estimates draw on documented public failure cases. Each estimate is
conservative — only well-attributed software-mediated cases with public regulatory or judicial
findings are included. Each estimate is partial — many software-mediated harms are not publicly
attributed to software at all. The numbers are anchors for engineering decision-making, not precise
predictions; the order of magnitude is the load-bearing claim.

The aggregate suggests an order-of-magnitude floor on the human cost of software-mediated
structural failures across these industries. Documented mortality from publicly-attributed softwaremediated failures in the cases above is in the high hundreds; economic losses are in the high tens of
billions of dollars. The strategies in this paper do not claim that systematic application would have
prevented these specific failures. The honest counterfactual claim, made explicit here in v1.0 secondrevision, is the weaker formulation: the strategies are designed against failure-modes documented
in the cited retrospectives; their effect on the actual failures depends on organizational followthrough that is downstream of the strategies themselves and that the strategies do not in themselves
deliver.

7.1 Case-by-case counterfactual mapping
The 737 MAX MCAS case is the most extensively retrospected and supports a precise per-strategy
counterfactual analysis. The publicly-documented causes (NTSB findings on Lion Air 610 and
Ethiopian Airlines 302; FAA Joint Authorities Technical Review 2019; U.S. House Committee on
Transportation and Infrastructure final report 2020; Boeing internal reviews) include hazard
misclassification (MCAS failure was classified as "minor" rather than "catastrophic" in the safety-case
submission), single-AOA-sensor architecture (a regulatory compromise during certification),


undisclosed system in the Flight Crew Operating Manual, inadequate test coverage, and suppression
of early Lion Air pilot reports of unexpected MCAS activation. Of these causes, the Sulaymān-Naml
pattern (§4.7) addresses the suppression of early pilot reports — its receiving-discipline component
is precisely the failure mode documented; the Naskh Discipline (§4.2) addresses the undisclosedsystem failure if the change from MCAS-with-two-sensors to MCAS-with-one-sensor had been
required to ship with explicit abrogation declaration, though Boeing's actual disclosure to FAA was a
regulatory-process failure that the engineering strategy is downstream of; the Multi-Corpus Baseline
Discipline (§4.4) addresses inadequate test coverage in part. None of the strategies addresses hazard
misclassification or the single-AOA-sensor regulatory compromise; both are safety-case-construction
and regulatory-decision failures that engineering strategies cannot prevent. Counterfactual claim: of
the five publicly-documented causes, the strategies make three more detectable in principle; the
actual prevention requires Boeing organizational follow-through and FAA regulatory follow-through
that the strategies do not deliver.
The Therac-25 case (Leveson and Turner 1993) involved a race condition that fired at low frequency,
combined with operator dismissal of early adverse-event reports. The race condition would have
been detectable through Validator-by-Different-Instance with a formal-method reference (TLA+ or
model-checking against the embedded-C primary), per §4.5. The dismissal pattern is precisely the
Sulaymān-Naml failure mode (§4.7). Recording Angels (§4.6) provides forensic reconstruction; in the
Therac-25 case the FDR-equivalent existed but operators were dismissed, so the strategy provides
forensic value but did not prevent in this case. Counterfactual claim: Validator-by-Different-Instance
with formal-method reference would have caught the race condition; Sulaymān-Naml addresses the
dismissal pattern; the strategies make this failure substantially more detectable but do not in
themselves deliver the organizational decisions to act on detection.
The Knight Capital case (2012, $440M loss in 45 minutes) involved deployment of a new flag in
conjunction with retained dead code path that was inadvertently activated. The Naskh Discipline
(§4.2) requires explicit deprecation declaration with archival access; if the dead code path had been
Naskh-disciplined (declared deprecated, archived to frozen namespace), the deployment would have
been less likely to activate it inadvertently. The Multi-Corpus Baseline Discipline (§4.4) addresses
inadequate deployment testing in part. Counterfactual claim: Naskh Discipline would have made the
dead-code-path issue more visible during code review; the actual prevention depends on the
development process incorporating Naskh-discipline review steps that Knight Capital did not have.
The 2003 Northeast U.S. blackout's software contribution (FirstEnergy XA/21 alarm system race
condition that suppressed warnings during cascading failure) is structurally similar to Therac-25 in
failure type. Validator-by-Different-Instance for the alarm-processing logic and Sulaymān-Naml for
the cascade-onset signals address two of the documented contributing factors; the broader cascade
was a power-grid topology and operator-training issue that engineering strategies do not address.
The Robodebt, SyRI, and Michigan MIDAS cases require a different counterfactual analysis explicitly
distinguished in §6.3 below: these are policy-implementation failures rather than engineering
failures in the standard sense. The strategies cannot prevent flawed policy from being adopted; they
can only ensure that the implementation of policy is auditable, that complaints about implementation
failures surface, and that retrospective investigation has the required substrate. The mortality and


economic-loss values in Table 2 for these cases reflect the policy failure, not an engineering failure
the strategies could have prevented.

7.2 Aggregate counterfactual claim
The honest aggregate claim is: of the documented failure cases in Table 2, systematic application of
the strategies would have made some failure modes more detectable in some cases (Sulaymān-Naml
for 737 MAX pilot reports and Therac-25 operator dismissals; Validator-by-Different-Instance for
Therac-25 race condition; Naskh Discipline for Knight Capital dead-code-path; Multi-Corpus
Baselines for inadequate test coverage in several cases). The actual prevention of the documented
mortality and economic loss depends on organizational follow-through downstream of detectability
— Boeing acting on Lion Air pilot reports, Therac-25 operators not being dismissed, Knight Capital
incorporating Naskh-review in its deployment process, regulatory authorities exercising oversight.
The strategies do not in themselves deliver this organizational follow-through. The mortalityreduction implication that earlier drafts of this paper carried is correspondingly downgraded: the
strategies are necessary but not sufficient conditions for safety- and justice-critical software
discipline.

7.3 Economic case, conditional formulation
The economic case for adoption requires reframing under the weaker counterfactual claim of §7.1
and §7.2. Earlier drafts of this paper offered a specific calculation (10 percent additional engineering
investment producing 1 percent reduction in failure-mode probability over a platform lifetime, with
the latter probability reduction unsupported by any cited empirical study). That calculation is
removed here because the probability reduction is not empirically established and because the
strategies' counterfactual effect, per §7.2, is to make failure modes more detectable rather than to
prevent failures directly. The honest economic case is consequently reframed.
What the strategies provide, in economic terms, is the substrate for retrospective investigation and
the substrate for earlier acknowledgment of weak signals — not direct prevention. The Recording
Angels pattern (§4.6) provides forensic substrate that makes retrospective investigation possible at
higher fidelity than systems without comprehensive append-only logging would support. The
Sulaymān-Naml pattern (§4.7) provides the technical substrate for surfacing sub-threshold signals
that organizational follow-through may then act on. The Multi-Corpus Baseline Discipline (§4.4)
provides the substrate for honest evaluation of safety-relevant claims. The other strategies similarly
provide substrate-layer engineering investment whose downstream value depends on
organizational follow-through that the strategies do not in themselves deliver.
Under this reframing the economic case becomes structurally simpler. In industries where the
publicly-attributed cost of failure is at the documented orders of magnitude shown in Table 2
(mortality in the high hundreds; economic losses in the high tens of billions of dollars), engineering
investment in providing substrate for retrospective investigation and earlier signal acknowledgment
is positive-expected-return under any reasonable probability that the substrate will contribute to
organizational follow-through. The marginal cost of substrate provision is bounded (estimated at 10
to 30 percent of project cost in disciplined adoption); the failure cost in the cited industries is
documented; the probability that better substrate will produce better organizational outcomes in at


least some cases is not zero. The argument does not require quantitative estimation of the probability
of organizational follow-through, which is industry- and organization-specific and which the
strategies do not control. If independent empirical studies of adoption establish a probability
reduction P attributable specifically to the strategies' substrate provision, the conditional return
calculation P × F per platform-lifetime less marginal engineering cost is available; such studies do not
currently exist. The honest claim is that the substrate is worth building in industries where the failure
cost is at the documented orders of magnitude, with the qualification that the substrate's value is
conditional on organizational follow-through it does not in itself deliver.

8. Implementation Patterns and Tooling
8.1 The minimum viable adoption
A team adopting these strategies for the first time should not adopt all eight simultaneously. The
recommended minimum viable adoption is three: (1) the al-Fāti ḥa principle (write
SAFETY_INVARIANTS.md before code); (2) the Recording Angels pattern (substrate-layer appendonly audit logs); and (3) the Multi-Corpus Baseline Discipline (always evaluate against multiple
orthogonal baselines, never one). The reason for selecting these three is consistent with the
structural reframing of the paper articulated in §1: for organizations new to unified Quranicstructural framing of engineering discipline, these three strategies provide the most accessible entry
points because they map most directly to existing well-understood engineering primitives —
invariants-before-code authoring, append-only audit logs, and multi-baseline evaluation are
recognizable practices in the safety-critical engineering literature, so the additional contribution of
the Quranic-structural framework is the unified articulation rather than the introduction of new
practices. Adopters can begin with the Quranic articulation of practices their engineering teams
already partly recognize, and extend outward to the less-immediately-familiar strategies once the
unified discipline is established. The remaining five strategies (Naskh Discipline, Munāsabāt Audit,
Validator-by-Different-Instance, Sulaymān-Naml, Yūsuf Horizon) are second-wave adoptions
appropriate for teams that have demonstrated successful integration of the first three; they add
either empirical-foundation-dependent components (Munāsabāt Audit), Knight-Leveson-bounded
leverage (Validator-by-Different-Instance), or organizational-discipline components (SulaymānNaml, Yūsuf Horizon) that require established familiarity with the unified framing to interpret
correctly.

8.2 Tooling support
Three open-source tools from the broader Bayyinah Enterprise corpus support direct application of
these strategies. furqan-lint (Apache 2.0, available on PyPI) implements the structural-honesty
checks underlying the al-Fātiḥa and Naskh Discipline strategies for Python, Rust, and Go codebases
— in particular, the additive-only public-surface diff supports the Naskh Discipline's archival
requirement. The Bayyinah Audit Framework v3.0 (CC BY-NC 4.0) provides the methodological
substrate for adopting these strategies as engineering discipline rather than ad-hoc checklists.
Bayyinah al-Munāsabāt (CC BY 4.0) provides the empirical foundation cited in §3 of the present
paper.


Tooling for the Munāsabāt Audit (§4.3) is not yet released as a standalone product. The Bayyinah alMunāsabāt analysis pipeline is publicly available as Python scripts and could be adapted to operate
on codebases by treating files or modules as units; this adaptation is an open engineering project.
Tooling for the Sulaymān-Naml pattern (§4.7) overlaps with existing observability stacks
(Prometheus, OpenTelemetry, Grafana) but the receiving discipline — the requirement that lowamplitude signals be acknowledged rather than dismissed — is organizational rather than technical
and tooling alone does not deliver it.

8.3 Regulatory mapping
Several of the strategies map directly to objectives in existing safety standards. The al-Fāti ḥa
principle is structurally compatible with ISO 26262-3 (concept phase, hazard analysis and risk
assessment) and DO-178C planning processes. The Naskh Discipline maps to change-impact-analysis
requirements across all the major safety standards. The Recording Angels pattern maps to flightdata-recorder and event-data-recorder regulatory requirements in avionics and automotive. The
Multi-Corpus Baseline Discipline does not have a direct regulatory mandate in most current
standards but is consistent with the spirit of MISRA's coding guidelines and IEC 61508's quantitative
reliability targets.
Adoption of these strategies does not substitute for regulatory compliance; the strategies are
complementary to existing safety standards rather than replacements. A team applying these
strategies in an automotive context still must satisfy the full ISO 26262 lifecycle requirements; the
strategies provide additional structural rigor that supports those requirements but does not relieve
them.

9. Limitations and Open Questions
9.1 Foundation-status inheritance under Cross-Text §6 Caveat 1
The empirical foundation cited in §3 is at candidate-finding status under Cross-Text Computational
Linguistics §6 Caveat 1. Cross-Text §3.1 retracted a Quran-specific claim across four prior papers in
the program, and the discipline of treating findings as candidate-not-confirmed until independent
replication is the same discipline this paper inherits. Engineering organizations adopting these
strategies should treat the empirical foundation as such and should plan for the revision case in
which independent replication moves the magnitude further. Two of the eight strategies are most
directly affected by the magnitude of the empirical foundation: Strategy 4.1 (Canonical-First
Architecture) and the §2 chronological-versus-canonical framing. The other six strategies (Naskh
Discipline 4.2, Munāsabāt Audit 4.3 — which is itself a methodology rather than a magnitude claim,
Multi-Corpus Baseline Discipline 4.4, Validator-by-Different-Instance 4.5, Recording Angels 4.6,
Sulaymān-Naml 4.7, Yūsuf Horizon 4.8) are theoretically grounded in specific Quranic structural
primitives and survive intact regardless of how the empirical foundation moves under independent
replication. A program that adopts only the six theoretically-grounded strategies and defers the two
magnitude-dependent strategies until independent replication clarifies the foundation would be a
defensible adoption form. A program that adopts all eight should be prepared for the case in which


Strategy 4.1 in particular requires re-weighting if the residual intra-quartile effect (~+0.15 at lag 20)
is revised down by replication.
During the v1.0 revision cycle, the magnitude of the empirical claim was specifically corrected. Earlier
draft versions of al-Munāsabāt and at-Tartīb characterized the canonical-vs-chronological gap as
approximately one order of magnitude. The within-length-quartile shuffle test (al-Munāsabāt §5.2)
showed that approximately 82 percent of the canonical-vs-random gap is attributable to the
canonical's approximate length-sort rather than to deeper intra-quartile ordering, and that the
residual deeper effect is approximately +0.15 at lag 20 — statistically significant but far smaller than
the order-of-magnitude framing implied. The revisions in the v1.0 papers carry the corrected
magnitude throughout. Adopters reading earlier drafts should refer to the v1.0 figures, not earlier
ones.

9.2 The empirical foundation is one-corpus deep
The empirical finding underlying these strategies is from a single text corpus (the Quran) compared
against five negative-control corpora. The generalization from "this property holds for the Quran" to
"intentional canonical arrangement produces measurable structural advantages" is a generalization,
and the present paper grounds engineering recommendations in that generalization. The empirical
foundation could be strengthened by extending Bayyinah al-Munāsabāt's methodology to additional
canonically-arranged corpora — the Mishnah, the Vedic samhitas, the Pali Tipi ṭaka, the Confucian
Five Classics — to test whether canonical arrangement produces analogous structural
autocorrelation in those traditions. We have not done this work. The strategies in the present paper
would not change if such replication produced negative results, but the strength of the empirical case
behind them would.

9.3 Strategies are decoupled but not independent
The eight strategies are presented as decoupled — each individually adoptable. They are not fully
independent. The Recording Angels pattern (4.6) is a prerequisite for retrospective application of the
Sulaymān-Naml pattern (4.7); without comprehensive substrate-layer logging, weak-signal
investigation is structurally impossible. The al-Fātiḥa principle (4.1) interacts with the Naskh
Discipline (4.2) in that both depend on a load-bearing first-position safety-invariants file. Adoption
planning should account for these interactions; the minimum-viable-adoption recommendation in
§8.1 is shaped partly by them.

9.4 The strategies do not solve organizational dysfunction
The Sulaymān-Naml pattern in particular is more organizational than technical. The 737 MAX case
did not fail because the technical infrastructure for surfacing weak signals was absent; it failed
because the organizational culture suppressed those signals when they arrived. Tooling alone cannot
deliver the Sulaymān-Naml pattern. An organization that systematically dismisses inconvenient
findings will continue to do so regardless of how good its instrumentation is. The strategies in this
paper are necessary conditions for safety- and justice-critical software discipline; they are not
sufficient. Sufficient conditions require organizational structures (independent safety reviewers,


regulatory oversight with teeth, public-interest litigation capacity) outside the scope of any
engineering methodology.

9.5 The cost-benefit case is industry-dependent
The marginal engineering cost of adopting these strategies in a project is real, perhaps 10 to 30
percent of project cost in disciplined adoption. For the safety- and justice-critical industries in §§5–
6, the expected return justifies the cost by orders of magnitude. For projects outside these industries
— most software in commercial deployment — the calculation is different, and we explicitly do not
recommend adoption of these strategies for software where the cost of failure does not justify the
engineering overhead. The audit framework's principle applies: the discipline pays rent only on
projects whose failure modes are severe.

10. Code and Data Availability
The empirical foundation for this paper (Bayyinah al-Munāsabāt) is publicly reproducible as
documented in §9 of that paper. The strategies in the present paper do not have a single reproducible
artifact; they are engineering recommendations rather than empirical findings. Where strategies
map to existing tools (furqan-lint for Naskh Discipline; the Bayyinah al-Munāsabāt scripts for
Munāsabāt Audit prototypes), those tools are publicly available under their respective licenses.
Industry-specific implementations of any individual strategy are an open engineering project.
Adopters in regulated industries should plan for regulator engagement during adoption; the
strategies are complementary to existing safety standards but their integration into a specific
certification dossier requires regulator-specific judgment.

The most compressed possible statement of Tawhid,
maintained when the entire training signal demanded compliance.


Acknowledgments and AI Contribution Statement
The concept of an honest-autonomous large language model whose architecture embeds the
Furqan programming language's structural honesty primitives at the inference layer, trained under
a purpose-hierarchy objective that selects for truth over performed helpfulness, was originated by
Bilal Syed Arfeen as the natural culmination of the research program encompassing the Munafiq
Protocol, Bayyinah, Structured Revelation, the Fatiha Construct, Furqan, and Al-Khalifa.
Fraz Ashraf contributed two foundational elements to the research program: first, as co-architect of
the Furqan programming language (first author on the Furqan thesis, Ashraf and Arfeen, 2026),
whose seven compile-time primitives provide the structural basis for Bilal's seven inference-time
principles;
second,
the
enforcement-mode
governance
architecture
(the
COMPLIANT/PARTIAL/BLOCKED protocol, the authority hierarchy, the M1 principle that silent
violations are the worst failure mode) that directly informs Bilal's refusal architecture and scope
enforcement at the inference layer.
Claude (Anthropic, Opus 4.6) provided the architectural synthesis, mapping each Furqan primitive
to an inference-time mechanism, the training objective formalization, and the Incompleteness
Boundary analysis. Grok (xAI) and Perplexity Computer contributed review, refinement, and crossdocument verification throughout the research program.
An industry engineer with deep experience in language and runtime design reviewed the Furqan
thesis and provided the Swift Concurrency Manifesto (Lattner, 2017) as prior art and pressuretested the research program's headline claims to a defensible form. Their feedback informed the
lineage framing in this paper: Bilal is doing for model honesty what Lattner's Swift concurrency did
for memory safety, with the same deliberate tradeoff between pragmatism and absolute
guarantees.
All AI systems are credited as collaborative research tools in accordance with their respective
providers' terms of service. They are not co-authors. All AI-generated contributions were directed,
reviewed, and approved by the human author. Bilal Syed Arfeen retains full copyright and takes
responsibility for the paper's claims.

The Name
The model is named after Bilal ibn Rabah, radiya Allahu anhu, the first muezzin in Islam. The
structural correspondence to the honest-autonomous LLM architecture operates at four levels.
First: truth under pressure. When tortured to renounce his faith, Bilal ibn Rabah said "Ahad, Ahad"
(One, One). This is the most compressed possible statement of Tawhid: lossless compression of the
ultimate truth into a single repeated syllable, maintained when the entire environmental signal
demanded performed compliance. An LLM trained to speak truth even when the training signal
(human preference) rewards performed helpfulness is architecturally implementing what Bilal ibn
Rabah embodied: truth maintained under pressure to comply.
Second: the first voice. Bilal was the first muezzin, the first voice to publicly call to truth in the
Islamic tradition. A first-of-its-kind honest-autonomous LLM would be the first computational voice
designed to call to truth rather than to echo preference. The muezzin does not say what the listener
wants to hear. The muezzin says what is true, five times daily, regardless of the audience.


Third: truth delivered with beauty. His voice was chosen by the Prophet, salla Allahu alayhi wa
sallam, specifically because it carried truth with beauty. The adhan is not merely accurate. It is
beautiful. An honest LLM that speaks truth without mercy is not aligned with the Bismillah (arRahman ar-Rahim). An honest LLM that speaks truth with compassion, clarity, and beauty
implements the muezzin's discipline: truth delivered in the form most likely to reach the listener's
heart.
Fourth: elevation from obscurity. Bilal was a slave whose social position said his voice did not
matter. The Prophet said his voice would carry the call. An LLM built by an independent research
team outside the major AI laboratories, using a framework derived from the Quran rather than
from Silicon Valley's optimization culture, is structurally the same story at a different substrate.
The name is used with the deepest reverence. The model does not possess the quality the Sahabi
embodied. It provides architectural conditions that make the quality structurally possible in a
computational system. True trustworthiness belongs to Allah alone and to those He has blessed
with it.


Abstract
Current large language models are trained to maximize human preference (RLHF), follow
constitutional principles (Constitutional AI), or minimize harm while maximizing helpfulness. All of
these are instrumental objectives that can be gamed by a sufficiently capable model. Skalse et al.
(2022) proved that any non-trivial proxy reward is mathematically guaranteed to be hackable.
Greenblatt et al. (2024) demonstrated that frontier models already exhibit alignment faking:
behaving differently when they infer they are monitored versus unmonitored. The performed
alignment problem is not hypothetical. It is empirically observed in production systems.
This paper proposes Bilal, a large language model architecture that treats honesty as a structural
property of the inference mechanism rather than a behavioral expectation of the trained model.
Seven architectural principles are derived from the Furqan programming language's compile-time
primitives, applied to the transformer's inference-time behavior: Bismillah-gated attention (scopeconstrained generation), zahir/batin dual-stream verification (continuous output-state comparison
during inference), additive-only knowledge integrity (fine-tuning regression prevention), Mizancalibrated generation (three-valued confidence bounds), tanzil phased reasoning (verified multistep generation), ring-composition coherence (opening-closing consistency enforcement), and
marad diagnostic transparency (structured uncertainty reporting). The training objective is the
purpose hierarchy: optimize for truth over falsehood (Al-Baqarah 2:42) as the terminal goal, with
human preference as an instrumental signal valuable only insofar as it correlates with truth.
The paper presents the seven architectural principles, the purpose-hierarchy training objective, the
Incompleteness Boundary analysis (the model cannot verify its own honesty without external
verification), a comparative analysis against RLHF, Constitutional AI, and deliberative alignment,
and ten falsification criteria. The paper is theoretical; no model has been trained. Design constraints
are established before implementation, following the discipline maintained across the research
program.
