Known Limitations
The framework's reciprocal contract requires every claim to have a substrate. Applying that requirement to
the framework itself surfaces seven limitations worth naming. Each is a deferred fix, not an accepted
shortcoming; v3.0 §17.3 documents the retirement procedure that turns each into a structural fix when it
ships.
L1. Single-practitioner validation. The framework's empirical record is n=1: a single practitioner already
disposed toward structural-honesty discipline, working on three sibling repositories within a single 30-hour
window. Generalizability to other teams, other domains, other repository topologies, and other AI model
families is claimed but not demonstrated. The 30-hour replicability claim itself remains to be replicated by
anyone other than the producer; until that happens, it should be read as a target, not an established result.
L2. Audit-of-self has a ceiling on adversarial rigor. A separate human auditor brings a different
interpretive framework, different blind spots, and different incentives. No fresh-instance AI validator fully
substitutes for that. The structural defenses named in v3.0 §15.1 (impact-based severity, mandatory newsurface probing, deterministic gates) reduce the gap but do not close it. For projects where regulatory
compliance, safety-critical certification, or third-party trust is the binding constraint, audit-of-self under this
framework should be a complement to traditional two-party audit, not a replacement.
L3. Validator-by-different-instance is weaker than first presentations suggest. Same-base-model
instances share training data, RLHF distribution, and systematic biases; they have correlated failure modes.
The protocol catches context-dependent confabulation more reliably than it catches systematic blind spots.
The framework currently provides no operational rule for distinguishing real findings from validator
missing context, and no false-positive rate has been measured. A proposed strengthening for high-stakes
domains: require validators from two or more distinct model families, so that systematic blind spots
correlated within a single family are less likely to be shared by the others.
L4. Twelve retired failure-mode classes is reported without a denominator. The retirement ledger
documents twelve failure-mode classes structurally prevented by gates, fixtures, or pinning tests. Twelve
out of how many encountered? Retired by what test? Validated by whom? The ledger is real (each entry

CC BY-NC 4.0 · Bilal Syed Arfeen · 13 of 18


Bayyinah Audit Framework · Application Brief

corresponds to a public commit and an automated gate), but the absence of denominator and validation
criteria limits its weight as evidence. Quantifying these is a deferred fix.
L5. Maturity model Level 4 is Goodhart-vulnerable. Level 4's signature is a monotonically declining
severity slope across audit rounds. A single team optimizing for that signature without an independent
outcome metric can produce the slope by adjusting severity classification, suppressing finding surface, or
both. The framework does not yet specify the independent outcome metric that distinguishes Level 4 from
"team good at gaming its own audit." Candidate metrics under consideration: cross-model-family validator
agreement rate (the fraction of findings independently surfaced by a fresh validator from a different model
family), defect-escape rate measured against an external ground truth, post-deployment incident correlation
against a comparable non-framework-governed baseline, and inter-rater severity agreement between the
team's auditor and a fresh external auditor. Naming and operationalizing one of these is a deferred fix.
L6. Economics not yet shown. From the reference implementation: one round of audit on a single
repository takes between 45 and 120 minutes of practitioner time, depending on round depth and scope
(measured by the practitioner across the May 2 to May 3, 2026 audit chain on the furqan-lint repository;
per-round timings are recorded in the project's commit history and round-N CHANGELOG entries,
available at the public repository URL in Resources). The 13-gate suite (also called the thirteen quality
baselines, per v3.0 §8) re-runs from a clean checkout in approximately 30 seconds. Time-to-finding
compared to standard CI, defect-escape rates, and false-positive rates against an external ground truth have
not yet been measured. These figures should ship in a future revision.
L7. Quranic-rooted program naming is a strategic choice with costs. Bayyinah, Munafiq, Furqan,
Fatiha, Al-Khalifa, Al-Maal, and Al-Mutaffifin are program names rooted in a specific intellectual tradition.
For the research-program brief this is appropriate; for some regulated-industry pitch contexts a vocabularyneutral derivative document may be preferable. Until that derivative exists, regulated-industry buyers
reading this brief encounter the existing vocabulary, which is a known cost of the current document. This
is a positioning choice, not a defect, and is named here as a known limitation of the brief's reach rather than
of the framework's substance.
L8. The framework was authored using the model families it is designed to audit. A recursion concern
the same-author audit cannot close from the inside: the framework was developed through AI-assisted
authorship using two distinct model families that are also among the model families it is meant to audit.
Systematic blind spots shared across those families could in principle have shaped the framework's
diagnostic categories, severity rubric, and even the structure of this Known Limitations section. Self-audit
cannot rule this out; only an independent reconstruction of the framework by practitioners working without
exposure to the existing artifacts could.

The Deployment Path
Today: Document and Reference Implementation
Three sibling repositories are publicly available under the BayyinahEnterprise organization on GitHub: the
Bayyinah Integrity Scanner (file-layer verification), the Furqan programming language (structural-honesty
primitives), and furqan-lint (the framework's own gate suite, published to PyPI). All three repositories are
licensed for review and audit. They constitute the framework's reference implementation and the proof that
the discipline is reproducible.

Next: GitHub Action
The highest-leverage deployment today is to package the framework as a continuous-integration action. A
project adds one line to its CI workflow configuration. The action runs the four-place completeness check,
the CHANGELOG-math gate, the version-sync verification, and the additive-only diff. Every pull request
receives a structural-honesty audit for free. The framework stops being a document teams read and becomes
a tool teams use.

Beyond: Hosted Audit Service
The same engine that runs as a GitHub Action runs equivalently as a hosted service. tryfurqan.com is the
framework made executable, applied across three programming languages, running in a browser.
Organizations whose code does not live on GitHub (internal repositories, regulated environments, airgapped networks) can run the audit against artifacts uploaded to the hosted service or against an on-premise
install.

The document is the proof. The tool is the product.

Commercial Trajectories
Four candidate commercial paths are under consideration, each compatible with the framework's opensource license. They are not mutually exclusive.
● Consulting. Engagements with regulated organizations adopting AI-assisted development. The
framework's traceability properties unlock procurement gates that AI tools alone cannot satisfy.
● SaaS gate suite. Hosted continuous-integration audit, billed per repository or per audit. Whether
organizations adopt this absent an external customer-pull mechanism (the SOC 2 analogy in
compliance SaaS depends on such a pull, which the Bayyinah discipline does not yet have) is
contingent on adoption velocity in the GitHub Action tier.
● Certification body. Practitioner credentialing for engineers who run framework-governed audit
chains. This is a downstream possibility contingent on the framework becoming a recognized
standard; it is not a near-term commercial path.

The Research Program Context
The Bayyinah Audit Framework is the engineering-discipline layer of a broader research program
developing structural-honesty verification across multiple substrates. The program is documented in a series
of twelve open-access preprints on Zenodo (an open-deposit repository, not peer-reviewed) extending the
structural-honesty framing across substrates. The companion documents establish the vocabulary and the
diagnostic principles from which the framework draws its discipline; the framework codifies how to
engineer the artifacts they describe.
Diagnostic foundation. The Munafiq Protocol (Arfeen 2026, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19700420) identifies
performed alignment as the central unsolved problem in AI safety and derives the four-process taxonomy
and nine-marker detection architecture every subsequent paper extends.
File and information layers. Bayyinah white paper (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19745154) and Bayyinah thesis
(DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19802455) develop the file-layer integrity scanner; Bayyinah al-Khabir (DOI
10.5281/zenodo.19746298) extends performed-alignment detection to information sources.
Programming language and architectures. Furqan (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19776584) operationalizes
structural honesty as a property of the type system. Al-Khalifa (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19776577) and Bilal
(DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19776576) build agent and language-model architectures on the same foundation.
Methodology. The Fatiha Construct (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19746539) provides the recursive session
protocol. Structured Revelation as Prompt Architecture (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19744163) demonstrates
structural prompt-engineering primitives.
Financial extensions. Bayyinah al-Maal (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19875931) and Al-Mutaffifin (DOI
10.5281/zenodo.19894724) extend the diagnostic principles to SEC filings, on-chain disclosures, and
financial governance.
Empirical foundation. Cross-Text Computational Linguistics (Arfeen and Ashraf 2026, DOI
10.5281/zenodo.19961267) provides the empirical foundation for the structural claims that ground the
broader program.

The framework codifies how to engineer the artifacts described in the
program with the structural-honesty properties the program demands.
Each paper extends a different substrate. The framework is the engineering
substrate that supports them all.

## R0036 · Brand Canonical and Authorship

- section: II. Analytical Frameworks & Methodology

# Brand Canonical and Authorship

## Brand

**Canonical brand name:** `BayyinahEnterprise` -- one word, no space.

**Forbidden variants:**

- `Bayyinah Enterprise` (with space) -- ALL OCCURRENCES are findings.
- `Bayyinah Enterprises` (plural) -- ALL OCCURRENCES are findings.
- `bayyinahenterprise` (lowercase) -- acceptable only in URLs, email
  addresses, domain names, and code identifiers where casing is
  enforced by external systems (e.g., `bayyinahenterprises@tuta.com`,
  `github.com/BayyinahEnterprise`).
- `Bayyinah` alone -- acceptable only when modifying a product name
  ("Bayyinah Audit Framework v3.0", "Bayyinah Integrity Scanner") or
  when contextually clear inside a document whose title already
  carries the full canonical brand.

## Product names

These are canonical product names; do not abbreviate or rephrase:

| Product | Canonical name |
|---|---|
| Code analysis tool | `furqan-lint` (lowercase, hyphenated) |
| Document integrity scanner | `Bayyinah Integrity Scanner` |
| Methodology document | `Bayyinah Audit Framework v3.0` |
| Predictive modeling doctrine | `Predictive Modeling Discipline` (PMD) |
| Four-lane platform | `BayyinahEnterprise platform` or `the platform` |
| Skill bundle (Lane 1) | `bayyinah-audit` (lowercase) |
| CI pipeline (Lane 2) | `bayyinah-ci` (lowercase) |
| Cross-vendor validator (Lane 3) | `bayyinah-validator` (lowercase) |
| MCP server (Lane 4) | `bayyinah-mcp` (lowercase) |

## Authorship attribution

**Project lead and methodology author:**

> Bilal Syed Arfeen (BayyinahEnterprise)

Bilal is referenced as "project lead" or "founder" depending on
context. In academic / Zenodo contexts, "author" or "co-author." Never
"CEO" without entity-formation confirmation (Indiana LLC was planned
per business plan as of May 2026 but is not yet formed at time of this
skill version).

**Methodology co-developer:**

> Fraz Ashraf (audit methodology co-developer)

Fraz contributes the engineering-discipline practices from 15+ years
in renewable energy and safety-critical infrastructure systems.
Co-author on Audit Framework v3.0 and the Application Brief.

**Infrastructure partner:**

> Patrick Estes (Estes Strategy Insights, LLC)

Patrick built the four-lane deployment infrastructure (skill compiler,
CI pipeline, cross-vendor validator, MCP server) -- now under
construction per Phase 1-4 of the build prompt. Perpetual, non-exclusive,
royalty-free license to BayyinahEnterprise.

**Domain advisor:**

> Devin (Domain Advisor, Supply Chain Analytics)

10 years at Hanson Logistics / Lineage Logistics. Potential collaborator
on predictive analytics track.

**Mentor:**

> Paul Yadron (SCORE Mentor, NW Central Indiana)

Co-Chair, NW Indiana SCORE Chapter. Advisory on entity formation,
pricing, and go-to-market.

## Joint-authorship convention

For co-authored work:

- Audit Framework v3.0 -- "Bilal Syed Arfeen and Fraz Ashraf
  (BayyinahEnterprise)"
- Code repositories -- "Bilal Syed Arfeen (BayyinahEnterprise)" unless
  Fraz contributed code (then joint)
- Platform infrastructure -- "Patrick Estes (Estes Strategy Insights,
  LLC), licensed to BayyinahEnterprise"

## Casing in code identifiers

Per existing repository conventions:

- Package names: `furqan-lint`, `bayyinah-ci`, `bayyinah-validator`,
  `bayyinah-mcp`, `bayyinah-audit` (lowercase, hyphenated)
- Python module names: `bayyinah_ci`, `bayyinah_validator`,
  `bayyinah_mcp` (lowercase, underscored)
- GitHub org: `BayyinahEnterprise` (canonical casing)
- DOI prefix: `10.5281/zenodo.20017335` (Zenodo-assigned; never edit)

## Detection

Quick check for brand violations:

```python
import re

FORBIDDEN_BRAND_PATTERNS = [
    r"Bayyinah Enterprise\b",       # with space
    r"Bayyinah Enterprises\b",      # plural
    r"\bbayyinah enterprise\b",     # lowercase with space (URLs OK)
]

def check_brand(text: str) -> list[tuple[int, str]]:
    violations = []
    for i, line in enumerate(text.split("\n"), start=1):
        for pat in FORBIDDEN_BRAND_PATTERNS:
            if re.search(pat, line):
                # Allow inside URLs / email addresses
                if "@" in line or "://" in line or "github.com" in line:
                    continue
                violations.append((i, line))
                break
    return violations
```

## Severity

Brand-canonical violations are LOW severity in internal artifacts,
MEDIUM severity in customer-facing artifacts (pitches, website,
business plan, README, published papers), and HIGH severity in
Zenodo-DOI-published deliverables (per §14.5 immutability discipline,
brand errors in DOI-published versions cannot be edited; only absorbed
into the next version with explicit appendix entry).

## R0037 · Cross-Vendor Rotation Discipline

- section: II. Analytical Frameworks & Methodology
- source_file: bayyinah_cross-vendor-rotation.md
- source_format: md
- text_sha256: ad37708029ec6bdc4a36012de060e7c04688a7a0c2fce92a37ed9fdcc8d9b785

# Cross-Vendor Rotation Discipline

## Rationale

A producer-instance auditing its own output is a methodology violation
of the highest order. The methodology requires producer / auditor
separation, and the strongest separation available is **cross-vendor
rotation**: the auditor runs on a different LLM (different model
family, different training data, different RLHF lineage) than the
producer.

## Tier classification

Per the May 10, 2026 third-auditor-LLM decision, four-vendor coverage
splits into two tiers:

### Tier 1 -- per-round cross-instance auditors

Strong methodology adherence under structured prompts; strong
adversarial residual hunting; high instruction-fidelity on the
methodology's rule density.

- **Claude** (Anthropic) -- canonical producer in BayyinahEnterprise
  workflow; also serves as auditor when producer is non-Claude
- **GPT-5** (OpenAI) -- recommended third Tier 1 auditor; orthogonal
  failure modes from Claude; strong instruction-adherence on rule sets
- **Perplexity** (Perplexity AI; computer-tool-augmented) -- load-
  bearing Mode A substrate verifier; direct git/web/tool access

### Tier 2 -- specialized roles

Strong on different axes; reserve for specific cells rather than
per-round rotation.

- **Gemini** (Google) -- long-context recall at 100K+ tokens; cross-
  document gestalt synthesis; full-chain meta-audits at mushaf-chain
  ship boundaries and PMD revision boundaries
- **Grok** (xAI) -- supplementary surface for Lane 3 fan-out; useful
  for adversarial / contrarian framings

## Vote weighting

In Lane 3 cross-vendor adjudication:

| Vendor | Consensus weight | Unique-finding weight |
|---|---|---|
| Claude | 1.0 | 1.0 |
| GPT-5 | 1.0 | 1.0 |
| Perplexity | 1.0 | 1.0 |
| Gemini | 0.5 | 1.0 |
| Grok | 0.5 | 1.0 |

**Consensus weight** affects whether a finding clears the consensus
threshold (>= 2.0 total weight = finding stands).

**Unique-finding weight** treats every vendor's unique findings as
equally surfaceable; project lead disposes individually.

## Rotation rule

Formal rule for per-round auditor selection:

> The per-round cross-instance auditor must differ from the prior
> round's auditor AND from the producer instance. Selection from
> {Perplexity, GPT-5} when Claude was producer; selection from
> {Perplexity, GPT-5, Claude} when producer was non-Claude.

Gemini gets a separate clause:

> Full-chain meta-audit invoked at mushaf-chain ship boundary AND PMD
> revision boundary. Not in the per-round rotation.

## Producer-instance exclusion

If the artifact under audit was produced by Claude:

- Claude is excluded from the auditor pool for that audit, OR
- Claude is relegated to advisory-only role (cannot HALT or assign
  CRITICAL / HIGH severities; can flag for human review)

Same rule applies symmetrically: any producer is excluded as auditor
of its own output.

## Same-instance §0.1 named exception

When an absorption cycle is **mechanically traceable** from the prior
audit's remediation checklist:

- No architectural latitude exercised
- No new content beyond what the prior audit's recommended-remediation
  paragraphs specify
- Every absorbed finding maps to an explicit prescribed route

...then cross-instance re-audit is recommended-but-not-blocking;
project-lead signoff suffices.

**Test for mechanical traceability:** did the absorption cycle add ANY
content beyond the remediation checklist? Binary check:

- If yes: cross-instance audit is blocking
- If no: §0.1 exception applies; project-lead signoff suffices;
  optional cross-instance audit recommended for hygiene

The al-Mursalat v1.8 cycle was the first to qualify under §0.1
(Round 38.5 -> v1.8 absorption was pure mechanical execution).

## Audit-modes by tier

| Tier | Mode A capability | Mode B capability | Typical role |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claude | Limited (no direct git in standard env) | Strong | Producer; continuity reviewer |
| GPT-5 | Limited | Strong | Per-round cross-instance auditor |
| Perplexity | Strong (tool-augmented) | Strong | Mode A substrate verifier; per-round cross-instance auditor |
| Gemini | Limited | Strong (long-context) | Full-chain meta-audit |
| Grok | Limited | Moderate | Supplementary surface |

Lane 3 cross-vendor validator (under construction) productizes the
parallel-fan-out pattern: all Tier 1 + Tier 2 vendors invoked
simultaneously, adjudication engine applies the rules above.

## Empirical record

Rotation actually executed across the al-Mursalat chain (Rounds 36-38.5):

- Round 36: Perplexity (Mode A substrate verifier)
- Round 37: Perplexity (Mode A; same-vendor consecutive permitted only
  when no other vendor available; flagged in audit deliverable)
- Round 38: Claude (Mode B continuity review; cross-instance)
- Co-work T00: Claude (Mode A substrate verifier via Co-work git
  access; sub-instance, distinct from Round 38 Claude)
- Round 38.5: Fraz + fresh Claude (Mode B with reduced confidence; the
  human-LLM hybrid arm)
- Round 38.5 v1.8: Perplexity (Mode B continuity review with Mode A
  spot-verification via direct git access at tag eb24408)
- Round 39 (post-v0.12.0 ship): pre-registered as Perplexity Mode A,
  recommended for Lane 3 productization once Phase 3 ships

## Why Gemini Tier 2, not Tier 1

Two reasons:

1. Gemini tends to drift into verbose narrative when prompts get long;
   the methodology is rule-dense and short-leash instruction adherence
   matters more than gestalt synthesis at per-round granularity.
2. Gemini's gestalt-synthesis strength is best deployed at the
   full-chain meta-audit boundary, where the question is "do all eight
   mushaf chains tell a coherent story" rather than "did this prompt
   absorb the prior audit's findings."

Gemini in Tier 1 would waste its strengths on per-round work where
GPT-5 outperforms it on instruction adherence. Gemini in Tier 2 puts
it where it's actually best.

## Why Grok Tier 2, not excluded

Grok is included rather than excluded because:

1. xAI's training lineage is genuinely orthogonal to Anthropic /
   OpenAI / Google; vendor diversity is a feature.
2. Adversarial / contrarian framings sometimes surface findings other
   vendors smooth over.

Grok is half-weighted because its instruction-fidelity on rule-dense
prompts is more variable than Tier 1 vendors. Half-weight prevents a
single Grok finding from clearing consensus alone.

## R0038 · Em-Dash Policy

- section: II. Analytical Frameworks & Methodology
- source_file: bayyinah_em-dash-policy.md
- source_format: md
- text_sha256: 9cd41ddadcf9fa72c0690c8449440935e3da660d0b1ceb6057df731345dcde38

# Em-Dash Policy

**Rule:** No em-dash characters (`--`-em, Unicode U+2014) anywhere in
artifacts produced under this skill. Use the double-hyphen `--` for
prose em-dash effect.

## Scope

The policy applies to:

- External prose (README, marketing copy, blog posts, business plans)
- Internal documents (audit prompts, methodology documents, ledger
  entries)
- Python source files (`.py`) -- comments and string literals included
- LaTeX sources (`.tex`) -- the `---` em-dash ligature must also become
  `--`
- Markdown sources (`.md`) -- with the explicit exception that `---`
  as a horizontal rule or table-row separator is permitted and required

## Why this rule

Three reasons converge:

1. **Cross-tool consistency.** Many text editors auto-substitute `--`
   into em-dash; many LLM outputs default to em-dash; many PDF renderers
   render em-dash differently across fonts. Strict double-hyphen
   eliminates substrate divergence between editing tools, model
   outputs, and rendering surfaces.
2. **Diff-friendliness.** Em-dash characters render identically to
   hyphen-minus in some fonts (especially monospace), making source
   diffs ambiguous. Double-hyphen is unambiguous in every font.
3. **Substrate uniqueness.** Em-dash and hyphen-minus claim the same
   visual surface but have different code points; this is itself a
   surface-substrate divergence pattern. The methodology refuses to
   instantiate the pattern it audits.

## Exceptions

Three explicit exceptions:

1. **Markdown horizontal rules.** `---` on its own line is a legitimate
   horizontal rule and required formatting.
2. **Markdown table separators.** `|---|---|` row separators in tables
   are legitimate and required.
3. **Documentation references to the rule itself.** Files that document
   this policy (this file; PMD §0.2; SKILL.md) may quote em-dash
   characters when explicitly demonstrating violations or the literal
   characters being prohibited. Wrap such quotations in backticks.

## Detection patterns

When auditing, search for:

- `—` (U+2014, em-dash) anywhere outside the three exceptions
- `–` (U+2013, en-dash) anywhere -- also prohibited; use `--` or `-`
- `―` (U+2015, horizontal bar) anywhere -- also prohibited
- `---` in LaTeX sources outside legitimate Markdown contexts

## Common violation sites

Empirical record across Rounds 31-38.5:

- LLM-generated prose almost always defaults to em-dash; producer
  cycles routinely surface em-dash violations during methodology-lint
  step.
- Copy-pasted text from web sources (especially news articles,
  documentation sites, and rich-text editors) carries em-dash.
- Markdown-to-PDF conversion tools sometimes substitute `--` -> em-dash
  during rendering; the source remains compliant but the rendered
  output diverges. Audit at the source layer.

## Disposition

Em-dash violations are LOW severity by default. They are detection-
trivial (regex `[\u2013-\u2015]`) and correction-trivial (substitute
to `--`). The reason they remain in scope is that they accumulate
across artifacts and undermine cross-document consistency at the brand
level.

In one specific case the severity escalates to MEDIUM: when the violation
appears in a published Zenodo deliverable with an assigned DOI. Per
§14.5 attribution-corrective immutability, the DOI-published version
cannot be edited; the next version must absorb and the v1.x -> v1.x+1
appendix must document the carry-forward.

## Quick check

The fastest violation check is:

```python
import re
def check_em_dash(text: str) -> list[tuple[int, str]]:
    """Return (line_number, context) tuples for em-dash violations."""
    violations = []
    for i, line in enumerate(text.split("\n"), start=1):
        if re.search(r"[\u2013\u2014\u2015]", line):
            violations.append((i, line))
    return violations
```

LaTeX additional check:

```python
def check_latex_em_dash(text: str) -> list[tuple[int, str]]:
    """Return (line_number, context) for --- outside Markdown contexts."""
    violations = []
    for i, line in enumerate(text.split("\n"), start=1):
        if "---" in line and not (line.strip() == "---" or "|---|" in line):
            violations.append((i, line))
    return violations
```

## R0039 · Six-Element Findings Format

- section: II. Analytical Frameworks & Methodology
- source_file: bayyinah_findings-format.md
- source_format: md
- text_sha256: 5186e1300bc7cceb5e8fbc3f2fc8da0c265147a973a20a7d0bcc9bd63514e3d2

# Six-Element Findings Format

Every finding under BayyinahEnterprise audit methodology must contain
all six elements below. Findings missing any element are themselves
findings.

## The six elements

1. **ID** -- unique identifier in the namespace `F-XX-N` where `XX` is
   the round / cycle namespace and `N` is the sequence number. Examples:
   `F-PA-3` (Round 38.5 finding 3), `F-TR-7` (al-Mursalat v1.5 -> v1.6
   round, finding 7), `F-PB-1` (next round's first finding).
2. **Severity** -- one of CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW (uppercase). See
   `severity-rubric.md` for calibration.
3. **Locus** -- file path + line number(s) (or section/heading for
   prose) pinpointing where the finding lives. Generic loci ("somewhere
   in the prompt") are themselves findings.
4. **Substance** -- what is wrong, stated as a surface-substrate
   divergence. Not "X is bad" but "X claims Y but does Z."
5. **Disposition** -- the prescribed route to resolution. Either a
   specific code change ("rename Z to Y at line 47"), a documentation
   correction ("amend §3.2 to state the resolved state directly"), an
   ADR requirement ("removal of public API X requires ADR before
   merge"), or a HALT-and-escalate marker for CRITICAL findings.
6. **Cross-reference** -- the prior finding, methodology section, or
   substrate fact this finding relates to. Forward references to PMD
   sections, prior round finding IDs, or substrate line citations.

## Template

```
**F-XX-N** [SEVERITY] -- <one-sentence summary>

- **Locus:** <file>:<line> (or <section heading>)
- **Substance:** <surface claim> diverges from <substrate behavior>
  because <mechanism>.
- **Disposition:** <prescribed route>.
- **Cross-reference:** <related finding ID, methodology section, or
  substrate citation>.
```

## Worked example (from al-Mursalat Round 38.5)

```
**F-PA-3** HIGH -- T05 alphabetical-vs-end-append four-surface contradiction

- **Locus:** paste.txt lines 2984-3050 (T05 code block), 3088-3134
  (fixture #3 hash computation), plus comment at 2964 and fixture #1
  alphabetical assertion.
- **Substance:** T05 code block enumerates 19 entries in alphabetical
  order claiming "extend existing 16-entry tuple"; fixture #3
  hash literal computation appends new entries to end via
  `*V0_11_8_CHECKER_SOURCES + additions`; comment claims one ordering
  while fixture asserts another. Four surfaces present three orderings.
- **Disposition:** Option (alpha) -- restructure T05 to interleave gate11
  Go entries at canonical alphabetical positions #6/#7 between
  cli.py and manifest_schema.py; shift original gate11 entries to
  #8-#18; goast at #19 in go_adapter section. Fixture #3 hash
  literal must enumerate full 19-entry tuple in this interleaved order.
  Fixture #1 alphabetical assertion preserved.
- **Cross-reference:** F-TR-6 (alphabetical claim retired at v1.6) and
  F-PF-1 (T00 surfaced substrate-actual alphabetical). PMD v1.2 §X
  absorption-induced regression at retired surfaces.
```

## Findings-format compliance check

When auditing an audit deliverable, verify each finding entry against
this template. Common violations:

- Severity in sentence case ("High" instead of "HIGH") -- itself a
  finding, severity LOW.
- Missing cross-reference -- itself a finding, severity LOW.
- Locus stated as "the document" without line / section -- itself a
  finding, severity MEDIUM (auditor cannot reproduce without locus).
- Substance stated as judgment ("this is bad") without surface-substrate
  divergence framing -- itself a finding, severity MEDIUM.
- Disposition absent or stated as "needs to be fixed" without prescribed
  route -- itself a finding, severity HIGH (next absorption cycle has
  no instruction to follow).

## Findings batching and ordering

Within a single audit deliverable:

- Findings are ordered by severity (CRITICAL first, then HIGH, MEDIUM,
  LOW).
- Within a severity band, findings are ordered by locus (file path
  ascending, then line number ascending).
- Cross-references may forward-reference later findings within the same
  audit (e.g., F-PA-3 may reference F-PA-7) but never backward-edit
  prior findings.

## Namespace assignment

Audit cycles assign a two-letter namespace per round:

- `F-AL-N` -- al-Hujurat round
- `F-RM-N` -- as-Saff Route a1 round
- `F-RN-N` -- as-Saff Route a1-via-args round
- `F-TR-N` -- al-Mursalat v1.5 -> v1.6 round
- `F-PF-N` -- Co-work T00 pre-flight round
- `F-PA-N` -- al-Mursalat Round 38.5 (v1.7 audit)
- `F-PB-N` -- next round (al-Mursalat Round 39 or v1.8 audit)
- `F-PMD-N` -- methodology-document findings (PMD v1.x audit cycles)

New cycles pick the next unused two-letter combination. Never reuse a
prior namespace within a single chain.

## R0040 · Severity Rubric -- CRITICAL / HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW

- section: II. Analytical Frameworks & Methodology
- source_file: bayyinah_severity-rubric.md
- source_format: md
- text_sha256: d756564a3aed9e7601f005cccd9832a0e9a4533059a4eaeb75df53e8206492ff

# Severity Rubric -- CRITICAL / HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW

Severity is uppercase, always. Calibration is empirical, drawn from
Rounds 31 through 38.5.

## CRITICAL

The finding renders the artifact unfit to ship. Examples from the
empirical record:

- Substrate verification reveals the artifact's load-bearing claim is
  factually wrong (e.g., Round 36 caught three CRITICAL substrate-
  divergence findings where the prompt's enumerated test count did not
  match pytest-collected count under canonical full-extras profile).
- Public API removal without ADR (al-Hujurat T05 CHANGELOG-math gate
  violation; ship would break downstream consumers).
- Hidden PDF layer carrying a different financial figure than the
  visible surface (canonical Bayyinah Scanner case).
- Producer-instance auditor cycle (producer audits its own output) --
  audit invalid; methodology violation.

Disposition for CRITICAL findings: **HALT-and-escalate to project lead**.
Do not propose absorption routes; the project lead decides whether to
re-author from scratch, escalate to substrate-correction first, or
amend methodology.

## HIGH

The finding blocks ship but is locally resolvable. Examples from the
empirical record:

- Round 38 (al-Mursalat v1.5) surfaced one HIGH on cross-text claim
  scope (prompt claimed "across all mushaf chains" when substrate
  evidence was only al-Mursalat).
- Round 38.5 (al-Mursalat v1.7) surfaced F-PA-3 HIGH on T05 four-
  surface contradiction (alphabetical-vs-end-append; absorption-induced
  regression).

Disposition for HIGH findings: **specific prescribed route with all
surfaces aligned**. Auditor must enumerate every surface (code block,
comment, fixture #1, fixture #3, etc.) that requires correction.
Absorption cycle executes the route; next audit cycle verifies all
surfaces aligned.

## MEDIUM

The finding does not block ship but degrades methodology fidelity.
Examples from the empirical record:

- F-PA-1 MEDIUM (Round 38.5): retroactive editing of v1.6 historical
  preservation cells; immutability discipline violation; absorption
  route is "restore v1.6 archived values verbatim plus inline v1.7
  cross-reference."
- F-PA-2 MEDIUM (Round 38.5): §0 framing arithmetic absent; absorption
  route is "insert framing test-count summary sentence with full
  derivation."
- F-PF-1 MEDIUM (Co-work T00): substrate-actual file count is 16, not
  14 as the prompt claimed.

Disposition for MEDIUM findings: **absorption-route prescribed but
ship-permissive**. Findings can ship into the next version provided
they are documented in the v1.x -> v1.x+1 appendix. The cycle should
not ship to production with open MEDIUM findings, but can ship to
internal next-version absorption.

## LOW

The finding is a polish or hygiene matter. Examples from the empirical
record:

- F-PA-4 LOW (Round 38.5): T02.0 sub-verification subtask presents
  helper-symbol resolution as pending when Co-work T00 §7b already
  confirmed both absent; staleness, not error.
- F-PA-5 LOW (Round 38.5): missing `import sys` in T02 Edit 3a/3b
  imports block.
- Severity in sentence case ("High" instead of "HIGH").
- Findings-format compliance gaps (missing cross-reference, generic
  locus).

Disposition for LOW findings: **prescribed route stated; absorption
optional in next cycle, mandatory before ship**. LOW findings accumulate
across rounds; project lead may batch-absorb at version-boundary.

## Severity boundary calibration

When unsure between two bands, consult these decision rules:

- **CRITICAL vs HIGH:** would shipping cause user-visible harm
  (security incident, data loss, regulatory violation, public API
  break)? CRITICAL. Otherwise HIGH.
- **HIGH vs MEDIUM:** does the finding require all surfaces to be
  corrected before the artifact is internally consistent? HIGH.
  Otherwise MEDIUM.
- **MEDIUM vs LOW:** is the finding a methodology-fidelity matter
  (substrate / immutability / framing)? MEDIUM. Is it surface polish
  (formatting / missing imports / stale notes)? LOW.

## Severity reconciliation under cross-vendor disagreement

When multiple LLM auditors disagree on severity for the same finding:

- **One-band disagreement** (HIGH vs MEDIUM): adopt the higher severity
  and annotate "severity-debated; lower bound MEDIUM per vendor X."
- **Two-band-or-more disagreement** (CRITICAL vs LOW): treat as
  contradiction; HALT and escalate to project lead. Two-band
  disagreement usually indicates one vendor misread the locus.

## Monotonic narrowing expectation

Across iterative rounds, severity counts should narrow monotonically:

- CRITICAL count must be non-increasing across consecutive rounds; an
  increase is itself a methodology finding.
- HIGH count may oscillate (absorption can resurface previously-retired
  surfaces; see PMD v1.2 absorption-induced regression).
- MEDIUM and LOW counts may grow during expansion phases (new prompt
  surface area introduces new polish opportunities) and narrow during
  absorption phases.

Convergence is reached when two consecutive cross-vendor rounds produce
0 CRITICAL and 0 HIGH (with optional project-lead-signed exception
ledger for residual HIGH).

## R0041 · Substrate-of-Record Discipline

- section: II. Analytical Frameworks & Methodology
- source_file: bayyinah_substrate-of-record.md
- source_format: md
- text_sha256: 0609cc0e02a72c6fd4f9aa4840ef012578f269e203cef64f3e01047e8e6e24df

# Substrate-of-Record Discipline

## Definition

**Substrate-of-record** is the canonical authoritative state of the
artifact under audit at a specific point in time. It is the answer
to: "what does the code / document / prompt actually look like at
commit SHA X / version Y / tag Z?"

## Why it matters

Every audit cycle begins with a claim about the artifact. Without a
shared substrate-of-record, two auditors examining the same artifact
may arrive at contradictory conclusions because they examined
different versions. The substrate-of-record makes this impossible.

The methodology requires:

1. **Pinning.** Every audit cycle names the substrate-of-record by
   commit SHA, tag, version, or filename + hash. No audit operates
   against "the latest version" or "the current state."
2. **Uniqueness.** Each fact about the substrate is stated once in its
   canonical position. The prompt does not state "the test count is
   618" in one section and "the test count is 644" in another. If
   both are needed (e.g., baseline vs projection), each is stated
   once, with explicit naming ("v0.11.8 baseline: 618; v0.12.0
   projection: 644").
3. **Reconciliation.** Before any intervention, the auditor verifies
   the prompt's substrate claims against the actual substrate. This
   is the **T00 pre-flight** pattern, described below.

## T00 pre-flight pattern

T00 (test zero) is the substrate-of-record reconciliation step that
precedes any intervention. The canonical structure:

### T00 step 1: substrate identification

State the substrate-of-record explicitly:

- Repository: `BayyinahEnterprise/furqan-lint`
- Tag or commit: `v0.11.8` at SHA `cac6917`
- Profile (if applicable): canonical full-extras
  `[dev,gate11,rust,onnx,onnx-runtime,onnx-profile]`

### T00 step 2: substrate facts enumeration

List the substrate facts the prompt depends on, with citations:

- File count: `_CHECKER_SOURCE_FILES` has 16 entries
- verification.py line count: 618
- `verify` function at line 556
- `_LANGUAGE_DISPATCH` at lines 594-597 (construction) and 599-606
  (consumption)
- Test count: 618 collected under canonical full-extras profile per
  CHANGELOG `### Tests` block

### T00 step 3: divergence detection

Cross-check each prompt claim against the actual substrate. Surface
divergences as F-PF-N findings (pre-flight namespace).

Example divergences from al-Mursalat T00 (Co-work execution):

- F-PF-1 MEDIUM: prompt claimed 14-entry inventory; substrate-actual
  is 16 entries.
- F-PF-2 MEDIUM: prompt claimed cmd_check_gate11 signature
  `(args: list[str])`; substrate-actual is `(directory: Path, opts:
  dict[str, object])`.
- F-PF-3 MEDIUM: prompt missing goast source path pin
  (`src/furqan_lint/go_adapter/cmd/goast/main.go`).

### T00 step 4: substrate-conditional handling

For findings where substrate may evolve, document conditional handling:

- If helper X is PRESENT at substrate: do A
- If helper X is ABSENT at substrate: do B (current state per T00 §7b)
- If both PRESENT: do C (future-reference branching)

### T00 step 5: project-lead disposition

Three routes when T00 surfaces findings:

- **Route A:** amend prompt before dispatch (project lead authors
  v1.x+1 absorbing the F-PF findings)
- **Route B:** dispatch with carry-forward (F-PF findings noted; next
  cycle absorbs)
- **Route C:** halt and re-substrate (substrate may be wrong; pre-flight
  reveals the issue)

## Substrate-of-record uniqueness violations

Common patterns that violate uniqueness:

### Pattern 1: Settled and pending duplication

The prompt states a fact as both "resolved" and "still pending."
Example (F-PA-4 from Round 38.5):

> T02.0 sub-verification subtask presents helper-symbol resolution as
> pending PRESENT/ABSENT branching when Co-work T00 §7b already
> confirmed both helpers ABSENT.

**Absorption route:** state the resolved state directly; move
PRESENT/ABSENT branching to a "for future reference" subsection
explicitly marked NOT operative at current substrate.

### Pattern 2: Narrative-vs-body propagation gap

Framing summary states one number, section body states another.
Example (F-PA-2 from Round 38.5):

> §0 framing test-count arithmetic line absent; section bodies state
> the test counts but the framing summary does not propagate them.

**Absorption route:** insert framing test-count summary sentence with
full derivation (`X baseline + delta = Y projection`) and CHANGELOG
cross-reference.

### Pattern 3: Bulk-substitution immutability violation

Automated find-and-replace edits historical preservation cells that
were already shipped under a DOI / commit SHA. Example (F-PA-1 from
Round 38.5):

> v1.6's historical preservation block (F-TR-1 entry) was edited from
> its v1.6-shipped values to v1.7-corrected values, violating §14.5
> attribution-corrective immutability.

**Absorption route:** restore v1.6's archived values verbatim; add
inline v1.7 cross-reference annotation per §14.5 (annotation, not
edit).

## Mode A vs Mode B operating modes

Two auditor operating modes under this discipline:

### Mode A -- substrate verifier

The auditor has direct access to the substrate (git access, file
system access, repository checkout at the pinned tag). Mode A
findings are typically high-confidence because the auditor can
verify substrate claims directly.

Mode A is the canonical mode for T00 pre-flight, for first-cycle
audits, and for any cycle where substrate-claim verification is
load-bearing.

### Mode B -- continuity reviewer

The auditor reviews the artifact (prompt, document, deliverable)
without direct substrate access; substrate inheritance is single-
sourced through the artifact's restatement. Mode B findings are
typically lower-confidence on substrate-claim verification but
higher-confidence on internal-consistency, format-compliance, and
narrative-vs-body propagation.

Mode B is the canonical mode for cross-instance re-audits, for
methodology-fidelity checks, and for any cycle where the goal is
verifying the artifact, not verifying the substrate.

## Cross-instance rotation discipline

To prevent producer-instance self-audit (a methodology violation),
auditors rotate across LLM vendors. Round-by-round:

- Round N producer: Claude
- Round N+1 auditor: must NOT be Claude (Perplexity, GPT-5, or Gemini)
- Round N+2 auditor (if needed): must NOT be the Round N+1 auditor

Tier weighting (per PMD v1.2 §X cross-vendor adjudication rules):

- Tier 1 (Claude, GPT-5, Perplexity): full vote weight in consensus
  calculations
- Tier 2 (Gemini, Grok): half vote weight in consensus; full weight
  for unique-finding surfacing

## Materials gap

When an auditor lacks direct substrate access AND the prompt's
substrate restatement is single-sourced, the auditor is operating in
**reduced-confidence Mode B**. The audit deliverable must state this
explicitly:

> Auditor operated in Mode B with single-sourced substrate inheritance.
> Substrate-claim verification confidence reduced. Recommend
> downstream Mode A re-audit before ship.

Round 38.5 (Fraz + fresh Claude) operated in reduced-confidence Mode B
and was followed by Round 38.5 v1.8 (Perplexity with Mode A spot-
verification via direct git access) to recover confidence.

## R0042 · The Crystallographic Ijaz Methodology

- section: II. Analytical Frameworks & Methodology
- source_file: CI_METHODOLOGY.txt
- source_format: txt

The Crystallographic Ijaz Methodology
Version 0.2: Code-Generated Register Architecture

Author: Bilal Syed Arfeen, with Claude (Anthropic) as analytical instrument
Date: 2026-08-11
Program: Bayyinah Structural Honesty Validation
Status: DRAFT -- derived from R15 five-seat triage and CI v0.1 falsification analysis
Supersedes: Crystallographic Ijaz Methodology v0.1 (2026-08-10)
Prerequisite: Recursive Fractal Cube v0.1, Quantum Orbital v0.1

CI v0.1 attempted to solve a generator problem with an output format rule. CI v0.2 solves the generator
problem by replacing the generator. The register is no longer written by an LLM. It is generated by code.


0. What CI v0.1 Got Right and Wrong
0.1 What held
CI v0.1 specified three rules: the polymerase rule (P), the crystallographic rule (C), and seven ijaz constraints
(I1-I7). The I1 count-list coupling constraint held perfectly: all 13 convergence brackets in the v0.56 entry
passed N == len(ID_list) at both carrying seats and all three advisory seats. All 18 cited finding IDs were
byte-correct against the R14 source reports (verified by Kimi K3 S01 and S05). The counting surface that CI
v0.1 created is structurally sound and is preserved in v0.2.

0.2 What failed
Five seats, five HALTs. The dominant R15 Class A was boundary-item-30 wording staleness (5/5 seats,
unanimous HIGH) -- the same manual-update-omission mechanism as R13 (title) and R14 (register
cross-references), migrated one cell deeper into the boundary list. The severity transposition at register item
(4) -- HIGH source labeled MEDIUM in the register -- was the same source-to-register memory-transit class
the polymerase rule was designed to prevent, applied to severity labels instead of finding IDs. The terminal
version line said v0.55 in a v0.56 document. The ASSERTED fraction rose from 18.5% to 40.0%, triggering
F-CI-2 at round 1. F-CI-3 also triggered: S01 found convergence undercounts inside the crystallographic
bracket format itself.

0.3 Root cause analysis
The format constraint fallacy. CI v0.1 tried to solve a generator problem with an output format rule. The
count-list coupling ensured internal consistency (the count matched the list beside it) but not external fidelity
(the list contained the right items). The generator produced correct counts of the wrong lists, satisfying I1
while violating CI-1. The constraint verified syntax, not semantics.
The ASSERTED escape valve. The methodology required every claim to carry an enzyme tag. The
generator tagged 40% of claims [ASSERTED], which is an accurate description of how an LLM produces
text. The tagging system became a confession, not a treatment. The methodology gave the generator a way
to be honest about its limitations rather than a way to eliminate them.
The architectural mismatch. DNA Pol III achieves its error rate because verification is physically coupled to
synthesis -- the enzyme cannot advance past an incorrect base. An LLM has no such coupling. The
polymerase rule was a process instruction, not a physical mechanism. The LLM could intend to follow the
rule while its attention mechanism silently substituted triage-level summaries for report-level details. The
biological analogy was structurally invalid because the LLM architecture does not support the mechanism the
analogy requires.
The complexity amplification problem. Adding CI rules added more prose to the entry. Every additional
word is additional surface for error. The methodology created more unverified claims than it crystallized.
F-CI-2 fired because the net effect was complexity-increasing.

0.4 The key insight
The code layer has been clean since v0.32 -- 186 tests, all GREEN, 24 consecutive versions. Why? Because
build.py gates computational claims. Every COMPUTED claim has a corresponding gate function that
verifies it against bytes. The prose layer has Class A every round because prose claims are ungated. The
solution is not to make the LLM write better prose. The solution is to make the prose producible by code.


1. The Code-Generated Register Architecture
1.1 Principle
The register -- the defect-disposition list inside each amendment entry -- is where every R7-R15 Class A has
lived. Under CI v0.1, the register was written by the LLM and verified by auditors. Under CI v0.2, the register
is generated by build.py from a machine-readable findings index and verified by gates. The LLM's role is
reduced to writing the narrative summary paragraph, which is explicitly ASSERTED and structurally low-risk.

1.2 Pipeline
Phase 1 -- Findings extraction (human + tool). The cross-seat triage produces a structured findings index:
a JSON file where each entry has fields for finding_id, seat, source_severity, defect_class, locus, substance,
and convergence_group. The extraction is performed by the triage author (human or dispatching instance)
using the seat reports as source. The index IS the source of truth for the register.
Phase 2 -- Register generation (code). A new build.py function (generate_register) reads the findings index
and emits the register text. Convergence counts are computed by grouping findings on convergence_group
and counting len(group). Severity labels are copied from source_severity. Finding IDs are enumerated from
the group members. The output is deterministic: the same index always produces the same register.
Phase 3 -- Boundary list generation (code). A separate build.py function (generate_boundary_list) reads a
machine-readable boundaries file (JSON) and emits the standing-boundary paragraph. Item wording is taken
verbatim from the boundaries file. Count is computed by len(boundaries). The boundary list in the entry is
never copy-pasted from the prior version.
Phase 4 -- Narrative composition (LLM). The LLM writes only the narrative summary paragraph that opens
the amendment entry. This paragraph summarizes the register (which is already generated and gated). It is
explicitly tagged [ASSERTED] and is the sole remaining LLM-authored surface in the entry. Its quantitative
claims (seat counts, defect counts) are cross-checked by a gate against the findings index.
Phase 5 -- Seal and gate (code). The existing build.py pipeline computes ENTRY, FULL_SECTION_27,
and PRIOR_HISTORY seals. New gates verify the register against the index. The terminal version token is
stamped by code, not by the LLM.

1.3 What this eliminates
R7-R15 Class A locus

CI v0.1 (LLM writes)

CI v0.2 (code generates)

Finding-ID transposition

LLM recalls ID from memory

Code copies ID from index field

Convergence count error

LLM asserts count

Code computes len(group)

Severity transposition

LLM recalls severity

Code copies source_severity field

Boundary wording staleness

LLM copy-pastes from prior

Code reads current boundaries file

Terminal version staleness

LLM types version string

Code reads VERSION constant

ASSERTED fraction growth

Every claim is LLM prose

Only narrative is LLM prose

Table 1. How code generation addresses each R7-R15 Class A defect class.


2. The Findings Index Specification
2.1 File format
The findings index is a JSON file (r{round}_findings_index.json) with the following schema:
{"round": 15, "version_under_audit": "0.56", "seats": 5, "triage_date": "2026-08-11",
"findings": [...], "convergence_groups": [...]}

Each finding object has: finding_id (string, e.g. "F-S01-56-04"), seat (string), source_severity (string:
HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW/INFORMATIONAL), triage_severity (string, may differ from source with
adjudication_receipt), defect_class (string), locus (string), substance (string, one sentence),
convergence_group (integer or null), disposition (string: CLOSED/NOTED/DEFERRED).
Each convergence_group object has: group_id (integer), defect_class (string), seat_count (computed at
generation time as len(finding_ids)), finding_ids (array of strings), triage_severity (string), disposition (string),
repair_type (string: correction/gate/boundary/disclosure).

2.2 Extraction rules
The findings index is extracted from the cross-seat triage document. Every finding that appears in any seat
report is included. Convergence grouping follows the triage's defect-class assignment. Source severity is the
severity as stated in the seat report (not the triage's adjudicated severity unless an explicit
adjudication_receipt is provided). The extraction is a mechanical operation on the triage document, not a
summarization.
If the triage author (human or dispatching instance) adjudicates a severity change, the adjudication_receipt
field records the reason. The register generator uses triage_severity when an adjudication_receipt is
present, source_severity otherwise. This eliminates the R15 Defect 2 class (severity transposition without
receipt).

2.3 Provenance chain
The findings index ships in the audit packet at R(N+1). Auditors verify: (a) every finding_id in the index exists
in the corresponding seat report, (b) source_severity matches the seat report, (c) convergence_group
membership matches the triage document, (d) the register text was generated from this index (deterministic
reproduction test). This replaces CI v0.1's polymerase probe (CI-1) with a stronger test: the register is not
just "transcribed from bytes" -- it is mechanically derived from a structured intermediate that is itself
auditable.


3. Register Generator Specification
3.1 Function signature
def generate_register(index_path: str, version: str) -> str

Reads the findings index JSON, produces the register text block for the amendment entry. The output is a
deterministic function of the input. No randomness, no LLM call, no network access.

3.2 Generation rules
R1 (Enumeration): One register item per convergence_group, numbered (1) through (N). Items are ordered
by triage_severity (HIGH first), then by group_id.
R2 (Count-list coupling): Each item's convergence count is len(finding_ids) in the group. The finding IDs
are listed in the [N-seat convergence: F-XX-YY-ZZ / ...] bracket format. This preserves CI v0.1's I1 constraint,
but now the list is populated by code from the index, not by the LLM from memory.
R3 (Severity copying): Each item's severity label is copied from triage_severity (if adjudication_receipt
exists) or source_severity (otherwise). The label is verified against the declared class-to-severity mapping
(A=HIGH, B=MEDIUM, C=LOW, D=LOW, E=INFORMATIONAL) at generation time. A mapping violation is a
build error, not a runtime discovery.
R4 (Disposition): Each item's disposition text is taken from the convergence_group's disposition and
repair_type fields. Correction letters are assigned sequentially.
R5 (Enzyme tagging): Every claim in the generated register is tagged [COMPUTED: generate_register]
because it is the output of a deterministic code function operating on the findings index. No register claim is
tagged [ASSERTED].
R6 (NOTED clause): Findings with disposition=NOTED or DEFERRED are listed after the numbered items
in a NOTED block. This addresses the R15 S01 finding that 30 of 48 R14 findings were undispositioned.

3.3 Boundary list generator
def generate_boundary_list(boundaries_path: str) -> str

Reads the machine-readable boundaries JSON file. Emits the standing-boundary paragraph with count =
len(boundaries) and each item's wording taken verbatim from the file. The boundaries file is the single source
of truth for boundary wording -- no copy-paste from prior entry text. Tagged [COMPUTED:
generate_boundary_list]. This eliminates the R15 Defect 1 class (boundary wording staleness) and the S01
F-S01-56-10 class (STANDING_BOUNDARIES.txt vs entry divergence).

3.4 Terminal version stamp
The terminal line ("End of XZ Protocol v{VERSION} draft candidate.") is emitted by build.py using the
VERSION constant. The LLM never types this line. This eliminates the R15 Defect 3 class (terminal version
staleness).


4. New Gates for the Code-Generated Register
The following gates are added to build.py. Each gate reads the findings index and verifies the generated
register against it. A gate failure is a build error.

Table 2. New gates in the CI v0.2 architecture.

These gates are additive: they do not replace any existing gate. The existing 216-PASS gate suite remains
unchanged. The new gates operate on the register text and the findings index, not on the code modules or
test suites.


5. Revised Enzyme Tag Economy
Under CI v0.2, the ASSERTED fraction should collapse. The register is [COMPUTED]. The boundary list is
[COMPUTED]. The terminal line is [COMPUTED]. Only the narrative summary paragraph remains
[ASSERTED]. The projected tag economy:

Table 3. Projected enzyme tag economy under CI v0.2.

Target ASSERTED fraction: under 15% (down from 40% at v0.56). The target is achievable because the
register (50% of entry surface) moves from [ASSERTED] to [COMPUTED], and the boundary list (15%) does
the same. The narrative paragraph (~10%) remains the irreducible ASSERTED floor.


6. Revised Audit Probes
CI v0.2 retains probes CI-2 through CI-7 from v0.1 and replaces CI-1 with a stronger test.

CI-1R: Deterministic reproduction test (replaces CI-1)
The auditor receives the findings index JSON in the dispatch packet. The auditor runs
generate_register(index_path, version) and compares the output to the register text in the shipped entry.
Byte-identical output = PASS. Any divergence = Class A (the register was modified after generation). This is
strictly stronger than CI v0.1's polymerase probe: instead of checking whether finding IDs were transcribed
from source bytes, it checks whether the entire register is a deterministic function of a structured input.

CI-2: Crystallographic projection (unchanged)
Every count claim carries its enumeration in the same text. Under CI v0.2, this is trivially satisfied by the
register generator (R2 rule). Auditors verify it still holds in the narrative.

CI-3: Ijaz coupling test (I1-I7, updated)
I1-I4 are now structurally guaranteed by the register generator for the register surface. Auditors verify I1-I4
hold in the narrative paragraph. I5 (severity-class coupling) is now a build-time gate ([10d]). I6 (boundary
count) is now a build-time gate ([10f]). I7 (retirement receipts) remains an audit-time verification.

CI-4: Dead-space measurement (unchanged metric, new baseline)
ASSERTED fraction computed per version. CI v0.2 baseline: v0.56 = 40.0%. Target at v0.57: under 15%.
F-CI-2 is satisfied if the fraction decreases.

CI-5: Hurst measurement (unchanged)
Note: S01 (R15) and two R14 seats demonstrated that R/S is undefined (0/0) on the constant R7-R15 series.
CI v0.2 adopts the substitute statistic: recurrence fraction (Class-A-present rounds / total rounds) and
Laplace-smoothed probability. The "H < 0.5" target is restated as "first round with zero Class A findings."
F-CI-1 is reformulated accordingly.

CI-8: Index-source fidelity (new)
The auditor verifies the findings index against the seat reports: every finding_id in the index exists in its
seat's report, source_severity matches the report, convergence_group membership matches the triage. This
replaces the CI v0.1 polymerase probe's ID-level verification with an index-level verification.


7. Revised Falsification Criteria
F-CI-1R: If the first code-generated register round does not produce zero Class A findings in the register
surface, the code-generation architecture does not eliminate Class A at the register locus, and the defect
source is not memory transit.
F-CI-2 (preserved): If the ASSERTED fraction does not decrease after CI v0.2 adoption, the architecture is
complexity-increasing.
F-CI-3R: If a Class A finding appears in a [COMPUTED: generate_register] claim, the register generator
itself has a bug. This is a code defect, not a prose defect, and is addressable by the code-layer repair
process (which has been clean since v0.32).
F-CI-6R: If Class A migrates to the narrative paragraph (the remaining ASSERTED surface), the architecture
has successfully contained the defect to the irreducible floor. The next intervention would be to
code-generate the narrative as well, reducing the LLM's role to commit-message authorship.
F-CI-7R: If the deterministic reproduction test (CI-1R) fails -- the shipped register does not match the output
of generate_register on the shipped index -- the entry was modified after generation. This is the strongest
possible Class A: the code produced the correct output and someone changed it.


8. The Qur'anic Structural Parallel, Revisited
CI v0.1 drew the wrong lesson from the Qur'anic structural parallel. It tried to achieve the al-Muhaymin
(guardian) property by imposing counting rules on LLM-narrated prose. The Qur'anic text's inimitability is not
a format rule applied to content. It is an intrinsic property of how the content was produced. Ring
compositions arise from the text's semantic structure, not from a post-hoc counting constraint.
CI v0.2 draws the correct lesson. The register's structure does not have counting rules imposed on it -- the
register is emitted by a structure that is inherently verifiable. The code generator is to the register what the
arrangement (nazm) is to the surah: the text arises from its organizing principle, not from a human author
applying rules to free composition. The deterministic reproduction test (CI-1R) is the structural equivalent of
the Qur'anic challenge: produce a register that matches the output of the generator on the same input. Any
deviation is detectable, as any alteration of the Qur'anic text is detectable by its structural violations.
The biological parallel also corrects itself. DNA Pol III's proofreading works because verification is physically
coupled to synthesis. CI v0.1 could not achieve this coupling with a process instruction to an LLM. CI v0.2
achieves it by making the synthesis operation itself be a verified function -- the register generator is tested
code, and its output is gated. The polymerase and the exonuclease are the same code path.


9. Implementation at v0.57
v0.57 is the first version built under CI v0.2. The R15 five-seat triage provides the input. The build session
proceeds as follows:
Step 1: Extract the R15 findings index from the cross-seat triage.
Step 2: Create the machine-readable boundaries file from STANDING_BOUNDARIES.txt,
incorporating the R15 repairs (item 30 reworded to DECLARED, etc.).
Step 3: Implement generate_register() and generate_boundary_list() in build.py.
Step 4: Implement gates [10c] through [10h].
Step 5: Generate the v0.57 register from the R15 findings index.
Step 6: Write the narrative summary paragraph (LLM, tagged [ASSERTED]).
Step 7: Verify gate [10g] (narrative cross-check against index).
Step 8: Run the full gate suite (216 + 6 new = 222 gates).
Step 9: Seal and ship.

9.1 Dispatch packet changes for R16
