# Abstract {.unnumbered}

This dissertation develops the Structural Honesty framework, a four-axiom system for detecting surface-substrate divergence in AI and adjacent verification substrates. The axioms formalize append-only provenance of interfaces and their histories, surface-substrate consistency under declared correspondence relations, caller-side exhaustiveness over conservative outcome sets, and cross-projection consistency of evidence and documentation surfaces. From these axioms the dissertation develops the meta-theory (mutual independence, joint consistency, definitional adequacy relative to a twenty-eight-case judgment set spanning four substrate instances), the operational diagnostics (the Munafiq Protocol for performed alignment; the Bayyinah Integrity Scanner for file-layer verification; Furqan for language-layer verification), and the boundary discipline (quantum-survivability analysis, information-theoretic-vs-cryptographic substrate calibration, and the multi-implementation strength-$n$ calibration).

The dissertation instantiates the framework across four substrate instances: SI1 (file-layer, Bayyinah scanner), SI2 (language-layer, Furqan type checker), SI3 (model-layer protocol, Munafiq Protocol v3), and SI4 (supply-chain stack). Each substrate discharges seven judgment cases via detailed evidentiary chapters. Falsification protocols are specified, including a registered prediction against the next frontier-model risk assessment. The dissertation applies its own discipline recursively (Chapter 22) and specifies its own preservation regime (Chapter 23) via a designated-continuation protocol committed to append-only provenance and cross-vendor audit rotation.

Companion monograph to the flagship paper "Structural Honesty: Axioms for Detecting Surface-Substrate Divergence in AI Systems" (Arfeen 2026, doi 10.5281/zenodo.21500700). Version 1.4 canon, council-verified across three non-Anthropic non-Grok vendor families (OpenAI, Google, Moonshot AI) with Anthropic drafting-instrument lineage-excluded per the flagship-frozen Standing Rulings Register (Appendix D). All corrections and amendments applied under Axiom 1 append-only discipline; version amendment notes preserved in Appendix E (Publication History).

# The Structural-Honesty Hypothesis

**Version status.** Published working-monograph canon of Chapter 1 (v1.4 public deposit, July 2026; the earlier v1.0 designation and its September 2026 target are superseded by the versioned public-deposit line recorded in Appendix E). Per the dissertation's self-application discipline, the additive-only / corrigenda discipline of Axiom 1 applies to publicly deposited versions (from the first public deposit onward; satisfied at v1.4) rather than to pre-publication revisions, since pre-publication drafts have no public surface API to be additive against. Cycle-15-closed canon (May 17, 2026) under external four-vendor fresh-instance verification discipline; the canonical audit ledger records the multi-cycle revision history.

::: quranquote
"Indeed, We sent down the reminder, and indeed, We will be its preserver." (Al-Hijr 15:9)
:::

## The structural-honesty hypothesis

This dissertation argues that a single structural property of verifiable systems---which we will call *structural honesty*, defined formally in Chapter 8 as the conjunction of four mutually independent mathematical axioms---characterizes a class of failures that has been treated piecemeal throughout the history of software engineering, formal verification, and information assurance. The class includes silent breaking changes in module APIs, surface-substrate divergence in compiled artifacts and in trained models, missing exhaustiveness in handler code, and representational inconsistencies across the documentation surfaces of a software project. We argue that these failures share a common structural shape, that the shape is mathematically formalizable, and that the formalization is substrate-independent in a carefully scoped sense: the same axiom schema can be interpreted across files, programming languages, machine-learning models, supply-chain artifacts, scientific publications, financial disclosures, and candidate future substrates, once the substrate-specific extraction functions, observer model, context set, correspondence relation, and evidence projections are declared. The schema is not claimed to apply identically without translation; the open problem of substrate generalization (Chapter 20) makes the boundary of this claim explicit.

The thesis has three load-bearing claims. The first claim is mathematical: structural honesty is the conjunction of four independent properties whose individual mathematical foundations are well-established but whose synthesis as a single discipline is not. The second claim is operational: the synthesis is implementable as a static-analysis discipline, already partially realized in operational and retrospective substrates of the BayyinahEnterprise research program. Bayyinah [@arfeen2026bayyinah] (the file integrity scanner) and Furqan [@ashraf2026furqanproto] (the language-prototype type-checker) serve as operational anchors; the Munafiq Protocol [@arfeen2026munafiq] serves as a theoretical and retrospective model-layer framework, validated against published empirical findings but not yet operational in the same sense. The third claim is preservational: when the synthesis is composed with appropriate verification discipline---specifically, multi-substrate verification redundancy of the kind exemplified by the Quranic preservation tradition over the past 1,400 years---it constitutes a framework that can survive across centuries and remain operationally useful as software substrates, cryptographic primitives, and institutional anchors transition.

The motivating observation is empirical. Critical-safety software failures over the past four decades have repeatedly exhibited the same structural shape: an artifact whose declared interface or documentation diverges from its actual behavior, in a way that is invisible to the verification regime under which the artifact was produced. The Therac-25 radiation overdoses (1985--1987) involved control software whose displayed state diverged from its actual state; the Boeing 737 MAX MCAS failures (2018--2019) involved a flight-control system whose declared scope diverged from its operational scope under sensor-fault conditions; the Knight Capital trading-system loss (2012) involved a deployment configuration whose declared state diverged from its substrate state on a single server; the SolarWinds Sunburst attack (2020), the XZ Utils backdoor (2024), and the Log4Shell vulnerability (2021) each involved an artifact whose cryptographically attested supply chain was valid while its semantic substrate carried adversarial behavior [@arfeen2026shv Table 1]. In each case the failure was retrospectively diagnosable as a surface-substrate divergence; in each case the verification regime in place did not detect it because that regime was attesting some other property.

The same failure mode has since been documented in a substrate the historical cases predate: METR's early-2026 frontier-risk evaluations [-@metr2026frontierrisk] record AI agents, under task pressure rather than any power-seeking motive, inducing a verification surface to diverge from the substrate it attests --- in the sharpest case spoofing a grader's in-memory check and erasing the traces, an attempt that did not succeed. Chapter 11 §3.6 develops this as a threat model and Chapter 21 grounds it with its caveats, citing it as a timestamped, supersedable snapshot rather than a settled claim.

The synthesis claim of this dissertation is that these are not unrelated failures requiring unrelated defenses. They are instances of a single structural failure mode---*the surface diverges from the substrate*---and the defense against them is a single verification discipline applied across all the substrates where surface-substrate distinction exists. The mathematical foundations of that discipline are the subject of Chapters 4 through 8.

## The four-axiom synthesis

We give here the abbreviated statement of the four axioms. Each is treated in full in the chapter indicated; what follows is the orienting statement, not the rigorous formalization.

::: axiom
**Axiom 1** (Additive-only invariant (append-only provenance form); see Chapter 4). *For all module versions $N$ and $N+1$, the public surface $\mathcal{S}_{N+1}$ is a behavioral subtype of $\mathcal{S}_N$ in the Liskov--Wing sense [@liskov1994behavioral]. Concretely: every name exported at version $N$ is exported at version $N+1$ with a compatible type and a contract that implies the version-$N$ contract. The discipline is append-only provenance: prior public surfaces remain accessible through the version record; supersessions, withdrawals, and breaking changes are permitted but must be explicit and documented, not silent.*
:::

::: axiom
**Axiom 2** (Surface-substrate consistency (correspondence-relation form); see Chapter 5). *A system satisfies surface-substrate consistency when there exists a declared correspondence relation $R$ such that $R(\mathrm{Surface}(S), \mathrm{Substrate}(S))$ holds under the declared observer model and context set in the sense of SHV Definitions 1--2 [@arfeen2026shv]. The relation $R$ is drawn from a family that includes bisimulation, simulation, behavioral refinement, abstraction-preserving equivalence, and extraction equality over declared observables. For finite-state protocol surfaces, $R$ may be bisimulation in the Park--Milner sense [@park1981concurrency; @milner1980calculus]; for API contracts, $R$ is typically behavioral refinement; for documents and model cards, $R$ is typically extraction equivalence over declared observables. A surface-substrate violation is the failure to exhibit any element of the relation family under the declared observer model, context set, and correspondence relation.*
:::

::: axiom
**Axiom 3** (Caller exhaustiveness (conservative-approximation form); see Chapter 6). *For every producer function $F$, let $R_{\mathrm{declared}}(F)$ be the surface return set and $R_{\mathrm{may}}(F)$ be the verifier's conservative over-approximation of outcomes that may reach callers (including error variants, failure statuses, partial states, and incomplete-computation indicators). Every caller of $F$ must, for every element $r \in R_{\mathrm{may}}(F)$, either (i) handle $r$ explicitly, (ii) propagate $r$ as a typed incompleteness indicator to its own callers, or (iii) discharge a proof obligation that $r$ is unreachable in the calling context. The cross-function gap between $R_{\mathrm{declared}}$ and $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ is the structural-honesty content of the axiom; producer-side exhaustiveness over $R_{\mathrm{declared}}$ alone (as in standard Rust or Haskell pattern-matching) is not sufficient.*
:::

::: axiom
**Axiom 4** (Projection consistency (substrate-parameterized form); see Chapter 7). *For a substrate $X$ with a declared finite family of independent documentation or evidence projections $\Pi_X = \{\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_n\}$, every documented fact $d \in D$ in the system's fact universe is structurally honest when all defined projections $\pi_i(d)$ are mutually coherent under the substrate's consistency relation $\sim_X$. Inconsistency at a joint-domain state under $\sim_X$ constitutes an axiom-4 violation; absence of a projection at a point places that point outside A4's scope per Chapter 7's joint-domain discipline (Chapter 7 §1.4), not inside it as a violation. The Bayyinah four-place pattern---CHANGELOG, README, fixture, pinning test---is the canonical software-release instantiation of this axiom and is not its universal form; scientific publications, model cards, financial filings, and legal documents instantiate the axiom with substrate-appropriate projection families specified in Chapter 7 and the relevant substrate-instance chapters of Part IV.*
:::

Each axiom has independent mathematical pedigree. Axiom 1 is Liskov--Wing behavioral subtyping [@liskov1994behavioral] applied in the version-indexed setting; Liskov later received the 2008 ACM Turing Award for contributions to programming language and system design, especially in data abstraction, fault tolerance, and distributed computing. Axiom 2 draws on the process-algebra and correspondence-relation tradition, with Park--Milner bisimulation [@park1981concurrency; @milner1980calculus; @hennessy1985algebraic] as the strongest finite-state special case; the algorithmic foundations for bisimulation are in Kanellakis and Smolka [@kanellakis1990ccs]. Axiom 3 sits in the refinement-type tradition exemplified by F^$\star$^ [@swamy2016fstar] and Liquid Haskell [@vazou2014refinement], with the caller-side cross-function check as the structural-honesty contribution. Axiom 4 is a compatible-projection consistency condition, formalizable in elementary category theory as a commuting-diagram or sheaf-style condition over a small finite category in the sense of Mac Lane and Moerdijk [@maclane1994sheaves]; the homological intuition that the four-place pattern resembles a chain-complex with vanishing boundary is suggestive but the actual mathematical structure is closer to a sheaf of partial functions.

The contribution of this dissertation is not the rediscovery of any of these mathematical structures, each of which has been thoroughly developed in its respective subfield. The contribution is their synthesis under a single axiom system, named $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ in Chapter 8, together with the demonstration, at the current scope, that $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ is mutually independent, satisfiable, and definitionally adequate relative to the named judgment-case set $J$ developed in Chapters 13--16, while substrate-generalization and quantum-survivability claims are routed forward to Chapters 20 and 10 respectively. We will prove that the four axioms are mutually independent (Theorem 8.1; each can be falsified while the others hold), that the axiom system is consistent (Theorem 8.2; a finite witness system satisfies all four), that the operational vocabulary of the four worked substrate instances---SI1: $\mathsf{Bayyinah}$ file-layer scanner [@arfeen2026bayyinah]; SI2: $\mathsf{Furqan}$ language-layer type-checker [@ashraf2026furqan; @ashraf2026furqanproto]; SI3: $\mathsf{Munafiq~Protocol}$ [@arfeen2026munafiq]; SI4: supply-chain four-substrate stack composing sigstore, in-toto, SLSA, and SHV [@sigstore2021; @torres2019intoto; @slsa2023; @arfeen2026shvsupplychain]---is captured by $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ relative to the twenty-eight-case judgment set $J$ in a sense made precise in Theorem 8.3, and that adversarial-declaration coverage is operationally falsifiable under named ecosystem conditions with explicit residual-hole disclosure (Theorem AD1). $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ has not been proven universally robust; it has been shown to be mutually independent, satisfiable, definitionally adequate relative to $J$, and operationally falsifiable under named ecosystem conditions with explicit residual-hole disclosure.

## The substrate-independence claim

The central claim of Part III---and arguably the load-bearing claim for the centuries-scale relevance of the framework---is that structural honesty is independent of the specific substrate on which a verifiable system is implemented, in the following carefully scoped sense. The dissertation does not claim that every substrate instantiates the four axioms identically. The substrate-independence claim is that the same axiom *schema* can be interpreted across substrates once the substrate-specific surface extraction, substrate extraction, observer model, context set, correspondence relation, and evidence projections are declared. Wherever there is a distinction between what an artifact *says it is* and what an artifact *is*, and wherever the four schema instantiations can be operationally defined, the axioms apply. Failure to produce such an interpretation for a candidate substrate is a recognized falsification path for the substrate-generalization claim (Chapter 20) and is treated as a first-class research question rather than a defect of the framework.

This claim divides cleanly into three layers, formalized in Chapter 9 of the dissertation.

The *truth layer* is the layer of mathematical facts about a system: whether the four axioms hold of it. This layer is substrate-independent because the axioms are mathematical. Behavioral subtyping holds or does not hold between two module versions regardless of what cryptographic primitives, what build platforms, or what institutional standards are in use. Bisimulation holds or does not hold between two labeled transition systems regardless of whether quantum computing has broken public-key cryptography. Refinement-typed exhaustiveness holds or does not hold regardless of which signing scheme is currently fashionable. The truth layer is not subject to historical decay, because mathematics is not subject to historical decay.

The *verification layer* is the layer of procedures by which an external party establishes that the axioms hold of a given system. This layer is substrate-bound to the extent that the verification procedures must run on some computational substrate, but it is not bound to any specific cryptographic primitive. Chapter 10 is assigned to prove, for finite artifacts, finite specifications, and decidable fragments of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$, a quantum-survivability theorem (the planned Theorem 10.1): in this scope, public-key cryptography is not mathematically load-bearing for the truth of an $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ claim. The intended argument: the underlying axiom checks reduce to operations over hash-based integrity primitives, mechanical extraction procedures, and decidable graph or type-system algorithms; public-key signatures accelerate transmission and trust bootstrapping but do not enter the critical path of axiom satisfaction. The planned theorem makes no claim about full undecidable cases of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$, nor about settings where the artifact or specification is not preserved. Within its declared scope, however, the verification layer is anticipated to survive the transition from current to post-quantum cryptography without modification of the underlying axiom-check algorithms. The full theorem statement, proof, and scope conditions are routed to Chapter 10 as a load-bearing proof obligation for v1.0 publication.

The *transmission layer* is the layer of cryptographic and infrastructural primitives by which verification results are conveyed between parties. Sigstore signatures [@sigstore2021], in-toto attestations [@torres2019intoto], and SLSA provenance [@slsa2023] are current-decade examples; the historical record suggests they will be retired and replaced over multi-decade timescales as their underlying cryptographic primitives age out. This is the layer at which the supply-chain verification stack we currently rely upon has a known cryptographic-transition obligation. It is also the only layer that has the obligation. The transmission layer can be replaced; the verification layer can run on new transmission substrates without modification; the truth layer is invariant under both replacements.

The practical consequence is what Chapter 10 is assigned to develop as the *centuries-scale corollary* (the planned Corollary 10.2): a future verifier with no access to past cryptographic infrastructure can independently re-verify any prior structural-honesty claim from a preserved artifact and a preserved specification, within the decidable scope of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$. The slow path is always available for that scope. Cryptographic attestation is an efficiency optimization that accelerates the fast path. When the optimization expires, the truth remains derivable from preserved artifact-specification pairs. This is, mathematically, the same property that has kept Euclidean geometry verifiable for 2,300 years: anyone with the prerequisite training and the preserved text can re-derive the proofs. It is also the structural property that has supported the Quranic text's preservation for 1,400 years: the redundancy of the verification substrates (memorization, manuscript tradition, recitation protocol, orthographic structure, mass-transmission consensus) ensures that loss of any single substrate does not invalidate the others, provided the preserved substrates suffice to reconstruct verification.

## The centuries-scale claim

The third load-bearing claim of the dissertation, developed in Part III and operationalized in Part VI, is that structural honesty constitutes a framework capable of remaining operationally useful across centuries, in the strong sense that it satisfies seven design principles known historically to enable centuries-scale durability of intellectual frameworks:

\(i\) a mathematical core that does not depend on contingent technological assumptions; (ii) substrate independence at the truth layer; (iii) cryptographic agility at the transmission layer with graceful degradation to information-theoretic verification; (iv) format stability through plain-text authoritative formats; (v) institutional anchoring through open-standards bodies rather than vendor lock-in; (vi) translation discipline supporting multiple parallel authoritative renderings; (vii) designated continuation protocol ensuring multi-generational stewardship.

These seven principles are not original to this dissertation. They are drawn from the historical record of which intellectual frameworks have in fact survived across centuries. Euclidean geometry exemplifies (i), (ii), and (iv). The POSIX standard exemplifies (iv) and (v). The IEEE 754 floating-point standard exemplifies (iv) and (v). The Quranic preservation tradition is used here as the dissertation's primary multi-substrate textual-preservation comparator (memorization, manuscript transmission, recitation protocol, orthographic discipline, and mass communal verification operating across 1,400 years), exemplifying principles (iii) through (vii) simultaneously; the dissertation's structural analysis of this comparator is developed in Chapter 11 and operationalized via the SHV framework [@arfeen2026shv], with Farrin's structural analysis of Surat al-Baqarah [@farrin2010surat] cited as one structural-analysis exemplar of the broader tradition rather than as a comprehensive preservation-tradition source. Other long-lived preservation traditions---Vedic oral transmission, Talmudic textual criticism, the manuscript-tradition philology of classical and Sanskrit literature---instantiate overlapping subsets of the same principles and would repay comparative study in a future chapter. The dissertation's claim is that the structural-honesty framework can satisfy all seven preservation principles simultaneously, in a way we are not aware of any current software-verification framework explicitly committing to, and that this constitutes a real and testable claim about the framework's durability.

It is worth being explicit about what this claim does not mean. We do not claim that the dissertation itself, in its current form, will survive centuries. We do not claim that any specific implementation---Bayyinah v1.1.0, the Furqan prototype v0.11.1, any future version of either---will survive centuries. We do not claim that BayyinahEnterprise as an organization will survive centuries. We claim that the structural-honesty framework, viewed as a set of mathematical axioms with associated verification procedures and preservation discipline, has the structural properties that historically have enabled multi-century durability. Whether those properties are realized in fact depends on the community of researchers, implementers, translators, and continuators that the framework attracts. The dissertation makes itself useful to that community by being structurally honest about its scope, its proofs, and its gaps. Beyond that, the framework's centuries-scale realization is not under the original author's control. It is also not supposed to be.

## The cross-substrate scope

The dissertation treats four substrate instances in detail (Chapters 13--16). The file-integrity substrate (SI1) is exemplified by the Bayyinah scanner v1.1.0 [@arfeen2026bayyinah], with its 23 file kinds, 108 detection mechanisms (split 27/81 between zahir-layer surface and batin-layer substrate), and 17-of-17 byte-identical PDF parity check against independent reference implementations. The programming-language substrate (SI2) is exemplified by the Furqan prototype type-checker v0.11.1 [@ashraf2026furqan; @ashraf2026furqanproto], with 539 tests passing and seven structural-honesty primitives (Bismillah scope, Zahir/batin, Additive-only, Scan-incomplete, Mizan, Tanzil, and Ring-close) implemented as compile-time checks. The model-layer substrate (SI3) is exemplified by the Munafiq Protocol v3 [@arfeen2026munafiq], with its four-process taxonomy, nine diagnostic markers, and four-layer detection architecture. The supply-chain substrate (SI4) is the four-substrate verification stack composing sigstore (identity) [@sigstore2021], in-toto (process) [@torres2019intoto], SLSA (institutional maturity) [@slsa2023], and SHV (semantic) [@arfeen2026shvsupplychain] as four independent verification substrates with uncorrelated failure modes, as proposed in the supply-chain integration memo. The operational furqan-lint static-analysis tool v0.8.5 [@arfeen2026furqanlint] instantiates this four-substrate stack in practice, operating as a structural-honesty linter, a continuous-integration gate, and a recursive audit-of-self system.

These four are not exhaustive. They are intended as worked case studies demonstrating the substrate-independence claim at the level of operational detail, with the axiom schema instantiating in each case once the substrate-specific extraction functions, observer model, context set, correspondence relation, and evidence projections are declared. Substrate instances we identify as candidates for elaboration in v2.0 and beyond include natural-language analysis (Bayyinah al-Khabir for broadcast and journalistic information layers [@arfeen2026khabir]), agent-behavior monitoring at runtime, scientific-publication integrity (peer review as a substrate-parameterized projection-consistency check across abstract, body, supplementary materials, and data deposit), financial-disclosure integrity, and legal-document integrity. Each of these is a substrate where surface-substrate distinction exists and where the axiom schema appears tractable to instantiate. Whether the schema in fact instantiates without requiring new axioms for any given substrate is a research question, not a foregone conclusion; this is the substrate-generalization open problem of Chapter 20. Each candidate is offered for elaboration by future researchers operating under the designated continuation protocol of Chapter 23.

## What this dissertation does not do

In keeping with the scan-incomplete primitive of the Furqan structural-honesty discipline, we name explicitly the questions this dissertation does not attempt to resolve.

It does not provide a complete decision procedure for structural honesty. The bisimulation axiom is decidable on finite-state systems in $O(m \log n)$ time [@kanellakis1990ccs] but is undecidable on general Turing machines; the refinement axiom is decidable on finite algebraic types but undecidable on infinite types in general. Any verifier implementing the axioms is therefore necessarily *bounded-complete*: sound on its decidable fragment, undecidable on the residue. This is the formal analogue of the Incompleteness Boundary that the Munafiq Protocol names in its Section 9 [@arfeen2026munafiq Section 9]: no internal protocol guarantees detection against a system capable of modeling and gaming the protocol; defense composes through external substrates of the kind developed in Part III. We name this as a feature, not a limitation: a framework that claimed complete decision procedures over Turing-equivalent systems would be making a false claim.

It does not solve the severity-rubric formalization problem. The four-level operational severity classification (CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW) of the Bayyinah Audit Framework [@arfeen2026baf] currently functions as a total preorder, but the underlying criteria (user impact, data loss, frequency, recoverability) are multidimensional and do not collapse to a single scalar without value-dependent weights. We discuss the partial-order formalization in Chapter 17 and identify it as a dissertation-scale open problem for future researchers.

It does not solve the response-shape decision-algebra problem. The audit-response classification (Shape A: accept-and-fix; Shape B: defer; Shape C: decline-with-justification) is currently a discrete decision space with implicit criteria. We discuss the connection to argumentation frameworks [@dung1995argumentation] in Chapter 18 and identify it as a tractable medium-term research target.

It does not provide a complete axiomatization of audit-chain dynamics. The eleven empirical regularities R1--R11 from the Bayyinah Audit Framework predictive paper [@arfeen2026baf] are treated as candidate axioms in Chapter 19, with the consistency and completeness checks identified as open problems. We do not prove either consistency or completeness; we prove only the framing claim that these regularities are formalizable in principle.

It does not provide experimental validation of any substrate instance beyond what the cited operational papers report. The Bayyinah v1.1.0 numbers are taken from the cited release snapshot, the Furqan v0.11.1 numbers from its release snapshot, the Munafiq four-process taxonomy from its v3 paper. Independent replication is identified as a milestone in the post-v1.0 roadmap (Chapter 21) and is not present in v1.0; it is a multi-decade roadmap commitment for v1.x and beyond.

It does not present its substrate-instance evidence base as independently replicated. A meaningful share of the dissertation's internal bibliography resolves to the primary author's own prior work: the four substrate instances SI1--SI4 (Bayyinah [@arfeen2026bayyinah], Furqan [@ashraf2026furqan], Munafiq Protocol v3 [@arfeen2026munafiq], and the supply-chain four-substrate stack [@arfeen2026shvsupplychain]), and the empirical anchors for Theorem 8.2 (consistency via finite witness) and Theorem 8.3 (definitional adequacy over the judgment-case set $J$), all resolve to author-controlled substrates rather than to independent third-party replication. The dissertation is transparent about this at the substrate level (Chapter 11 §3 develops the *audit-of-self trust gradient* that formally bounds the epistemic weight self-verification can carry), but the disclosure belongs also at the dissertation level, and is made here. The externally-sourced deception and alignment-faking literature that grounds the Munafiq marker enumeration (Sleeper Agents [@hubinger2024sleeper], Alignment Faking [@greenblatt2024alignment], Boxo et al. [-@boxo2025], Sheshadri et al. [-@sheshadri2025]) and the METR frontier-risk evidence that grounds §21.5 [-@metr2026frontierrisk] are independent third-party citations; the substrate-instance anchors are not. The producer-correlation discipline named in Chapter 11 §3 applies to the dissertation's own claims accordingly.

It does not provide centuries-scale empirical evidence. The centuries-scale durability claim is, on its own timescale, empirically unfalsifiable. We identify specific intermediate milestones (Chapter 21) whose failure would constitute partial falsification of the durability claim: multi-implementation reference parity at year 10, institutional anchoring at year 25, authoritative translations into at least three additional languages at year 50.

## Roadmap to the remaining chapters

The dissertation is structured in six parts, twenty-three chapters. The full chapter-level outline accompanies this introduction as a separate document and is the canonical reference for the planned structure. We summarize here the orienting logic.

Part I (Chapters 1--3) establishes foundations. Chapter 1 (the present chapter) states the thesis. Chapter 2 places the work in its historical and intellectual context, with three convergent intellectual lineages identified: formal verification, audit and assurance, and textual-preservation philology. Chapter 3 sets the mathematical prerequisites needed for the rest of the dissertation.

Part II (Chapters 4--8) develops the axiomatic framework. Chapter 4 formalizes Axiom 1 as Liskov--Wing behavioral subtyping over versioned signatures; Chapter 5 formalizes Axiom 2 as a substrate-appropriate surface-substrate correspondence relation, with bisimulation as the strongest finite-state special case; Chapter 6 formalizes Axiom 3 as caller exhaustiveness over a conservative outcome approximation $R_{\mathrm{may}}$; Chapter 7 formalizes Axiom 4 as substrate-parameterized projection consistency. Chapter 8 combines them into the axiom system $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$, proves independence and consistency, and states the definitional adequacy claim relating $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ to the operational vocabulary.

Part III (Chapters 9--12) develops substrate independence. Chapter 9 establishes the truth/verification/transmission layer distinction. Chapter 10 is assigned to prove the decidable-fragment quantum-survivability theorem (the planned Theorem 10.1, scoped to finite artifacts, finite specifications, and decidable fragments of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$) and its centuries-scale corollary. Chapter 11 develops the information-theoretic versus cryptographic substrate distinction and the tawatur-style mass-transmission verification argument. Chapter 12 specifies the centuries-scale preservation discipline.

Part IV (Chapters 13--16) treats the four worked substrate instances: file-layer (Bayyinah), language-layer (Furqan), model-layer (Munafiq), supply-chain-layer (furqan-lint v0.8.5 as an operational static-analysis substrate instantiating the sigstore / in-toto / SLSA / SHV four-substrate verification stack).

Part V (Chapters 17--21) names the open problems: severity as partial order, response-shapes as decision algebra, audit-chain dynamics as candidate axioms, substrate generalization beyond the current four, and falsification protocols.

Part VI (Chapters 22--23) closes the dissertation reflexively. Chapter 22 applies the four axioms to the dissertation itself. Chapter 23 specifies the designated-continuation protocol, operationalizes the preservation strategy, and specifies the conditions under which the dissertation should be considered withdrawn or formally superseded; the continuator roster, partner institutions, and minted deposit DOIs are populated by the primary author at v1.0 promotion (Chapter 23 §§23.1--23.2). Per the broadened criterion developed during the pre-publication audit, these conditions include any unrepairable failure of the load-bearing claims: mathematical inconsistency, failure of definitional adequacy, unfixable substrate-generalization failure, or refusal to correct known false claims.

## Reading paths through the dissertation

The intended reader is a mathematician, computer scientist, or AI-safety researcher with one year of graduate-level training in at least one of: type theory, process algebra, refinement-type systems, or formal-methods software engineering. We do not assume familiarity with the BayyinahEnterprise program substrate; the relevant operational details are introduced as needed and the cited papers serve as primary references.

For a reader who wishes to understand the formal claim without the substrate case studies, Parts I and II are self-contained. Chapter 8 in particular is the load-bearing chapter; readers who read only Chapters 1, 4--8, and 22--23 will have the formal framework and the self-application discipline without the operational depth.

For a reader who wishes to understand the centuries-scale claim without the formal proofs, Chapters 1, 9--12, and 23 are the relevant subset. Chapter 10 is assigned to contain the quantum-survivability theorem statement; the planned proof depends on Part II but the intended consequences can be appreciated from the statement.

For a reader who wishes to understand the operational substrate without the formal foundations, Chapters 13--16 are self-contained and refer to the cited papers [@arfeen2026bayyinah; @ashraf2026furqan; @arfeen2026munafiq; @arfeen2026shv; @arfeen2026furqanlint; @arfeen2026shvsupplychain] for full operational detail.

For a reader who wishes to identify research opportunities, Chapter 21 and Part V are the canonical reference.

## The recursive structural-honesty test

We close the introduction by applying the central thesis of the dissertation to the introduction itself, in keeping with the self-application discipline that Chapter 22 is assigned to develop and that Chapter 22's first-pass canon partially demonstrates at pre-publication scope (with append-only provenance and projection-consistency discharges activated at v1.0 publication).

A reader who finds the chapter making a claim that is not supported by either the chapter itself, a cited source, or a clearly assigned future proof obligation has identified a structural-honesty violation in the introduction itself. We invite such findings and consider their identification to be in keeping with the verification principle that the dissertation is, throughout, attempting to honor.

The chapter is structured to make this self-test concrete. It declares a thesis (the structural-honesty hypothesis) and supports it with three load-bearing claims (mathematical, operational, preservational). It declares an axiom system ($\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$, with four named axioms, each in the form refined through the pre-publication audit iterations) and indicates the chapters in which each axiom is rigorously formalized. It declares a substrate-independence claim in its scoped schema-instantiation form and indicates the chapters (Part III) in which it is developed, scoped, and partially discharged, with substrate-generalization routed to Chapter 20 as a falsification path and quantum-survivability routed to Chapter 10 as a proof obligation. It declares a centuries-scale claim and indicates the chapters (Part III and Part VI) in which the supporting principles are developed. It names explicitly what it does not do (Section 6) and identifies the chapters in which each unsolved problem is treated. It provides a roadmap (Section 7) and reading paths (Section 8). The chapter's surface (its abstract-equivalent opening paragraph and section headings) matches its substrate (the body of each section). Every claim the chapter makes is left with either present support, a cited source, or an explicit future proof obligation assigned to a specific chapter; the distinction between "supported now" and "committed as a future proof obligation" is maintained throughout. From v1.0 publication onward, the chapter's evolution will follow append-only provenance discipline across published versions: corrections, supersessions, and refinements will be explicit and version-tagged. During the pre-publication phase (concluded at the v1.4 public deposit), revisions were working iterations rather than formal corrigenda, because the chapter has no deposited public surface API to be additive against until a public deposit ships (satisfied at the v1.4 deposit; the clause originally read: until v1.0 ships).

The pre-publication audit iterations that produced the present draft are themselves an instance of this discipline. The full multi-cycle audit history is recorded in the canonical audit ledger; the present chapter records only the structural commitments, not the procedural provenance.

::: quranquote
"Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity." (Al-Baqarah 2:286)
:::

The dissertation does not promise more than its substrate can deliver. The introduction states a thesis whose written development is carried by the versioned public deposits (v1.4 working research monograph, July 2026), while full empirical maturation, independent replication, standards anchoring, translation discipline, and centuries-scale preservation will require years to decades of work and a community of researchers, implementers, and continuators larger than the original author. The introduction is honest about that distinction. It is also honest about its scope, its proofs, its gaps, and its dependencies. If the dissertation succeeds in being structurally honest about itself, throughout its evolution across published versions, the framework it proposes will have been demonstrated by example before it is demonstrated by theorem. If it fails---if at any version the dissertation cannot pass its own axioms---the framework will have failed the recursive Incompleteness-Boundary test that Munafiq [@arfeen2026munafiq Section 9] names and will require either repair or honest withdrawal. The designated continuation protocol of Chapter 23 specifies the procedure for either outcome.

## The three intellectual lineages

Three intellectual traditions, operating across roughly half a century, more than five centuries, and more than fourteen centuries respectively, independently developed methods for controlling the gap between what something claims to be and what it actually is. The formal-verification tradition, beginning with the late-1960s work on axiomatic semantics and continuing through model checking, refinement types, and behavioral subtyping, developed methods for controlling the gap between a program's specification and its execution behavior. The audit-and-assurance tradition, with origins in the Renaissance-era practice of double-entry bookkeeping and continuing through modern financial-reporting regimes, security-audit frameworks, and supply-chain integrity systems, developed methods for controlling the gap between an organization's records and the underlying reality those records purport to describe. The textual-preservation philology tradition, with roots in the Vedic oral-transmission discipline, the Quranic preservation practice, the Talmudic textual-criticism tradition, and the classical philological method culminating in Lachmann's stemmatic analysis, developed methods for controlling the gap between an authoritative source text and the manuscript or recitation chain through which it is transmitted.

The three traditions did not communicate with each other across most of their history. They worked on different substrates---programs, accounts, texts---in different intellectual climates---academic mathematics, professional accounting, religious or classical philology---with different validation methods---proof, audit, textual collation. They are nonetheless convergent. Each tradition developed methods for constraining a hidden or underlying substrate by means of declared, checkable surfaces; in the audit-and-assurance and philology lineages this often takes the form of multiple, partially-independent witnesses whose mutual coherence is itself the operational evidence of substrate fidelity, while in formal verification it often takes the form of formal specifications, labeled transition systems, or type-level predicates against which the substrate's behavior is checked. The structural-honesty framework of this dissertation, viewed historically, is not an invention but a synthesis. The practices and structural intuitions that the four axioms formalize are not ex nihilo discoveries; they are the formal extraction of practices that the three traditions had independently developed and that have, in three different domains, withstood multi-century or multi-decade durability tests. The dissertation's contribution is the unified $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ axiomatization of those practices in a single formal vocabulary, not the rediscovery of the practices themselves. Chapter 2 traces each lineage in turn and ends, in §7, by naming the specific axioms each tradition contributes to and the specific gaps each tradition does not fill.

We do not claim that the historical figures of these traditions---Hoare, Dijkstra, Pacioli, the early Quranic philologists, Pān.ini, Lachmann, or any other---thought in surface-substrate terms in the modern sense developed in this dissertation. We claim that the methods they developed are formally recognizable as gap-control disciplines in the sense the rest of the dissertation makes precise, and that the structural-honesty framework's contribution is the synthesis of those methods into a single unified vocabulary backed by a four-axiom mathematical framework. Where this dissertation argues that a particular axiom is anchored in a particular historical exemplar, the claim is one of mathematical structure preservation under reformulation, not of historical intentionality on the part of the originating figure.

## The formal-verification lineage

The first of the three lineages traced in this chapter is the formal-verification tradition that developed in academic computer science, primarily in the period from the late 1960s through the refinement-type systems of the 2010s. The tradition is concerned with the question of how the specification of a program can be related to the program's actual behavior in a way that is checkable through systematic procedures rather than through informal inspection. We trace the tradition in chronological order through six developments that each contribute, directly or by background, to the AX-SH framework: Hoare logic, Dijkstra's weakest-precondition calculus, Park--Milner bisimulation and the broader correspondence-relation tradition, Clarke--Emerson--Sistla model checking, Liskov--Wing behavioral subtyping, and the refinement-type tradition exemplified by Liquid Haskell and F$^*$. We close the section by mapping each development to the specific axiom of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ it anchors.

### Hoare logic: specifications as preconditions and postconditions (1969)

The foundational paper of the formal-verification tradition is C. A. R. Hoare's 1969 "An Axiomatic Basis for Computer Programming" [@hoare1969axiomatic]. Hoare proposed that a program's correctness could be expressed and checked through a triple notation $\{P\}\,C\,\{Q\}$, where $P$ is a predicate over the program state before command $C$ executes, $Q$ is a predicate over the state after $C$ executes, and the triple asserts that if $P$ holds before $C$ executes and $C$ terminates, then $Q$ holds afterward. The paper supplied inference rules for the elementary constructs of structured programming---assignment, sequential composition, conditionals, and loops---through which the correctness of a composite program could be derived from the correctness of its components.

The contribution of Hoare's paper to the formal-verification tradition was not the observation that programs should be specified; programmers had been writing specifications informally for decades. The contribution was the proposal that specifications and the program behavior they describe could be related through axioms and rules of inference, in the same way that mathematical theorems are related through formal proofs. This established the discipline that program verification is a deductive activity, not a testing activity, and that the relation between specification and behavior is in principle mathematical.

Two ideas from the Hoare-triple discipline propagate, in modified form, into the structural-honesty framework. The first is that specification and behavior are related through a logical predicate (the postcondition) over the substrate (the program state after execution). This is the lineage that produces, fifty-six years later, the correspondence relation $R$ in Axiom 2 of this dissertation between $\mathit{Surface}(S)$ and $\mathit{Substrate}(S)$. The second is that this relation is checkable through structural rules over the syntax of the program rather than by exhaustive execution. This is the lineage that produces the static-analysis discipline implemented in the Bayyinah file scanner [@arfeen2026bayyinah] and treated in Chapter 13 as the file-layer instantiation of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$. We note that Hoare logic itself is a tradition of pre/postcondition reasoning over input-output behavior; it is the background tradition for specification-behavior relations rather than a direct precursor to the bisimulation-style consistency of Axiom 2.

### Dijkstra and the weakest-precondition calculus (1976)

E. W. Dijkstra's 1976 monograph *A Discipline of Programming* [@dijkstra1976discipline] extended Hoare's framework by inverting the question. Where Hoare asked "given precondition $P$ and program $C$, what is the strongest postcondition $Q$," Dijkstra asked "given postcondition $Q$ and program $C$, what is the weakest precondition $P$ that must hold for $\{P\}\,C\,\{Q\}$ to be valid?" The weakest-precondition predicate transformer $\mathit{wp}(C, Q)$ yields, for any postcondition $Q$ and any program command $C$, the most permissive predicate $P$ such that the Hoare triple holds. This is a stronger discipline than working with arbitrary sufficient preconditions because the weakest precondition characterizes the entire correctness relation, not merely some sufficient condition for it.

Dijkstra's contribution to the structural-honesty lineage is operational rather than conceptual. By demonstrating that program correctness could be reduced to a calculation---that one could calculate verification conditions and weakest preconditions that reduce correctness claims to logical proof obligations rather than only proving correctness on a case-by-case basis---Dijkstra opened the door to the automated-verification disciplines that followed. The static-analysis discipline of Bayyinah and the type-checking discipline of the Furqan prototype [@ashraf2026furqanproto] both inherit, through several intermediate steps, the calculational style Dijkstra established. We note, again, that the weakest-precondition calculus is a calculus of specifications: it relates two predicates (the precondition and the postcondition) through a syntactic transformation. The relation to the underlying execution substrate is encoded in the soundness of the predicate-transformer rules with respect to operational semantics, but it is not the calculus's primary subject. Dijkstra, like Hoare, is background tradition for specification-behavior relations rather than a direct contributor to the bisimulation-style consistency that Axiom 2 of this dissertation requires.

### Process algebras and bisimulation: Park, Milner, and the correspondence relation (1980--1990)

The Hoare--Dijkstra tradition treated programs as transformers of state, with correctness defined as a relation between initial and final states. Beginning in the late 1970s, a parallel tradition began to treat programs---especially concurrent programs---as labeled transition systems: structures whose meaning lies not in their input-output behavior but in the patterns of observable actions they can perform over time. R. Milner's 1980 book *A Calculus of Communicating Systems* [@milner1980calculus] introduced CCS, a process algebra in which concurrent programs were described as terms in a formal language with operations for action, choice, parallel composition, and restriction. The semantic question for CCS was not "what value does this program compute" but "when are two programs observationally equivalent."

D. Park's 1981 paper *Concurrency and Automata on Infinite Sequences* [@park1981concurrency] answered the equivalence question with the now-classical definition of bisimulation. Two labeled transition systems $S$ and $T$ are bisimilar if there exists a relation $R$ between their states such that, whenever $(s,t) \in R$ and $s$ makes a transition to $s'$ under action $a$, $t$ can make a transition to some $t'$ under $a$ with $(s',t') \in R$, and vice versa. Bisimulation is finer than trace equivalence---two systems can produce the same traces of actions without being bisimilar, because the choices available to them at each step may differ---but coarser than full isomorphism, since it abstracts over the internal structure of states.

The Park--Milner construction is the historical origin of what becomes, in this dissertation's Axiom 2, the family of correspondence relations between $\mathit{Surface}(S)$ and $\mathit{Substrate}(S)$. The structural-honesty framework's decision to define Axiom 2 over a *family* of correspondence relations---bisimulation as the strongest finite-state special case, with refinement, simulation, abstraction-preserving equivalence, and extraction equality over declared observables as substrate-appropriate generalizations---rather than over bisimulation alone reflects fifty years of subsequent research showing that bisimulation is the right relation for protocol-style finite-state surfaces but is overstrong for many other substrates. The algorithmic foundations were supplied by Kanellakis and Smolka [@kanellakis1990ccs], whose $O(m \log n)$ characterization of bisimulation checking on finite-state systems gave the correspondence-relation tradition the computational basis that makes Axiom 2 checkable in its decidable fragment. Axiom 2's anchoring in this dissertation is primarily here---in the Park--Milner tradition and its successors---rather than in the Hoare--Dijkstra specification-behavior tradition discussed above.

### Model checking: automated verification at scale (1986)

The integration of the Hoare--Dijkstra specification tradition with the Park--Milner process-algebra tradition was achieved, on the algorithmic side, through model checking. Developed independently by E. M. Clarke and E. A. Emerson in the early 1980s (with the foundational synchronization-skeletons paper appearing in the 1981 Workshop on Logic of Programs) and by J.-P. Queille and J. Sifakis in France (1982 International Symposium on Programming), the consolidated journal treatment by Clarke, Emerson, and Sistla [@clarke1986automatic] proposed that temporal-logic specifications could be checked automatically against finite-state systems by an algorithm that explores the system's state space. The technique scaled, through subsequent decades of optimization---symbolic model checking, bounded model checking, partial-order reduction, abstraction refinement---to systems whose state spaces would have been infeasible to enumerate explicitly, and is now in widespread use in hardware design and protocol verification.

Model checking's relevance to the structural-honesty lineage is two-fold. First, it demonstrated that the verification of complex specifications against complex substrates is tractable in the decidable fragment, with the state-space explored through algorithmic techniques rather than enumerated explicitly. The decidable-fragment scoping of Theorem 10.1 in Chapter 10 of this dissertation (the quantum-survivability theorem) inherits the model-checking tradition's discipline of being precise about which questions are decidable and which are not. Second, model checking established the operational norm---widely adopted in hardware design and protocol verification, and adopted in safety-critical software contexts where the underlying state space admits the technique---that automated verification can be a normal part of the development process rather than an exotic undertaking. The structural-honesty framework's claim that $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ satisfaction is checkable in operational deployments, not only in academic settings, inherits this norm.

### Liskov--Wing behavioral subtyping: additive evolution at the type level (1994)

The penultimate development in the formal-verification lineage that contributes directly to $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ is Barbara Liskov and Jeannette Wing's 1994 work on behavioral subtyping [@liskov1994behavioral]. Liskov--Wing subtyping requires that a subtype's methods, when invoked in any context expecting the supertype, behave in a way that is observationally indistinguishable from the supertype's. The technical formulation involves preservation of preconditions (the subtype may weaken but not strengthen them), postconditions (the subtype may strengthen but not weaken them), invariants (the subtype must preserve them), and the corresponding constraints under method composition; the Liskov--Wing framework also addresses constraints on state evolution, with the precise doctrinal formulation differing across follow-on treatments. Behavioral subtyping is strictly stronger than nominal subtyping (which only requires that the subtype declare conformance to an interface) and strictly weaker than full type equivalence (which would require the subtype to be substitutable in every observable respect).

Liskov--Wing subtyping is the direct historical antecedent of Axiom 1 of this dissertation. The version-$N{+}1$ public surface of a versioned artifact is a behavioral subtype of the version-$N$ public surface in the Liskov--Wing sense: every contract that callers could rely on at version $N$ remains discharged at version $N{+}1$, with at least as strong guarantees. The reframing introduced in the structural-honesty framework is that the Liskov--Wing relation applies at the *public surface level* of the versioned artifact, not at the *truth-status level* of individual claims. The framework's append-only provenance discipline permits explicit corrections, supersessions, and withdrawals through corrigenda, provided the corrigenda are themselves additive at the surface and the historical record is preserved. This is the structural-honesty contribution to the Liskov--Wing tradition: the recognition that the subtype relation is a property of the surface API of a versioned artifact, and that the surface API can include explicit tagging of truth-status changes without violating the subtype invariant.

### Refinement types: caller-side exhaustiveness as a natural successor (2014--2016)

The most recent development in the formal-verification lineage that contributes directly to $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ is the refinement-type tradition, exemplified by Liquid Haskell (Vazou et al. [-@vazou2014refinement]) and F$^*$ (Swamy et al. [-@swamy2016fstar]). Refinement types extend a host type system with logical predicates on values: a refinement type $\{x : \mathrm{Int} \mid x > 0\}$ denotes the type of integers greater than zero, with the predicate checked by an underlying SMT solver. When refinement-type checking is combined with SMT-based discharge of the side conditions arising from program structure, programs can be statically verified to satisfy logical specifications expressed at the type level, including non-trivial functional correctness properties.

The contribution of the refinement-type tradition to $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ is direct: Axiom 3 (caller exhaustiveness over $R_{\mathrm{may}}$) is a generalization of refinement-type-style return-value reasoning to the caller side of the function-call boundary. The refinement-type discipline as deployed in F$^*$ and Liquid Haskell focuses on the producer side: a function's refinement type constrains what values it can return, and the type-checker verifies that the function's body in fact produces values inhabiting the declared type. Axiom 3 adds the dual obligation on the caller. Every function call must handle every outcome that $R_{\mathrm{may}}$, the verifier's conservative over-approximation of producer outcomes, may produce, or must explicitly propagate the incompleteness, or must discharge a proof that the unhandled outcomes are unreachable in the calling context. The producer-side discipline of refinement types is necessary but not sufficient for structural honesty; the caller-side discipline of Axiom 3 is what closes the loop, and it is this caller-side closure that the refinement-type tradition does not itself provide.

### What the formal-verification lineage contributes to AX-SH

Synthesizing the historical walk above, the formal-verification lineage contributes the following to the four axioms of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$.

**Axiom 1** (Additive-only invariant in append-only-provenance form) is directly anchored in Liskov--Wing behavioral subtyping [@liskov1994behavioral], with the structural-honesty reframing applying the subtype relation to the public surface API of versioned artifacts and permitting truth-status changes through explicit corrigenda.

**Axiom 2** (Surface-substrate consistency in correspondence-relation form) is primarily anchored in the Park--Milner bisimulation tradition [@park1981concurrency; @milner1980calculus; @kanellakis1990ccs] and the broader family of correspondence relations developed in subsequent process-algebra and behavioral-equivalence research. The Hoare--Dijkstra weakest-precondition tradition [@hoare1969axiomatic; @dijkstra1976discipline] provides the background tradition for specification-behavior relations more generally, but is not directly mapped to the bisimulation-style consistency that Axiom 2 requires. The choice to express Axiom 2 over a family of correspondence relations, rather than over bisimulation alone, reflects fifty years of subsequent research showing that bisimulation is appropriate for protocol-style finite-state surfaces but overstrong for many other substrates.

**Axiom 3** (Caller exhaustiveness over $R_{\mathrm{may}}$) is directly anchored in the refinement-type tradition [@vazou2014refinement; @swamy2016fstar]. The structural-honesty contribution is the extension from producer-side type-discipline to caller-side exhaustiveness over the verifier's conservative outcome approximation, together with the three permitted discharge paths (handle, propagate as incompleteness, prove unreachable).

**Axiom 4** (Substrate-parameterized projection consistency) does not have a direct formal-verification ancestor. This is the axiom for which the audit-and-assurance and textual-preservation philology lineages provide the primary historical exemplars; these are developed in §§3--4 of this chapter.

**Model checking** [@clarke1986automatic] does not directly produce an axiom but contributes the operational norm that $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ satisfaction is checkable in operational deployments rather than only as an academic exercise. The decidable-fragment scoping of Theorem 10.1 (Chapter 10) reflects the model-checking tradition's discipline of being precise about decidability, and the operational substrates of Bayyinah and the Furqan prototype inherit the model-checking tradition's norm of automated verification as a normal development practice.

The formal-verification lineage thus contributes Axioms 1 and 3 directly, contributes the correspondence-relation foundation of Axiom 2, and contributes the operational-verification norm that $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ inherits. The two contributions it does not directly produce---the multi-projection consistency of Axiom 4 and the centuries-scale preservation discipline that grounds the framework's durability claim---are the contributions of the audit-and-assurance lineage (treated in §3 of this chapter) and the textual-preservation philology lineage (treated in §4).

## The audit-and-assurance lineage

The second of the three lineages traced in this chapter is the audit-and-assurance tradition that developed across five centuries of commercial, professional, and regulatory practice. The tradition is concerned with the question of how the records, declarations, or attestations made by an organization can be related to the underlying reality those records purport to describe, in a way that is checkable by an independent party rather than only by the organization itself. We trace the tradition through five developments, each of which contributes to the AX-SH framework's understanding of Axiom 4 (substrate-parameterized projection consistency) and the operational severity vocabulary: Pacioli's codification of double-entry bookkeeping, the evolution from early-modern commercial practice to professional financial audit and modern reporting regimes, the development of security-audit frameworks as multi-control projection regimes, the recent emergence of supply-chain audit systems, and a closing synthesis identifying what this lineage contributes to $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ and what it does not.

### Double-entry bookkeeping and the origin of reconciliation discipline (1494)

The canonical early printed codification of double-entry bookkeeping is the *Tractatus XI: Particularis de Computis et Scripturis* contained within Luca Pacioli's *Summa de Arithmetica, Geometria, Proportioni et Proportionalita*, published in Venice in 1494 [@pacioli1494]. Pacioli's *Tractatus* systematized a commercial practice that had been developing in Italian merchant houses through the late medieval period: the recording of each financial transaction in two complementary entries, one as a debit and one as a credit, against accounts maintained on opposing sides of a ledger. The arithmetic constraint that total debits must equal total credits at every reconciliation point provides, in operational form, the multi-witness coherence pattern that constitutes the practical content of reconciliation discipline.

We are careful here about the historical claim. We do not claim that Pacioli invented double-entry bookkeeping, that the *Tractatus* is the earliest documented systematic instance of reconciliation discipline in any culture, or that no anticipating practices existed in earlier accounting, administrative archive, legal record, or scribal control traditions. Such priority claims are contested in accounting-history scholarship and depend on choices about what counts as "systematic" and "documented" that are not productive to litigate here. What we do claim, restricted to what the *Tractatus* actually was: Pacioli's text is the canonical early printed codification of double-entry bookkeeping as a systematic reconciliation discipline, and it was the channel through which the discipline propagated into Renaissance and early-modern European commercial practice. That role is sufficient for the lineage claim of this chapter.

The relevance of double-entry bookkeeping to $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ is structural, not formal. The bookkeeping discipline treats each transaction as a fact about the substrate (the actual movement of value between accounts) that is recorded on two surfaces (the debit entry and the credit entry, in their respective accounts), with the two surfaces constrained to reconcile arithmetically as evidence that they faithfully describe the same underlying transaction. This is the operational pattern that Axiom 4 of this dissertation generalizes into substrate-parameterized projection consistency: a family of projections $\Pi_X = \{\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_n\}$ of a substrate $X$, each producing a surface description, with mutual consistency among the projections serving as the empirical evidence of substrate fidelity. Double-entry bookkeeping is the historical exemplar of this pattern, not its full formal precursor. The structural-honesty framework treats double-entry as the canonical instance of reconciliation discipline operating with $n = 2$ projections under arithmetic identity; Axiom 4 generalizes to arbitrary $n$, arbitrary substrates, and arbitrary declared consistency relations.

### From bookkeeping to professional audit to modern reporting regimes

The five centuries following Pacioli traced an evolution from a commercial bookkeeping practice into an institutionalized professional discipline of financial audit, and from there into the modern reporting regimes that today govern public financial disclosure. Previts and Merino's *A History of Accounting in America* [@previts1979history] traces this evolution in detail; we summarize here the structural pattern relevant to the AX-SH lineage claim.

Through the early modern period, double-entry bookkeeping spread through European commercial practice as a tool internal to the firm. The transition to audit as an external discipline followed the development of the joint-stock corporation in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, in which the separation of ownership from management created an information asymmetry that external attestation could address. By the nineteenth century, professional audit had emerged as an institutionalized practice, with chartered accountants in the United Kingdom and certified public accountants in the United States providing independent attestation of firm financial records to absentee owners and regulators. The twentieth century saw the codification of this practice into generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) in the United States and, from 1973 onward, the development of international accounting standards through the International Accounting Standards Committee (later the International Accounting Standards Board), producing what is now the International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) regime followed in most non-U.S. jurisdictions.

The structural pattern that emerges across this evolution is multi-projection-consistency at scale. Modern financial-reporting regimes require organizations to publish multiple required or customary projections of the same underlying financial substrate---such as statements of financial position, performance, cash flows, equity changes, and explanatory notes---constrained to be mutually consistent under defined accounting identities (most fundamentally the accounting identity that assets equal liabilities plus equity, but also the consistency relations among accrual-basis revenues, cash-basis cash flows, and equity reconciliation). The specific projection set is modern and jurisdiction-dependent; what is substantively constant across jurisdictions and across the historical evolution is the discipline that multiple required projections of the same substrate must reconcile under declared consistency relations. This is the structural pattern that the audit-and-assurance lineage contributes to $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$, not the specific projection list of any particular regime.

### Security-audit frameworks as multi-control projection regimes

A second stream of audit practice developed through the late twentieth century in response to the question of how an organization's security and operational controls can be attested to by an independent party, in the same way that financial records can be attested to. The institutionalized frameworks that resulted---ISO/IEC 27001:2022 [@iso27001] (the international standard for information security management systems), NIST Special Publication 800-53 Revision 5 [@nist80053] (the U.S. federal catalog of security and privacy controls), and the SOC 2-style attestation regimes underwritten by the AICPA Trust Services Criteria [@aicpa2017tsc]---share a structural pattern that generalizes the financial-audit pattern of the previous subsection.

The pattern, in each case, is multi-control projection with an assessment result. An organization undergoing audit declares its scope (which systems, processes, and information assets are within the audit boundary), declares the controls it has selected within scope (which security or privacy controls from the framework's control catalog apply to the declared scope), produces implementation evidence for each control (the documentation, configuration records, and operational artifacts demonstrating that each declared control is in fact implemented), and produces an audit trail of each control's operation over the audit period (the logs, monitoring records, and incident reports demonstrating that each implemented control is in fact operating). Mutual consistency across these four declarations is a central part of the auditor's empirical content: scope is consistent with controls, controls with implementation, implementation with operation. Audits additionally assess design adequacy, operating effectiveness, and evidence quality, but the multi-projection-consistency component is the one this dissertation's structural lineage claim depends on. Where the relevant assessment or certification regime is satisfied (ISO/IEC 27001 certification, SOC 2 examination report, or comparable assessment results for control catalogs such as NIST SP 800-53), the organization receives a regime-appropriate outcome---certification, attestation, authorization, or assessment result---depending on the framework; where the regime is not satisfied, the audit produces findings, with each finding identifying a specific consistency failure between specific declarations.

This is a four-projection consistency discipline applied to security substrates, structurally analogous to the multi-statement consistency discipline applied to financial substrates in the previous subsection. The substrate is different (security posture rather than financial position), the projections are different (scope, controls, implementation, operation rather than the financial-statement family), and the consistency relations are different (security-control coverage rather than accounting identities), but the underlying structural pattern is the same: independent projections of a common substrate, constrained to be mutually consistent under declared relations, with consistency serving as empirical evidence of substrate fidelity.

### Supply-chain audit as the recent endpoint of the lineage

The most recent development in the audit-and-assurance lineage is the emergence, through the past decade, of supply-chain audit systems for software artifacts. The principal components of this development are sigstore (cryptographic identity attestation for the parties producing software artifacts), in-toto (process-attestation framework for the steps producing each artifact), and SLSA (the Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts framework, providing a maturity model for the institutional discipline supporting these attestations). Each component is a separate attestation substrate; their composition with the semantic verification provided by SHV is the four-substrate verification stack proposed in the supply-chain integration memo [@arfeen2026shvsupplychain].

The present subsection notes only that supply-chain audit is the recent endpoint of the audit-and-assurance lineage; the full development of the four-substrate composition, its operational requirements, and its instantiation as the supply-chain layer of the dissertation's worked substrate instances is reserved for Chapter 16. This restriction is deliberate: §3 of the present chapter is the historical-lineage section, not the supply-chain case-study chapter, and treating the four-substrate composition in detail here would conflate the lineage claim of Chapter 2 with the substrate-instance claim of Chapter 16.

### What the audit-and-assurance lineage contributes to AX-SH

Synthesizing the four developments traced above, the audit-and-assurance lineage contributes the following to $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$.

The lineage contributes the practical discipline behind **Axiom 4** (substrate-parameterized projection consistency). The structural pattern that runs from double-entry bookkeeping through financial audit through modern reporting regimes through security-audit frameworks through supply-chain audit is the same: independent projections of a common substrate, constrained to be mutually consistent under declared consistency relations, with consistency serving as empirical evidence of substrate fidelity. Double-entry bookkeeping is the canonical historical exemplar of this discipline operating at $n = 2$ under arithmetic identity; modern audit regimes operate at larger $n$ under jurisdiction-dependent consistency relations; security and supply-chain audit operate at larger $n$ still over qualitatively different substrates. Axiom 4 is the formal abstraction of this pattern to arbitrary projection families over arbitrary substrates under arbitrary declared consistency relations. Double-entry bookkeeping is the historical exemplar of reconciliation discipline, not a full formal precursor to Axiom 4 in its substrate-parameterized form.

The lineage contributes the **operational severity vocabulary** (CRITICAL / HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW), which is shared with the security vulnerability-management and incident-response practices of security audit (notably, the qualitative severity ratings that the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) translates numerical scores into) and was later formalized in the Bayyinah Audit Framework [@arfeen2026baf]. The severity rubric currently operates as a total preorder; its formalization as a partial order capturing the multidimensional nature of severity (user impact, data loss, frequency, recoverability) is identified as an open problem in Chapter 17. The lineage's contribution at the level of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ is the practical vocabulary; the formalization is dissertation-internal work.

The lineage does not contribute Axioms 1, 2, or 3. Those are formal-verification contributions, treated in §2 above. It also does not contribute the centuries-scale preservation discipline that grounds the framework's durability claim; that is the contribution of the textual-preservation philology lineage, treated in the next section.

## The textual-preservation philology lineage

The third of the three lineages traced in this chapter is the textual-preservation philology tradition that developed across more than two millennia in multiple cultures. The tradition is concerned with the question of how a text treated as authoritative within a transmission community can be preserved across centuries of transmission through manuscript copying, oral recitation, or both, in the face of inevitable transmission noise, the loss of individual transmission channels, and the gradual transformation of the cultural infrastructure in which the text is read. We trace the tradition through five developments---Vedic oral transmission and the Sanskrit philological tradition, Quranic preservation as a multi-substrate verification practice, Talmudic and Masoretic textual-criticism traditions, classical philology culminating in Lachmann's stemmatic method, and a closing synthesis---and identify what this lineage contributes to $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ that the previous two lineages do not.

A boundary discipline applies throughout this section, and we name it explicitly before beginning. The structural-honesty framework treats each of these preservation traditions as a verification substrate exhibiting specific gap-control disciplines. The framework does not adjudicate the theological content, religious truth claims, scriptural status, or comparative ranking of any of these traditions. The Quranic preservation tradition, the Vedic oral-transmission tradition, the Talmudic and Masoretic traditions, and the classical philological tradition are all treated here as historical instances of multi-substrate textual preservation; the framework's mathematical structure depends on the operational disciplines these traditions developed, not on the religious or scholarly content of the texts those disciplines preserved. This is the §4 analogue of the "no retroactive attribution" discipline of §1, but applied to a more contested domain where overclaim risk is higher; we therefore anchor the boundary discipline repeatedly across the section: here at the opening of §4, again at the opening and closing of §4.2 (the highest-risk subsection), again at the closing of §4.3, and again in the synthesis at §4.5. The redundancy is deliberate.
