The canonical audit ledger records the multi-cycle revision history including the full cycle-14-arc absorption details (C14-P1 through C14D-P1).

## Mathematical objects and notation

### Purpose of Chapter 3

Chapter 3's role within the dissertation is to introduce the mathematical objects, notation, and conventions that the four axiom chapters (Chapters 4--7) and the definitional-adequacy theorem chapter (Chapter 8) use as standing foundation. Chapter 3 does not state or prove any of the four axioms of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$; the axiom statements and their formal development are the work of Chapters 4--7. Chapter 3 does not establish decidability results for the structures it introduces; the rigorous decidability claims and the quantum-survivability claim are the work of Chapter 10. What Chapter 3 contributes is the vocabulary that those later chapters require: typed objects for the domain entities the axioms reason about, notational conventions for the variables that range over those domain entities, and the mathematical machinery (correspondence-relation families, refinement-type machinery, projection families) over which the axioms express constraints.

This boundary is operationally important. Each subsequent section of Chapter 3 is to be read as introducing machinery, never as asserting that the machinery satisfies any property; the properties are stated in Chapters 4--7 against the machinery introduced here. The discipline at the chapter level is parallel to the "no retroactive attribution" discipline of Chapter 2 §1, but applied within the dissertation rather than across historical lineages: introducing a mathematical object in Chapter 3 is not the same as asserting an axiom about it in Chapters 4--7.

### Finite-default convention

Throughout Chapter 3 and the axiom chapters that use its machinery, the working universe is by default finite. Public surfaces are finite artifacts (finite specifications, finite APIs, finite attestation documents); substrates are finite structures relative to a chosen observer model; correspondence relations are defined over finite-state systems unless explicitly extended; projection families are finite collections of projections. This convention allows Chapter 10 to formulate decidability and quantum-survivability claims over already-finite working objects rather than arbitrary mathematical structures.

Later chapters, especially Chapter 10, identify which finite or bounded fragments support rigorous decidability and quantum-survivability claims, and which extensions remain outside v1.0 scope. The finite-default convention is not a metaphysical claim about what exists; it is a working assumption that scopes the dissertation's formal results to a tractable fragment. Extensions to infinite or unbounded structures are identified as open problems in the Part V open-problem chapters (especially Chapter 20 for substrate-generalization limits and Chapter 21 for falsification protocols) where they remain unresolved at v1.0.

### Standing symbol set

Table [1](#tab:notation){reference-type="ref" reference="tab:notation"} introduces the standing symbol set used throughout the dissertation. Each symbol is introduced as a typed variable with explicit components; relationships among the symbols are not yet asserted (relationships are the work of Chapters 4--7).

::: {#tab:notation}
  **Symbol**                **Reading**
  ------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  $S$                       substrate identifier
  $\mathrm{Surface}(S)$     the public surface family associated with substrate $S$
  $\mathrm{Substrate}(S)$   the substrate-level entities that $\mathrm{Surface}(S)$ describes
  $O$                       observer model: typed limits on what a verifier can detect
  $K$                       context set: operational conditions under which claims are evaluated
  $R$                       correspondence relation between surface and substrate behaviors
  $R_{\mathrm{declared}}$   producer's declared possible outcome set or relation, used as the surface-level return/outcome claim compared against $R_{\mathrm{may}}$
  $R_{\mathrm{may}}$        verifier's conservative over-approximation of possible producer outcomes
  $\Pi_X$                   substrate-parameterized projection family $\{\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_n\}$ over substrate $X$
  $\sim_X$                  consistency relation over substrate $X$'s projection family

  : Standing symbol set for $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$.
:::

The symbols partition into three groups by role. The first group ($S$, $\mathrm{Surface}(S)$, $\mathrm{Substrate}(S)$) names the substrate and the two carrier objects associated with it. The second group ($O$, $K$) names the verification-regime parameters under which claims are evaluated. The third group ($R$, $R_{\mathrm{declared}}$, $R_{\mathrm{may}}$, $\Pi_X$, $\sim_X$) names the relations and projection families over which the axioms quantify. The axiom chapters draw freely from all three groups; Chapter 3 introduces each symbol once and uses it consistently.

### Notation-versus-claim discipline

The standing symbols introduced in §1.3 are notation, not assertions. Introducing $S$ in this chapter does not assert anything substantive about substrates beyond the typed-variable convention. Introducing $R$ does not assert that any specific correspondence relation holds for any specific (surface, substrate) pair. Introducing $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ does not assert that the conservative over-approximation is achieved by any specific verifier. Introducing $\Pi_X$ does not assert that any specific projection family is consistent under $\sim_X$, nor that any specific consistency relation $\sim_X$ has the properties an axiom will require. The notation supplies vocabulary that the axiom chapters use to state their constraints; the constraints themselves remain Chapters 4--7's work.

This discipline is the Chapter-3-level operational implementation of the "Chapter 3 introduces machinery, Chapters 4--7 state the axioms" boundary. The four axioms will be stated in §1 of their respective chapters using the notation introduced here; Chapter 3 prose should be readable independently of any axiom statement. A reader who reads only Chapter 3 should encounter a coherent vocabulary; a reader who proceeds to Chapter 4 should find the axiom statements stated against that vocabulary without any axiom content having been smuggled into Chapter 3.

## Domain objects

Section 2 introduces the four domain objects on which $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ operates: public surfaces, substrates, observer models, and contexts. Each is defined as a structured type with explicit components; each is illustrated with examples drawn from the three lineages traced in Chapter 2; each carries a deferral sentence specifying which axiom chapter will impose constraints relating the object to the others. The packaging of the four into a unified type system is summarized in §2.5 with the explicit axiom-deferral note.

### Public surfaces

A public surface is a formal artifact visible to callers, auditors, users, or other downstream verifiers. It is a structured type with explicit components: the *declared interface* (what the surface exposes), the *declared semantics* (what the surface says the substrate does), and the *declared behavior expectations* (what callers may rely on). Examples include the published API specification of a software library; the visible interface of a versioned protocol; the disclosed audit attestation of an organization undergoing SOC 2 attestation; and a textual witness treated as authoritative within a transmission community.

A public surface carries no constraint on what behavior the underlying substrate actually exhibits. The relation between surface declarations and substrate behavior is the work of Axiom 2 in Chapter 5; Chapter 3 supplies only the typed object.

### Substrates

A substrate is the underlying entity that a public surface describes, implements, summarizes, or exposes. It is a structured type with explicit components: the substrate's *actual state*, its *operational behavior*, and its *real interface* (as distinguished from the declared interface that the public surface exposes). Examples include the program whose API is the public surface; the organization whose financial position the financial-statement family projects; the manuscript tradition whose textual content the critical edition presents; the protocol implementation whose runtime behavior the published specification describes.

A substrate's relationship to its public surface is parameterized by the choice of correspondence relation $R$ from the family introduced in §3 (Block B). The axiom that constrains $R$ is stated in Chapter 5; Chapter 3 supplies only the typed substrate object and the relation family over which Chapter 5's axiom will quantify.

### Observer models

An observer model is a formal limit on what a caller, verifier, auditor, or user can distinguish or detect when interacting with a substrate through its public surface. It is a typed observation calculus specifying which behaviors are observable, with what precision, and under what conditions. Examples include a refinement-type caller with the full F^$\star$^ or Liquid Haskell type system available [@swamy2016fstar; @vazou2014refinement]; an audit-style auditor with sampled access to substrate state under a defined materiality threshold; a mass-transmission community of reciters with limited individual access but high aggregate coverage; a static analyzer with bounded inspection depth.

The observer model parameterizes what a verifier can observe or distinguish in a given verification regime. Later axiom chapters will specify which observable divergences constitute structural-honesty failures under a declared observer model. Chapter 3 supplies the observer-model typed object; the failure conditions are stated in Chapters 5 and 6.

### Contexts

A context is the set of operational conditions under which surface-substrate consistency claims are evaluated. It is a typed condition specification including workload range, deployment environment, audit scope, transmission community, and any other operational parameter that determines which substrate behavior is relevant to the claim being evaluated. Examples include the workload range under which a software library's API claims are evaluated; the audit scope of a SOC 2 engagement (which systems and processes are within the audit boundary); the textual-transmission community within which a manuscript tradition's variants are catalogued; the protocol-deployment environment within which a network-protocol specification is operationally meaningful.

Later chapters may evaluate the same surface/substrate pair under different contexts $K_1$ and $K_2$, allowing context-sensitive consistency claims to be stated explicitly rather than left implicit. The axiom chapters specify how context parameterizes their respective consistency relations; Chapter 3 supplies only the typed context object.

### Structured-type packaging and axiom deferral

Public surfaces, substrates, observer models, and contexts are packaged as structured types used by later chapters. The packaging is as follows. Surfaces are objects of a structured surface-type carrying declared-interface, declared-semantics, and declared-behavior components. Substrates are objects of a structured substrate-type carrying actual-state, operational-behavior, and real-interface components. Observer models are typed observation calculi specifying observability conditions. Contexts are typed condition specifications.

Subsequent axiom chapters will impose constraints that relate these objects. Axiom 1 (Chapter 4) will constrain how versioned surfaces evolve over time under the append-only-provenance discipline. Axiom 2 (Chapter 5) will constrain surface-substrate consistency under observer model $O$ and context $K$ for a chosen correspondence relation $R$. Axiom 3 (Chapter 6) will constrain caller-side coverage of $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ for callers reasoning about producer outcomes. Axiom 4 (Chapter 7) will constrain projection-family consistency under $\sim_X$ for projection families $\Pi_X$ over substrate $X$.

Chapter 3 supplies the typed objects and the relation/projection machinery; the axiom chapters impose the structural-honesty constraints. The vocabulary of §§1--2 is sufficient to state every axiom of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ once the relation and projection machinery of §§3--7 (Block B) is in place; that machinery is introduced in the next block of Chapter 3 and is used by Chapters 4--7 to express the axioms in their final form.

## Correspondence-relation families

Section 3 introduces the correspondence-relation machinery that Chapter 5 (Axiom 2) will use to state the surface-substrate consistency requirement. The machinery is presented in six subsections: §3.1 defines the relation family as a structured collection; §3.2 introduces the labeled-transition-system and structural-operational-semantics foundations on which the LTS-based members are defined; §3.3--§3.5 introduce the family members (bisimulation, simulation and refinement, abstraction-preserving equivalence and extraction equality); §3.6 introduces the relation-choice mechanism by which a substrate records which family member it uses. Chapter 5 will state the consistency requirement over the substrate's declared choice; Chapter 3 supplies only the machinery.

### Correspondence-relation family as a structured collection

A correspondence-relation family is a parametric collection of binary relations between public surfaces and substrate behaviors, indexed by structural parameters (observer model, context, finite-state-foundation choice). Each member of the family relates the declared behavior of a public surface to the operational behavior of the substrate it describes through a specific equivalence or refinement discipline. The family is not assumed to satisfy any uniform consistency property at the §3.1 level: members vary in strength, in symmetry, and in observer-sensitivity, and which member is the appropriate $R$ for a given substrate depends on the substrate's nature. The relation-strength ordering among family members is optionally representable as a preorder or small finite category in the sense of Mac Lane [@maclane1998categories]; this categorical-equivalence framing is the general categorical machinery on which Axioms 1 and 2 rely, with the sheaf-style machinery of §6.5 (relevant to Axiom 4 only) treated separately in the sense of Mac Lane and Moerdijk [@maclane1994sheaves].

Chapter 5 will use the relation family to state Axiom 2 by quantifying over the substrate's declared correspondence relation $R$. Chapter 3 supplies the family structure (members, relationships among members, declaration mechanism); the axiom statement is the work of Chapter 5.

### Labeled transition systems and structural operational semantics

We adopt the standard process-algebra notation for the LTS foundations used in §§3.3--3.4. A *labeled transition system* (LTS) is a triple $(Q, A, {\rightarrow})$ consisting of a set of states $Q$, a set of action labels $A$, and a transition relation ${\rightarrow} \subseteq Q \times A \times Q$. We write $p \xrightarrow{a} p'$ for $(p, a, p') \in {\rightarrow}$. The LTS provides the formal substrate over which finite-state correspondence relations are defined: bisimulation, simulation, and refinement are all definable as conditions on the transition structure of two LTSs that are to be compared.

*Structural operational semantics* (SOS), introduced by Plotkin [@plotkin2004structural], generates an LTS from program syntax through syntax-directed inference rules. Given a program, the SOS rules generate the LTS whose states are program configurations and whose transitions are derived from the SOS inference rules. The finite-default convention of MP1.2 means that we work with LTSs whose state and label sets are finite, so that the resulting transition relation is finite and the family relations of §§3.3--3.4 are decidable in the relevant fragment. Chapter 10 will discuss the formal decidability claims; Chapter 3 introduces only the foundational LTS/SOS machinery.

### Bisimulation

A *bisimulation* is a binary relation $\mathcal{R} \subseteq Q_1 \times Q_2$ between two LTSs $(Q_1, A, {\rightarrow}_1)$ and $(Q_2, A, {\rightarrow}_2)$ such that: (i) if $(p, q) \in \mathcal{R}$ and $p \xrightarrow{a}_1 p'$, then there exists $q'$ with $q \xrightarrow{a}_2 q'$ and $(p', q') \in \mathcal{R}$; (ii) symmetrically, if $(p, q) \in \mathcal{R}$ and $q \xrightarrow{a}_2 q'$, then there exists $p'$ with $p \xrightarrow{a}_1 p'$ and $(p', q') \in \mathcal{R}$. Two states are *bisimilar* when there exists a bisimulation that relates them.

Bisimulation was introduced by Park [@park1981concurrency] and developed within Milner's process-calculus tradition [@milner1980calculus]; Hennessy and Milner introduced the modal-logical characterization in their 1980 ICALP paper [@hennessy1980observing], with subsequent algebraic-laws work [@hennessy1985algebraic]. The Hennessy-Milner theorem establishes that, under suitable image-finite assumptions on the LTS, bisimilarity coincides with modal equivalence in Hennessy-Milner logic: two states are bisimilar exactly when they satisfy the same modal formulas. The algorithmic foundations for deciding bisimilarity over finite-state LTSs are due to Kanellakis and Smolka [@kanellakis1990ccs]; modern theoretical treatment appears in Sangiorgi [@sangiorgi2012bisimulation].

Bisimulation is treated as the strongest standard finite-state behavioral equivalence used in this dissertation, under the declared observer model and the relevant finite/image-finite assumptions. The qualifier "treated as" is deliberate: stronger equivalences exist in the literature (graph isomorphism, hereditary history-preserving equivalence in true-concurrency settings), but bisimilarity is the strongest behavioral equivalence that the dissertation's observer-model machinery (§2.3) is designed to express, under the finite/image-finite scoping that the modal-characterization results require. Chapter 5 will state when bisimulation is the appropriate $R$ for a substrate; Chapter 3 introduces only the definition and the foundational results.

### Simulation and refinement

A *simulation* is the asymmetric directional weakening of bisimulation: a relation $\mathcal{R} \subseteq Q_1 \times Q_2$ such that condition (i) above holds ($Q_2$ can mimic $Q_1$'s transitions) but condition (ii) is dropped. $Q_2$ *simulates* $Q_1$ when there exists a simulation relating their initial states. Simulation is appropriate when the substrate-surface correspondence is asymmetric: the substrate may exhibit behaviors not declared by the surface (provided the declared behaviors are preserved), while the surface need not cover every substrate behavior.

*Refinement*, in the sense of Lynch and Vaandrager [@lynch1995simulations], is a variant of simulation used in distributed-systems and concurrency verification. A refinement is a forward simulation that additionally preserves the substrate's externally-visible action interface: the abstract specification (the public surface in our terminology) describes the externally-visible interface; the concrete implementation (the substrate) may have richer internal behavior; refinement asserts that every concrete execution corresponds to some abstract execution under the externally-visible action projection. Refinement is the natural correspondence relation for distributed-protocol verification, where the abstract specification captures the intended protocol behavior and the concrete implementation may include additional internal state and actions.

The relationships among bisimulation, simulation, and refinement are structural properties of the relations themselves: every bisimulation is a simulation by definition, and in many process- and distributed-system settings, refinement can be represented using simulation-like relations together with a preservation condition on externally visible behavior. Chapter 5 will state when each of these is the appropriate $R$ for a substrate; Chapter 3 introduces the family members without imposing a uniform choice.

### Abstraction-preserving equivalence and extraction equality

Not every substrate is naturally modeled as an LTS. A printed financial report, an AI model card, an attestation document, a manuscript: these are static artifacts whose "behavior" is what an observer extracts from them under a defined extraction procedure, not a sequence of transitions. For substrates of this form, the correspondence-relation family extends beyond LTS-based relations to include abstraction-preserving equivalence and extraction equality.

*Abstraction-preserving equivalence* is a relation $\mathcal{R}$ between substrates defined via a designated abstraction map $\alpha: \mathrm{Substrate} \to \mathrm{AbstractDomain}$. Two substrates are abstraction-equivalent when their $\alpha$-images are equal in the abstract domain. The relation is parameterized by the abstraction map, which captures what aspect of the substrate the correspondence relation is sensitive to: for a financial report, $\alpha$ might map a balance sheet to the equation "assets equal liabilities plus equity"; for an attestation document, $\alpha$ might map an audit report to a control-evidence pairing; for a manuscript, $\alpha$ might map a witness to its stemmatic position and variant readings.

*Extraction equality* is a closely related notion in which a defined extraction procedure $\varepsilon: \mathrm{Substrate} \to \mathrm{Surface}$ produces a derived artifact from each substrate, and two substrates are extraction-equal when their $\varepsilon$-outputs are equal. The procedure $\varepsilon$ formalizes "what the substrate is taken to mean" for the purposes of comparison: for a manuscript, $\varepsilon$ might be the editorial reading procedure that produces a canonical text from a witness; for a model card, $\varepsilon$ might be the extraction procedure that produces the model's stated capabilities from the card's structured fields.

Abstraction-preserving equivalence and extraction equality are both non-LTS correspondence forms: neither requires that the substrate have a transition structure. They are appropriate for substrates including philological texts, AI model cards, financial reports, and attestation documents. Chapter 5 will state when these forms are the appropriate $R$ for a substrate; Chapter 3 introduces them as additional members of the correspondence-relation family.

### Relation-choice mechanism

The relation-choice mechanism is the structured field by which a substrate records which correspondence relation $R$ from the family it will use. For a software-library substrate, the mechanism might be a declaration in the library's specification document that "this library's surface-substrate consistency is verified under bisimilarity over the LTS generated by the library's API surface." For a financial-report substrate, the mechanism might be a declaration in the audit attestation that "the report's surface-substrate consistency is verified under abstraction-preserving equivalence with respect to the jurisdiction-specified accounting identity." For a manuscript substrate, the mechanism might be a declaration in the critical edition's apparatus that "the textual-witness correspondence is verified under extraction equality with respect to the editorial reading procedure $\varepsilon$."

The declaration is itself a public-surface object (it appears on the surface where downstream verifiers can read it) and is therefore subject to the discipline of Chapter 4 (versioned surfaces, append-only-provenance under Axiom 1). Chapter 5 will state the Axiom 2 requirement over the declared choice. Chapter 3 introduces the choice mechanism as the structured slot; Chapter 5 will state what it means for a substrate's behavior to satisfy the surface-substrate consistency condition under the declared choice.

The choice mechanism keeps the relation-family approach tractable: rather than asserting a single uniform correspondence relation across all substrates of all types, the framework permits per-substrate declarations recorded as structured fields. Different substrate types are likely to use different family members (LTS-based bisimulation for protocols, abstraction-preserving equivalence for financial reports, extraction equality for manuscripts), and the declaration mechanism is what allows the same axiom statement (Axiom 2 in Chapter 5) to apply uniformly across the substrate types without requiring a uniform correspondence relation across them.

## Versioned public surfaces and behavioral subtyping

Section 4 introduces the versioned-surface apparatus that Chapter 4 (Axiom 1) will use to state the append-only-provenance discipline. The apparatus is presented in five subsections: §4.1 defines version-indexed public-surface families as the typed objects over which Axiom 1 quantifies; §4.2 introduces behavioral subtyping between versions in the Liskov-Wing sense; §4.3 distinguishes compatible extension from silent breaking change at the surface level; §4.4 introduces truth-status tags as explicit surface objects; §4.5 introduces historical-record preservation as the object-level apparatus. Chapter 4 will state Axiom 1 over this apparatus; Chapter 3 supplies only the machinery.

### Version-indexed public-surface families

A version-indexed public-surface family is a sequence $S_0, S_1, \ldots, S_n$ of public surfaces indexed by version, with each successive $S_{i+1}$ representing a published revision of $S_i$. We use $S_i$ as §4-local notation for the $i$-th version of the public-surface family $\mathrm{Surface}(S)$ associated with substrate $S$; the standing symbol $S$ from Table 3.1 remains the substrate identifier. The version index tracks the temporal evolution of the surface: $S_0$ is the initial published version, $S_1$ is the first revision, and so on. The family is finite by the MP1.2 finite-default convention; the version index ranges over a finite ordinal set $\{0, 1, \ldots, n\}$ for some $n$.

The family is not assumed to satisfy any inheritance property between successive versions at the §4.1 level. Chapter 4 will state Axiom 1 over the family by imposing the append-only-provenance discipline. Chapter 3 introduces the typed family as an object; the discipline that constrains evolution between adjacent versions is the work of Chapter 4.

### Behavioral subtyping between versions

Behavioral subtyping in the Liskov-Wing sense [@liskov1994behavioral] is a binary relation between two versions of a public surface at the typed-interface level: $S_{i+1}$ is a behavioral subtype of $S_i$ when callers whose assumptions are valid under $S_i$'s declared interface continue to have those assumptions preserved under $S_{i+1}$'s declared interface (equivalently, $\mathcal{S}_{N+1} <: \mathcal{S}_N$, expressing the behavioral-subtype relation that Chapter 1 §2 Axiom 1 states in Liskov-Wing prose, with Chapter 8 §1.2 Witness M1 instantiating the relation at the type-signature level using plain $S_{t+1}$-versus-$S_t$ notation for the per-version contract). The relation captures the intuition that a successor version honors the contracts of its predecessor: callers built against $S_i$ do not break when $S_{i+1}$ is substituted.

Behavioral subtyping over public surfaces extends the original Liskov-Wing notion (which was stated for class-instance substitutability in object-oriented programming) to general public-surface artifacts: versioned APIs, versioned protocol specifications, versioned audit attestations, versioned editions of textual artifacts. The substitutability test in each case is whether a caller programmed against the predecessor surface continues to function against the successor surface, under the caller's declared dependencies on the predecessor.

Chapter 3 introduces the behavioral-subtyping relation as the structural relation between adjacent versions; Chapter 4 will use it when stating the Axiom 1 append-only-provenance discipline across the version-indexed surface family.

### Compatible extension versus silent breaking change

A surface-level transition from $S_i$ to $S_{i+1}$ is a *compatible extension* when $S_{i+1}$ is a behavioral subtype of $S_i$ and any additions to $S_{i+1}$ are additive: new capabilities, new optional parameters, new endpoints that do not interfere with the semantics of existing declarations. Compatible extension preserves what callers already rely on and adds new affordances they may or may not use.

A surface-level transition is a *silent breaking change* when $S_{i+1}$ is not a behavioral subtype of $S_i$ (callers programmed against $S_i$ break against $S_{i+1}$) and the breaking change is not accompanied by an explicit corrigendum (truth-status tag, §4.4) marking what was changed and why. Silent breaking change is the surface-evolution pattern that Chapter 4 will treat as the relevant structural-honesty failure mode under Axiom 1: the surface changed, callers relying on it broke, and the change was not declared.

Chapter 3 introduces the discrimination vocabulary (compatible extension versus silent breaking change); Chapter 4 will use this vocabulary to distinguish permitted compatible extensions from impermissible silent breaks. The formal invariant Axiom 1 imposes over surface evolution is the work of Chapter 4.

### Truth-status tags

A truth-status tag is an explicit surface object marking a change to previously-declared content. The dissertation uses three tags. A *correction* tag indicates that a prior claim on the surface was wrong and is revised: the predecessor surface contained an assertion the producer no longer endorses, the successor surface replaces that assertion with a revised one, and the correction tag attaches to the change. A *supersession* tag indicates that a prior claim is replaced by a newer claim that takes precedence: the predecessor's claim was not necessarily wrong, but the newer claim is the operative one going forward. A *withdrawal* tag indicates that a prior claim is no longer maintained or defended: the producer is no longer asserting the predecessor's claim, but does not necessarily replace it with a substitute.

The tags are surface objects, not silent mutations. The predecessor surface remains visible in the version history with the tag attached; the successor surface includes the revised, superseded, or withdrawn claim along with the tag identifying which prior claim it modifies. Chapter 4 will use the tags to formalize the corrigenda discipline that distinguishes append-only-provenance-with-corrections from silent rewriting.

### Historical-record preservation

Historical-record preservation is the object-level apparatus that ensures the historical record across $S_0, S_1, \ldots, S_n$ remains accessible and verifiable. The apparatus has three components: *archived versions* (each $S_i$ is preserved in archived form alongside its successors, available to downstream verifiers who need to compare versions); *corrigenda registers* (the truth-status tags of §4.4 are recorded in a register that lists which tags apply to which version transitions); *retention discipline* (the archived versions and corrigenda registers are retained for the period during which the surface's claims may be relied upon).

Chapter 4 will use this apparatus to state the append-only-provenance invariant that Axiom 1 imposes. Chapter 3 supplies the typed objects (archived versions, corrigenda registers, retention discipline) that the invariant operates over; the invariant statement is the work of Chapter 4.

## $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ machinery and caller-side coverage

Section 5 introduces the $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ machinery that Chapter 6 (Axiom 3) will use to state the caller-coverage obligation. The machinery is presented in five subsections: §5.1 introduces $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ as the verifier's conservative over-approximation of producer outcomes; §5.2 distinguishes $R_{\mathrm{declared}}$ from $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ as standing-symbol objects; §5.3 introduces substrate-specific over-approximation disciplines; §5.4 introduces the caller-side coverage vocabulary; §5.5 positions the caller-side discipline as an extension of producer-side refinement-type discipline. Chapter 6 will state Axiom 3 over this machinery; Chapter 3 supplies only the machinery.

### $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ as conservative over-approximation

$R_{\mathrm{may}}$ is the verifier's typed object representing the set of possible producer outcomes that a caller must be prepared to handle. The construction is conservative: $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ includes every outcome that the verifier cannot rule out, possibly more outcomes than the producer actually exhibits. Conservatism is what makes the construction tractable: the verifier need only over-approximate the actual outcome set, not compute it precisely.

For a software producer, $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ might be the set of return values, exception types, and side-effect classes that a static analyzer cannot prove to be impossible for the producer's procedure. For an audited organization, $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ might be the set of control-failure modes that an auditor cannot rule out within the engagement's scope. For a document extractor, $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ might be the set of interpretations that an automated extractor cannot disambiguate without further evidence. Chapter 3 introduces $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ as the typed object; Chapter 6 will state Axiom 3 over it.

### Distinguishing $R_{\mathrm{declared}}$ from $R_{\mathrm{may}}$

$R_{\mathrm{declared}}$ and $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ are both standing symbols in Table 3.1, but they play different roles. $R_{\mathrm{declared}}$ is the producer's declared possible outcomes: what the producer says, on the surface, that the substrate can do. $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ is the verifier's conservative over-approximation: what the verifier cannot rule out, conservatively.

$R_{\mathrm{declared}}$ and $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ are distinct standing-symbol objects that may or may not overlap; the relationship between them is not constrained at the §5.2 level. The relationship between $R_{\mathrm{declared}}$ and $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ depends on the substrate and the verification regime; Chapter 6 will state the caller-exhaustiveness obligation that quantifies over whatever relationship between them obtains in a given verification context.

Chapter 3 introduces the distinction between $R_{\mathrm{declared}}$ and $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ as standing-symbol objects. The caller-exhaustiveness obligation that quantifies over these objects is the work of Chapter 6.

### Substrate-specific over-approximation disciplines

Different substrate types use different methods to compute $R_{\mathrm{may}}$. Four exemplar disciplines illustrate the parameterization.

*Type-level over-approximation* uses the producer's declared type as the over-approximation: the set of values inhabiting the type is the set of possible producer outcomes. The refinement-type tradition---F^$\star$^ [@swamy2016fstar], Liquid Haskell [@vazou2014refinement]---extends this with refinement predicates that further constrain the type-level over-approximation; the predicates are part of the producer's declaration, and the over-approximation incorporates them.

*Static-analysis over-approximation* uses a static analyzer to compute the set of values, exception types, or side-effect classes that the analyzer cannot prove to be impossible for the producer. The analysis is bounded in depth (per the MP1.2 finite-default convention) and produces a conservative over-approximation by construction in the abstract-interpretation tradition originated by Cousot and Cousot [@cousot1977abstract].

*Audit-style over-approximation* uses an auditor with scope-bounded access to enumerate possible control-failure modes within a defined audit scope. The audit attestation declares which scope was examined and what failure modes were ruled out; failure modes outside the declared scope or not ruled out remain in $R_{\mathrm{may}}$.

*Document-extraction over-approximation* uses an automated extractor to enumerate possible interpretations of an ambiguous document. The extractor's output is the set of interpretations consistent with the document; the over-approximation is conservative because the extractor enumerates all plausible interpretations rather than committing to one.

Chapter 3 introduces these substrate-specific disciplines as parameterizations of the $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ construction; Chapter 6 will state Axiom 3 over the substrate's declared discipline.

### Caller-side coverage vocabulary

Given $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ for a producer, later chapters will frame caller use of that producer in terms of a coverage question: what does the caller do with each outcome in $R_{\mathrm{may}}$? The dissertation's caller-side coverage vocabulary supplies three discharge categories.

*Handled*: the caller has explicit logic for the outcome. When the outcome occurs, the caller takes a specific action---catching the exception, branching on the return value, processing the alternative document interpretation, escalating the control-failure mode to a defined incident response.

*Propagated-as-incomplete*: the caller acknowledges the outcome without having explicit handling logic for it, and propagates it to its own caller with an incompleteness annotation. The incompleteness is declared rather than hidden: the caller's own surface reflects that it does not handle this outcome, and the discharge obligation transfers upward to whichever component the caller is, in turn, called by.

*Proven-unreachable*: the caller proves that the outcome cannot occur in its calling context. The proof might be a refinement-type discharge (the type system rules out the outcome), a static-analysis result (the analyzer proves unreachability), or an audit attestation (the auditor confirms the outcome is outside the relevant scope).

Chapter 3 introduces the three-category vocabulary as caller-side discharge slots; Chapter 6 will state the caller-exhaustiveness obligation using this vocabulary.

### Caller obligations as extension of producer-side refinement-type discipline

The producer-side refinement-type tradition---F^$\star$^ [@swamy2016fstar], Liquid Haskell [@vazou2014refinement]---requires producers to satisfy refinements declared in their signatures: the producer's actual behavior must conform to the type-level refinements the producer published. This is producer-side discipline: the producer's obligations are stated against the producer's own declarations.

The dissertation's structural-honesty discipline extends this by adding caller-side obligations. Where the producer-side tradition requires the producer to satisfy its own refinements, the dissertation additionally addresses callers: callers face discharge obligations over $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ in the three-category vocabulary of §5.4. The caller-side discipline complements rather than replaces the producer-side discipline: the producer still must satisfy its declarations; additionally, the caller must discharge its obligations against the verifier's over-approximation of what the producer might do.

Chapter 3 positions the caller-side discipline as an extension of the producer-side tradition; Chapter 6 will state Axiom 3 as the formal caller obligation that complements the producer-side refinement-type framework.

## Projection families and consistency relations

Section 6 introduces the projection-family machinery that Chapter 7 (Axiom 4) will use to state the substrate-parameterized projection-consistency requirement. The machinery is presented in six subsections: §6.1 defines projection families $\Pi_X$ as finite structured collections; §6.2 introduces projection domains and partiality; §6.3 introduces substrate-specific consistency relations $\sim_X$; §6.4 catalogues the motivating projection-family exemplars from Chapter 2's three lineages and from contemporary computational practice; §6.5 introduces sheaf-style and commuting-diagram vocabulary as compact descriptions; §6.6 records the deferral to Chapter 7. Chapter 7 will state Axiom 4 over this machinery; Chapter 3 supplies only the machinery.

### Projection family $\Pi_X$ as a finite structured family

A projection family $\Pi_X = \{\pi_1, \pi_2, \ldots, \pi_n\}$ over substrate $X$ is a finite collection of projections, each $\pi_i$ being a function from substrate states (or substrate facts) to a typed view. The family is finite by the MP1.2 finite-default convention; the index set is a finite ordinal range $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ for some $n$. Each member $\pi_i$ is a typed object with explicit domain and range; the family $\Pi_X$ is the typed object that collects them.

The family is not assumed to satisfy any consistency property at the §6.1 level. Chapter 7 will state Axiom 4 over the family by imposing the substrate-specific consistency requirement under $\sim_X$ (§6.3). Chapter 3 introduces the typed family as an object; the consistency requirement that relates the family members is the work of Chapter 7.

### Projection domains and partiality

Each projection $\pi_i$ has an explicit domain $\mathrm{dom}(\pi_i) \subseteq \mathrm{Substrate}(X)$ over which it is defined; outside the domain, $\pi_i$ is partial (no projection value is produced). Different projections in the family may have different domains: $\pi_1$ may project from a strictly larger subset of substrate states than $\pi_2$, or the two domains may overlap without one containing the other.

Partiality is structurally important. A substrate fact need not be projectable into every member of $\Pi_X$; some substrate facts may lie in the domain of $\pi_1$ and $\pi_3$ but outside the domain of $\pi_2$ and $\pi_4$. Later chapters will formulate consistency checks only on regions where the relevant projections are jointly defined: the test "do $\pi_1$ and $\pi_2$ agree on substrate fact $x$" presupposes $x \in \mathrm{dom}(\pi_1) \cap \mathrm{dom}(\pi_2)$. Chapter 7 will state when joint definability implies mutual coherence under $\sim_X$; Chapter 3 supplies the partiality structure.

### Substrate-specific consistency relations $\sim_X$

For each substrate $X$, the consistency relation $\sim_X$ is the substrate-specific relation later used to express when two projection outputs are compatible, where both are defined on the same underlying fact. The relation $\sim_X$ varies by substrate: arithmetic identity for double-entry bookkeeping (debit projection and credit projection agree under arithmetic equality); jurisdiction-specified accounting identity for modern financial reporting (balance-sheet, income-statement, and cash-flow projections agree under GAAP- or IFRS-defined relationships); control-evidence-attestation consistency for security audit (control-design, evidence-collection, and operational-effectiveness projections agree under the attestation framework's consistency rules); variant-record-comparison for textual-preservation philology (manuscript-witness projections agree when stemmatic relationships predict their variant readings).

Chapter 3 introduces the consistency-relation parameter $\sim_X$ without yet requiring mutual coherence. Chapter 7 will state when projections in $\Pi_X$ are required to cohere under $\sim_X$; the coherence requirement is the work of Chapter 7.

### Motivating projection-family examples

The dissertation's motivating projection-family examples serve as exemplars for Axiom 4's structure, drawn from the three lineages traced in Chapter 2 and from contemporary computational practice.

Double-entry bookkeeping [@pacioli1494] supplies the original $n=2$ projection family: each transaction produces a debit projection and a credit projection over the chart of accounts, with the consistency relation being arithmetic identity (total debits equal total credits per transaction). The bookkeeping practice predates the formal mathematical machinery by approximately five centuries.

Modern financial reporting [@previts1979history] extends the projection-family approach to multiple statement projections: balance sheet, income statement, statement of cash flows, statement of changes in equity. The consistency relation in this case is jurisdiction-specified (GAAP in the United States, IFRS internationally), and the projections must agree under jurisdiction-specific accounting identities such as retained-earnings reconciliation across statements.

Multi-control audit [@iso27001; @nist80053; @aicpa2017tsc] supplies a projection family of scope, control, evidence, and operational-effectiveness projections, with the consistency relation being the attestation framework's defined consistency rules (for SOC 2, the AICPA Trust Services Criteria define when scope, controls, evidence, and operations cohere).

Manuscript cross-witnessing [@timpanaro2005lachmann; @reynolds2013scribes; @tov2012textual; @strack1996introduction] supplies a projection family in which each manuscript witness produces a textual-reading projection, and the consistency relation is stemmatic: witnesses related by descent from a common ancestor are expected to agree on inherited readings, while disagreements indicate either independent error or variant transmission.

Recitation chains for Quranic transmission supply a multi-substrate projection family in which hifz (oral memorization), manuscript witness, tajwid (recitational ruleset), riwayat (transmission chain), and communal verification each project over the textual substrate, with the consistency relation being the multi-substrate cross-coherence that the verification community treats as authoritative; the dissertation's structural framing of this multi-substrate apparatus is developed in the SHV synthesis paper [@arfeen2026shv] rather than in single-surah literary-structural analyses such as Farrin [@farrin2010surat], which is cited elsewhere only as a structural-analysis exemplar (per Chapter 1 §4 and Chapter 2 §4.2 scoping).

Software-release projection families [@arfeen2026shvsupplychain] supply a contemporary example in which sigstore (cryptographic signing), in-toto (build-provenance attestation), SLSA (supply-chain integrity levels), and SHV (structural-honesty verification) each project over a software-release substrate, with the consistency relation being the supply-chain-consistency framework that downstream consumers rely on.

These exemplars are motivating examples, not the axiom statement. Chapter 7 abstracts the pattern to substrate-parameterized form; Chapter 3 supplies only the exemplars.

### Sheaf-style and commuting-diagram vocabulary

The projection-family-with-consistency-relation structure can be described using sheaf-inspired and presheaf-style restriction vocabulary in compact categorical form. Mac Lane and Moerdijk [@maclane1994sheaves] develop the sheaf-theoretic machinery in detail; the vocabulary relevant to the dissertation is the small-finite-category restriction of that machinery. A projection family $\Pi_X$ over a substrate $X$ with consistency relation $\sim_X$ can be described using sheaf-inspired / presheaf-style restriction vocabulary over a small finite category, where each projection plays the role of a section over a local view, and restriction maps express comparison across overlaps. Whether the consistency relation $\sim_X$ additionally satisfies the gluing condition (that sections agreeing on overlaps extend uniquely to a global section) is not claimed here and is not required for Chapter 3's prerequisite role; Chapter 7 will determine which structural properties $\sim_X$ is required to satisfy. No gluing or uniqueness condition is asserted at the Chapter 3 prerequisite level.

In compact commuting-diagram form: for projections $\pi_i, \pi_j$ in $\Pi_X$ with overlapping domains, the consistency relation $\sim_X$ relates the restriction $\pi_i \upharpoonright (\mathrm{dom}(\pi_i) \cap \mathrm{dom}(\pi_j))$ to the restriction $\pi_j \upharpoonright (\mathrm{dom}(\pi_i) \cap \mathrm{dom}(\pi_j))$, where each side denotes the projection restricted to the joint domain.

The categorical vocabulary supplies the formal apparatus for stating Axiom 4 compactly. The analogy with sheaves is structural and notational, not a claim that projection families are sheaves in the full topos-theoretic sense; the relevant restriction is to small finite categories under the MP1.2 finite-default convention. Chapter 3 introduces the apparatus; Chapter 7 uses it to state the axiom.

### Deferral to Chapter 7

Chapter 7 will state when defined projections in $\Pi_X$ are required to mutually cohere under $\sim_X$---that is, when the projection family is required to satisfy Axiom 4 (substrate-parameterized projection consistency). Chapter 3 supplies the typed projection family (§6.1), the partiality structure (§6.2), the substrate-specific consistency relation (§6.3), the motivating exemplars (§6.4), and the sheaf-style vocabulary (§6.5). Chapter 7 supplies the axiom statement; Chapter 3 supplies only the prerequisites.

## Decidable-fragment discipline and chapter handoff

Section 7 introduces the decidable-fragment discipline and identifies the candidate fragments for which the dissertation will attempt to establish decidability in Chapter 10. The discipline is presented in five subsections: §7.1 defines the decidable-fragment scoping discipline; §7.2 lists the candidate fragments; §7.3 distinguishes candidate from proven; §7.4 names unbounded and infinite cases as outside v1.0 scope; §7.5 closes Chapter 3 with the handoff to Chapter 4. Chapter 10 supplies the rigorous decidability and quantum-survivability proofs. Chapter 3 supplies only the discipline and the candidate identification.

### Decidable-fragment discipline

The dissertation's v1.0 verification claims are scoped by declared boundedness assumptions; where no bounded or decidable fragment is established, the relevant claim is marked as an open problem or continuation target. The decidable-fragment scoping discipline is the formal-methods analog of the scope-declaration discipline familiar from professional audit, which states the scope of an audit engagement before stating the audit results: the SOC 2 attestation declares what was within the audit's scope and what was not, and the audit opinion is meaningful only within the declared scope.

Chapter 3 introduces this scope-declaration discipline as a methodological commitment for the formal results to follow. The actual fragments and their rigorous decidability proofs are the work of Chapter 10; Chapter 3 commits to the discipline that those proofs will be scoped explicitly.

*Standing convention.* Throughout this dissertation, Chapter 8 §2's finite-witness construction (T82) operates within whatever decidable fragment Chapter 10 establishes; T82 itself does not prove general decidability conditions. This routing convention is stated once here and is not restated at each subsequent occurrence in Chapter 3 where decidability is referenced.

### Candidate decidable fragments

The dissertation identifies the following candidate fragments as plausibly establishable based on standard formal-methods results. *Finite-state correspondence relations* over the LTS foundations of §3.2, where standard bisimulation and simulation problems have well-studied decision procedures over finite-state systems. *Finite version histories* over the version-indexed surface families of §4.1, where compatible-extension-versus-silent-break determination is plausibly decidable when both versions are represented as finite-state LTS structures and the behavioral-subtyping relation is decidable over those LTS representations---the precise decidability conditions depend on the underlying semantic model and are established in Chapter 10. *Bounded $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ approximations* over the substrate-specific over-approximation disciplines of §5.3, where the caller-coverage three-category vocabulary is plausibly decidable when $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ is finitely representable. *Finite projection families* over the projection-family structure of §6.1, where the joint-definability condition and the consistency relation $\sim_X$ are plausibly decidable when $\Pi_X$ is finite and $\sim_X$ is decidable per substrate type.

Each candidate is identified as a fragment where decidability appears tractable; the rigorous decidability proofs are deferred to Chapter 10. Chapter 3 supplies the candidate identification, not the proofs.

### Candidate versus proven distinction

The methodological discipline that distinguishes candidate decidable fragments from proven decidable fragments is structurally important. Chapter 3's candidate listings (§7.2) are not commitments that the fragments are decidable; they are commitments that the dissertation will attempt to establish their decidability in later chapters and will explicitly mark any candidate that fails to establish as an open problem in the Part V open-problem chapters (especially Chapters 20 and 21).

The candidate-versus-proven distinction is the formal-methods analog of the conjecture-versus-theorem distinction familiar from pure mathematics: a candidate fragment is a conjecture that decidability holds within the fragment; a proven fragment is a theorem that decidability holds within the fragment. Chapter 3 makes only the conjectures; Chapter 10 supplies the rigorous decidability and quantum-survivability proofs.

### Unbounded and infinite cases outside v1.0 scope

The dissertation v1.0 explicitly excludes the following cases from its rigorous decidability claims. *Unbounded $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ approximations* (where the over-approximation is not finitely representable, for example $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ over an infinite-state probabilistic producer) are outside v1.0 scope. *Infinite-state correspondence relations* (where the underlying LTS has infinitely many states) are outside v1.0 scope unless explicitly handled by a later chapter. *Infinite version histories* (where the version index ranges over an infinite ordinal) are outside v1.0 scope. *Infinite projection families* (where $|\Pi_X|$ is infinite) are outside v1.0 scope.

The scope exclusion is the structural-honesty companion to the decidable-fragment discipline of §7.1: the dissertation declares what it does not claim to prove, just as it declares what it does claim to prove. Open problems in this excluded space are identified in the Part V open-problem chapters (especially Chapter 20 for substrate-generalization limits and Chapter 21 for falsification protocols) for the v1.0 release; future work may address some of them in later versions of the framework.

### Chapter 3 hands off to Chapter 4

Chapter 3 closes by summarizing what the prerequisites supply and what Chapter 4 will use them for. The prerequisites supply: typed objects for surfaces, substrates, observer models, and contexts (§§1--2); the correspondence-relation family with LTS/SOS foundations, bisimulation, simulation, refinement, abstraction-preserving equivalence, and extraction equality (§3); the versioned-surface and behavioral-subtyping apparatus with compatible-extension-versus-silent-break vocabulary, truth-status tags, and historical-record preservation (§4); the $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ construction with substrate-specific over-approximation disciplines and the caller-side coverage three-category vocabulary (§5); the projection-family and consistency-relation machinery with exemplars from the three Chapter-2 lineages and from contemporary practice plus the sheaf-style vocabulary (§6); and the decidable-fragment discipline with candidate fragments and scope-exclusion declarations (§7).

Chapter 4 will use these prerequisites to state Axiom 1 as the append-only-provenance invariant over the versioned-surface family from §4. The handoff statement marks the boundary between the prerequisites chapter (Chapter 3) and the first axiom chapter (Chapter 4). Subsequent axiom chapters (Chapters 5, 6, 7) will use the prerequisites from §§3, 5, 6 to state Axioms 2, 3, 4. The integrative-evaluation chapter (Chapter 8) will use the finite-default and scope-declaration discipline of §7 to scope its four integrative-evaluation results (T81 mutual independence; T82 finite-witness consistency; T83 definitional adequacy; AD1 adversarial-declaration coverage); the decidability-and-quantum-survivability chapter (Chapter 10) will use the same discipline to scope its rigorous decidability and quantum-survivability theorems.
