# Axiom 1 (Append-Only Provenance)

**Version status.** Full chapter canon (§§1--3) after cycle-15 first-encounter cycle-14d-equivalent verification (May 16--17, 2026) under external four-vendor fresh-instance verification discipline. Chapter 4 states Axiom 1, develops its three structural conditions (compatible extension, corrigenda discipline, historical-record preservation), identifies three primary failure patterns, explores six edge cases, illustrates across SI1--SI4, articulates the target-stability dependency Axiom 2 has on Axiom 1, and hands off to Chapter 5. Cycle-15 absorbed C4RV-P1 (§1.7 decidability-routing alignment with cycle-14d Chapter 3 §7 stabilized form) and C4RV-P2 (§1.5 within-section labeling drift fix). The canonical audit ledger records the multi-cycle revision history.

## Axiom 1: Append-Only Provenance

Section 1 states and develops Axiom 1, the first of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$'s four axioms. Axiom 1 governs the temporal evolution of public surfaces: it requires that successive versions of a public surface satisfy append-only provenance, with compatible extensions and explicitly-tagged corrections, supersessions, and withdrawals as the only permitted transitions, and with the historical record preserved across versions. The section is presented in seven subsections: §1.1 supplies the formal statement; §1.2 formalizes the compatible-extension condition; §1.3 formalizes the corrigenda-tagging discipline; §1.4 formalizes the historical-record preservation condition; §1.5 identifies three primary failure patterns; §1.6 illustrates Axiom 1 across the four worked substrate instances; §1.7 closes with proof obligations and the forward reference to Chapter 8's definitional-adequacy theorem.

### Formal statement of Axiom 1

For every substrate $S$ with version-indexed public-surface family $S_0, S_1, \ldots, S_n$ (using the §4-local notation of Chapter 3 §4.1, in which $S_i$ denotes the $i$-th version of the public-surface family $\mathrm{Surface}(S)$ associated with substrate $S$; the standing symbol $S$ from Chapter 3 Table 3.1 remains the substrate identifier), the family satisfies *append-only provenance*: for every successive pair $(S_i, S_{i+1})$, either (i) $S_{i+1}$ is a behavioral subtype of $S_i$ in the Liskov-Wing sense from Chapter 3 §4.2 (callers whose assumptions are valid under $S_i$'s declared interface continue to have those assumptions preserved under $S_{i+1}$'s declared interface), in which case the transition is a compatible extension, or (ii) $S_{i+1}$ is accompanied by an explicit corrigendum---a truth-status tag from Chapter 3 §4.4's three-tag set $\{\text{correction}, \text{supersession}, \text{withdrawal}\}$---marking what changed and the truth-status category under which the change is published. The historical record is preserved across $S_0, S_1, \ldots, S_n$ per the historical-record apparatus of Chapter 3 §4.5.

This is Axiom 1: append-only provenance over versioned public surfaces.

The axiom is a single requirement with three structural conditions: compatible extension (§1.2), corrigenda discipline (§1.3), and historical-record preservation (§1.4). When all three conditions hold across the version-indexed family, Axiom 1 is satisfied; when one or more conditions fail, the failure manifests in one of three primary failure patterns identified in §1.5.

### Behavioral-subtyping condition for compatible extension

A version transition $S_i \to S_{i+1}$ is a *compatible extension* when two structural conditions hold.

\(i\) $S_{i+1}$ is a behavioral subtype of $S_i$ in the Liskov-Wing sense [@liskov1994behavioral] as introduced in Chapter 3 §4.2: callers whose assumptions are valid under $S_i$'s declared interface continue to have those assumptions preserved under $S_{i+1}$'s declared interface.

\(ii\) The additions to $S_{i+1}$ are *additive*: new optional parameters with defaults; new endpoints that do not interfere with the semantics of existing declarations; new declared semantics that preserves the assumptions valid under $S_i$'s declared semantics; new components that callers programmed against $S_i$ are free to ignore.

The two conditions together capture the intuition that compatible extension is what callers programmed against $S_i$ should be able to ignore: their existing dependencies continue to be honored (condition (i)), and any new capabilities are opt-in rather than mandatory (condition (ii)). A version transition that satisfies both (i) and (ii) is a compatible extension and requires no corrigendum: the transition extends the surface without modifying any prior commitment.

### Corrigenda discipline using correction/supersession/withdrawal tags

When a version transition is not a compatible extension---when $S_{i+1}$ either breaks behavioral subtyping with $S_i$ or makes a non-additive change---Axiom 1 requires an explicit corrigendum: a truth-status tag (Chapter 3 §4.4) accompanies the transition, identifying which prior surface element is modified and the truth-status category under which the change is published.

The three truth-status categories from Chapter 3 §4.4 each classify a specific kind of non-compatible change.

A *correction tag* classifies a transition in which a prior claim is modified because the prior claim was wrong. The successor surface replaces the prior claim with a revised one; the correction tag identifies the prior claim being corrected and marks the change as a correction. The correction tag does not erase the prior claim; the historical record (§1.4) preserves both the original incorrect claim and the corrected successor.

A *supersession tag* classifies a transition in which a prior claim is replaced by a newer claim that takes precedence without the prior claim being wrong per se. The supersession tag identifies the prior claim being superseded and marks the change as a supersession. Examples include a deprecated API endpoint replaced by a successor endpoint with different (but not contradictory) semantics; an audit attestation replaced by a more recent attestation that supersedes the prior period.

A *withdrawal tag* classifies a transition in which a prior claim is no longer maintained or defended, without necessarily being replaced. The withdrawal tag identifies the prior claim being withdrawn and marks the change as a withdrawal. Examples include an API endpoint deprecated and removed without successor; an audit firm withdrawing a prior attestation following discovery of material misstatement.

In all three cases, the corrigendum is a public-surface object: the truth-status tag appears on the surface at the version transition. The historical record (§1.4) preserves the predecessor surface alongside its successor; the corrigenda register lists which tags apply to which version transitions.

### Historical-record preservation condition

Axiom 1 requires that the historical record across $S_0, S_1, \ldots, S_n$ remain accessible and verifiable. The historical-record preservation apparatus of Chapter 3 §4.5 has three components, and Axiom 1 imposes a condition on each.

*Archived versions*: each $S_i$ is preserved in archived form alongside its successors $S_{i+1}, S_{i+2}, \ldots, S_n$. Preservation here is not "the current version is the only visible version"; predecessors remain visible to downstream verifiers who need to compare versions, audit the version sequence, or verify a corrigendum's claims about what was modified.

*Corrigenda registers*: the truth-status tags of §1.3 are recorded in a register that lists which tags apply to which version transitions. The register is a public-surface object: it appears on the surface where downstream verifiers can read it, parallel to how the truth-status tags themselves appear on the surface. The register's purpose is to make the corrigenda history navigable: a verifier examining the transition $S_i \to S_{i+1}$ can look up which tags apply.

*Retention discipline*: the archived versions and corrigenda registers are retained for the period during which the surface's claims may be relied upon. The retention period is substrate-dependent: for audit attestations, the retention period extends through the audit-engagement scope; for software API versions, the retention period extends through the version's published deprecation timeline; for manuscript critical editions, the retention period extends through the scholarly community's expected reliance on the edition.

The three components together make the version-indexed family $S_0, S_1, \ldots, S_n$ inspectable: a verifier can examine the full version history, the corrigenda register, and the retained archives to determine whether Axiom 1's conditions are satisfied.

### Three primary failure patterns

Chapter 4 §1.5 identifies three primary Axiom 1 failure patterns within the Chapter 4 formalization. Each pattern is a structural failure of one or more of the conditions of §1.2 (compatible extension), the corrigenda-tagging requirement of §1.3, or the historical-record preservation condition of §1.4. The exhaustiveness of the three-pattern characterization across all possible failure forms is deferred to Chapter 8's definitional-adequacy work; Chapter 4 §1.5 identifies these three as the primary patterns the axiom treats as failures.

*Silent deletion*: an element of $S_i$ is removed from $S_{i+1}$ without a withdrawal tag in the corrigenda register. The transition violates §1.2(i) (behavioral subtyping: callers programmed against the removed element break against the successor) and §1.3 (no corrigendum was published for the removal). The structural-honesty failure is that the surface was modified without declaration: callers who relied on the deleted element have no recorded acknowledgment that it was deleted, and no successor pointer is available.

*Silent semantic weakening*: an element of $S_i$ has its declared semantics weakened in $S_{i+1}$ without a correction or supersession tag. Weakening occurs when, for example, a stronger guarantee is replaced by a weaker one (an API method that previously guaranteed sorted output now returns unsorted output; an audit attestation that previously asserted a strong control now asserts only a weaker variant). The transition may or may not violate §1.2(i) depending on how strictly the caller relies on the prior guarantee, but it always violates §1.3 when no corrigendum is published. The structural-honesty failure is the same: the surface was modified without declaration.

*Untagged breaking change*: any other behavioral-subtyping violation between $S_i$ and $S_{i+1}$ that is not accompanied by an explicit corrigendum. This pattern covers behavioral-subtyping breaks that are not categorizable as deletion or semantic weakening but that nonetheless violate §1.2(i) without a §1.3 tag. The structural-honesty failure is general: the surface broke its predecessor's contract without declaring the break.

In each case, the failure pattern is a structural violation of one or more of the §1.2/§1.3/§1.4 conditions. Whether the three patterns exhaust the failure modes of Axiom 1 within the four-substrate scope is part of Chapter 8's definitional-adequacy proof obligation.

### Examples across the four worked substrate instances

Axiom 1 operationalizes differently for each of the four substrate instances from Section 5 of the audit ledger. The following examples illustrate the axiom's application across SI1--SI4; secondary illustrative examples (software APIs, audit attestations, textual witnesses, AI model cards) appear in subsequent chapters as general illustrations when explicitly marked.

*SI1 --- Bayyinah file-layer scanner.* The Bayyinah scanner [@arfeen2026bayyinah] publishes versioned releases, each with a public surface comprising the file-kinds list, the detection-mechanism list, the zahir-layer/batin-layer split, the PDF byte-identical parity check, and the scan-incomplete primitive. Compatible extensions include the addition of new file-kinds, new detection mechanisms, and new diagnostic outputs that do not interfere with existing semantics. Breaking changes---e.g., removal of a detection mechanism, weakening of the zahir-layer/batin-layer classification---require explicit corrigenda in the release-notes register. The historical record is preserved through the version-control system, with each release tagged and archived. Axiom 1 governs the surface evolution of Bayyinah across release versions.

*SI2 --- Furqan language-layer type-checker.* The Furqan type-checker [@ashraf2026furqan; @ashraf2026furqanproto] publishes versioned releases, each with a public surface comprising the implemented-constructs list, the test-suite results, and the compile-time-check semantics. Compatible extensions include the addition of new constructs, new compile-time checks, and additional test coverage that does not regress existing checks. Breaking changes---e.g., removal of a previously-implemented construct, weakening of a compile-time check from "must" to "should"---require explicit corrigenda. The historical record is preserved through versioned releases with archived test-suite results. Axiom 1 governs the surface evolution of Furqan across release versions.

*SI3 --- Munafiq model-layer protocol.* The Munafiq Protocol document [@arfeen2026munafiq] publishes versioned editions, each with a public surface comprising the four-process taxonomy, the nine diagnostic markers, and the four-layer detection architecture. Compatible extensions include the addition of new diagnostic markers, refinements to process descriptions that strengthen rather than weaken the protocol, and new architecture details consistent with the four-layer structure. Breaking changes---e.g., removal of a diagnostic marker, replacement of a process in the taxonomy---require explicit corrigenda in the version-change log. The historical record is preserved through versioned editions with archived predecessors. Axiom 1 governs the surface evolution of the Munafiq Protocol across editions.

*SI4 --- Supply-chain four-substrate stack.* The supply-chain stack composes sigstore (identity layer) [@sigstore2021], in-toto (process layer) [@torres2019intoto], SLSA (institutional layer) [@slsa2023], and SHV (semantic layer) [@arfeen2026shvsupplychain]. Each layer publishes versioned releases with public surfaces (sigstore: identity-attestation format; in-toto: link-attestation format; SLSA: build-integrity-level specification; SHV: structural-honesty surface). Compatible extensions and explicit corrigenda apply to each layer's surface evolution. The historical record is preserved through each layer's release-management discipline. Axiom 1 governs the surface evolution of each layer separately, with cross-layer compatibility tracked through the stack's composition discipline.

In each case, existing release-management practices---version control, release notes, deprecation policies, and attestations---provide substrate-specific mechanisms that can support Axiom 1's structural conditions. Chapter 4 §1.6's contribution is to recognize that these existing practices can be viewed as instances of a single structural-honesty discipline that Axiom 1 formalizes.

### Proof obligations and relationship to Chapter 8 definitional adequacy

Chapter 4 §1.7 closes the Axiom 1 development by identifying its proof obligations and the relationship to Chapter 8's definitional-adequacy theorem.

The Axiom 1 proof obligations within Chapter 4 are three.

*Well-formedness*: Axiom 1 is well-formed as a structural condition over the version-indexed surface families introduced in Chapter 3 §4. This is verified by the construction in §§1.1--1.4: each of the three structural conditions (compatible extension, corrigenda discipline, historical-record preservation) is defined over typed objects from Chapter 3 §4, and the conjunction of the three conditions is itself well-typed.

*Decidability scope*: Axiom 1's compatible-extension and corrigenda-tagging conditions are candidates for decidable treatment in the finite-default fragment of Chapter 3 §7, assuming finite version histories, a finite truth-status-tag set, and a finite or otherwise decidable behavioral-subtyping check. Chapter 10 carries the rigorous decidability burden; Chapter 8 §2's finite-witness construction (T82) operates within whatever decidable fragment Chapter 10 establishes. Outside the finite-default fragment (infinite version histories, infinite-state behavioral-subtyping settings), Axiom 1 remains structurally well-defined but its decidability is not claimed for v1.0.

*Exhaustiveness of the three primary failure patterns*: whether the three patterns of §1.5 exhaust the failure modes of Axiom 1 within the four-substrate scope. This is a definitional-adequacy question---whether the three patterns are sufficient to classify every Axiom 1 failure observable in SI1--SI4---and the exhaustiveness claim is deferred to Chapter 8.

The relationship to Chapter 8: Chapter 8 is assigned the definitional-adequacy proof---whether Axiom 1, together with the other three axioms of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ (Axiom 2 in Chapter 5, Axiom 3 in Chapter 6, Axiom 4 in Chapter 7), captures the operational SHV/Furqan/Munafiq vocabulary across the scoped substrate instances. Chapter 8 will evaluate whether the A1.1--A1.5 classifications are definitionally adequate for the scoped operational vocabulary: whether behaviors classified as compatible extension (§1.2) or properly-tagged corrigendum (§1.3) correspond to behaviors the operational vocabulary treats as structurally honest, and whether behaviors classified as failure patterns (§1.5) correspond to behaviors the operational vocabulary treats as structurally dishonest.

Chapter 4 supplies Axiom 1 statement and the three structural conditions; Chapter 8 supplies the definitional-adequacy proof. This closes Chapter 4 §1.

## Axiom 1 edge cases and boundary cases

Section 2 explores Axiom 1's behavior in edge cases that §1's formal statement does not fully illuminate. Each subsection identifies a structural edge case and shows how the axiom's three conditions (§1.2 compatible extension, §1.3 corrigenda discipline, §1.4 historical-record preservation) apply or fail in that case. The edge cases are not a new failure taxonomy beyond §1.5's three primary patterns; they are structurally distinct cases of Axiom 1's existing conditions, with their relationship to the §1.5 taxonomy deferred to Chapter 8's definitional-adequacy work.

### Corrigendum-on-corrigendum

Truth-status tags are themselves public-surface objects: Chapter 3 §4.4 introduced them as surface objects, not silent mutations. Axiom 1 therefore applies to corrigenda the same way it applies to any surface element: a corrigendum that turns out to be wrong must itself be modified through a tagged transition, not through silent overwrite.

When a producer publishes a correction tag, supersession tag, or withdrawal tag and later determines that the tag itself was misapplied, the resolution is recursive: a meta-corrigendum is published that explicitly references the prior tag, identifies the modification, and is itself recorded in the corrigenda register. The meta-corrigendum carries one of the same three categories (correction/supersession/withdrawal) and is governed by §1.3's discipline; the historical record (§1.4) preserves both the prior tag and its meta-corrigendum so that downstream verifiers can navigate the full corrigenda history. The recursion is bounded by the finite-default convention that bounds the version-indexed family: corrigenda chains are finite, the corrigenda register is finite, the meta-corrigenda are themselves entries in the register.

### Mistaken withdrawal

A specific instance of corrigendum-on-corrigendum is mistaken withdrawal: a withdrawal tag was applied to a claim that, on later review, should have been retained or corrected rather than withdrawn. The discovery may come from internal review (the producer realizes the withdrawal was hasty), from external feedback (a user or auditor identifies that the withdrawn claim was substantively correct), or from a substantive change in the producer's position (the claim was withdrawn pending further analysis, and the analysis subsequently supports re-asserting the claim).

The resolution depends on the substantive situation. If the original withdrawal was wrong (the claim should have been retained), the meta-corrigendum is a correction-of-the-withdrawal: the withdrawal tag is itself corrected, the claim is restored, and the restoration is recorded. If the situation has changed (the claim is now defensible again under new conditions), the meta-corrigendum is a supersession of the withdrawal: the withdrawal is replaced by an updated claim. In both cases, the original withdrawal remains visible in the historical record alongside its meta-corrigendum, so the full history (claim then withdrawal then restoration or supersession) is navigable.

### Supersession chains

When a claim is superseded multiple times in sequence---$S_i$'s claim replaced in $S_{i+1}$ with a successor, then $S_{i+1}$'s replacement replaced again in $S_{i+2}$---Axiom 1 requires each transition to carry its own supersession tag. The chain does not collapse: $S_{i+1}$'s claim remains visible in the historical record alongside $S_i$'s and $S_{i+2}$'s, and the corrigenda register lists both supersession events.

The chain structure is what enables downstream verifiers to reason about the surface's evolution. A verifier examining $S_{i+2}$'s current claim can navigate the corrigenda register to discover that this is the second supersession of $S_i$'s original claim, with $S_{i+1}$'s intermediate claim as the first supersession. The verifier can then evaluate whether the chain reflects refinement (each supersession improving precision), correction-with-supersession (a correction tag applied first, then later refinement), or other evolution patterns. Supersession chains do not require a maximum length or a canonical resolution; what they require is that each link in the chain be tagged and preserved.

### Deprecation timelines

Withdrawal tags often carry a deprecation timeline: a claim is first announced as deprecated (intent to withdraw, but the claim remains active and supported), then enters active deprecation (the claim is no longer recommended for new use but is still operational), then is formally withdrawn (the claim is no longer maintained or defended).

The timeline structure is part of the withdrawal tag itself: each tag carries the dates at which the claim transitions through the deprecation states, and the corrigenda register records the full timeline. A verifier examining a deprecated-but-not-yet-withdrawn claim can determine, from the tag, when the formal withdrawal will take effect and what alternative claim (if any) will succeed it. The deprecation-timeline structure does not change Axiom 1's compatible-extension or historical-record conditions; it elaborates the withdrawal tag's content so that downstream verifiers can plan their reliance on the claim. The historical record (§1.4) preserves the timeline alongside the claim, so the full deprecation history remains inspectable.

### Archive loss as historical-record preservation failure

Archive loss is the canonical edge case for the historical-record preservation condition of §1.4. It occurs when predecessor surfaces, corrigenda registers, or retained archives are no longer accessible for the period during which the surface's claims may be relied upon. The loss may be deliberate (a producer intentionally deletes a predecessor surface), accidental (storage corruption, retention-policy misapplication), or systemic (a substrate's infrastructure does not preserve historical records by default).

Archive loss violates the §1.4 historical-record preservation condition directly: the preservation requirement is that each $S_i$ remain accessible alongside its successors, that the corrigenda register list the applicable tags, and that the retention discipline maintains both. When any of these fails, Axiom 1 fails on the preservation side, regardless of whether any §1.2 or §1.3 condition was violated on the evolution side.

This is not introduced as a fourth exhaustive peer category alongside the §1.5 primary patterns. The §1.5 patterns (silent deletion, silent semantic weakening, untagged breaking change) are evolution-side failures concerning what happens between consecutive versions; archive loss is a preservation-side failure concerning what happens to predecessor versions in storage. The two failure-types operate on different aspects of Axiom 1 (§1.2/§1.3 conditions versus §1.4 condition), and the relationship between their respective taxonomies is part of Chapter 8's definitional-adequacy analysis.

### Version-history forks

When two divergent successors $S_{i+1}^A$ and $S_{i+1}^B$ are produced from the same predecessor $S_i$, the version history is no longer a linear sequence but a branching structure. Examples include a software library forked into two maintained variants (one branch tracks long-term-support stability, the other tracks rapid feature evolution); an audit attestation split into two scoped sub-attestations (one branch covers the original engagement scope, the other covers a narrower follow-on scope); a manuscript critical edition succeeded by two competing later editions, each with its own apparatus.

Axiom 1 applies to each branch independently: $S_{i+1}^A, S_{i+2}^A, \ldots$ must satisfy Axiom 1's conditions as a version-indexed family, and $S_{i+1}^B, S_{i+2}^B, \ldots$ likewise. The shared predecessor $S_i$ remains visible in the historical record of both branches. The fork structure itself is recorded in both branches' corrigenda registers, so a downstream verifier can navigate from either branch's history to the shared predecessor and from there to the other branch if desired.

Axiom 1 does not specify how forked branches should be reconciled, whether one branch should be considered authoritative, or whether the fork itself indicates a structural-honesty failure. These are substantive questions that depend on the substrate's context and are not part of Axiom 1's invariant.

## Operational substrates and Chapter 5 handoff

Section 3 reviews how Axiom 1 operates across the four worked substrate instances introduced in Chapter 2 and Section 5 of the audit ledger (SI1--SI4), articulates the structural dependency that subsequent axioms have on Axiom 1, and hands off to Chapter 5. The review in §3.1 is illustrative and preparatory rather than a substantive substrate-adequacy finding; detailed substrate adequacy remains deferred to Chapters 13--16 and Chapter 8.

### Substrate-by-substrate operational surface practices for SI1--SI4

Each of the four worked substrate instances has existing operational practices that can support some or all of Axiom 1's structural conditions. The review here identifies the support mechanisms and the places where additional explicit surface support would be needed; substantive substrate adequacy is the work of the case-study chapters (Chapters 13--16) and the definitional-adequacy theorem chapter (Chapter 8).

*SI1 --- Bayyinah file-layer scanner*: existing practices that can support Axiom 1 include semantic-versioned releases (version-indexed surface family per §1.1); release notes and changelogs (corrigenda registers per §1.4); explicit deprecation announcements (deprecation timelines per §2.4); version-control archives (historical-record preservation per §1.4). Additional explicit surface support would be needed for behavioral-subtyping verification across versions, to support §1.2's compatible-extension condition rigorously rather than informally.

*SI2 --- Furqan language-layer type-checker*: existing practices that can support Axiom 1 include the versioned test-suite results, which provide concrete evidence relevant to behavioral-subtyping preservation, especially when successor test suites retain predecessor coverage. Release notes and changelogs serve as the corrigenda register. Additional explicit support would be needed for truth-status tags on individual construct removals or weakenings, currently informal in release notes rather than formally structured.

*SI3 --- Munafiq model-layer protocol*: existing practices that can support Axiom 1 include versioned editions of the protocol document and version-change logs. The historical record is preserved through the document's revision history. Additional explicit support would be needed for formal truth-status tags on diagnostic-marker changes (currently described in narrative form rather than tagged) and for behavioral-subtyping verification of process-taxonomy refinements.

*SI4 --- Supply-chain four-substrate stack*: each of the four layers (sigstore, in-toto, SLSA, SHV) has its own release-management discipline. Sigstore's identity-attestation format and in-toto's link-attestation format both support versioned releases with explicit deprecation. SLSA's build-integrity-level specification has explicit level transitions that can be read as supersession events. SHV's structural-honesty surface itself is the focus of this dissertation and is intended to support Axiom 1 explicitly. Additional explicit support would be needed for cross-layer compatibility tracking, so that supersession in one layer can be related to compatible-extension or supersession in dependent layers.

In each case, the review identifies where the substrate's existing practices align with Axiom 1's conditions and where additional surface support would strengthen the alignment. Whether the existing practices are definitionally adequate for the substrate's structural-honesty needs is the work of Chapter 8.

### How Axiom 1 stabilizes the target surface for Axiom 2

Axiom 1 supplies a stable, inspectable versioned public surface against which Axiom 2 (Chapter 5) can evaluate surface-substrate consistency. Without append-only provenance, a surface may shift silently over time, making it unclear which public commitment Axiom 2 should compare to the substrate.

The structural dependency operates as follows. Axiom 2 will state a condition relating the public surface to the underlying substrate's actual behavior. For this consistency check to be well-targeted, the verifier needs to know which surface version is being checked. If the surface has been silently modified between when the substrate's actual behavior was observed and when Axiom 2's check is applied, the consistency claim becomes ambiguous: is it a claim about the substrate-behavior-versus-original-surface, or the substrate-behavior-versus-current-surface? When Axiom 1 is satisfied, its append-only-provenance discipline resolves the ambiguity by preserving the surface version at the time of observation (per §1.4) and tagging any subsequent modifications (per §1.3), so the verifier can identify which surface version is the relevant target.

This is a structural dependency about target stability, not a statement of Axiom 2's content. Axiom 2 itself is stated in Chapter 5; what Chapter 4 supplies is the surface stability that makes the Axiom 2 statement well-targeted.

### Chapter 5 handoff

Chapter 5 will state Axiom 2 over the correspondence-relation family from Chapter 3 §3, using the now-Axiom-1-honest surfaces of Chapter 4. When Axiom 1 is satisfied, Chapter 5 can treat the relevant surface version and its corrigenda history as stable inputs to Axiom 2: the public commitments are clear (the current $S_n$ surface plus its history), the version transitions are tagged (corrigenda register navigable), and the historical record is preserved (predecessor surfaces archived).

Chapter 5 will state how the surface compares to the substrate; Chapter 4 has stated how the surface evolves over time. Together, the two axioms cover the temporal and substrate-correspondence dimensions of structural honesty. Axioms 3 and 4 (Chapters 6 and 7) cover the verifier-side caller-coverage and substrate-side projection-consistency dimensions, completing the four-axiom synthesis $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$. This closes Chapter 4.

## Axiom 2: Surface-Substrate Consistency under Declared Observer Model and Context Set

Section 1 states and develops Axiom 2, the second of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$'s four axioms. Axiom 2 governs the relationship between a substrate's public surface and the substrate itself: it requires that the surface be consistent with the substrate at the level of observability that a declared observer model $O$ permits, within the operational conditions specified by a declared context set $K$, using a declared correspondence relation $R$ drawn from Chapter 3 §3's family. Axiom 2 is a claim of relativized consistency---consistency under declared $(O, K, R)$---not a claim of full truth or universal correspondence. The section is presented in eight subsections: §1.1 supplies the formal statement; §1.2 formalizes the observer-model declaration discipline; §1.3 formalizes the context-set declaration discipline; §1.4 formalizes the correspondence-relation choice from Chapter 3 §3's family; §1.5 formalizes the satisfaction predicate evaluated under the three declarations; §1.6 identifies three primary failure patterns; §1.7 illustrates Axiom 2 across the four worked substrate instances; §1.8 closes with proof obligations and the forward reference to Chapter 8's definitional-adequacy theorem.

### Formal statement of Axiom 2

For every substrate $S$ with public surface $\mathrm{Surface}(S)$ and substrate object $\mathrm{Substrate}(S)$ (using the Chapter 3 §2 notation in which $\mathrm{Surface}(S)$ and $\mathrm{Substrate}(S)$ are the typed surface and substrate objects associated with substrate $S$), declared observer model $O$ (Chapter 3 §2.3), declared context set $K$ (Chapter 3 §2.4), and declared correspondence relation $R$ chosen from the correspondence-relation family of Chapter 3 §3, Axiom 2 requires that the consistency condition $R(\mathrm{Surface}(S), \mathrm{Substrate}(S))$ holds at the observability level that $O$ permits, within the operational conditions specified by $K$.

This is Axiom 2: surface-substrate consistency under declared $(O, K, R)$.

The axiom is a single requirement with three declaration disciplines and one satisfaction predicate: §1.2 observer-model declaration, §1.3 context-set declaration, §1.4 correspondence-relation choice, and §1.5 the satisfaction predicate evaluated under the three declarations. The axiom is not a claim of full truth or universal correspondence between $\mathrm{Surface}(S)$ and $\mathrm{Substrate}(S)$; consistency is claimed at the declared $(O, K, R)$ resolution, not beyond it. When all three declarations are made and the satisfaction predicate holds under them, Axiom 2 is satisfied; when the satisfaction predicate fails or the declarations themselves are misdeclared, the failure manifests in one of three primary failure patterns identified in §1.6.

### Observer-model declaration discipline

The observer model $O$ is a typed observation calculus (Chapter 3 §2.3) specifying which behaviors of the substrate are observable, with what precision, and under what conditions. Different observer models yield different consistency claims: an observer with the full $F^\star$ [@swamy2016fstar] or Liquid Haskell [@vazou2014refinement] refinement-type calculus has access to a richer behavior space than an audit-style sampled observer; a mass-transmission community of reciters with high aggregate coverage has different observability than a single individual reciter; a static analyzer with bounded inspection depth has different observability than an exhaustive symbolic-execution observer.

Axiom 2 requires $O$ to be declared explicitly as part of the consistency claim. The declaration is a public-surface object: the observer model under which consistency is claimed appears on the surface, where downstream verifiers can read it. Without explicit $O$-declaration, the consistency claim is ambiguous between different observer choices; with explicit $O$-declaration, the claim is specific and verifiable. The $O$-declaration discipline operationalizes the principle that consistency claims must specify what is observable, not assert observability simpliciter.

### Context-set declaration discipline

The context set $K$ is a typed condition specification (Chapter 3 §2.4) declaring the operational conditions under which the consistency claim applies. Different contexts yield different substrate behaviors: a software substrate may behave differently under load, in different deployment environments, with different inputs, under different sandboxing regimes; an audit substrate may yield different attestations under different engagement scopes, materiality thresholds, or compliance regimes; an AI-model substrate may produce different outputs under different prompts, temperature settings, or fine-tuning configurations.

Axiom 2 requires $K$ to be declared explicitly. Like $O$, the context set is a public-surface object: the operational conditions under which consistency is claimed appear on the surface. Without explicit $K$-declaration, the consistency claim is ambiguous between different contexts (consistency under what conditions, in what deployment, for which inputs); with explicit $K$-declaration, the conditions are specific. The $K$-declaration discipline operationalizes the principle that consistency claims must specify the operational regime, not assert universal applicability.

### Correspondence-relation choice from family

The correspondence relation $R$ is chosen from Chapter 3 §3's correspondence-relation family, following the relation-choice mechanism of Chapter 3 §3.6. The family is not assumed to satisfy uniform consistency properties; members vary in strength, in symmetry, and in observer-sensitivity, and which member is the appropriate $R$ for a given substrate depends on the substrate's nature. Bisimulation [@park1981concurrency; @milner1980calculus] is an appropriate $R$ when the declared claim requires symmetric finite-state behavioral equivalence under the declared observer model and the relevant finite/image-finite assumptions. Simulation and refinement are appropriate choices when the declared claim is directional or implementation-refinement oriented. Abstraction-preserving equivalence is the appropriate choice when extraction equality is the consistency criterion.

Axiom 2 requires $R$ to be declared, with the substrate-appropriate choice from the family. Like $O$ and $K$, $R$ is a public-surface object: the correspondence relation under which consistency is claimed appears on the surface, identifying which structural notion of correspondence the claim invokes. The $R$-declaration discipline operationalizes the principle that consistency claims must specify the structural-correspondence notion, not assert consistency simpliciter.

### Surface-substrate satisfaction predicate

When $O$, $K$, and $R$ are all declared per §§1.2--1.4, the satisfaction predicate for Axiom 2 is: $R(\mathrm{Surface}(S), \mathrm{Substrate}(S))$ holds at the $O$-permitted observability level, within $K$-specified contexts. The predicate is evaluated under the three declarations; the value of the predicate depends on (i) which $O$ is declared, (ii) which $K$ is declared, (iii) which $R$ is declared, and (iv) the actual substrate-surface relationship at the $O$-observable level within $K$.

Axiom 2 consists of three declaration disciplines ($O$, $K$, $R$) plus the satisfaction predicate evaluated under those declarations. The predicate is not a fourth declaration: producers declare $O$, $K$, $R$; the satisfaction predicate's truth-value is computed from the declarations and the substrate-surface relationship. The producer commits to $(O, K, R)$ and to the claim that the predicate holds under them; verifiers can evaluate whether the predicate actually does hold under those declarations.

### Three primary failure patterns

Within the Chapter 5 formalization, Axiom 2 has three primary failure patterns. Each pattern is a violation of the consistency claim under the declared $(O, K, R)$; the patterns are not claims of full-truth failure but of declaration-relative failure. The exhaustiveness of the three-pattern characterization across all possible failure forms is deferred to Chapter 8's definitional-adequacy work; Chapter 5 §1.6 identifies these three as the primary patterns the axiom treats as failures.

*Observable inconsistency*: $R$ fails at the declared $(O, K)$. The surface and substrate diverge at the observability level $O$ permits within $K$-contexts. The structural-honesty failure is that the producer's consistency claim does not hold even at the declared resolution: the surface claims one thing about the substrate's $O$-observable behavior in $K$-contexts, but the substrate's actual $O$-observable behavior in $K$-contexts is something else.

*Scope misdeclaration*: the public surface presents or is used as if it supports a broader observer model or context set than the declared $(O, K)$ actually covers. The Axiom 2 failure is the surface's misstatement, obscuring, or overextension of its own consistency claim. If the narrower scope is explicit and downstream users rely on observations or contexts beyond it, the issue is caller-side or governance-side reliance and is not by itself an Axiom 2 violation; Axiom 2 fails when the surface itself misstates the scope of its consistency claim. This distinction preserves the consistency-not-truth discipline: Axiom 2 governs the surface's honesty about its own scope, not the downstream verifier's reliance discipline (which is the territory of Axiom 3 in Chapter 6).

*$R$-misdeclaration*: the declared $R$ is the wrong choice from the family. Consistency may hold under some $R$ in the Chapter 3 §3 family, but not the $R$ that the surface's claims actually rely on. For example, the surface may claim correspondence under bisimulation when only a weaker simulation relation actually holds; the failure is not that no correspondence exists, but that the declared $R$ does not hold.

In each case, the failure pattern is a structural violation of one or more of §§1.2--1.5 conditions. Whether the three patterns exhaust the failure modes of Axiom 2 within the four-substrate scope is part of Chapter 8's definitional-adequacy proof obligation.

### Examples across the four worked substrate instances

For each of the four worked substrate instances from Section 5 of the audit ledger, the consistency claim under declared $(O, K, R)$ operationalizes differently. The following examples are illustrative; substantive adequacy of these $(O, K, R)$ choices for each substrate is the work of Chapter 8 and Chapters 13--16.

*SI1 --- Bayyinah file-layer scanner.* The Bayyinah scanner [@arfeen2026bayyinah] declares an observer $O$ comprising the test-harness assertions over scanner outputs (file-kinds list, detection-mechanism list, zahir-layer/batin-layer classification, PDF parity, scan-incomplete primitive). $K$ is the scoped-input context set (declared file types, specified probe categories, declared scanning regime such as production-mode vs developer-mode). $R$ is typically a refinement or simulation relation, depending on whether the surface claims the scanner returns exactly the declared kinds (bisimulation appropriate) or at least the declared kinds (simulation appropriate). Axiom 2 holds for Bayyinah when, under the test-harness observer's assertions within the scoped-input regime, the scanner's actual behavior satisfies the declared $R$ with respect to the public file-kinds surface.

*SI2 --- Furqan language-layer type-checker.* The Furqan type-checker [@ashraf2026furqan; @ashraf2026furqanproto] declares an observer $O$ comprising the test-suite assertions (callers whose assumptions correspond to passing the published test suite). $K$ is the scoped-program context set (declared program kinds, specified type-system features, declared compilation regime). $R$ is typically a refinement relation: the type-checker's surface claims compile-time guarantees over typed programs, and the substrate, as observed through the declared test-suite observer, supports those guarantees when the observed checker behavior preserves them for programs in $K$. Axiom 2 holds for Furqan when, under the test-suite observer for programs in $K$, the type-checker's behavior refines the public type-system-feature surface under the declared $R$.

*SI3 --- Munafiq model-layer protocol.* The Munafiq Protocol [@arfeen2026munafiq] declares an observer $O$ comprising the eval-prompt sampling (declared prompt categories, sampled outputs under specified prompting conditions). $K$ is the scoped-context context set (declared prompt types, specified evaluation conditions, declared model-deployment regime). $R$ is typically abstraction-preserving equivalence between the protocol's declared markers and the model's actual outputs: the declared markers correspond to specific behavioral categories, and the substrate (actual model behavior) satisfies the protocol when its outputs fall into the corresponding categories. Axiom 2 holds for the Munafiq protocol when, under the eval-prompt observer's sampling within $K$, the model's outputs satisfy the abstraction-preserving correspondence to the declared markers.

*SI4 --- Supply-chain four-substrate stack.* Each of the four layers has its own $(O, K, R)$. Sigstore [@sigstore2021]: $O$ is the identity-attestation observer (cryptographic signature verification); $K$ is the cryptographic-verification context set (declared signature algorithms, certificate authorities, time-validity windows); $R$ is signature-validity (the surface signature matches the substrate identity under the declared cryptography). In-toto [@torres2019intoto]: $O$ is the link-attestation observer (provenance-chain verification); $K$ is the build-step context set (declared build pipeline, specified provenance requirements); $R$ is the provenance-chain relation (the surface link-attestations correspond to the substrate build steps). SLSA [@slsa2023]: $O$ is the build-integrity observer (level-classification verification); $K$ is the release context set (declared release types, specified maturity requirements); $R$ is the level-classification relation (the surface level claim corresponds to the substrate build practices). SHV [@arfeen2026shvsupplychain]: $O$ is the structural-honesty observer; $K$ is the surface-evolution context set (declared four-axiom-applicable contexts); $R$ is the four-axiom-satisfaction relation (the surface structural-honesty claims correspond to the substrate's actual four-axiom satisfaction).

In each case, the declared $(O, K, R)$ makes the consistency claim specific and verifiable rather than ambiguous. The substrate-specific $(O, K, R)$ choices are illustrative and substrate-appropriate; detailed adequacy of these choices remains the work of Chapter 8 and Chapters 13--16.

### Proof obligations and relationship to Chapter 8 definitional adequacy

Chapter 5 §1.8 closes the Axiom 2 development by identifying its proof obligations and the relationship to Chapter 8's definitional-adequacy theorem.

The Axiom 2 proof obligations within Chapter 5 are three.

*Well-formedness*: Axiom 2 is well-formed as a structural condition over the Chapter 3 §2 typed objects ($\mathrm{Surface}(S)$, $\mathrm{Substrate}(S)$, $O$, $K$) and the Chapter 3 §3 correspondence-relation family. This is verified by the construction in §§1.1--1.5: each of the three declaration disciplines is defined over typed objects from Chapter 3 §2; the satisfaction predicate is evaluated over the Chapter 3 §3 family member chosen by the $R$-declaration; the conjunction of the three declarations and the satisfaction predicate is itself well-typed.

*Decidability scope*: Axiom 2's satisfaction predicate is a candidate for decidable treatment in the finite-default fragment of Chapter 3 §7, assuming finite $O$, finite $K$, finite-state $R$ from the Chapter 3 §3 family, and finite-state substrate. Chapter 10 carries the rigorous decidability burden; Chapter 8 §2's finite-witness construction (T82) operates within whatever decidable fragment Chapter 10 establishes. Outside the finite-default fragment (infinite-state substrates, infinite $O$, infinite $K$), Axiom 2 remains structurally well-defined but its decidability is not claimed for v1.0.

*Exhaustiveness of the three primary failure patterns*: whether the three patterns of §1.6 exhaust Axiom 2's failure modes within the four-substrate scope. This is a definitional-adequacy question---whether the three patterns are sufficient to classify every Axiom 2 failure observable in SI1--SI4---and the exhaustiveness claim is deferred to Chapter 8.

The relationship to Chapter 8: Chapter 8 is assigned the definitional-adequacy proof---whether Axiom 2, together with the other three axioms of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ (Axiom 1 from Chapter 4, Axiom 3 from Chapter 6, Axiom 4 from Chapter 7), captures the operational SHV/Furqan/Munafiq vocabulary across the scoped substrate instances. Chapter 8 will evaluate whether the §1.1 formal statement, the §§1.2--1.4 three declarations, the §1.5 satisfaction predicate, and the §1.6 failure patterns are definitionally adequate for the scoped operational vocabulary: whether behaviors classified as consistent under declared $(O, K, R)$ correspond to behaviors the operational vocabulary treats as structurally honest, and whether behaviors classified as failure patterns correspond to behaviors the operational vocabulary treats as structurally dishonest.

Chapter 5 supplies Axiom 2 statement, the three declaration disciplines, the satisfaction predicate, and the three primary failure patterns; Chapter 8 supplies the definitional-adequacy proof. This closes Chapter 5 §1.

## Axiom 2 edge cases and boundary cases

Section 2 explores Axiom 2's behavior in edge cases that §1's formal statement does not fully illuminate. Each subsection identifies a structural edge case under one of the three declaration disciplines (§1.2 observer-model, §1.3 context-set, §1.4 correspondence-relation) or the joint Axiom-1/Axiom-2 interaction, and shows how Axiom 2 applies or fails in that case. The edge cases are not a new failure taxonomy beyond §1.6's three primary patterns; they are structurally distinct cases of Axiom 2's existing conditions, with their relationship to the §1.6 taxonomy deferred to Chapter 8's definitional-adequacy work.

### Observer-model edge cases

The observer-model declaration discipline of §1.2 requires that the consistency claim specify $O$ explicitly. Three edge cases extend the discipline to scenarios §1.2 does not directly address.

*Multiple declared observers.* When a consistency claim is made under $\{O_1, O_2, \ldots\}$---for example, both a test-suite observer and an audit-style sampled observer---the composition semantics matters. Intersection (consistency holds at the intersection of observable behaviors), union (consistency holds across the union), product (consistency holds for each observer separately combined into a joint observation), hierarchy (one observer dominates), and weighted aggregation (consistency holds at some declared aggregation function) are different constructions yielding different consistency claims. Axiom 2 does not commit Chapter 5 to a single universal composition semantics; instead, the composition semantics must itself be declared as part of the $O$-field for the relevant substrate. The producer who claims consistency under $\{O_1, O_2\}$ must also declare which composition rule applies.

*Composite observer models.* A single observer model may be constructed from sub-observers---for example, a refinement-type observer composed of multiple type-system components. The composition operation (Cartesian product of observation spaces, sequential composition, parallel composition) is itself part of the $O$-declaration. Axiom 2 treats the composite as a single declared $O$ once the composition is specified.

*Observer mismatch.* The declared $O$ differs from the actual verifier access. For example, the surface declares a refinement-type observer with full $F^\star$ access, but a downstream verifier only has Liquid Haskell or static-analysis-with-bounded-depth access. The mismatch is not an Axiom 2 failure (Axiom 2's consistency claim is under the declared $O$); it is a verifier-side scoping issue. Whether the verifier with restricted access can still rely on the consistency claim is the territory of Axiom 3 ($R_{\mathrm{may}}$ handling of caller-side observation gaps).

Each of these edge cases is an application of A2.2's declaration discipline in a structurally distinct scenario; none introduces a new condition on the axiom.

### Context-set edge cases

The context-set declaration discipline of §1.3 requires that the consistency claim specify $K$ explicitly. Three context-set edge cases extend the discipline.

*Context-set evolution.* $K$ may change over time. A substrate's declared context set in version $v_1$ may differ from its declared context set in version $v_2$---for example, a software API that initially supports only POSIX deployment contexts is later extended to support Windows contexts, changing the declared $K$. Because $K$ is part of the public consistency claim, changes to $K$ across versions are themselves public-surface changes and are governed by Axiom 1's append-only-provenance discipline (Chapter 4 §§1.2--1.4 apply): $K$-extensions are compatible extensions when callers programmed against the prior $K$ can continue to rely on the same consistency claim, and $K$-restrictions are corrigenda-tagged transitions when the prior $K$ is being withdrawn or superseded.

*Context-set narrowing.* $K$ may be initially over-broad (claiming consistency in many contexts) and then narrowed to handle resource constraints or to acknowledge unsupported contexts. The narrowing is a corrigenda event under Axiom 1: the producer is withdrawing or correcting the prior claim that consistency holds in the broader $K$. The narrower $K$ must be tagged appropriately in the corrigenda register.

*Context-set expansion.* $K$ may be initially narrow (claiming consistency only in a small set of contexts) and then expanded to cover additional contexts after verification. The expansion is a compatible extension when the prior consistency claims remain valid in the original $K$ and additional consistency claims are established for the new contexts. Like all surface-evolution events, $K$-expansion is governed by Axiom 1's compatible-extension discipline (Chapter 4 §1.2).

In each case, the edge case is an application of A2.3's declaration discipline plus Axiom 1's surface-evolution governance for $K$-changes on the public surface. The structural-honesty discipline routes $K$-evolution through Axiom 1 so that downstream verifiers can navigate $K$-changes through the same corrigenda discipline that applies to other surface elements.

### $R$-family edge cases

The correspondence-relation-choice discipline of §1.4 requires $R$ to be chosen from Chapter 3 §3's family and declared. Three $R$-family edge cases extend the discipline.

*$R$ re-declaration.* A previously-declared $R$ may be replaced by a different $R$ from the family---for example, a surface initially claiming consistency under bisimulation may be re-declared to claim consistency under simulation (weaker) or under abstraction-preserving equivalence (orthogonal). Because the declared $R$ is part of the public consistency claim, $R$-redeclaration is itself a public-surface change governed by Axiom 1: the prior $R$-claim is either superseded (replaced by a stronger or differently-scoped $R$) or corrected (the prior $R$ was the wrong choice) and must be tagged in the corrigenda register.

*$R$-family changes.* The underlying correspondence-relation family of Chapter 3 §3 may itself be updated---for example, a new member is added to the family in a subsequent version of Chapter 3 (a Chapter 3 patch). If the new member becomes the declared $R$ for some substrate, the $R$-redeclaration discipline applies. If the family update affects a previously-declared $R$ (e.g., a refinement of bisimulation's definition under different observer-model assumptions), the substrate's $R$-declaration may need to be re-stated with the updated $R$-definition; the re-statement is itself a surface-evolution event under Axiom 1.

*Declared-$R$ becomes obsolete.* A substrate may evolve such that, as observed through the declared $O$ within the declared $K$, the declared $R$ is no longer satisfied, but a different $R$ in the family is. For example, a software substrate initially supporting a bisimulation claim with respect to its surface may evolve such that only a simulation claim now holds under the declared $(O, K)$. The structural-honesty options are: declare a corrigendum identifying the bisimulation claim as no longer valid and supersede it with a simulation claim; or correct the surface to match the substrate's current behavior under the declared $(O, K)$. Either option is governed by Axiom 1's corrigenda discipline.

In each case, $R$-changes that affect the public surface are surface-evolution events governed by Axiom 1's versioning and corrigenda discipline (Chapter 4 §§1.2--1.4). The $R$-declaration discipline of A2.4 operates within each version of the surface; transitions between versions are A1 territory.

### Joint Axiom-1-Axiom-2 interaction

Axioms 1 and 2 interact along a single structural dimension: Axiom 1 governs how the public surface evolves through time, including how the declared $(O, K, R)$ evolves; Axiom 2 evaluates consistency at any given surface version under that version's declared $(O, K, R)$. The two axioms operate on different aspects of the same surface, and their interaction is well-defined when each governs its respective aspect cleanly.

The structural relationship is as follows. At any given surface version $S_i$, with declared $(O_i, K_i, R_i)$, Axiom 2 evaluates whether $R_i(S_i, \mathrm{Substrate}(S))$ holds at the $O_i$-permitted level within $K_i$-contexts; this is a per-version consistency check. As the surface evolves through versions $S_0, S_1, \ldots, S_n$ under Axiom 1, the declared $(O, K, R)$ at each version may change. Each change is a surface-evolution event governed by Axiom 1's compatible-extension and corrigenda disciplines (Chapter 4 §§1.2--1.3): compatible-extension transitions preserve the prior consistency claim while extending it; corrigenda-tagged transitions modify or withdraw the prior consistency claim with explicit tagging.

§2.4 is not a re-statement of either axiom. Axiom 1 supplies the surface-evolution governance (covering $O$, $K$, and $R$ as they appear on the public surface); Axiom 2 supplies the per-version consistency claim under whatever $(O, K, R)$ is declared at that version. When both axioms hold, the surface evolves honestly (Axiom 1) and the consistency claim at each version is satisfied under the declared $(O, K, R)$ for that version (Axiom 2). When Axiom 1 holds but Axiom 2 fails at some version, the surface is honest about its evolution but the substrate has diverged from the claimed correspondence under the current $(O, K, R)$. When Axiom 2 holds but Axiom 1 fails (e.g., silent surface modification), the per-version consistency claim is meaningful but the version history is unreliable for downstream verifiers.

## Operational substrates and Chapter 6 handoff

Section 3 reviews how Axiom 2 operates across the four worked substrate instances introduced in Chapter 2 and Section 5 of the audit ledger (SI1--SI4), articulates the structural dependency that Axiom 3 has on Axiom 2, and hands off to Chapter 6. The review in §3.1 is illustrative and preparatory rather than a substantive substrate-adequacy finding; detailed substrate adequacy remains deferred to Chapters 13--16 and Chapter 8.

### Substrate-by-substrate operational surface practices for SI1--SI4 under Axiom 2

Each of the four worked substrate instances has existing operational practices that can support some or all of Axiom 2's declaration disciplines. The review here identifies the support mechanisms and the places where additional explicit surface support would be needed; substantive substrate adequacy is the work of the case-study chapters (Chapters 13--16) and the definitional-adequacy theorem chapter (Chapter 8).

*SI1 --- Bayyinah file-layer scanner.* Existing practices that can support Axiom 2 include the test-harness specification (declaring $O$ as the assertions over scanner outputs), the scoped-input documentation (declaring $K$ as the file types and probe categories), and the README's correspondence-criterion specification (declaring $R$ as refinement or simulation depending on exactness vs at-least-ness claims). Additional explicit surface support would be needed for explicit $(O, K, R)$ packaging---currently the three declarations are spread across test-harness scripts, README documentation, and scanner output assertions rather than packaged as a single declared consistency claim.

*SI2 --- Furqan language-layer type-checker.* Existing practices that can support Axiom 2 include the test-suite results (the declared $O$ is implicitly the test-suite observer), the documented program kinds (declaring $K$), and the published type-system features (the $R$ relation is implicit in what the type-checker claims to enforce). Additional explicit surface support would be needed for formal $R$-declaration (currently the relation is implicit in the test-suite-and-documentation combination) and for explicit composition-semantics if the test-suite observer is composed with other observers (e.g., static-analysis observers in CI).

*SI3 --- Munafiq model-layer protocol.* Existing practices that can support Axiom 2 include the eval-prompt specification (declaring $O$ as the prompt-sampling observer), the declared evaluation conditions (declaring $K$), and the marker-output correspondence specification (declaring $R$ as abstraction-preserving equivalence between markers and outputs). Additional explicit surface support would be needed for explicit failure-pattern documentation under the three primary patterns of §1.6 (currently failure descriptions are informal rather than structured under observable inconsistency, scope misdeclaration, and $R$-misdeclaration).

*SI4 --- Supply-chain four-substrate stack.* Each of the four layers (sigstore, in-toto, SLSA, SHV) has its own $(O, K, R)$ operational practices. Sigstore's identity-attestation format supports observer declaration (cryptographic verification), context declaration (algorithm and time-validity windows), and $R$ declaration (signature-validity). In-toto's link-attestation format supports observer declaration (provenance-chain verification), context declaration (build-step specification), and $R$ declaration (provenance-chain relation). SLSA's level specification supports observer declaration (build-integrity verification), context declaration (release types), and $R$ declaration (level-classification relation). SHV's structural-honesty surface is intended to support all three declarations explicitly. Additional explicit support would be needed for cross-layer $(O, K, R)$ consistency tracking, so that a downstream verifier checking the full stack can navigate each layer's $(O, K, R)$ and reason about how they compose.

In each case, the review identifies where existing practices can support Axiom 2's declaration disciplines and where additional explicit surface support would strengthen the alignment. Whether the existing practices are definitionally adequate for the substrate's structural-honesty needs is the work of Chapter 8.

### How Axiom 2 prepares the caller-coverage analysis for Axiom 3

Axiom 2 supplies an input to the caller-coverage analysis that Axiom 3 (Chapter 6) will perform. When a producer presents an Axiom 2 consistency claim under declared $(O, K, R)$, Chapter 6 can ask: which callers' assumptions fall within that declared scope, and which possible outcomes must be handled under $R_{\mathrm{may}}$?

The structural dependency operates as follows. Each caller has its own observation regime---what features of the substrate the caller observes, in what contexts, under what correspondence assumptions. Chapter 6 will make this caller-side observation regime precise; Chapter 5 uses the phrase only to name the caller's observed features, contexts, and correspondence assumptions for the purpose of the handoff. When a producer publishes an Axiom 2 consistency claim under declared $(O, K, R)$, each caller's observation regime can be compared to the declared $(O, K)$: callers whose observation regime fits within $(O, K)$ are covered by the Axiom 2 claim; callers whose observation regime extends beyond $(O, K)$ are not covered by the Axiom 2 claim but may still be supported under the conservative over-approximation $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ (Chapter 3 §5).

Chapter 6 will state the Axiom 3 caller-side condition using $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ to reason about callers whose observation regimes extend beyond declared $(O, K)$. The specific $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ discipline (whether through refinement-type caller-side reasoning, substrate-side over-approximation, or per-substrate caller-coverage vocabulary) is the work of Chapter 6.

This is a structural dependency about caller-scope, not a statement of Axiom 3's content. Axiom 3 can be stated whether or not Axiom 2 is satisfied; what changes when Axiom 2 fails or is absent is the input to caller-coverage analysis. When Axiom 2 is satisfied under declared $(O, K, R)$, the consistency claim is an input that Chapter 6 can use to identify covered callers and characterize $R_{\mathrm{may}}$-required handling of uncovered callers. When Axiom 2 is unsatisfied, the failed or absent A2 claim is itself part of the caller's verification context, and Chapter 6's caller-coverage check must account for the missing consistency foundation.

### Chapter 6 handoff

Chapter 6 will state Axiom 3 using $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ from Chapter 3 §5. When Axiom 2 is satisfied under declared $(O, K, R)$, that consistency claim can serve as one input to the caller-coverage analysis: callers whose observation regimes fit within $(O, K)$ are covered, callers whose regimes extend beyond $(O, K)$ require $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ handling. When Axiom 2 is not satisfied, Chapter 6 can still state the caller-side coverage obligation, but the failed or absent A2 claim must be visible as part of the caller's verification context.

Chapter 6 will state how callers should reason about producer outcomes under $R_{\mathrm{may}}$; Chapter 5 has stated how the producer's consistency claim is specified under declared $(O, K, R)$. Together, the two axioms cover the producer-side consistency claim and the caller-side coverage check. Axioms 1 and 4 (Chapters 4 and 7) cover the temporal-evolution and substrate-projection-consistency dimensions, completing the four-axiom synthesis $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$. This closes Chapter 5.
