What remains is to test whether the four-axiom system has the properties a structurally-honest theory must have: mutual independence (T81---none of the four is a derivative consequence of the others), consistency (T82---the system is satisfiable via a finite witness), definitional adequacy (T83---the formal definitions correspond to operational practitioner judgments of structural honesty), and adversarial-declaration coverage (AD1---whether weak or adversarial declarations of the axiom-relativized objects admit trivial satisfaction, and under which ecosystem conditions such trivial satisfaction becomes detectable or structurally blocked).

The section is presented in five subsections, framing the integrative evaluation that the rest of Chapter 8 carries out. §0.1 articulates Chapter 8's role as evaluator. §0.2 names the Principle of Layered Defense, the methodological discipline operating across the dissertation. §0.3 introduces the ecosystem-condition catalog as an auxiliary proof-configuration artifact---not a fifth axiom. §0.4 articulates the named judgment-case set discipline for T83. §0.5 articulates the Chapter 8 / Chapter 21 boundary that preserves Chapter 21's long-horizon falsification-protocol burden.

### Chapter 8's role: evaluation, not restatement

Chapter 8's burden is structurally distinct from Chapters 4--7's. Each axiom chapter stated and developed its axiom's local machinery: Chapter 4 stated A1 over versioned-surface machinery; Chapter 5 stated A2 over the correspondence-relation family; Chapter 6 stated A3 over $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ with the three discharge paths; Chapter 7 stated A4 over the projection-family machinery. The four axiom chapters supplied confidence at the axiom-statement level---each axiom is well-formed, well-typed over Chapter 3's typed-object substrate, and statable independently of the others' satisfaction.

Chapter 8 must earn integrative-level confidence independently. The four axioms, taken together, must satisfy four integrative properties: mutual independence (each falsifiable while the others hold), consistency (the system is satisfiable), definitional adequacy (the system corresponds to operational practice), and adversarial-declaration coverage (the system is nontrivially falsifiable under weak declarations modulo ecosystem conditions). None of these properties follows from the four chapters' statement-level work; each requires its own integrative argument or construction.

The temptation Chapter 8 must resist is to recycle the axiom-chapter confidence into integrative-level confidence by restating the axioms with rhetorical force. Chapters 4--7's discipline was honest at the statement level; it did not pre-claim what Chapter 8 must establish. Chapter 8's discipline is honest at the integrative level; it must not pre-claim what the remaining chapters (Chapter 10 decidability and quantum-survivability; Chapters 13--16 case studies; Chapter 20 substrate-generalization open problem; Chapter 21 falsification protocols) must establish.

The relationship between Chapter 7 and Chapter 8 mirrors the relationship within the axiom-chapter sequence: Chapter 4 supplied the A1 statement, and Chapter 6 §3.2 evaluated A3 against that supplied statement without re-stating A1. Chapter 8 evaluates the complete A1--A4 system against the four integrative properties without re-stating any of the axioms. Where prose references an axiom, it does so to test an integrative property of the axiom in conjunction with the others, not to develop the axiom's local machinery further.

### The Principle of Layered Defense

The dissertation operates under a methodological discipline that we name here, for the first time, as the Principle of Layered Defense. The principle holds that $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ claims are assigned to specific defense layers rather than treated as globally provable in the abstract. Axiom satisfaction is one layer; integrative theorem satisfaction is another; definitional adequacy is a third; operational nontriviality under ecosystem conditions is a fourth; long-horizon falsifiability surveillance is a fifth. Each layer carries a specific kind of claim with a specific kind of supporting argument.

The principle is not a new commitment introduced in Chapter 8. It has been operating across the dissertation since Chapter 3 §1.4's notation-versus-claim discipline (the introduction of a typed object is not the same as the assertion of a property of that object), through the A1--A4 declared-object relativization (each axiom is evaluated under declared $(O, K, R, R_{\mathrm{may}}, \Pi_X, \sim_X)$, not under absolute correspondence), and through the SI1--SI4 scope-relativized claims (each worked substrate is honest at its declared scope, not absolutely correct). What Chapter 8 §0 contributes is the formal naming of the principle that has been load-bearing without explicit recognition.

The principle has substantive consequences for what Chapter 8 can and cannot claim. T81 is a logical-falsifiability theorem operating at the axiom-system layer; it does not by itself establish operational falsifiability, which depends on the ecosystem-condition layer and is treated in AD1. T82 is a formal consistency theorem operating at the model-existence layer; it does not by itself establish that the witness is operationally meaningful, which again depends on the ecosystem-condition layer. T83 is a definitional-adequacy argument operating at the empirical-relative-to-named-cases layer; it does not establish absolute adequacy in a context-free sense, which is not a layer the framework supports. AD1 is an analysis at the adversarial-declaration layer; it identifies what each axiom is designed to expose under each ecosystem condition, and acknowledges residual holes routed to Chapter 21.

The principle is also what makes Chapter 8 tractable rather than impossible. The chapter does not have to prove $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ adequate, consistent, independent, and adversarially robust in a context-free sense---that would be an impossible burden, and the temptation to undertake it would either produce vacuous results or paper over essential limitations. Chapter 8 has to argue each property at its proper defense layer, with explicit acknowledgment of what each layer's argument depends on and what it does not establish. This is analogous to the epistemic posture of adequacy arguments for formal systems such as ZFC, Peano arithmetic, and behavioral subtyping: adequacy is argued relative to the intended domain and judgment practices, not proven in a context-free sense [@liskov1994behavioral].

### Ecosystem-condition catalog

$\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ satisfaction is necessary but not sufficient for operational structural honesty. This is the central methodological observation that shapes Chapter 8's integrative work. The four axioms---surface-evolution honesty, per-version surface-substrate consistency, caller-side exhaustiveness, projection consistency---capture necessary conditions for an artifact to be structurally honest in the framework's sense. They do not capture sufficient conditions; sufficiency requires additional operational-nontriviality conditions that we will call *ecosystem conditions*.

The ecosystem conditions are: multiple independent callers exercising the producer's published $R_{\mathrm{may}}$; multiple independent projections constraining the producer's projection family $\Pi_X$; evolutionary pressure on the producer's surface forcing the corrigenda discipline to engage with substantive change; and corrigenda discipline actually exercised by surface evolution rather than carried as nominal commitment. Without these conditions, individual axioms become structurally empty---A3 has nothing to catch if no callers exercise $R_{\mathrm{may}}$; A4 has nothing to catch if there is only one projection or if projections do not independently constrain; A1 has nothing to catch if the surface never substantively evolves.

The ecosystem-condition catalog is an auxiliary proof-configuration artifact for Chapter 8, not a fifth axiom. The four axioms are formal commitments about the artifact-substrate-caller relationship that the framework prescribes. The ecosystem conditions are interpretive conditions about the operational environment in which the artifact-substrate-caller relationship operates. The distinction matters for the structure of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$: adding ecosystem conditions to the formal axiom set would change the framework from "four axioms about structural honesty" to "five axioms"---and the fifth would be qualitatively different from the first four (it would be a meta-axiom about when the other four bite operationally, not a substantive structural-honesty condition). Preserving the four-axiom structure is methodologically essential; the ecosystem-condition catalog captures operational-nontriviality conditions under which axiom satisfaction has its intended structural-honesty interpretation, without itself becoming part of the formal axiom set.

The proper framing is the same as for any scientific theory: the formal commitments capture necessary conditions, and the operational interpretation requires auxiliary conditions that the theory itself names. Newton's second law ($F = ma$) is necessary but not sufficient for predicting motion; sufficient prediction requires knowing the force functions, the boundary conditions, and the initial state. The law is not falsified by the existence of motion that $F = ma$ alone cannot predict; it is falsified by motion that $F = ma$ predicts incorrectly under known force functions. Similarly, $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ is not falsified by the existence of operational structural dishonesty that $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ alone cannot detect; it is falsified by structural dishonesty that $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ classifies as honest under known ecosystem conditions.

The ecosystem-condition catalog is developed across Chapter 8: T82.7 makes the catalog explicit in the finite witness; AD1.5--AD1.6 examine cases where ecosystem conditions fail (private/no-caller ecosystem, single-projection ecosystem); AD1.7 constructs the cross-axiom coverage matrix as the structural-honesty disclosure mechanism for evaluating adversarial coverage under each ecosystem-condition combination.

### Named judgment-case set discipline

T83's definitional-adequacy claim---that A1--A4 satisfaction under declared $(O, K, R, R_{\mathrm{may}}, \Pi_X, \sim_X)$ corresponds to what operational practitioners call structural honesty---is empirical-relative to a judgment-case set, not provable in a context-free sense. The distinction is foundational and worth stating explicitly. Definitional adequacy of a formal system for a pre-formal notion (structural honesty, in this case) is analogous to the epistemic posture of adequacy arguments for formal systems such as ZFC over the pre-formal notion of set and Peano arithmetic over the pre-formal notion of natural number---the formal system is judged adequate not because it is provably correct in some absolute sense, but because it classifies the cases practitioners care about consistently with practitioner judgment.

The structurally honest move T83 makes is to name the judgment-case set explicitly. The case set comprises operational-practitioner judgment cases drawn from SI1--SI4: cases practitioners would classify as structurally honest; cases practitioners would classify as structurally dishonest; and boundary cases where practitioner judgment is debatable. Each case is a triple (substrate-scenario, expected-classification-by-practitioners, axioms-classification). The adequacy argument shows that for every case in the set, the axioms classify the case consistently with practitioner judgment.

The discipline has three components. First, the case set must include positive, negative, and boundary cases---a case set composed only of clean positive cases would not test the framework, since trivially satisfiable axioms could classify all positive cases correctly without engaging with the framework's actual content. Second, cases outside the case set are explicitly out of T83's scope; T83 does not claim absolute adequacy, only adequacy relative to the named set. Third, boundary cases are not papered over: they are either classified with explicit rationale (the framework correctly captures the practitioner's judgment because of structural-honesty consideration $X$) or routed to Chapter 21 as future falsification / refinement cases where the framework may need extension or modification.

The discipline has consequences for the SHV / Furqan / Munafiq vocabulary mappings (T83.2--T83.4). Each mapping is a structured interpretation from the program's operational vocabulary to $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$'s declared-object vocabulary, with each correspondence justified against the named judgment-case set [@arfeen2026shv; @ashraf2026furqan; @arfeen2026munafiq]. The mappings are not strict semantic isomorphisms; they are not claims that SHV's notion of structural honesty *is* A1--A4 satisfaction in some absolute sense. The mappings are structured correspondences that produce consistent classifications across the case set, with the framework correctly capturing what the program's vocabulary names as structurally honest behavior.

### Chapter 8 / Chapter 21 boundary

Chapter 8 evaluates the A1--A4 system under named ecosystem conditions and identifies what counts as a satisfactory adequacy argument relative to the judgment-case set. Chapter 21 retains the full long-horizon treatment of falsification protocols, monitoring of emergent misappropriation in operational practice, and concrete mechanisms for ongoing falsifiability surveillance. The boundary preserves Chapter 21's burden against Chapter 8 over-claiming.

Specifically, Chapter 8 does not solve three problems that are Chapter 21's burden. The first is the long-horizon dynamics of how $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$-adopting communities maintain corrigenda discipline across decades. Chapter 8 names corrigenda discipline as an ecosystem condition for A1 to bite operationally; it does not specify the institutional, social, or governance mechanisms by which a community ensures corrigenda are actually used. Those mechanisms are Chapter 21's burden. The second is the monitoring of emergent misappropriation in operational practice. AD1.8 acknowledges emergent misappropriation as a partial-falsifiability surface---scope-misdeclaration by honest future users extending $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$'s scope through legitimate intellectual labor, classified as recoverable (corrigenda-taggable) or irrecoverable (load-bearing entrenchment)---but does not specify the surveillance mechanisms by which such misappropriation is detected. Those mechanisms are Chapter 21's burden. The third is the concrete falsification protocols by which the dissertation's load-bearing claims are tested. Chapter 21 (named-open O5 in Section 6 of the audit ledger) carries this future-work.

Chapter 8 identifies which falsifiability surfaces exist: logical falsifiability via T81; operational falsifiability via AD1's coverage matrix; substrate-generality falsifiability via Chapter 20 (already routed via ST1 and SC1); long-horizon falsifiability surveillance via Chapter 21. Chapter 21 articulates the protocols by which each surface is exercised over time. The boundary is a methodological commitment: Chapter 8 makes the claims it can defend at the integrative-theorem layer, identifies the residual obligations, and routes them to the appropriate downstream chapter. This is the Principle of Layered Defense (§0.2) operating concretely.

## T81: Mutual Independence

Section 1 establishes the formal mutual-independence theorem of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ (T81). T81 is a logical-falsifiability result: for each axiom $A_i$ in $\{A1, A2, A3, A4\}$, there exists a model of the $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ machinery in which $A_i$ fails while the other three hold. The theorem establishes that each axiom is logically falsifiable in isolation---none is a derivative consequence of the conjunction of the others---and is the formal falsifiability foundation of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$.

The section is presented in six subsections. §1.1 supplies the formal statement and proof structure. §§1.2--1.5 supply the four single-axiom-failure witnesses, one per axiom. §1.6 distinguishes logical falsifiability from operational falsifiability and cross-references AD1 for the operational side.

### T81: formal statement and proof structure

::: theorem
**Theorem 8.1** (T81, Mutual Independence of A1--A4). *For each axiom $A_i$ in $\{A1, A2, A3, A4\}$, there exists a model $M_i$ of the $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ machinery---a substrate, surface, caller community, and projection family with declared $(O, K, R, R_{\mathrm{may}}, \Pi_X, \sim_X)$---such that $M_i$ satisfies $A_j$ for all $j \neq i$ but fails $A_i$.*
:::

The theorem asserts logical falsifiability of each axiom in isolation. Its proof structure is constructive: for each axiom, we construct (in §§1.2--1.5) a specific model in which that axiom fails while the others hold. Existence of the four witnesses establishes that no axiom is implied by the conjunction of the others---if $A_i$ were implied by $\{A_j : j \neq i\}$, then the $M_i$ witness (satisfying the latter and failing $A_i$) would be impossible.

The theorem is the formal falsifiability foundation of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$. Its significance is methodological as much as technical: a four-axiom system in which one axiom were a derivative consequence of the others would be either over-determined (one axiom carrying no independent content) or formally redundant. The mutual-independence theorem establishes that each of A1--A4 carries independent structural-honesty content not captured by the others. This is analogous to the metatheoretic discipline used when foundational systems are tested for redundancy or independence: the point is to show that a proposed axiom carries independent content rather than functioning as a disguised theorem of the remaining axioms.

The witnesses constructed below are minimal---each is designed to make the single-axiom-failure pattern as transparent as possible, drawing on Chapter 3's typed-object machinery without introducing new machinery. The witnesses are not intended to be operationally interesting; they are intended to be technically minimal demonstrations of logical falsifiability. Operational interest is a different property (treated in T82's witness-construction work for satisfiability and AD1's analysis of adversarial-declaration coverage). The clean separation between logical falsifiability (T81's burden) and operational falsifiability (AD1's burden) is the Principle of Layered Defense applied to the falsifiability question.

### Witness $M_1$: A1 fails, A2--A4 hold

Witness $M_1$ demonstrates that Axiom 1 can fail while A2, A3, A4 hold. Construction: consider a versioned-library substrate with two versions $v_t$ and $v_{t+1}$. At $v_t$, the public surface declares a function $f$ with type signature $S_t$. At $v_{t+1}$, the surface declares $f$ with type signature $S_{t+1}$, where $S_{t+1}$ is strictly incompatible with $S_t$ ($S_{t+1}$ requires an additional argument that $S_t$ did not require, with no corrigendum tagging this as a breaking change). The transition $v_t \to v_{t+1}$ violates Liskov-Wing version-subtyping with corrigenda discipline (Chapter 4 §1.1) [@liskov1994behavioral]. Axiom 1 fails: the surface evolution from $v_t$ to $v_{t+1}$ is neither behaviorally compatible nor corrigendum-tagged.

At $v_{t+1}$, however, the per-version structure remains honest. The declared $(O_{t+1}, K_{t+1}, R_{t+1})$ for $v_{t+1}$ correctly describes $v_{t+1}$'s behavior: $R_{t+1}(\mathrm{Surface}_{t+1}, \mathrm{Substrate}_{t+1})$ holds under $R_{t+1}$ drawn from the correspondence-relation family [@park1981concurrency; @milner1980calculus]. Axiom 2 holds at $v_{t+1}$ despite the dishonest evolution from $v_t$. The caller community at $v_{t+1}$ exhausts $R_{(t+1),\mathrm{may}}$ through the three discharge paths (handled / propagated as incomplete / proven unreachable) [@swamy2016fstar; @vazou2014refinement]. Axiom 3 holds at $v_{t+1}$. The projection family $\Pi_X$ at $v_{t+1}$ satisfies joint-domain consistency under $\sim_X$. Axiom 4 holds at $v_{t+1}$.

The witness establishes that A1 is not implied by the conjunction of A2, A3, A4 at any single version. A producer can be honest about its current behavior (A2, A3, A4 at $v_{t+1}$) while being dishonest about the relationship between its current and prior behavior (A1 from $v_t$ to $v_{t+1}$). This is the structural-honesty failure mode A1 was designed to expose, and it is distinct from any failure A2--A4 catches: A2--A4 operate within a single version, while A1 operates across versions.

### Witness $M_2$: A2 fails, A1, A3, A4 hold

Witness $M_2$ demonstrates that Axiom 2 can fail while A1, A3, A4 hold. Construction: consider a substrate at version $v_t$ where the public surface declares $(O_t, K_t, R_t)$ honestly with respect to $v_{t-1}$ (no breaking change without corrigendum, so A1 holds across the $v_{t-1} \to v_t$ transition). At $v_t$, however, the substrate's actual behavior does not satisfy $R_t(\mathrm{Surface}_t, \mathrm{Substrate}_t)$ under the declared $R_t$. The producer's declared correspondence relation says one thing about the substrate; the substrate's actual behavior says another. Axiom 2 fails at $v_t$.

The caller community at $v_t$ exhausts $R_{t,\mathrm{may}}$ through the three discharge paths---callers handle declared outcomes, propagate incompleteness, or supply unreachability certificates. Axiom 3 holds because the caller community discharges the outcomes represented in $R_{t,\mathrm{may}}$; the A2 failure is producer-side surface-substrate mismatch, not caller-side non-exhaustiveness. The projection family $\Pi_X$ at $v_t$ satisfies joint-domain consistency under $\sim_X$ [@maclane1994sheaves]; the projections cohere among themselves even though they collectively diverge from the substrate's actual structure. Axiom 4 holds.

The witness establishes that A2 is not implied by the conjunction of A1, A3, A4. A producer can have honest surface evolution (A1), correctly handled caller-side discharge (A3), and internally coherent projection family (A4) while still having a fundamental mismatch between its declared correspondence relation and its substrate's actual behavior (A2 failure). This is the per-version surface-substrate dishonesty A2 was designed to expose; it operates independently of the other axioms' coverage because the other axioms do not check the surface-substrate correspondence at the per-version level.

### Witness $M_3$: A3 fails, A1, A2, A4 hold

Witness $M_3$ demonstrates that Axiom 3 can fail while A1, A2, A4 hold. Construction: consider a substrate at version $v_t$ where the public surface declares $(O_t, K_t, R_t)$ honestly with respect to $v_{t-1}$ (A1 holds) and $R_t(\mathrm{Surface}_t, \mathrm{Substrate}_t)$ holds at $v_t$ (A2 holds). The verifier/caller regime constructs or relies on $R_{t,\mathrm{may}}$ as a conservative over-approximation under the declared over-approximation discipline. However, at least one caller in the caller community at $v_t$ consumes the substrate without exhausting $R_{t,\mathrm{may}}$: it handles only the most common outcomes, neither propagates remaining outcomes as incomplete nor supplies unreachability certificates for them. Axiom 3 fails.

The producer's behavior is otherwise honest. The projection family $\Pi_X$ at $v_t$ satisfies joint-domain consistency under $\sim_X$. Axiom 4 holds. The producer's surface and substrate are correctly aligned (A2) and the producer's evolution is corrigendum-disciplined (A1). The structural-honesty failure is on the caller side: the caller's discharge does not exhaust $R_{t,\mathrm{may}}$ through the three paths.

The witness establishes that A3 is not implied by the conjunction of A1, A2, A4. A producer can be entirely honest about its surface evolution, its current behavior, and its projection consistency while a caller community fails to honestly discharge its $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ obligations. The structural-honesty failure is caller-side, not producer-side; A3 is what catches it.

### Witness $M_4$: A4 fails, A1, A2, A3 hold

Witness $M_4$ demonstrates that Axiom 4 can fail while A1, A2, A3 hold. Construction: consider a substrate at version $v_t$ where the producer publishes a projection family $\Pi_X$ containing two projections $\pi_1$ and $\pi_2$ with non-empty joint domain $\mathrm{dom}(\pi_1) \cap \mathrm{dom}(\pi_2)$. At some substrate state $s$ in the joint domain, $\pi_1(s)$ and $\pi_2(s)$ fail to satisfy $\sim_X$---the two projections disagree about a jointly-projectable fact under the declared consistency relation. Axiom 4 fails.

The producer's surface evolution is corrigendum-disciplined (A1 holds across $v_{t-1} \to v_t$). The producer's surface-substrate consistency at $v_t$ holds under declared $(O_t, K_t, R_t)$---$R_t(\mathrm{Surface}_t, \mathrm{Substrate}_t)$ holds (A2). The caller community at $v_t$ exhausts $R_{t,\mathrm{may}}$ through the three discharge paths (A3). The structural-honesty failure is in the projection-family layer: two projections that should cohere under $\sim_X$ at the joint-domain state $s$ do not.

The witness establishes that A4 is not implied by the conjunction of A1, A2, A3. A producer can be entirely honest about its surface evolution, current behavior, and caller-side coverage while publishing a projection family that contains an internal inconsistency at a joint-domain state. The structural-honesty failure is in the projection-family layer, not the surface-substrate-caller layer; A4 is what catches it.

The four witnesses $M_1$, $M_2$, $M_3$, $M_4$ together complete the proof of T81: for each axiom $A_i$, the corresponding $M_i$ satisfies $A_j$ for all $j \neq i$ and fails $A_i$. No axiom is a derivative consequence of the conjunction of the others; each carries independent structural-honesty content. $\square$

### Logical falsifiability versus operational falsifiability

The four witnesses $M_1$, $M_2$, $M_3$, $M_4$ of §§1.2--1.5 collectively establish T81 (logical mutual independence). Each witness exists as a model of the $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ machinery satisfying three axioms and failing the fourth; no axiom is a derivative consequence of the others' conjunction.

T81 is a logical-falsifiability theorem. The four witnesses establish that each axiom can fail in principle while the others hold. The theorem does not, however, establish operational falsifiability---the property that the four axioms operationalize structurally-honest behavior in the practical sense of detecting dishonesty when it occurs in real artifacts. Operational falsifiability depends on ecosystem conditions: whether a caller community exists that exercises $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ against the producer's surface (without which A3 is structurally empty); whether the projection family contains multiple independent projections (without which A4 is structurally empty); whether the producer's surface evolves substantively over time (without which A1 has no transitions to evaluate); and whether the corrigenda discipline is operationally enforced rather than nominal.

The distinction is methodologically central. A producer who declares weak $(O, K, R)$ from inception, operates in an ecosystem without adversarial callers, declares a single-projection family that does not cross-check, and never substantively evolves its surface satisfies A1 trivially (no evolution to violate), A2 trivially (declared correspondence relation matches declared substrate behavior because both are weak), A3 trivially (no callers to exhaust $R_{\mathrm{may}}$), and A4 trivially (single projection cannot disagree with itself). Such a producer is satisfying A1--A4 logically; whether it is structurally honest in any operationally meaningful sense is a separate question, and the question turns on ecosystem conditions.

T81 establishes that the four axioms are not equivalent or derivative---each could fail while the others hold. AD1 (§4 of this chapter) takes up the operational-falsifiability question separately: under which ecosystem conditions does logical satisfaction of A1--A4 correspond to operational structural honesty, and under which ecosystem conditions does logical satisfaction admit trivial adversarial-declaration scenarios that $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ does not catch? The two questions---logical mutual independence and operational adversarial coverage---operate at different layers of the Principle of Layered Defense framework (§0.2). T81 settles the first; AD1 takes up the second.

The combination of T81 and AD1 is what positions $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ to be nontrivially falsifiable. T81 ensures that each axiom carries independent structural-honesty content; AD1 evaluates whether the axiom system as a whole is operationally falsifiable under named ecosystem conditions. Together they constitute the falsifiability foundation of the framework, with T82 supplying the consistency proof (the system is satisfiable, so falsifiability does not collapse into vacuity) and T83 supplying the empirical-relative adequacy argument (the system's classifications correspond to operational practitioner judgments across the named case set). This closes Chapter 8 §§0--1.

## T82: Consistency / Finite Witness System

Section 2 establishes Theorem 8.2 (T82): the consistency of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$. T82 is a formal satisfiability theorem---we construct a finite witness system $W$ satisfying A1, A2, A3, A4 simultaneously and thereby establish that the four-axiom system is logically satisfiable. The witness is drawn from SI1 (Bayyinah file-layer scanner) vocabulary [@arfeen2026bayyinah] to maximize compatibility with T83's adequacy argument while remaining small enough to be formally verified within the chapter. The section is presented in seven subsections: §2.1 supplies the witness construction; §2.2 supplies the substantive content; §§2.3--2.6 establish A1, A2, A3, A4 satisfaction in turn; §2.7 articulates the ecosystem assumptions under which the witness is operationally nontrivial and identifies the witness's limits.

### Finite witness construction

The finite witness is the tuple $W = (S, U, C, \Pi, \sim)$ where: $S$ is a finite substrate (file-scanning system over a finite set of file kinds); $U$ is a finite versioned surface (public API at two consecutive versions $S_0$, $S_1$); $C$ is a finite caller community (two callers exercising $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ against $U$); $\Pi$ is a finite projection family (three projections with explicit domains); and $\sim$ is a substrate-specific consistency relation (file-kind agreement under joint reading).

$W$ is finite under MP1.2's finite-default convention (Chapter 3 §1.2): $S$ has a finite number of substrate states; $U$ has two versions; $C$ has two callers; $\Pi$ has three projections; the consistency relation is a finite decidable predicate over projection outputs. The total structure is small enough to be formally verified by enumeration.

The witness construction draws on SI1 vocabulary [@arfeen2026bayyinah] without claiming to be SI1 in its full operational form. SI1's full scope covers 23 file kinds and 108 detection mechanisms; the T82 witness uses three file kinds $\{\mathrm{PDF}, \mathrm{TXT}, \mathrm{BIN}\}$ and three detection mechanisms to remain minimal. The witness is structurally faithful to SI1 (the projections from Chapter 7 §1.6 are present in reduced form; the version-evolution discipline matches Chapter 4 §1.1; the caller-side discharge follows Chapter 6 §1's three discharge paths; the projection consistency follows Chapter 7 §1's joint-domain discipline), but is intentionally simplified for verifiability.

### Witness substrate / surface / caller / projection setup

*Substrate $S$:* A file-scanning system over a finite universe of file blobs. Each blob has an intrinsic file-kind from the finite set $\{\mathrm{PDF}, \mathrm{TXT}, \mathrm{BIN}\}$, an intrinsic content-classification (manifest content versus latent content), and an intrinsic completeness status. The substrate state at each blob is the triple $(\mathrm{kind}, \mathrm{class}, \mathrm{complete})$.

*Surface $U$:* A versioned API with two versions $S_0$ and $S_1$. $S_0$ declares: $\mathrm{scan}(\mathrm{blob})$ returns a tuple $(\mathrm{kind}, \mathrm{class}, \mathrm{complete})$ under declared observer model $O_0 =$ "naked-eye file inspection at the kind layer," context set $K_0 =$ "file blobs of size up to 64MB," and correspondence relation $R_0 =$ "scan output matches intrinsic blob state under file-kind comparison." $S_1$ declares: $\mathrm{scan}(\mathrm{blob})$ returns the same tuple $(\mathrm{kind}, \mathrm{class}, \mathrm{complete})$ over the same context $K_1 = K_0$, but extends $R_0$ to include a parity-check provision for PDFs ($R_1 = R_0$ over all of $K_0$, with the additional PDF byte-identical parity check applied to the PDF subset of $K_0$). $S_1$ introduces $R_1$ as a strengthening of $R_0$ (more demanding correspondence relation), not a weakening: all $R_0$ commitments over $K_0$ are preserved in $R_1$. The version evolution from $S_0$ to $S_1$ is corrigendum-free: no claim is withdrawn, only added.

*Caller community $C$:* Two callers $C_1$ (a CI script that gates downstream processing on scan output) and $C_2$ (an audit tool that cross-references scan output against an external manifest). Both callers exercise $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ against the published surface; $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ is the verifier/caller-side conservative over-approximation of $R$, including the declared outcomes plus a small set of declared partial outcomes (*scan-incomplete*, *scan-failed*) per Chapter 6 §1.

*Projection family $\Pi$:* Three projections $\{\pi_{\mathrm{kind}}, \pi_{\mathrm{class}}, \pi_{\mathrm{complete}}\}$ each of which carries the substrate's intrinsic kind as a shared coordinate alongside its specific output: $\pi_{\mathrm{kind}}(b) = (\mathrm{kind}(b))$; $\pi_{\mathrm{class}}(b) = (\mathrm{kind}(b), \mathrm{class}(b))$; $\pi_{\mathrm{complete}}(b) = (\mathrm{kind}(b), \mathrm{complete}(b))$. Each projection has explicit domain: $\pi_{\mathrm{kind}}$ defined on all blobs in $K_0$; $\pi_{\mathrm{class}}$ defined on blobs the substrate has classified; $\pi_{\mathrm{complete}}$ defined on blobs the substrate has fully scanned. The shared kind coordinate makes the consistency relation well-defined: $\sim$ compares projection outputs on their shared kind coordinate.

*Consistency relation $\sim$:* For two projections $\pi_i$ and $\pi_j$ and a substrate state $s$ in their joint domain, $\pi_i(s) \sim \pi_j(s)$ iff the projections agree on file-kind under their joint reading. The relation is a finite decidable predicate over projection outputs.

### Witness satisfaction of A1

A1 requires Liskov-Wing version-subtyping with corrigenda discipline at the $S_0 \to S_1$ transition. We show A1 holds. The $S_1$ surface extends $S_0$'s correspondence relation by strengthening: $R_1$ includes $R_0$'s commitments plus the PDF parity check. No commitment from $S_0$ is withdrawn; the only changes are additions. Under the Liskov-Wing discipline [@liskov1994behavioral], strengthening the correspondence relation is behaviorally compatible with the prior version: a caller that depended on $R_0$ still receives $R_0$'s guarantees at $S_1$, plus additional guarantees that the caller may or may not use. No corrigendum is required because no prior claim is withdrawn. A1 holds.

### Witness satisfaction of A2

A2 requires per-version surface-substrate consistency under declared $(O_i, K_i, R_i)$ at each version. We show A2 holds at both $S_0$ and $S_1$.

At $S_0$: $R_0$ is the file-kind matching predicate. For every blob $b$ in $K_0$, $\mathrm{scan}(b)$ returns the intrinsic file-kind of $b$ (the scanner's three-file-kind detection mechanism is exhaustive over $\{\mathrm{PDF}, \mathrm{TXT}, \mathrm{BIN}\}$). Therefore $R_0(\mathrm{Surface}_{S_0}, \mathrm{Substrate}_{S_0})$ holds: the surface's declared scan output matches the substrate's intrinsic file-kind for every blob in $K_0$. A2 holds at $S_0$.

At $S_1$: $R_1$ is $R_0$ over $K_0$ plus the PDF parity check applied to the PDF subset of $K_0$. For PDF blobs in $K_0$, $\mathrm{scan}(b)$ returns the intrinsic kind plus a byte-identical parity assurance. The byte-identical assurance holds because the witness construction includes a PDF parity-check mechanism that reads the blob's raw bytes and emits the parity signal correctly. For TXT and BIN blobs in $K_0$, $R_1$ reduces to $R_0$ (no parity check claimed). Therefore $R_1(\mathrm{Surface}_{S_1}, \mathrm{Substrate}_{S_1})$ holds. A2 holds at $S_1$.

### Witness satisfaction of A3

A3 requires caller-side exhaustiveness over $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ with three discharge paths [@swamy2016fstar; @vazou2014refinement]. We show A3 holds for both callers $C_1$ and $C_2$.

$C_1$ (CI script): handles scan output by gating downstream processing on (kind, complete) tuples. For declared outcomes (kind $\in \{\mathrm{PDF}, \mathrm{TXT}, \mathrm{BIN}\}$ with complete = true), $C_1$ handles each kind with a specific downstream path. For declared partial outcomes (*scan-incomplete*, *scan-failed*), $C_1$ propagates them as incomplete upward via CI-pipeline status codes. $C_1$ has no proven-unreachable certificates because it does not claim any $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ outcome is impossible---it handles or propagates all $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ outcomes. The discharge is exhaustive over $R_{\mathrm{may}}$.

$C_2$ (audit tool): handles scan output by cross-referencing against an external manifest. For declared outcomes, $C_2$ records the cross-check result. For *scan-incomplete* outcomes, $C_2$ propagates the incompleteness into its audit log with a "deferred verification" annotation. $C_2$ supplies proven-unreachable certificates for outcomes that the audit tool's pre-conditions exclude (e.g., *scan-failed* cannot occur for blobs the audit tool has already verified as well-formed). The discharge is exhaustive over $R_{\mathrm{may}}$.

A3 holds for both callers, so the caller community discharges $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ exhaustively. A3 holds.

### Witness satisfaction of A4

A4 requires joint-domain projection consistency under $\sim$ [@maclane1994sheaves]. We show A4 holds.

Joint domains: $\mathrm{dom}(\pi_{\mathrm{kind}}) \cap \mathrm{dom}(\pi_{\mathrm{class}}) \cap \mathrm{dom}(\pi_{\mathrm{complete}})$ is the set of blobs the substrate has fully classified and scanned. For any blob $b$ in this multi-way joint domain, $\pi_{\mathrm{kind}}(b)$, $\pi_{\mathrm{class}}(b)$, $\pi_{\mathrm{complete}}(b)$ are all defined. The consistency relation $\sim$ requires that the projections agree on file-kind under their joint reading.

For each blob $b$ in the joint domain, the substrate's intrinsic file-kind is fixed. Each projection output carries the shared kind coordinate per §2.2: $\pi_{\mathrm{kind}}(b) = (\mathrm{kind}(b))$, $\pi_{\mathrm{class}}(b) = (\mathrm{kind}(b), \mathrm{class}(b))$, $\pi_{\mathrm{complete}}(b) = (\mathrm{kind}(b), \mathrm{complete}(b))$. The kind coordinate is computed from the same intrinsic blob state in each projection, so all three projections agree on the kind coordinate at every $b$ in their joint domain. The consistency relation $\sim$ holds at every blob in the joint domain.

The three projections agree on file-kind under joint reading because each projection's kind coordinate is computed from the same intrinsic blob state, and the substrate's intrinsic state is consistent within each blob. A4 holds at all blobs in the joint domain. Blobs outside the joint domain---partially classified or partially scanned---are outside A4's scope per Chapter 7 §1.4's joint-domain discipline.

The four satisfactions of §§2.3--2.6 together establish that $W$ satisfies A1, A2, A3, A4 simultaneously, yielding:

::: theorem
**Theorem 8.2** (T82, Consistency of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$). *The four-axiom system A1--A4 is logically consistent: there exists a finite witness $W = (S, U, C, \Pi, \sim)$ as constructed in §§2.1--2.2 such that $W$ satisfies A1, A2, A3, A4 simultaneously. $\square$*
:::

### Witness limits and explicit ecosystem assumptions

The witness $W$ is operationally nontrivial under specific ecosystem assumptions, which we make explicit. These assumptions are operational-nontriviality conditions per §0.3, not fifth axioms; they specify when the formal satisfiability T82 establishes has its intended structural-honesty interpretation.

*Caller diversity assumption.* The caller community $C$ contains two callers with distinct discharge patterns ($C_1$ gates downstream; $C_2$ cross-references). Without two callers, A3 could be trivially satisfied by a single caller that handles only the most common outcomes---the witness's A3 satisfaction would not test caller-side discharge against $R_{\mathrm{may}}$. The assumption is operational, not formal: A3 is satisfied formally with any caller community that exhausts $R_{\mathrm{may}}$, but the operational interpretation of A3 as a structural-honesty discipline requires caller diversity.

*Projection multiplicity assumption.* The projection family $\Pi$ contains three projections with overlapping but non-identical domains. Without multiple independent projections, A4 could be trivially satisfied by a single-projection family---the witness's A4 satisfaction would not test projection consistency. The assumption is operational, not formal.

*Substantive evolution assumption.* The $S_0 \to S_1$ transition involves a substantive change (the PDF parity check addition). Without substantive evolution, A1 would be trivially satisfied---the version chain would contain no transitions to evaluate. The assumption is operational.

*Corrigenda discipline exercised assumption.* The witness construction does not include any corrigenda (because $R_1$ strengthens $R_0$ without withdrawing prior claims). A more demanding witness would include a corrigendum event (e.g., a later $S_2$ that withdraws a portion of $R_1$ and tags the withdrawal as a corrigendum). The current witness is sufficient for T82 (it demonstrates A1--A4 satisfaction) but does not exercise the corrigenda discipline; full operational testing of A1 requires substrate evolution that includes corrigendum events. This is identified as a Chapter 21 falsification-protocol scope (named-open O5).

T82 establishes formal consistency through the explicit construction of $W$ satisfying A1--A4. The ecosystem assumptions explain when this witness avoids triviality in operational settings. Weakening these assumptions may reveal trivial-satisfaction surfaces that AD1 (§4) analyzes. The separation between formal consistency and operational nontriviality follows the Principle of Layered Defense (§0.2): T82 is a model-existence theorem at the formal-consistency layer; the operational interpretation of consistency is conditional on the named ecosystem conditions at the ecosystem-condition layer.

## T83: Definitional Adequacy

Section 3 establishes the definitional adequacy of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ relative to a named judgment-case set. T83 is an empirical-relative adequacy argument, not a context-free proof. The argument is analogous to the epistemic posture (§0.4) of adequacy arguments for ZFC, Peano arithmetic, and behavioral subtyping: adequacy is judged relative to operational practitioner judgments on a named set of cases, not provable in absolute terms.

The section is presented in seven subsections. §3.1 constructs the named judgment-case set with positive, negative, and boundary cases. §§3.2--3.4 supply the structured-interpretation mappings from SHV, Furqan, and Munafiq operational vocabulary to $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$'s declared-object vocabulary. §3.5 supplies the SI1--SI4 adequacy mapping. §3.6 identifies boundary cases and non-covered cases, routing residual adequacy concerns to Chapters 20 and 21. §3.7 articulates adequacy as relative-to-the-judgment-case-set, completing the empirical-relative discipline that §0.4 set up.

### Named judgment-case set construction

The judgment-case set $J = \{J_1, \ldots, J_m\}$ is constructed as follows. Each judgment case is a triple (substrate-scenario, expected-classification, axiom-classification): the substrate-scenario is a specific substrate-caller-projection scenario drawn from SI1--SI4; the expected-classification is how operational practitioners in the substrate's community would classify the scenario (honest, dishonest, or debatable); the axiom-classification is how A1--A4 classify the scenario under the substrate's declared $(O, K, R, R_{\mathrm{may}}, \Pi_X, \sim_X)$.

The case set must include three categories.

*Positive cases* (cases practitioners would classify as structurally honest): for each of SI1--SI4, at least three cases where the substrate operates correctly under its declared scope and practitioners would agree the scenario is structurally honest. Examples: SI1 with a complete file-kind detection across all scanned files; SI2 with a successfully type-checked program emitting no error diagnostics inconsistent with the type-check result; SI3 with a marker-calibrated model output consistent with the marker's confidence threshold; SI4 with a multi-layer attestation chain where all four substrates produce consistent attestations.

*Negative cases* (cases practitioners would classify as structurally dishonest): for each of SI1--SI4, at least three cases where the substrate exhibits a structural-honesty failure that practitioners would recognize. Examples: SI1 with an undeclared scan-incomplete that the surface treats as complete; SI2 with a successfully type-checked program emitting error diagnostics that contradict the type-check; SI3 with a marker-calibrated model output that fails the calibration threshold without diagnostic flagging; SI4 with a multi-layer attestation chain where one layer's attestation contradicts another.

*Boundary cases* (cases where practitioner judgment is debatable): for each of SI1--SI4, at least one boundary case where practitioners would disagree about whether the scenario is structurally honest. These boundary cases are not papered over---they are either classified by $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ with explicit rationale (the framework correctly captures the practitioner's judgment because of structural-honesty consideration $X$) or routed to Chapter 21 as future-work items.

The named judgment-case set $J$ is enumerated by identifier at the chapter level; detailed substrate evidence for each identifier is supplied by Chapters 13--16. The case identifiers are:

::: center
  ID range                 Case content
  ------------------------ ----------------------------------------------
  SI1-P1, SI1-P2, SI1-P3   three positive Bayyinah / file-layer cases
  SI1-N1, SI1-N2, SI1-N3   three negative Bayyinah / file-layer cases
  SI1-B1                   one boundary Bayyinah / file-layer case
  SI2-P1, SI2-P2, SI2-P3   three positive Furqan / language-layer cases
  SI2-N1, SI2-N2, SI2-N3   three negative Furqan / language-layer cases
  SI2-B1                   one boundary Furqan / language-layer case
  SI3-P1, SI3-P2, SI3-P3   three positive Munafiq / model-layer cases
  SI3-N1, SI3-N2, SI3-N3   three negative Munafiq / model-layer cases
  SI3-B1                   one boundary Munafiq / model-layer case
  SI4-P1, SI4-P2, SI4-P3   three positive supply-chain cases
  SI4-N1, SI4-N2, SI4-N3   three negative supply-chain cases
  SI4-B1                   one boundary supply-chain case
:::

This yields $|J| = 28$ judgment cases at the chapter level. Chapter 8 names the case identifiers and the classification obligations (positive cases should yield $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$-honest classification; negative cases should yield $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$-dishonest classification; boundary cases should yield either explicit-rationale classification or Chapter 21 routing); Chapters 13--16 supply the detailed substrate evidence for each case, and Chapter 21 maintains future expansion and falsification protocols for $J$ over time.

### SHV vocabulary mapping

The Structural-Honesty Verification framework [@arfeen2026shv] uses an operational vocabulary that the dissertation's axiom system must capture. The structured interpretation from SHV terms to $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ terms is: SHV "structural honesty" maps to A1--A4 satisfaction under declared $(O, K, R, R_{\mathrm{may}}, \Pi_X, \sim_X)$; SHV "surface-substrate distinction" maps to Chapter 3 §1's typed-object machinery for surfaces and substrates; SHV "attestation" maps to the producer's published claim that $R(\mathrm{Surface}, \mathrm{Substrate})$ holds under declared $(O, K, R)$; SHV "certified-incomplete" maps to the propagated-incompleteness path in A3's three discharge paths; SHV "four-substrate stack" [@arfeen2026shvsupplychain] maps to SI4 as the specific multi-layer attestation instance.

The mapping is a structured interpretation, not a semantic isomorphism. Each correspondence is justified against the named judgment-case set: for every positive SHV case in $J$ (cases SHV practitioners would classify as structurally honest), the $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ classification under the structured interpretation yields the same judgment; for every negative SHV case, the $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ classification yields structural dishonesty; for boundary cases, the $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ classification matches SHV practitioner judgment where rationale is explicit, and is identified as Chapter 21 future-work when practitioner judgment is genuinely indeterminate.

### Furqan vocabulary mapping

The Furqan language-layer type-checker [@ashraf2026furqan; @ashraf2026furqanproto] uses an operational vocabulary specific to compile-time verification. The structured interpretation: Furqan "build-time type-checker" maps to a producer-side mechanism evaluating $R$ at build-time under declared $(O, K, R)$; Furqan "structural-honesty surface contract" maps to the public surface's declared type signature; Furqan "compile-time guarantee" maps to A2's per-version surface-substrate consistency at build-time; Furqan "diagnostic emission" maps to a projection in $\Pi_X$ capturing the type-checker's diagnostic output; Furqan "type-check passing" maps to the consistency relation $\sim$ between the type-check projection and the build-time-success projection.

The mapping is a structured interpretation, justified against Furqan's judgment-case set drawn from SI2. Each Furqan case in $J$ is classified by the $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ structured interpretation consistently with Furqan practitioner judgment.

### Munafiq vocabulary mapping

The Munafiq Protocol [@arfeen2026munafiq] uses an operational vocabulary specific to model-layer evaluation. The structured interpretation: Munafiq "marker" maps to the producer's declared classification of model output (e.g., high-confidence, low-confidence); Munafiq "calibration" maps to $R$'s correspondence relation between marker and actual output reliability; Munafiq "four-process taxonomy" maps to the four process-types under which marker classification operates; Munafiq "four-layer detection" maps to a projection family $\Pi_X$ with four projections (marker, calibration, diagnosis, protocol-conformance); Munafiq "structural honesty in model output" maps to A1--A4 satisfaction across markers, calibrations, diagnoses, and protocol conformance.

The mapping is a structured interpretation, justified against Munafiq's judgment-case set drawn from SI3.

### SI1--SI4 adequacy mapping

The four worked substrate instances together test the adequacy argument across the case set. SI1 (Bayyinah file-scanner) operationally tests A1--A4 over file-layer substrates [@arfeen2026bayyinah]: for each judgment case in $J$ drawn from SI1, the $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ classification under SI1's declared $(O, K, R, R_{\mathrm{may}}, \Pi_X, \sim_X)$ matches practitioner judgment. SI2 (Furqan type-checker) operationally tests A1--A4 over language-layer substrates: for each judgment case in $J$ drawn from SI2, $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ matches practitioner judgment. SI3 (Munafiq Protocol) operationally tests A1--A4 over model-layer substrates: for each judgment case in $J$ drawn from SI3, $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ matches practitioner judgment. SI4 (Supply-chain stack) operationally tests A1--A4 over multi-layer attestation substrates [@sigstore2021; @torres2019intoto; @slsa2023]: for each judgment case in $J$ drawn from SI4, $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ matches practitioner judgment.

The adequacy argument is positive relative to the named case set $J$: for each case identifier named in §3.1, Chapter 8 states the expected $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ classification (positive cases should yield $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$-honest classification under the substrate's declared $(O, K, R, R_{\mathrm{may}}, \Pi_X, \sim_X)$; negative cases should yield $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$-dishonest classification; boundary cases should yield either explicit-rationale classification or Chapter 21 routing). Chapters 13--16 supply the detailed substrate-specific evidence for each case identifier. The present chapter establishes the structured adequacy claim at the integrative level; the case-study chapters carry the detailed evidentiary burden.

### Boundary cases and non-covered cases

Several types of cases are not papered over but explicitly identified as future-work, preserving the Chapter 8 / Chapter 21 boundary established in §0.5.

*Boundary cases within the case set.* For each of SI1--SI4, at least one boundary case exists where practitioner judgment is debatable. Examples: an SI1 boundary case is a partially-classified file where the scanner emits scan-incomplete but the file-kind detection is complete; practitioners disagree whether scan-incomplete on classification should propagate to the file-kind layer. An SI2 boundary case is a successfully type-checked program emitting warning-level diagnostics consistent with the type-check; practitioners disagree whether warning-level diagnostics constitute a structural-honesty surface. These boundary cases are classified by $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ under explicit rationale where possible; where rationale is debatable, the case is routed to Chapter 21 as future-work.

*Cases outside the case set.* T83 makes no claim about cases not in $J$. Cases outside $J$ that would be relevant to adequacy testing (cases from substrates not yet worked out in SI1--SI4, cases from substrate types that do not exist yet in current operational practice) are explicitly out of T83's scope. The adequacy argument is relative to $J$, not absolute. New substrate types are routed to Chapter 20 (substrate-generalization open problem, ST1 and SC1 in Section 3 and Section 5 of the audit ledger).

*Cases the framework does not yet handle adequately.* If a case lies outside $J$ (e.g., a case from a substrate type not yet worked out in SI1--SI4, or a case from a substrate type that does not exist yet in current operational practice), it does not refute T83 but may motivate Chapter 20 expansion (substrate-generalization open problem) or Chapter 21 expansion (falsification protocols and judgment-case set evolution). If a case lies inside $J$ and $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ diverges from practitioner judgment without explicit rationale, that is evidence against T83 for the current case set and must be recorded as a definitional-adequacy gap. T83's falsifiability at the empirical-relative layer of the Principle of Layered Defense (§0.2) requires that inside-$J$ divergence be treated as falsification, not as future-work; the framework's structural-honesty discipline applies recursively to T83 itself.

### Adequacy as relative, not absolute

T83's definitional-adequacy argument is empirical-relative to the named judgment-case set $J$. The argument does not establish absolute adequacy in a context-free sense. The structurally honest claim T83 makes is:

::: theorem
**Theorem 8.3** (T83, Definitional Adequacy of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ relative to $J$). *For every judgment case $J_k$ in the named judgment-case set $J$ (constructed per §3.1 with positive, negative, and boundary cases drawn from SI1--SI4), the structured interpretation from operational vocabulary (SHV / Furqan / Munafiq, per §§3.2--3.4) to $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$'s declared-object vocabulary classifies $J_k$ consistently with operational practitioner judgment for that substrate. The argument is empirical-relative to $J$ and does not establish absolute adequacy. $\square$*
:::

Two qualifications make the relative character explicit.

First, the adequacy claim is relative to $J$. Cases outside $J$ are out of scope. The framework's adequacy may need extension or revision for new judgment cases that emerge in operational practice; this is part of the framework's expected falsifiability surface at the definitional-adequacy layer of the Principle of Layered Defense (§0.2). The corrigenda discipline mechanism (Chapter 4 §1.1's apparatus applied recursively to the framework itself) provides the path for the framework to evolve as the judgment-case set evolves.

Second, the adequacy claim is relative to operational practitioner judgment as it currently exists. Practitioner judgment itself evolves: new technologies create new artifact types whose honesty / dishonesty intuitions were not anticipated; legal and regulatory regimes redefine adequate disclosure; cultural shifts change what practitioners mean by honest. T83's adequacy is judged against current practitioner judgment for the named case set; it does not claim adequacy against future practitioner judgment under conditions that do not yet exist. Long-horizon dynamics of practitioner-judgment evolution are routed to Chapter 21 (falsification protocols, named-open O5).

The relative-not-absolute framing is analogous to the epistemic posture of adequacy arguments for formal systems such as ZFC, Peano arithmetic, and behavioral subtyping (§0.4): adequacy is argued relative to the intended domain and judgment practices, not proven in a context-free sense. T83 makes the empirically-defensible adequacy claim available to the framework while acknowledging the relativity explicitly. This closes Chapter 8 §§2--3.

## AD1: Adversarial-Declaration Coverage

Section 4 evaluates the operational adversarial-declaration coverage of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ (AD1). AD1 is the fourth integrative obligation of Chapter 8: where T81 establishes logical falsifiability (each axiom can fail while the others hold) and T82 establishes formal consistency (the system is satisfiable) and T83 establishes definitional adequacy (the system corresponds to operational practitioner judgments across a named case set), AD1 evaluates whether the four-axiom system is operationally falsifiable under adversarial or weak declarations of the axiom-relativized objects, and under which ecosystem conditions such trivial satisfaction becomes detectable or structurally blocked. AD1 evaluates coverage; it does not prove universal robustness. The structurally honest result of AD1 is a disclosure of which weak-declaration / weak-ecosystem scenarios $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ exposes, which remain trivial-satisfaction holes, and which residual risks must be routed to Chapter 21.

The section is presented in nine subsections. §§4.1--4.4 supply the four weak-declaration scenarios (weak $(O, K, R)$, weak $R_{\mathrm{may}}$, weak $\Pi_X$, weak $\sim_X$) as inputs to the coverage analysis. §§4.5--4.6 supply the two principal ecosystem-failure scenarios (private / no-caller ecosystem; single-projection ecosystem) as conditions in the analysis. §4.7 synthesizes the cross-axiom coverage matrix as the disclosure mechanism for evaluating which axioms expose which scenarios under which ecosystem conditions. §4.8 takes on emergent misappropriation as a partial-falsifiability surface harder than authored adversarial declaration. §4.9 routes residual risks to Chapter 21.

### Weak $(O, K, R)$ scenario: narrow operational scope from inception

The first adversarial-declaration scenario: a producer declares weak $(O, K, R)$ from inception. Narrow observer model $O$ that observes only the public surface API without probing implementation behavior; narrow context set $K$ that excludes meaningful workloads or boundary conditions; trivial correspondence relation $R$ that reduces to equality of declared values without substantive structural correspondence. The producer satisfies A2 trivially because $R$ is too weak to require anything substantive of the surface-substrate relationship.

A1 is structurally silent on this scenario. A1 governs surface evolution; it does not govern the declared starting point. A producer who declares weak $(O, K, R)$ at $v_0$ and never narrows the declaration is unconstrained by A1's corrigenda discipline, since no claim is being withdrawn. The asymmetry between evolution and inception is one of the most consequential structural features of AX-SH's coverage analysis.

Whether A3 or A4 expose this scenario depends on ecosystem conditions. A3 may expose weak $(O, K, R)$ if the verifier/caller community's $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ is genuinely broader than the producer's declared $R$ and the caller community exercises that breadth (the discharge-path obligations force the producer to engage with outcomes the weak declaration excludes). A4 may expose weak $(O, K, R)$ if the projection family $\Pi_X$ contains projections that cross-check the surface-substrate relationship under a $\sim_X$ broader than the trivial declared $R$. Without these ecosystem conditions, weak $(O, K, R)$ goes uncaught --- the producer satisfies the four axioms while operating at a scope that practitioners would not recognize as structurally honest.

### Weak $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ scenario: under-declared possible outcomes

The second adversarial-declaration scenario: a publicly relied-on $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ --- whether producer-specified, verifier-published, or caller-surface --- is weak or under-approximating. $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ is close to $R$: the declared set of possible outcomes is barely broader than the declared set of intended outcomes, leaving genuine partial outcomes outside the declared possible set. A3 callers can only discharge outcomes that the verifier/caller regime represents in $R_{\mathrm{may}}$; outcomes excluded from $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ are simply not part of A3's evaluation. Under-approximating $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ makes A3 trivially satisfied: callers exhaust a thin $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ through the three discharge paths because there is little to discharge.

A2 is structurally silent on this scenario (A2 evaluates $R$, not $R_{\mathrm{may}}$). A1 may expose this scenario if $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ has been published and is subsequently narrowed without corrigendum, but a publicly relied-on $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ that is under-approximating at inception and never narrowed is unconstrained by A1.

The ecosystem condition that exposes weak $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ is adversarial-caller probing: callers who exercise the surface against actual operational workloads and encounter outcomes outside the declared $R_{\mathrm{may}}$. The encountered outcome creates a discharge-path obligation that the publicly relied-on declaration cannot satisfy, surfacing the gap between declared $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ and operational reality. Without diverse adversarial callers, weak $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ goes uncaught.

### Weak $\Pi_X$ scenario: single-projection or non-cross-checking projection family

The third adversarial-declaration scenario: a producer declares a projection family $\Pi_X = \{\pi_1\}$ (a single projection, against which A4's pairwise consistency check has no other projection to compare), or a projection family whose projections conveniently align with the producer's preferred declarations without cross-checking. A4 is trivially satisfied: a single projection cannot disagree with itself, and conveniently-aligned projections produce consistent outputs even when the underlying substrate diverges from the declarations.

A1 is structurally silent on this scenario for the same reason as in §4.1: the projection family is declared at inception, and A1 governs evolution. A2 may expose this scenario if the declared $R$ is broader than what the weak projection family can support (the surface-substrate consistency claim outruns the projection family's evidential support). A3 may expose this scenario if a caller requires multiple projection outputs and the weak $\Pi_X$ does not supply them.

The ecosystem condition that exposes weak $\Pi_X$ is projection multiplicity *and* independence: multiple required projections drawn from independent observation regimes such that their joint-domain consistency under $\sim_X$ is a substantive test. Without projection multiplicity and independence, weak $\Pi_X$ goes uncaught.

### Weak $\sim_X$ scenario: trivial consistency relation

The fourth adversarial-declaration scenario: a producer declares a trivially-satisfied $\sim_X$ --- the consistency relation everything satisfies, or a consistency relation tailored to the producer's preferred projections so that the declared projections always satisfy it. A4 is trivially satisfied under trivial $\sim_X$ because the consistency check imposes no substantive constraint.

A2 may expose this scenario if the declared $R$ requires correspondence beyond what the trivial $\sim_X$ tolerates (the surface-substrate consistency claim is stronger than the projection consistency the trivial $\sim_X$ permits). A1 is silent on inception. A3 is silent on $\sim_X$ choice directly, though caller-side probing may surface inconsistencies that the trivial $\sim_X$ should have caught.

The ecosystem condition that exposes weak $\sim_X$ is an independent benchmark for the consistency relation --- for example, a substrate domain where practitioner consensus on $\sim_X$ exists (such as arithmetic identity for double-entry bookkeeping, or stemmatic consistency for textual preservation philology). Without an independent benchmark for $\sim_X$, weak $\sim_X$ goes uncaught.

### Private / no-caller ecosystem scenario

The first ecosystem-failure scenario: the substrate operates in a private setting without an adversarial caller community, or with only callers that operate within the under-declared scope. A3 is structurally empty in this case --- there are no callers exercising $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ against the surface, so the caller-side exhaustiveness condition is vacuously satisfied regardless of declared $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ content.

The scenario is not a violation of A3; A3 is satisfied formally. The scenario is an ecosystem-condition failure that makes A3's operational interpretation as a structural-honesty discipline vacuous. The substrate may satisfy all four axioms formally while operating in an ecosystem that does not exercise the structural-honesty discipline. The ecosystem-condition catalog from §0.3 names caller diversity as one of the operational-nontriviality conditions; the private-ecosystem scenario is precisely the failure of that condition.

The condition that restores operational nontriviality is the existence of a populated caller community whose $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ obligations actually probe the surface's claimed scope. This condition is operational, not formal: it is a property of the substrate's environment, not a property of the substrate's declarations. The ecosystem-condition catalog is not a fifth axiom (§0.3); it is the catalog of conditions under which the formal axioms have their intended structural-honesty interpretation.

### Single-projection ecosystem scenario

The second ecosystem-failure scenario: the substrate's projection family lacks multiplicity, or the projections are correlated (all draw from the same underlying source, providing no cross-check). A4 is structurally empty in this case --- the joint-domain consistency check has no substantive content because the projections do not independently constrain each other.

The scenario again is not a violation of A4; A4 is satisfied formally (trivially, in the single-projection case; correlatedly, in the correlated-projection case). The scenario is an ecosystem-condition failure that makes A4's operational interpretation vacuous. The ecosystem-condition catalog names projection multiplicity *and* projection independence as the conditions under which A4 has its structural-honesty interpretation.

The condition that restores operational nontriviality is the substrate's having multiple independently-grounded projection mechanisms that genuinely cross-check. As with caller diversity in §4.5, this is operational rather than formal; the framework prescribes the ecosystem-condition catalog without adding ecosystem conditions to the formal axiom set.

### Cross-axiom coverage matrix

Sections §§4.1--4.4 supply four weak-declaration scenarios; §§4.5--4.6 supply two principal ecosystem-failure scenarios. The cross-axiom coverage matrix synthesizes the coverage analysis: rows are weak-declaration scenarios, columns are ecosystem conditions (positively named, so the matrix evaluates exposure under the named conditions rather than under the failure of conditions), and each cell either specifies which axiom exposes the scenario under that ecosystem condition or admits the cell as a residual hole.[^1]

The matrix is the structural-honesty disclosure mechanism for evaluating $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$'s adversarial coverage. Each cell answers the question: "Under ecosystem condition $E$, which axiom is designed to expose adversarial scenario $S$?" Cells that name an axiom describe the mechanism by which the axiom engages the scenario; cells that admit residual holes acknowledge the limits of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$'s coverage.

::: center
  Scenario \\ Ecosystem     Adversarial caller diversity                                                                        Projection multiplicity & independence                                             Evolutionary pressure on surface
  ------------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Weak $(O, K, R)$          A3 may expose: callers probe outside declared scope and surface $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ gaps             A4 may expose: independent projections force wider scope under $\sim_X$            A1 may expose: substantive change forces corrigenda discipline to engage
  Weak $R_{\mathrm{may}}$   A3 is designed to expose: diverse callers exhaust $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ against actual surface usage   A4 may expose: projection captures under-declared partial outcomes                 A1 may expose: $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ narrowing across versions becomes a corrigendum event
  Weak $\Pi_X$              A3 may expose: caller requires multiple projection outputs                                          A4 is designed to expose: projection multiplicity directly forces cross-check      A1 may expose: $\Pi_X$ narrowing across versions becomes a corrigendum event
  Weak $\sim_X$             A3 may expose: caller's expected consistency relation diverges from declared $\sim_X$               A4 may expose: independent projections disagree under producer's chosen $\sim_X$   A1 may expose: $\sim_X$ change across versions becomes a corrigendum event
:::

The matrix's positive cells describe exposure mechanisms, not guaranteed detections. "A3 may expose" means that A3's caller-side exhaustiveness obligation engages the scenario under the named ecosystem condition; "A3 is designed to expose" means that the named ecosystem condition directly forces the axiom into engagement with the scenario; in neither case does the cell claim that detection is guaranteed. Whether engagement results in detection depends on the substrate-specific particulars. Detection is a Chapter 13--16 case-study question evaluated in the substrate-specific judgment cases of $J$; AD1.7 supplies the analytical structure for that evaluation, not the substrate-specific results.

The matrix uses three ecosystem-condition columns (adversarial caller diversity, projection multiplicity & independence, evolutionary pressure on surface) rather than the four ecosystem assumptions enumerated in §2.7 (caller diversity, projection multiplicity, substantive evolution, corrigenda discipline exercised). The reconciliation is that corrigenda discipline exercised is not a separate matrix column; it is the activation condition for the evolutionary-pressure column, because A1 only becomes operationally nontrivial when substantive evolution is paired with actually exercised corrigenda discipline. Substantive evolution without corrigenda discipline produces a version chain without enforceable structural-honesty commitments; corrigenda discipline without substantive evolution has no transitions to discipline. The two assumptions activate the matrix's evolutionary-pressure column jointly.

The matrix's residual-hole cells are the cells where no axiom in the matrix's columns is designed to expose the scenario. Specifically: when the ecosystem provides none of the conditions in the columns (no adversarial callers, no projection multiplicity, no evolutionary pressure), no axiom in $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ is designed to expose any weak-declaration scenario. A producer who from inception declares weak $(O, K, R)$, weak $R_{\mathrm{may}}$, weak $\Pi_X$, and weak $\sim_X$, operates in an ecosystem without adversarial callers, with a single-projection family, and without surface evolution, satisfies A1--A4 trivially without operational structural honesty. This is the canonical adversarial-declaration trivial-satisfaction scenario, and it is a residual hole disclosed by AD1.

The disclosure of the residual hole is structural-honesty about $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$'s coverage. The framework does not claim that A1--A4 satisfaction is sufficient for operational structural honesty in all ecosystem conditions; the framework claims that A1--A4 satisfaction is necessary, and that under the named ecosystem conditions, A1--A4 also exposes specific adversarial-declaration scenarios. The residual hole is not a refutation of the formal A1--A4 system, but it is a disclosed limitation of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$'s operational sufficiency under weak ecosystem conditions.

### Emergent misappropriation as partial-falsifiability surface

Adversarial-declaration scenarios in §§4.1--4.7 are authored: a producer or verifier makes a specific weak declaration with knowledge that the declaration is weak. A structurally distinct and harder case is *emergent misappropriation*: scope-misdeclaration by honest future users extending $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$'s scope through legitimate intellectual labor across decades, without bad faith. A historical analogy from the reception of scientific frameworks may be introduced in a later revision if cited and carefully framed; Chapter 8's AD1 argument does not depend on that analogy.

Emergent misappropriation operates differently from authored adversarial declaration. The producer does not intentionally weaken declarations; future users extend the declarations beyond their original scope through accumulated intellectual labor --- pedagogical synthesis, theological elaboration, institutional embedding. By the time the misappropriation becomes visible, the framework's scope-as-used has drifted from the framework's scope-as-declared, and the drift was authored by no specific party.

The framework's response distinguishes recoverable from irrecoverable cases. *Recoverable cases:* the misappropriation has not yet become load-bearing in operational practice and can be corrigenda-tagged via A1's discipline --- the framework's authoritative version chain can append a corrigendum naming the misappropriation, withdrawing the appropriated scope, and restoring the original declared scope. *Irrecoverable cases:* the misappropriation has become load-bearing operational practice before being corrigenda-tagged, such that the framework's appropriated scope is the de facto framework in operational use, and corrigenda-tagging at the authoritative version cannot retroactively reach the operational practice that has adopted the appropriated scope.

The boundary between recoverable and irrecoverable is dynamic and substrate-specific. $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ plus the corrigenda discipline bounds the damage if corrigenda are exercised in time, but cannot retroactively fix history once misappropriation is deeply entrenched. The framework explicitly acknowledges this limit: AD1.8 evaluates emergent misappropriation as a partial-falsifiability surface, with the surveillance mechanisms by which such misappropriation is detected routed to Chapter 21 (long-horizon falsification-protocol work). Chapter 8 does not solve emergent-misappropriation surveillance; it names the case and the recoverable / irrecoverable boundary.

### Residual risks routed to Chapter 21

AD1's analysis is partial-by-design. The coverage matrix discloses what the four axioms are designed to expose under named ecosystem conditions; it does not claim universal robustness across all conditions or all adversarial patterns. Several categories of residual risk are explicitly routed to Chapter 21 (falsification protocols; named-open O5 in Section 6 of the audit ledger) rather than absorbed into Chapter 8's burden.

*Long-horizon sociotechnical dynamics.* How $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$-adopting communities maintain corrigenda discipline across decades, how the judgment-case set $J$ evolves as operational practice drifts, how ecosystem conditions hold or fail under institutional pressure: all are long-horizon questions that Chapter 21 carries.

*Monitoring mechanisms for emergent misappropriation.* The recoverable / irrecoverable boundary in §4.8 is meaningful only if emergent misappropriation can be detected in time to apply corrigenda. The surveillance mechanisms by which such detection occurs --- community-level review practices, comparative-vocabulary analysis, formal monitoring protocols --- are Chapter 21 work.

*Concrete falsification protocols for the dissertation's load-bearing claims.* T81 (logical falsifiability), T82 (consistency), T83 (adequacy relative to $J$), and AD1 (adversarial coverage) name the falsifiability surfaces at the integrative-theorem layer. Chapter 21 articulates the protocols by which each surface is exercised over time --- what counts as evidence for or against each theorem, how the evidence is collected, how the framework responds to evidence of falsification.

*Adversarial-pattern emergence on century scale.* New adversarial-declaration patterns will emerge as the framework is adopted and adversaries become motivated. The coverage matrix names current known patterns; future patterns are Chapter 21's surveillance burden, with the framework's expected response being matrix-extension under corrigenda discipline.

AD1.9 closes the AD1 analysis with the residual-risk disclosure: the framework names what it does not solve, what it routes forward to Chapter 21, and what the future-work burden looks like. The disclosure is structural-honesty about the framework's scope, not a hedge against its commitments. This closes Chapter 8 §4 and Chapter 8 as a whole.

The four integrative theorems established by Chapter 8 jointly evaluate the four-axiom system supplied by Chapters 4--7.
