T81 (Theorem 8.1) establishes mutual independence: each axiom is logically falsifiable while the others hold, demonstrating that no axiom is a derivative consequence of the conjunction of the others. T82 (Theorem 8.2) establishes formal consistency: a finite witness drawn from SI1 vocabulary satisfies A1--A4 simultaneously, demonstrating that the axiom system is satisfiable. T83 (Theorem 8.3) establishes definitional adequacy relative to the named judgment-case set $J$ of twenty-eight cases (SI1-P1 through SI4-B1): the structured-interpretation mappings from SHV, Furqan, and Munafiq operational vocabulary to $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$'s declared-object vocabulary classify the cases in $J$ consistently with operational practitioner judgment, with detailed substrate evidence supplied by Chapters 13--16 and the boundary cases routed to Chapter 21 as required. AD1 evaluates adversarial-declaration coverage: the cross-axiom coverage matrix discloses which weak-declaration scenarios $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ exposes under which named ecosystem conditions, names the residual-hole scenarios where no axiom is designed to expose, and routes emergent-misappropriation surveillance plus long-horizon falsification protocols to Chapter 21.

The Principle of Layered Defense (§0.2) operates concretely across these four results. T81 sits at the logical-falsifiability layer. T82 sits at the formal-consistency / model-existence layer. T83 sits at the empirical-relative-to-named-cases layer. AD1 sits at the operational-falsifiability-under-named-ecosystem-conditions layer. Each result is argued at its proper layer with explicit acknowledgment of what the layer's argument establishes and what it does not. This is the integrative evaluation Chapter 8 was tasked to perform; the four-axiom theory of structural honesty supplied by Chapters 4--7 has now been tested for the four properties a structurally-honest theory must have.

::: summary
**Integrative Summary 1**. *Chapter 8 completes the integrative evaluation of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ at the statement-level theory's current scope. T81 establishes that A1--A4 are mutually independent at the logical-falsifiability layer. T82 establishes that the four-axiom system is formally consistent by constructing a finite witness satisfying A1--A4 simultaneously at the formal model-existence layer. T83 establishes definitional adequacy relative to the named twenty-eight-case judgment set $J$ at the empirical-relative layer, while preserving the falsifiability of that adequacy claim through the inside-$J$ versus outside-$J$ distinction. AD1 evaluates operational falsifiability under named ecosystem conditions at the operational-falsifiability layer and discloses the residual trivial-satisfaction hole that obtains under weak declarations together with weak ecosystem conditions. Thus $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ has not been proven universally robust; it has been shown to be mutually independent, satisfiable, definitionally adequate relative to $J$, and operationally falsifiable under named ecosystem conditions with explicit residual-hole disclosure. Long-horizon falsification protocols, emergent-misappropriation surveillance, substrate-generalization across substrate types beyond SI1--SI4, and decidability of the axiom-relativized objects are routed to Chapters 10, 20, and 21 as named-open obligations.*

## §1.0 Role and scope

A structural-honesty claim about a system can be made, checked, and conveyed; and the layer at which each of these happens is not the same. This chapter formalizes a distinction that Chapter 1 §3 introduced informally: that a claim of the form "system $S$ satisfies axiom $A_i$" lives simultaneously at three layers --- a *truth* layer of mathematical fact, a *verification* layer of checking procedure, and a *transmission* layer of conveyance infrastructure --- and that these three layers stand in a strict dependency relation that runs in one direction only.

The chapter's purpose is to make that three-layer architecture precise enough to carry weight in the chapters that follow. Chapter 10's central result --- that the verification of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ is survivable across the cryptographic transitions of the coming decades, including the post-quantum transition --- is a claim about *which layer* the fragility of cryptography belongs to. That claim cannot even be stated cleanly until the truth, verification, and transmission layers have been separated and their dependency direction established. Chapter 9 supplies that scaffolding; Chapter 10 builds the survivability theorem on it.

The scope of this chapter is the formal architecture: the three layer definitions (§§1.1--1.3), the dependency-direction theorem and its statement (§1.4), the substrate-binding properties that distinguish the layers (§1.5), the residence of the $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ satisfaction predicates across the three layers (§1.6), and the practical consequences for software supply-chain attestation (§1.7). Two topics are deliberately out of scope for this chapter and routed forward: the detailed cryptographic-primitive analysis of the transmission layer under transition pressure (Chapters 12 and 17), and the information-theoretic strengthening of the verification layer through independent re-derivation (Chapter 11). The chapter depends on the four axioms as stated in Chapters 4--7, whose satisfaction predicates are the truth-layer objects this chapter places.

## §1.1 The truth layer

The *truth layer* is the layer of mathematical facts about a system: whether each axiom holds of it. For an axiom $A_i \in \{\mathrm{A1}, \mathrm{A2}, \mathrm{A3}, \mathrm{A4}\}$ with satisfaction predicate $\Pi_{A_i}$, the truth-layer claim is the proposition $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$ --- the assertion that $A_i$ holds of $S$. This is a proposition about mathematical objects: the system $S$ and the axiom $A_i$ as defined in Chapters 4--7. Its content does not mention any verifier, any procedure, or any attestation.

Two properties distinguish the truth layer. The first is *substrate-independence*: the truth value of $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$ is fixed by $S$ and $A_i$ alone, and carries no parameter ranging over the computational substrate of any procedure that might evaluate it. Whether $A_i$ holds of $S$ is not a fact about software, or about any particular machine; it is a fact about the mathematical objects the axiom constrains. The second property is *non-decay*: so long as $S$ and $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ remain specifications of record, the truth value of $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$ does not change with time. The cryptographic transitions that will, over decades, retire one signature scheme in favor of another (§1.3) operate at a different layer entirely and cannot alter a truth-layer proposition. A claim that was true of $S$ under $A_i$ remains true of $S$ under $A_i$ regardless of what becomes of the infrastructure that once conveyed it.

It is worth stating plainly what the truth layer is not. It is not a claim that anyone has checked $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$, nor that anyone could. It is the bare mathematical fact, prior to and independent of any act of verification. The remaining two layers are precisely the layers at which checking and conveyance enter.

## §1.2 The verification layer

The *verification layer* is the layer of procedures by which an external party establishes that an axiom holds. A verification procedure $V_i$ is an algorithm that, given a system $S$ and an axiom $A_i$, returns "verified" if and only if $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$ holds, within the decidable fragment characterized in Chapter 10. The qualifier matters: $V_i$ is not claimed to decide $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$ in full generality, but to decide it within the finite-default fragment established as a standing convention in Chapter 3 §7, producing a finite witness of satisfaction or of violation in the manner of Chapter 8 §2's Theorem T82.

Two properties distinguish the verification layer. The first is that $V_i$ is *substrate-bound but not cryptographically-bound*. It is substrate-bound in the trivial and unavoidable sense that an algorithm must run somewhere: current implementations run on software, and future implementations may run on other computational substrates. But $V_i$'s *correctness* is invariant across any substrate that faithfully implements its algorithm --- correctness is a property of the algorithm, not of the silicon --- and, crucially, $V_i$'s correctness does not rest on any cryptographic-hardness assumption. The verification procedure is a faithful implementation of the predicate $\Pi_{A_i}$; it is not a cryptographic protocol whose soundness depends on the difficulty of factoring or of computing discrete logarithms. The second property is that $V_i$ is *finite-witness producing*: by the Chapter 8 §2 convention, a run of $V_i$ yields a finite object that exhibits the satisfaction or the violation, and that another party can re-check.

The verification layer is where the act of establishing a truth-layer claim takes place. It is bound to a substrate in the weak sense that computation must be embodied, but it is not bound to cryptography, and this independence is the hinge on which Chapter 10's survivability result turns.

## §1.3 The transmission layer

The *transmission layer* is the layer of cryptographic and infrastructural primitives by which verification results are conveyed between parties. Its constituents are the familiar machinery of contemporary software supply-chain attestation: digital signatures (as in sigstore's signing of artifacts), attestation formats (as in in-toto's binding of a claim to the inputs that produced it), provenance frameworks (as in SLSA's levels of build integrity), and the trust roots on which these depend --- certificate authorities, key servers, and transparency logs.

A transmission-layer mechanism conveys a claim of the form "party $P$ verified that $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$." It does not itself establish $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$. A signature binds a claim to a signing principal; verifying that signature establishes the *provenance* of the claim --- that $P$ asserted it --- not the *truth* of the claim. This distinction is the substance of the dependency-direction theorem stated in the next subsection, and its sharpest illustration is the cryptographically valid signature on a false claim: such an object is perfectly sound at the transmission layer and entirely silent about whether the claim it carries is true.

The property that distinguishes the transmission layer is *cryptographic contingency*. The trust a transmission-layer attestation commands depends on a cryptographic-hardness assumption, and such assumptions are not permanent. They are subject to multi-decade transitions: the historical migration from SHA-1 to SHA-2 retired a hash function whose collision resistance had failed, and the anticipated post-quantum transition will, when large-scale quantum computation arrives, retire the public-key schemes whose security rests on the hardness of factoring and discrete logarithms. The transmission layer is the layer at which this fragility lives, and §1.7 develops what follows from confining it there.

## §1.4 Theorem 9.1 (Layer Dependency Direction)

The three layers are not symmetric. They stand in a strict dependency relation that runs in one direction.

> **Theorem 9.1 (Layer Dependency Direction).** *The truth layer $T$, verification layer $V$, and transmission layer $\mathrm{Tr}$ satisfy the strict dependency relation $\mathrm{Tr} \to V \to T$, in which each layer depends on the one to its right; and the reverse does not hold. Specifically:*
>
> *(a) any transmission-layer attestation of $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$ has evidential force only by way of some verification-layer procedure $V_i$ that evaluated $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$ --- attestations convey a verdict, they do not produce one (a cryptographically valid attestation can exist without any such $V_i$, as the forged-signature case in §2.1 shows, but it then carries no warrant for the claim it conveys);*
>
> *(b) any verification-layer procedure $V_i$'s correctness criterion is defined relative to the truth-layer predicate $\Pi_{A_i}$ --- there is no notion of $V_i$ being correct independent of what $\Pi_{A_i}$ asserts;*
>
> *(c) the truth-layer claim $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$ holds or fails to hold independently of whether any $V_i$ exists or any $\mathrm{Tr}$ conveys it; and correspondingly the reverse dependencies do not hold --- $T$ does not depend on $V$ or $\mathrm{Tr}$, and $V$ does not depend on $\mathrm{Tr}$.*

The proof is supplied in §2, which discharges sub-claims (a), (b), and (c) separately and then establishes the non-reverse direction. The present subsection states the theorem; §1.5 draws out the substrate-binding consequences that the theorem makes available, and §1.6 applies the layered picture to the four $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ satisfaction predicates.

The directional reading is the one that matters for the rest of the dissertation. Because $\mathrm{Tr}$ depends on $V$ and $V$ depends on $T$, fragility introduced at the transmission layer cannot propagate leftward: a broken signature scheme compromises the conveyance of a verdict without touching either the procedure that produced the verdict or the mathematical fact the verdict reported.

## §1.5 Substrate-binding properties

The dependency direction of Theorem 9.1 licenses three distinct substrate-binding characterizations, one per layer, which §2 formalizes as Propositions 9.2 through 9.4.

The truth layer is *substrate-independent*. A truth-layer proposition $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$ has no substrate parameter; it is identical whatever computational substrate one might consider, because it is a statement about mathematical objects rather than about any embodiment of a procedure.

The verification layer is *substrate-bound but not cryptographically-bound*. A verification procedure $V_i$ must execute on some substrate, but its correctness is invariant across substrates that faithfully implement its algorithm, and --- the load-bearing point --- its critical path uses only primitives drawn from two primitive classes: (a) symmetric-cryptographic primitives such as hash functions, and (b) information-theoretic primitives. It uses no public-key primitive. The taxonomy of these primitive classes is to be characterized in Chapter 10 §1.1 (a forward chapter; not yet closed canon); at this chapter, the claim that $V_i$ stays within classes (a) and (b) is the classification that Chapter 10 then shows to be quantum-survivable.

The transmission layer is *cryptographically contingent*. Transmission-layer trust is conditional on a cryptographic-hardness assumption $H$; should $H$ fail --- as the public-key assumptions are expected to fail under large-scale quantum computation --- the attestation loses its trust value, while, by the substrate-independence of the truth layer and the cryptographic-independence of the verification layer, the truth-layer and verification-layer claims are untouched. This last proposition is the formal core of the chapter's quantum-survivability thesis, and it is the claim handed forward to Chapter 10's decidable-fragment primitive-class theorem.

## §1.6 Residence of the $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ satisfaction predicates

Each satisfaction predicate $\Pi_{A_i}$ decomposes across the three layers, and the decomposition is the same in shape for all four axioms. The *truth-layer component* of $\Pi_{A_i}$ is the mathematical proposition $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$ --- whether $A_i$ holds of $S$. The *verification-layer component* is the procedure $V_i$ that evaluates $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$ within Chapter 10's decidable fragment, drawing only on primitive classes (a) and (b). The *transmission-layer component* is the attestation infrastructure that conveys "$V_i$ confirmed $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$" between parties: the sigstore signature on $V_i$'s verdict, the in-toto link binding that verdict to its inputs, the SLSA provenance record situating it in a build.

This residence claim is not a notational convenience; it is the structural fact on which Chapter 10 rests. Stated for all four axioms, it asserts that public-key cryptography --- which lives entirely at the transmission layer --- is *not* in the critical path of either axiom satisfaction (a truth-layer matter) or axiom checking (a verification-layer matter). Section 3 discharges the residence claim axiom by axiom, for A1 through A4, and shows that the claim holds symmetrically: every $\Pi_{A_i}$'s verification-layer component uses at most a symmetric-cryptographic primitive and never a public-key one. The present subsection states the residence claim and its symmetry; §3 proves it per axiom and §3.5 instantiates it concretely.

## §1.7 Practical implications

The three-layer architecture has direct consequences for the supply-chain four-substrate stack studied as Substrate Instance 4 in Chapter 16, and these consequences are worth drawing out even before the per-axiom proofs of §3.

First, a sigstore signature on a build artifact is a transmission-layer attestation and nothing more: it conveys that some party signed a claim about the artifact. It is not a verification-layer procedure and establishes no axiom. When the public-key scheme underlying the signature fails --- whether under quantum attack or by any other route by which its hardness assumption is broken --- the signature loses its transmission-layer trust, but the underlying axiom-satisfaction claim does not thereby lose its truth-layer validity.

Second, and consequently, fallback to source-plus-specification verification is always available. A future verifier with no access to the public-key infrastructure of the past can re-execute the verification procedure $V_i$ on $(S, A_i)$ and re-establish $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$ directly, using only the primitive classes that §1.5 and §3 confine the verification layer to. The structural-honesty substrate of a system --- its truth-layer claims and the verification-layer procedures that re-establish them --- is in this sense durable across cryptographic transitions in a way that the attestation fabric is not.

Third, the in-toto and SLSA layers of the stack provide transmission-layer attestations that likewise depend on public-key primitives, and their cryptographic-transition obligation is therefore structural rather than incidental: tools in this family should plan explicitly for post-quantum public-key transitions or for alternative attestation mechanisms. The obligation is real, but it is localized. It belongs to the transmission layer, and it leaves the truth and verification layers unaffected --- which is precisely the localization that §3.5 walks through in concrete detail on the SI4 stack.

## §1.8 Proof obligations and successor-work routing

This chapter incurs four proof obligations, discharged in the sections that follow. The first is the proof of Theorem 9.1 (the Layer Dependency Direction), supplied in §2, which discharges sub-claims (a), (b), and (c) separately and establishes the non-reverse direction. The second is the formal statement of the substrate-binding properties as Propositions 9.2 through 9.4, also supplied in §2. The third is the per-axiom residence proof, supplied in §3, which places each $\Pi_{A_i}$'s truth-layer, verification-layer, and transmission-layer components for A1 through A4 and establishes the symmetry of the residence claim. The fourth is the practical-implications walkthrough on the SI4 stack, supplied in §3.5, which shows concretely how the cryptographic-transition obligation localizes to the transmission layer.

Three successor chapters build on this architecture. Chapter 10 (Quantum Survivability of Verification) operates within the verification-and-transmission architecture established here, proving that the verification procedures confined to primitive classes (a) and (b) are survivable across the post-quantum transition. Chapter 11 (Information-Theoretic versus Cryptographic Substrates) develops the strength of the verification layer through tawatur-style mass-transmission arguments, in which independent re-derivations of a verification result reinforce one another. Chapter 12 (Centuries-Scale Preservation Discipline) specifies multi-layer replication operating across all three layers: truth-layer preservation through the stability of specifications, verification-layer preservation through independent re-implementation, and transmission-layer preservation through cryptographic agility.

## §2 Proof of Theorem 9.1 and the substrate-binding propositions

### §2.0 The shape of the argument

Theorem 9.1 asserts a strict, directional dependency $\mathrm{Tr} \to V \to T$ with no reverse. The proof discharges the three sub-claims of §1.4 in turn --- (a) that the transmission layer depends on the verification layer, (b) that the verification layer depends on the truth layer, and (c) that the truth layer depends on neither, together with the two non-reverse facts that follow --- and then formalizes the substrate-binding characterizations of §1.5 as Propositions 9.2 through 9.4. Throughout, $S$ ranges over systems, $A_i$ over the four axioms of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$, $\Pi_{A_i}$ over their satisfaction predicates, and $V_i$ over verification procedures for $\Pi_{A_i}$ within the decidable fragment that Chapter 10 characterizes.

### §2.1 Sub-claim (a): the transmission layer depends on the verification layer

We must show that any transmission-layer attestation of $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$ has evidential force only by way of some verification-layer procedure $V_i$ that evaluated $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$. The argument turns on what an attestation *is* and what it *does*.

A transmission-layer object --- a sigstore signature, an in-toto link, an SLSA provenance record --- is produced by an attestation function that takes a claim and a signing key and returns a signed object: $\mathrm{Att}(\text{claim}, \text{key}) \mapsto \text{signature}$. This function does not take $S$, does not take $\Pi_{A_i}$, and performs no evaluation of whether $A_i$ holds of $S$. Its operation is purely cryptographic: it binds a claim to a principal. Verifying the resulting signature establishes that the named principal asserted the claim --- the claim's *provenance* --- and establishes nothing about the claim's *truth*.

The gap is exhibited sharply by the forged-but-valid signature on a false claim. Suppose a principal signs the claim "$\Pi_{A_i}(S)$" when in fact $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$ is false. The signature is cryptographically valid: it verifies against the principal's key, and the transmission layer reports no fault. Yet the claim it conveys is false. The transmission layer is, by construction, silent on this difference; it certifies who said what, not whether what was said is so.

It follows that an attestation's *evidential force* --- its capacity to count as warrant for believing $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$ --- presupposes that some verification procedure $V_i$ actually established $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$ upstream of the signing. This is the precise sense of the dependency, and it is worth stating carefully to avoid a misreading. The claim is not that a valid signature cannot exist without a prior $V_i$ run; the forged signature shows that it can. The claim is that the signature's *evidential* relation to the truth of $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$ exists only by way of an upstream verification: the attestation conveys a verdict, and its trustworthiness as evidence for the verdict is exactly the trustworthiness of the $V_i$ that produced the verdict. The transmission layer transports warrant; it does not manufacture it. Hence $\mathrm{Tr}$ depends on $V$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

### §2.2 Sub-claim (b): the verification layer depends on the truth layer

We must show that the correctness of any verification procedure $V_i$ is defined relative to the truth-layer predicate $\Pi_{A_i}$. This is a definitional dependency, and the proof is correspondingly direct.

A verification procedure $V_i$ is *correct* exactly when, for the systems in its decidable fragment,
$$V_i(S) = \text{``verified''} \iff \Pi_{A_i}(S) \text{ holds.}$$
The right-hand side of this biconditional is a truth-layer proposition. The very statement of what it means for $V_i$ to be correct quantifies over $\Pi_{A_i}$'s content: there is no notion of "$V_i$ is correct" that can be stated without reference to the truth-layer fact the procedure is meant to track. A procedure that returned "verified" on some other condition --- one not coextensive with $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$ within the fragment --- would not be an incorrect verifier of $\Pi_{A_i}$; it would be a verifier of something else. Correctness for $V_i$ is individuated by $\Pi_{A_i}$.

The decidable-fragment qualifier does not weaken the dependency; it sharpens it. By the standing convention of Chapter 3 §7 and the finite-witness construction of Chapter 8 §2 (Theorem T82), $V_i$ produces, within its fragment, a finite witness exhibiting the satisfaction or the violation of $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$. That witness is checkable precisely because it is a witness *for the truth-layer proposition*: its adequacy is judged against $\Pi_{A_i}$. Hence $V$ depends on $T$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

### §2.3 Sub-claim (c) and the non-reverse direction

We must show that $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$ holds or fails independently of whether any $V_i$ exists or any attestation conveys it, and that correspondingly the reverse dependencies fail: $T$ depends on neither $V$ nor $\mathrm{Tr}$, and $V$ does not depend on $\mathrm{Tr}$.

For sub-claim (c) itself: $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$ is a proposition whose only free terms are the system $S$ and the axiom $A_i$, both fixed mathematical objects under the definitions of Chapters 4--7. The proposition contains no variable ranging over verifiers, procedures, or attestations. Its truth value is therefore determined by $S$ and $A_i$ alone, and is what it is whether or not anyone ever checks it. This is sub-claim (c).

The non-reverse direction follows by two ablations (the third non-reverse fact, $T \perp \mathrm{Tr}$, is already subsumed by sub-claim (c), since a truth-layer proposition independent of all verification is a fortiori independent of the attestations that convey verification). *First* ($T \perp V$): remove every verification procedure from the world. The proposition $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$ retains its truth value, because that value was never a function of any procedure --- it was fixed by $S$ and $A_i$. So $T$ does not depend on $V$. *Second* ($V \perp \mathrm{Tr}$): remove every attestation mechanism, every signing key, every transparency log. A verification procedure $V_i$ can still be run on $(S, A_i)$, and by Chapter 8 §2 it still produces a finite witness of satisfaction or violation; nothing in $V_i$'s operation consults a transmission-layer object. So $V$ does not depend on $\mathrm{Tr}$.

Combining (a), (b), and (c): the dependency relation is the strict chain $\mathrm{Tr} \to V \to T$, and the two ablations show there are no reverse edges. This completes the proof of Theorem 9.1. $\qquad\blacksquare$

### §2.4 The substrate-binding propositions

The dependency direction just established licenses three propositions, one per layer, formalizing the substrate-binding characterizations stated informally in §1.5. Their statements are recorded in spec-canon at T9.13; their proofs follow.

> **Proposition 9.2 (Truth-layer substrate-independence).** *For any computational substrates $\sigma, \sigma'$, the proposition $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$ is identical: it carries no substrate parameter.*

*Proof.* $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$ is a statement about the mathematical objects $S$ and $A_i$. A substrate $\sigma$ enters the picture only as a possible site of execution for a procedure, and $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$ mentions no procedure. There is thus no place in the proposition for a substrate parameter to occur, and the proposition one obtains "under $\sigma$" is syntactically and semantically the proposition one obtains under $\sigma'$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

> **Proposition 9.3 (Verification-layer substrate-boundedness without cryptographic-boundedness).** *A verification procedure $V_i$ requires some substrate $\sigma$ on which to execute; its correctness is invariant across any $\sigma$ that faithfully implements its algorithm; and its critical path uses only primitives from two primitive classes --- (a) symmetric-cryptographic and (b) information-theoretic --- and no public-key primitive.*

*Proof.* The first clause is the truism that an algorithm must be embodied to run. The second clause follows from the definition of correctness in §2.2: correctness is the biconditional $V_i(S) = \text{``verified''} \iff \Pi_{A_i}(S)$, a property of the algorithm's input-output relation, and any substrate faithfully implementing the algorithm realizes the same relation. The third clause --- that the critical path stays within classes (a) and (b) and uses no public-key primitive --- is the per-axiom claim discharged in §3 below, where each of $V_{A_1}, \dots, V_{A_4}$ is exhibited and its primitive usage classified. (The taxonomy of primitive classes (a) and (b) is to be characterized in Chapter 10 §1.1, a forward chapter; at this chapter the third clause is the classification result, established here per axiom, which Chapter 10 then takes as the hypothesis of its quantum-survivability theorem.) $\qquad\blacksquare$

> **Proposition 9.4 (Transmission-layer cryptographic contingency).** *Transmission-layer trust is contingent on a cryptographic-hardness assumption $H$; if $H$ fails, the attestation loses its trust value, while the truth-layer and verification-layer claims are unaffected.*

*Proof.* A transmission-layer attestation commands trust only insofar as its signature scheme is unforgeable, which holds only under a hardness assumption $H$ (for current public-key schemes, the hardness of factoring or of discrete logarithms). Should $H$ fail --- as the public-key assumptions are expected to fail under large-scale quantum computation --- forgery becomes feasible and the attestation no longer warrants belief in its conveyed claim. But by Proposition 9.2 the truth-layer proposition $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$ is substrate- and assumption-independent, and by Proposition 9.3 the verification procedure $V_i$ uses no public-key primitive in its critical path; neither is touched by the failure of $H$. The loss is confined to the transmission layer. $\qquad\blacksquare$

Proposition 9.4 is the formal core of the chapter's quantum-survivability thesis. It localizes cryptographic fragility to the transmission layer and hands the verification layer's primitive-class confinement (Proposition 9.3, discharged per axiom in §3) forward to Chapter 10, which proves that confinement to classes (a) and (b) is survivable across the post-quantum transition.

---

## §3 Residence of the satisfaction predicates and the SI4 walkthrough

### §3.0 What §3 proves, and the division of labor with Chapter 10

Section 3 discharges the residence claim of §1.6: that each satisfaction predicate $\Pi_{A_i}$ decomposes across the three layers, and that the decomposition is symmetric in the load-bearing respect --- every $V_i$'s critical path uses at most a symmetric-cryptographic primitive and never a public-key one. The section proceeds axiom by axiom (§§3.1--3.4), concludes the symmetry (§3.4), and instantiates the whole picture on the supply-chain stack of Substrate Instance 4 (§3.5).

One division of labor must be stated at the outset to forestall a circularity worry. Chapter 9 *classifies*: for each axiom it exhibits the verification procedure and identifies which primitive classes its critical path uses. Chapter 10 *proves survivability*: it takes "the critical path uses only classes (a) and (b)" as a hypothesis and shows the procedure survives the post-quantum transition. The symmetry conclusion of §3.4 is the classification result --- "no public-key primitive in any $V_i$'s critical path" --- not the survivability theorem. Chapter 9 does not assume what Chapter 10 proves; it supplies the classified input that Chapter 10's theorem consumes.

### §3.1 A1 (append-only provenance)

The truth-layer component of $\Pi_{A_1}$ is the proposition that $S$'s provenance record is append-only and corrigenda-disciplined, in the sense fixed by Axiom 1 in Chapter 4. The verification-layer component is the procedure $V_{A_1}$ that scans the provenance record for non-append mutations and checks the integrity of its hash chain: each entry commits to its predecessor by hash, and a tampered or reordered history fails the chain check. This is a finite-witness procedure --- the witness is the offending entry, or the verified chain --- and its only cryptographic ingredient is the hash function, a primitive of class (a), symmetric-cryptographic. No public-key primitive appears in $V_{A_1}$'s critical path. The transmission-layer component is the attestation that conveys "$V_{A_1}$ confirmed A1 for $S$" --- typically a sigstore signature over the verdict, an in-toto link binding it to the inputs, an SLSA record situating it.

That the A1 verification critical path uses only hash-chaining is the residence fact for A1, and it is the one axiom whose verification touches cryptography at all. Even here the cryptography is symmetric, of the kind transparency logs already rely on, and is the kind Chapter 10 is assigned to show survives the post-quantum transition.

### §3.2 A2 (surface-substrate consistency)

The truth-layer component of $\Pi_{A_2}$ is the proposition that $\mathrm{Surface}(S)$ is consistent with $\mathrm{Substrate}(S)$ under the declared correspondence relation $R$, in the sense fixed by Axiom 2 in Chapter 5. The verification-layer component is the procedure $V_{A_2}$ that checks the correspondence appropriate to the declared claim --- a bisimulation, simulation, or refinement check, drawn from the relation family of Chapter 5 §1.4 --- within the decidable fragment of Chapter 3 §7, producing a finite witness. This is a behavioral-equivalence computation over typed objects; it consults no cryptographic primitive of any class. The transmission-layer component is, as before, the attestation of the $V_{A_2}$ verdict. The residence fact for A2 is therefore stronger than for A1: $V_{A_2}$'s critical path contains no cryptographic primitive at all.

### §3.3 A3 (caller-side exhaustiveness)

The truth-layer component of $\Pi_{A_3}$ is the proposition that caller-side coverage over $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ provides defensible exhaustiveness, in the sense fixed by Axiom 3 in Chapter 6. The verification-layer component is the procedure $V_{A_3}$ that checks caller coverage against the conservative over-approximation $R_{\mathrm{may}}$, confirming for each outcome in the caller's scope that it is handled, propagated-as-incomplete, or proven-unreachable --- the three discharge paths of Chapter 6 §§1.1--1.4, with $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ itself constructed under the over-approximation discipline of Chapter 3 §§5.1 and 5.4. This is a finite-witness set-coverage check; like $V_{A_2}$ it consults no cryptographic primitive. The transmission-layer component is the attestation of the verdict. The residence fact for A3: no cryptographic primitive in $V_{A_3}$'s critical path.

### §3.4 A4 (substrate-parameterized projection consistency), and the symmetry conclusion

The truth-layer component of $\Pi_{A_4}$ is the proposition that the projection family is consistent across substrate parameterization, in the sense fixed by Axiom 4 in Chapter 7. The verification-layer component is the procedure $V_{A_4}$ that checks projection consistency across the substrate-parameter family using the local-section and restriction-map machinery of Chapter 7 §1, within the decidable fragment, producing a finite witness. This machinery is algebraic, not cryptographic; $V_{A_4}$'s critical path contains no cryptographic primitive. The transmission-layer component is the attestation of the verdict.

The four per-axiom results now combine. For A1, the verification critical path uses a symmetric-cryptographic primitive (hash-chaining) and no public-key primitive. For A2, A3, and A4, the verification critical path uses no cryptographic primitive at all. In every case, then, the verification of an $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ axiom uses *at most* a symmetric-cryptographic primitive and *never* a public-key one. This is the symmetry conclusion: public-key cryptography is absent from the critical path of every $V_i$. It is the residence claim of §1.6 discharged, and --- as the division of labor in §3.0 stressed --- it is the classified hypothesis that Chapter 10's Quantum-Survivable Verification Theorem requires. $\qquad\blacksquare$

### §3.5 The SI4 walkthrough

The supply-chain four-substrate stack of Substrate Instance 4 (Chapter 16) instantiates the three-layer architecture concretely, and walking through it makes the localization of cryptographic fragility tangible.

Consider a build artifact moving through the stack. It carries a sigstore signature, an in-toto attestation binding it to its build inputs, and an SLSA provenance record --- three transmission-layer objects. The structural-honesty claims about the artifact, that it satisfies A1 through A4, are truth-layer facts. The procedures that re-establish those claims --- $V_{A_1}$ through $V_{A_4}$, with the primitive usage classified in §§3.1--3.4 --- are verification-layer activities. It is worth stating explicitly, since the stack's most visible machinery is its signing infrastructure, that structural-honesty verification itself lives at the verification layer, not the transmission layer: running $V_{A_i}$ on the artifact is a verification act, and the signature that later conveys its verdict is a separate, transmission-layer act.

Now suppose the public-key hardness assumption underlying the sigstore signature fails --- under quantum attack, or by any other route by which the assumption is broken. By Proposition 9.4 the transmission-layer attestations lose their trust value: the signatures can no longer be relied upon as unforgeable. But by Propositions 9.2 and 9.3 the truth-layer claims remain valid and the verification-layer procedures remain re-runnable: a verifier with no access to the compromised infrastructure can re-execute $V_{A_1}$ through $V_{A_4}$ on the artifact's source and specification and re-establish A1 through A4 directly, using only the primitive classes §§3.1--3.4 confine them to. The fallback to source-plus-specification verification, named in §1.7, is exactly this re-execution.

The conclusion is the chapter's thesis made concrete: when the cryptography of the attestation fabric ages out, the obligation to migrate falls entirely on the transmission layer. The structural-honesty substrate --- the truth-layer claims and the verification-layer procedures that re-establish them --- is untouched, and is in this precise sense durable across the cryptographic transitions that the attestation fabric is not. The general survivability of that durability across the post-quantum transition is the burden of Chapter 10; what Chapter 9 has shown is that the burden falls where Chapter 10 can discharge it --- on a verification layer confined to symmetric and information-theoretic primitives.

## §1.0 Role and scope

Chapter 10 carries two burdens, and it is worth saying at the outset that they are distinct burdens that happen to be discharged in the same place. The first is the dissertation's central long-horizon result: that the verification of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ survives the cryptographic transitions of the coming decades, the post-quantum transition foremost among them. The second is a piece of formal housekeeping that five earlier chapters deferred to this one: the characterization of the *decidable fragment* within which $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ verification actually runs. The two are independent in principle --- one could imagine a dissertation that proved survivability without ever pinning down decidability, or vice versa --- but they meet here because the survivability theorem is most naturally stated relative to the very fragment the housekeeping defines.

The first role, *quantum survivability*, builds directly on Chapter 9. Chapter 9 separated the truth, verification, and transmission layers and classified, axiom by axiom, which cryptographic primitives the verification procedures actually use; its §3.4 reached the conclusion that no $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ verification procedure places a public-key primitive in any critical path. That conclusion is the load-bearing hypothesis of the present chapter. Chapter 10 does not re-establish it. It takes Chapter 9 §3.4 as given and proves the consequence: that a verification procedure built only from the surviving primitive classes remains sound and executable against an adversary holding a large-scale quantum computer. The division of labor is the one Chapter 9 §3.0 set down explicitly --- Chapter 9 classifies; Chapter 10 proves survivability from that classification --- and the present chapter is written to honor it without slippage.

The second role, the *decidability burden*, is Chapter 10's own contribution rather than an inheritance. Chapters 4 through 7 each close their decidability-scope subsection --- §1.7 for A1, A3, and A4, and §1.8 for A2 --- with a forward-pointer to "Chapter 10's decidable fragment," and Chapter 8 §2's finite-witness construction (T82) operates, in its own words, within whatever decidable fragment Chapter 10 establishes. This chapter closes those pointers by characterizing, uniformly across the four axioms, what it means for an $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ fragment to be decidable.

The scope of this opening section is the apparatus that the two roles require: the primitive-class taxonomy by which survivability is judged (§1.1); the decidable-fragment framework (§1.2) and its per-axiom instantiation (§1.3); the quantum threat model and the definition of "quantum-survivable" (§1.4); the statement of Theorem 10.1 (§1.5) and of its centuries-scale Corollary 10.2 (§1.6); and the practical consequences for software supply-chain attestation (§1.7), before the proof obligations are routed forward (§1.8). Three topics are deliberately out of scope and handed onward: the information-theoretic strengthening of the verification layer through $n$-fold independent re-implementation (Chapter 11); the operational discipline of preserving artifacts and specifications across long horizons (Chapter 12); and the genuinely undecidable fragments, together with settings in which the artifact or specification has not been preserved, which are routed to the open-problems treatment (Chapter 17) and the falsification analysis (Chapter 21).

## §1.1 The primitive-class taxonomy

Survivability is a claim about how a procedure fares against a particular adversary, and so it must be indexed to the cryptographic primitives the procedure relies on. This section fixes a three-way classification of primitives by their resilience to quantum attack. It is the same taxonomy Chapter 9 §1.5 and Proposition 9.3 invoked as a scoped forward-assumption, named there but characterized here; closing that forward-reference is part of this section's work.

The first class, **(a) symmetric-cryptographic primitives**, comprises hash functions, symmetric ciphers, and message-authentication codes. These are *quantum-weakened but survivable*. The sharpest general quantum attack against them is Grover's algorithm, which accelerates unstructured search quadratically; against a primitive offering $n$ bits of classical security, Grover reduces the effective security to roughly $n/2$ bits. The mitigation is bounded and one-time: doubling the relevant parameter --- moving from SHA-256 to SHA-512, or from AES-128 to AES-256 --- restores the original security margin. There is no unbounded escalation here, a point that matters for the centuries-scale claim and is made precise in §1.4 and discharged in §2.

The second class, **(b) information-theoretic and non-cryptographic primitives**, comprises bit-identical equality checks, decidable graph- and type-system algorithms, mechanical extraction of structure from an artifact, and the $n$-fold independent-re-implementation reference-parity that Chapter 11 will develop. These are *quantum-unconditional*. The unifying property of the class is the absence of any computational-hardness assumption, and it covers two superficially different things under one heading: primitives that are information-theoretically secure in the cryptographic sense, and plain non-cryptographic computation that has no "security" to break in the first place. A bit-identical comparison of two artifacts does not become easier to subvert because an adversary has a quantum computer; there is nothing in it for a quantum algorithm to attack. Because the class rests on no hardness assumption, no quantum algorithm bears on it at all.

The third class, **(c) public-key primitives**, comprises RSA, Diffie--Hellman, and the elliptic-curve schemes ECC and ECDSA. These are *quantum-broken*. Shor's algorithm solves integer factorization and the discrete-logarithm problem in polynomial time on a large fault-tolerant quantum computer, and the security of every primitive in this class reduces to the hardness of one of those problems.

The taxonomy thus partitions into the *survivable* classes (a) and (b) and the *broken* class (c). The whole of Chapter 10's survivability argument turns on a single structural fact, established in Chapter 9 and consumed here: that $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ verification lives entirely within classes (a) and (b).

## §1.2 The decidable-fragment framework

The decidability burden is discharged by saying, once and uniformly, what a "decidable $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ fragment" is, and then instantiating that definition per axiom in §1.3. The framework rests on the finite-default fragment of Chapter 3 §7, the standing convention by which the dissertation treats state spaces as finite or otherwise decidable unless a construction explicitly requires otherwise.

A fragment is *decidable* when three conditions hold together. First, the underlying state spaces over which the axiom's satisfaction predicate quantifies are finite or otherwise decidable. Second, the equality, consistency, and subtyping checks that constitute the satisfaction predicate are themselves decidable relations. Third, the finite-witness construction of Chapter 8 §2 (T82) succeeds: there is a finitary object that witnesses satisfaction, or a finitary counterexample that witnesses violation. The third condition is what connects decidability to verification in the operational sense, since it is the finite witness that a verification procedure actually inspects.

The four-axiom decidable fragment is the conjunction of the four per-axiom decidable fragments characterized in §1.3: a system lies within it when each of the four satisfaction predicates is decidable in the sense just given. Theorem 10.1 is stated relative to this fragment, and its scope is exactly the fragment's scope; systems falling outside it are routed to Chapter 17, not silently assumed away.

## §1.3 Per-axiom decidable-fragment scope

The general framework of §1.2 specializes to four concrete sets of conditions, one per axiom. In each case the condition is a statement about decidability --- Chapter 10's own contribution --- while the question of which primitive classes the corresponding verification procedure uses is *not* settled here: it was settled in Chapter 9 §§3.1--3.4 and is consumed below as a citation, not re-derived.

For **A1** (append-only provenance), the satisfaction predicate is decidable under finite version histories, a finite set of truth-status tags, and decidable behavioral-subtyping, as routed from Chapter 4 §1.7. For **A2** (surface--substrate consistency), it is decidable under finite observer-model and context-set data $(O, K)$, a finite-state correspondence relation $R$ drawn from the family of Chapter 5 §1.4, and a finite-state substrate, with the relevant decidability scope at Chapter 5 §1.8. For **A3** (caller-side exhaustiveness over $R_{\mathrm{may}}$), it is decidable under a finite $R_{\mathrm{may}}$, finite caller-discharge specifications, and decidable invariant-verification for the proven-unreachable cases, as routed from Chapter 6 §1.7. For **A4** (substrate-parameterized projection consistency), it is decidable under finite projection families $\Pi_X$, finite joint domains, and a decidable consistency relation $\sim_X$, as routed from Chapter 7 §1.7.

In every one of the four cases, the fact that the verification procedure carries no public-key primitive in its critical path is established in Chapter 9 §§3.1--3.4 and consumed here. The reader who wishes to confirm that no class-(c) primitive lurks in any of these procedures is directed to Chapter 9, which owns that classification; the present section's claim is only that, given that classification, the satisfaction predicates are decidable under the stated finiteness conditions. Fragments that violate those conditions --- unbounded histories, undecidable consistency relations, and the like --- are undecidable and route to Chapter 17.

## §1.4 The quantum threat model

The adversary against which survivability is judged is one in possession of a large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computer: an adversary able to run Shor's and Grover's algorithms at the scales their asymptotic analyses assume. This is the standard post-quantum threat model, and the taxonomy of §1.1 was built to be read against it.

Against this adversary the three classes fare as §1.1 described. Class (c), public-key, is broken in polynomial time by Shor. Class (a), symmetric, is preserved at a bounded parameter increase: Grover's quadratic speedup halves the effective security level, and a one-time doubling of the output or key size restores it. Class (b), information-theoretic and non-cryptographic, is preserved unconditionally, because it rested on no hardness assumption for the adversary to dissolve.

This licenses the chapter's central definition. A procedure is **quantum-survivable** when it remains both sound and executable under this adversary, subject to two conditions: it may rely on class-(a) primitives only at bounded, one-time parameter increases, and it may not rely on any class-(c) primitive at all. The definition is deliberately operational --- "sound and executable," not merely "not provably broken" --- because the use to which it is put in Corollary 10.2 is the concrete re-execution of a verification procedure by a future party, not an abstract security reduction.

## §1.5 Theorem 10.1 (Quantum-Survivable Verification) --- statement

The chapter's principal result can now be stated.

> **Theorem 10.1 (Quantum-Survivable Verification).** Within the four-axiom decidable fragment of §1.2--§1.3, for each $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ axiom $A_i$ the verification procedure $V_i$ is quantum-survivable. Because, by Chapter 9 §3.4, the critical path of $V_i$ uses only primitives from classes (a) and (b) and never a class-(c) public-key primitive, $V_i$ remains sound and executable under the §1.4 quantum adversary, with at most bounded parameter increases for any class-(a) primitive it employs. Equivalently: $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ verification places no public-key primitive in any critical path, and therefore survives the post-quantum transition.

Two features of the statement deserve emphasis, both bearing on the discipline of the chapter. First, the hypothesis is Chapter 9 §3.4's conclusion, cited rather than re-derived; the theorem's antecedent "the critical path of $V_i$ uses only classes (a) and (b)" is precisely what Chapter 9 proved and what Chapter 10 is forbidden, by Chapter 9 §3.0's division of labor, from re-proving. Second, the statement is a statement only: the proof is routed to §2, where the survivability of classes (a) and (b) established in §1.4 is applied to the Chapter 9--classified critical paths within the §1.2 decidable fragment. Stating the theorem here and proving it there is the spec-then-prose boundary the dissertation has maintained since Chapter 3, not a deferral of difficulty.

## §1.6 Corollary 10.2 (centuries-scale re-verification) --- statement

The post-quantum transition is the nearest of a family of cryptographic-infrastructure losses the dissertation cares about, and Theorem 10.1 generalizes to the rest of that family in a single step.

> **Corollary 10.2 (centuries-scale re-verification).** Any future verifier with no access to past cryptographic infrastructure --- no key servers, no transparency logs, no live public-key roots of trust --- can independently re-verify any prior structural-honesty claim from the preserved artifact and specification alone, by re-executing $V_i$ within the decidable fragment. Confined to classes (a) and (b), $V_i$ requires no surviving public-key infrastructure to run.

The corollary's reach is wider than the post-quantum transition that motivates it. It speaks to durability across *arbitrary* loss of cryptographic infrastructure --- the disappearance of a certificate authority, the abandonment of a transparency log, the obsolescence of an entire signature ecosystem --- because the property it relies on is not that any particular scheme survives but that the verification procedure never needed one. Its proof, routed to §2, runs through Theorem 10.1 together with two results Chapter 9 hands forward: the source-plus-specification fallback of Chapter 9 §1.7, which guarantees that re-verification consults only the artifact and the specification, and Proposition 9.2's truth-layer substrate-independence, which guarantees that the proposition being re-verified has not itself decayed with time. The corollary is scoped, as the theorem is, to preserved artifact--specification pairs within the decidable fragment; the discipline of achieving that preservation is Chapter 12's subject.

## §1.7 Practical implications

The theorem and its corollary have concrete consequences for the software supply-chain stack that substrate instance SI4 (Chapter 16) models, and stating them sharpens the contrast between what the surviving verification layer guarantees and what the transmission layer must still manage.

The first consequence is that a signature --- a sigstore signature, in SI4's terms --- is an *efficiency optimization* on verification rather than a precondition for it. A signature lets a party accept a verification verdict without re-running $V_i$ itself, which is a real and worthwhile economy. But it is an economy, not a foundation: when the signature's public-key scheme breaks, the party can always fall back to re-running $V_i$ on the artifact and specification, exactly as Chapter 9 §1.7 provides. The second consequence follows immediately: that fallback path is *permanent*, not contingent on any cryptographic assumption, because $V_i$ itself depends on none. The slow path is always open.

The third consequence concerns where the post-quantum obligation actually falls. Sigstore, in-toto, and SLSA all depend on public-key signatures --- class (c) --- and therefore each carries a real cryptographic-transition obligation: each must, over the coming years, migrate to post-quantum public-key schemes. But that obligation is localized, by Chapter 9 Proposition 9.4, to the transmission layer. It never reaches the truth layer, where the proposition $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$ lives untouched, nor the verification layer, where $V_i$ runs without any public-key primitive at all. The supply-chain stack has post-quantum work to do; the point of Theorem 10.1 is that the work is confined to the layer that conveys verdicts, and leaves the layer that establishes them alone.

## §1.8 Proof obligations and successor-work routing

This section closes by recording what the remainder of the chapter must discharge and what it routes onward. Four obligations pass to §§2-3. The proof of Theorem 10.1 (§2) must apply the class-(a) and class-(b) survivability of §1.4 to the Chapter 9--classified critical paths, within the §1.2 decidable fragment. The proof of Corollary 10.2 (§2) must compose Theorem 10.1 with the Chapter 9 §1.7 fallback and Proposition 9.2. The per-axiom application (§3) must instantiate the theorem on each of A1 through A4 and on the SI4 stack. And the cryptographic-transition-obligation contrast (§3) must develop, against the sigstore/in-toto/SLSA case, the localization of the post-quantum obligation to the transmission layer.

Two successor chapters are routed forward from here. Chapter 11 strengthens class (b) through the $n$-fold independent re-implementation that yields reference-parity, a mass-transmission strengthening in the spirit of *tawatur*: many independent witnesses to the same structural fact. Chapter 12 develops the operational discipline of preserving artifacts and specifications across the centuries-scale horizon that Corollary 10.2 presupposes.

The boundary of §1 is the boundary the version status announced: this section has stated the taxonomy, the decidable-fragment framework, the threat model, the theorem, and the corollary. It has not proved the theorem or the corollary --- those are §2 --- and it has not re-derived Chapter 9's classification, which it consumes as the cited hypothesis of Theorem 10.1.

## §2 Proof of Theorem 10.1 and Corollary 10.2

### §2.0 The shape of the argument

Theorem 10.1 asserts that, within the four-axiom decidable fragment, each verification procedure $V_i$ is quantum-survivable. The proof is a composition argument over the primitive classes of §1.1, and it rests on a hypothesis it does not itself establish: that, by Chapter 9 §3.4, the critical path of every $V_i$ uses only primitives of classes (a) and (b) and never a class-(c) public-key primitive. That classification is Chapter 9's result, consumed here; the present section proves only the survivability that follows from it.

The argument proceeds in four steps. Two lemmas treat the surviving classes in isolation: Lemma 10.1a establishes that a class-(a) primitive remains sound and executable under the quantum adversary at a bounded, one-time parameter increase (§2.1), and Lemma 10.1b establishes that a class-(b) primitive is quantum-invariant (§2.2). The proof of Theorem 10.1 then composes these two facts over the Chapter 9--classified critical path (§2.3). Corollary 10.2 follows by combining the theorem with two results Chapter 9 hands forward (§2.4). The section closes with the boundedness property that the centuries-scale reading requires, and the scope conditions that bound the claim (§2.5). Throughout, $S$ ranges over systems, $A_i$ over the four axioms of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$, $\Pi_{A_i}$ over their satisfaction predicates, and $V_i$ over verification procedures for $\Pi_{A_i}$ within the decidable fragment of §1.2.

### §2.1 Lemma 10.1a: survivability of class-(a) primitives

> **Lemma 10.1a (class-(a) survivability).** Let $P$ be a symmetric-cryptographic primitive (a hash function, symmetric cipher, or message-authentication code) whose security rests on the infeasibility of an unstructured search over a space of size $2^n$. Under the quantum adversary of §1.4, $P$ remains sound at the bounded, one-time parameter increase $n \mapsto 2n$, and its executability is unaffected.

**Proof.** The strongest general quantum attack against a primitive of this kind is Grover's algorithm, which finds a marked element in an unstructured search space of size $N$ using $\Theta(\sqrt{N})$ evaluations, a quadratic speedup over the classical $\Theta(N)$. Applied to the search problem on which $P$'s security rests --- inverting the primitive on a target, or finding a forgery --- Grover reduces the adversary's work from order $2^n$ to order $2^{n/2}$. The effective security level is therefore at most halved, from $n$ bits to $n/2$ bits.

Two observations make this a *bounded* loss rather than the beginning of an erosion. First, Grover's quadratic speedup is optimal: the lower bound of Bennett, Bernstein, Brassard, and Vazirani establishes that no quantum algorithm solves unstructured search in fewer than $\Omega(\sqrt{N})$ queries, so there is no further quantum speedup beyond the quadratic for $P$'s security to lose. Second, the loss is recovered by a single doubling of the size parameter: replacing $P$ at $n$-bit security with the corresponding primitive at $2n$-bit security (for instance SHA-256 by SHA-512, or AES-128 by AES-256) restores the post-quantum effective security to $n$ bits, the pre-quantum margin. The increase is one-time --- it answers a fixed quadratic speedup, not a moving target --- and it is bounded, in that no iteration of the mitigation is required.

Executability is unaffected because the doubled-parameter primitive is an ordinary symmetric primitive, evaluated by the verifier exactly as the original was; the verification procedure that invoked $P$ now invokes its doubled-parameter counterpart, at the same asymptotic cost up to the constant implied by the larger parameter. Hence $P$ remains both sound and executable under the quantum adversary at the parameter increase $n \mapsto 2n$. $\square$

A remark on collision resistance, which is the security property the provenance hash-chaining of §3.1 will rely on. The generic quantum collision attack (the Brassard--Høyer--Tapp algorithm) is sometimes quoted as reducing collision resistance from $2^{n/2}$ to $2^{n/3}$; under the realistic accounting that charges for quantum memory, its advantage over classical collision search is smaller still. In either accounting the loss is bounded and is covered, conservatively, by the same one-time output-size doubling, so the lemma's mitigation applies to collision resistance without modification.

### §2.2 Lemma 10.1b: survivability of class-(b) primitives

> **Lemma 10.1b (class-(b) survivability).** Let $Q$ be an information-theoretic or non-cryptographic primitive --- a bit-identical equality check, a decidable graph- or type-system algorithm, a mechanical extraction, or an information-theoretically secure primitive. Under the quantum adversary of §1.4, $Q$ is quantum-invariant: it remains sound and executable without any parameter change.

**Proof.** The defining property of class (b) is the absence of any computational-hardness assumption. The proof splits on the two ways that absence can hold.

In the first case, $Q$ is a non-cryptographic computation: it computes a total function $f$ on a decidable domain --- whether two artifacts are bit-identical, whether a graph has a property, whether an extraction yields a given structure. The soundness of a verification step that invokes $Q$ is the assertion that $Q$ computes $f$ correctly, and this is a fact about the computation being carried out, not about any adversary's inability to solve a hard problem. A quantum computer can evaluate $f$ as well --- quantum computation subsumes classical computation --- but there is no security property for it to subvert: $Q$ has no secret, no hardness assumption, and no adversarial game in which a quantum speedup could matter. The introduction of quantum computational power cannot make a correct decidable computation incorrect.

In the second case, $Q$ is information-theoretically secure: its security holds against a computationally unbounded adversary, by definition of the term. An adversary equipped with a quantum computer is in particular a computationally bounded special case of an unbounded adversary, so $Q$'s security holds against it a fortiori.

In both cases the soundness of $Q$ is independent of any hardness assumption, and is therefore invariant under the introduction of quantum computational power. Executability is unaffected, since $Q$ is computed by the verifier identically regardless of the adversary's resources. Hence $Q$ is quantum-invariant. $\square$

### §2.3 Proof of Theorem 10.1

> **Theorem 10.1 (Quantum-Survivable Verification).** Within the four-axiom decidable fragment of §1.2--§1.3, for each $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ axiom $A_i$ the verification procedure $V_i$ is quantum-survivable.

**Proof.** Fix an axiom $A_i$ and its verification procedure $V_i$ within the decidable fragment. By Chapter 9 §3.4 --- the classification consumed as hypothesis, not re-derived here --- the critical path of $V_i$ uses only primitives of classes (a) and (b), and contains no primitive of class (c).

Within the decidable fragment, $V_i$ is a finite procedure, and each of its steps is of exactly one of three kinds: a step that invokes a class-(a) primitive, a step that invokes a class-(b) primitive, or a step of decidable control or data manipulation that invokes no cryptographic primitive at all. A step of the third kind is itself a non-cryptographic computation, hence class (b) by the taxonomy of §1.1, so the three kinds reduce to two for the purpose of the argument.

By Lemma 10.1a, every class-(a) step remains sound and executable under the quantum adversary at a bounded, one-time parameter increase. By Lemma 10.1b, every class-(b) step is quantum-invariant, remaining sound and executable without change. It remains to show that the finite composition of these steps that constitutes $V_i$ is itself sound and executable under the adversary.

Executability composes immediately: a finite sequence of individually executable steps is executable. For soundness, recall that $V_i$'s verdict on $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$ is a decidable function of the verdict-relevant results of its steps. Each step, by the two lemmas, contributes under the quantum adversary the same verdict-relevant result it contributes classically --- though what that preservation amounts to differs by class. A class-(b) step is quantum-invariant: it returns the identical output, the underlying computation being unchanged. A class-(a) step need not return an identical output --- a doubled-parameter hash yields a different digest --- but its security property is restored at the doubled parameter, so it accepts and rejects exactly as it did classically: a tampered provenance link still fails its collision check, a genuine one still passes. Either way the verdict-relevant contribution of each step is preserved, so the decidable function composing them returns a preserved value; hence $V_i$'s verdict under the quantum adversary equals its verdict in the absence of one, and $V_i$ is sound under the adversary. No quantum attack on the composed procedure can succeed without succeeding against some constituent step, and no constituent step is vulnerable; the decidable glue between steps introduces no cryptographic assumption and so opens no new attack surface. There is therefore no emergent vulnerability from composition.

Finally, because no class-(c) primitive appears anywhere in the critical path, Shor's algorithm has no target within $V_i$: its polynomial-time solution of factoring and discrete logarithm bears only on public-key primitives, of which $V_i$ uses none. The post-quantum break of class (c) thus does not touch $V_i$ at all.

Combining, $V_i$ remains sound and executable under the §1.4 quantum adversary, with at most bounded parameter increases for its class-(a) primitives and no reliance on any class-(c) primitive --- which is precisely quantum-survivability in the sense of §1.4. As $A_i$ was an arbitrary one of the four axioms, the conclusion holds for each. $\square$

### §2.4 Proof of Corollary 10.2

> **Corollary 10.2 (centuries-scale re-verification).** Any future verifier with no access to past cryptographic infrastructure can independently re-verify any prior structural-honesty claim from the preserved artifact and specification alone, by re-executing $V_i$ within the decidable fragment.

**Proof.** Let $(S, A_i)$ be a preserved artifact--specification pair within the decidable fragment, and consider a future verifier possessing $S$, the specification of $A_i$, and ordinary computational resources (including, in the strongest case, a quantum computer), but with no access to any past cryptographic infrastructure --- no key servers, no transparency logs, no live public-key roots of trust.

By Theorem 10.1, $V_i$ is quantum-survivable: it is sound and executable under the quantum adversary, using only primitives of classes (a) and (b) and requiring no class-(c) primitive, hence no public-key infrastructure of any kind. By Chapter 9 §1.7, the source-plus-specification fallback guarantees that an execution of $V_i$ consults only the artifact $S$ and the specification of $A_i$ --- not any transmission-layer attestation, signature, or log. The future verifier therefore has, in the preserved pair $(S, A_i)$, exactly the inputs $V_i$ requires, and by quantum-survivability it can execute $V_i$ on those inputs to a sound verdict on $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$.

It remains only to confirm that the verdict so obtained concerns the same proposition the original verification did. By Chapter 9 Proposition 9.2, the truth layer is substrate-independent and non-decaying: the truth value of $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$ is fixed by $S$ and $A_i$ alone and does not change with the passage of time or the loss of any infrastructure. The proposition the future verifier re-establishes is thus identical to the one originally established. Hence the future verifier independently re-verifies the prior structural-honesty claim from the preserved artifact and specification alone. $\square$

The corollary's reach, noted in §1.6, is now visible in the proof: nothing in it is specific to the post-quantum transition. The only properties used are that $V_i$ needs no public-key infrastructure (Theorem 10.1), that its execution needs only the preserved pair (Chapter 9 §1.7), and that the proposition does not decay (Proposition 9.2). Any loss of cryptographic infrastructure whatever --- not merely the retirement of pre-quantum public-key schemes --- leaves all three intact.

### §2.5 The boundedness property and scope conditions

The centuries-scale reading of Corollary 10.2 depends on a property already established inside the proof of Lemma 10.1a but worth isolating, because it is what distinguishes a survivable verification from one that merely defers its failure. The class-(a) mitigation is a *one-time, bounded* parameter increase, not an unbounded escalation. The reason is the optimality of Grover's algorithm: because no quantum search algorithm beats the quadratic speedup (§2.1), the security loss a class-(a) primitive can suffer to a quantum adversary is capped at one halving, and a single doubling of the size parameter answers it permanently. There is no sequence of ever-larger parameters to maintain, and so the verification's resource requirements do not grow without bound over the centuries-scale horizon. A verification whose cost escalated indefinitely could not honestly be called survivable at that horizon; this one does not.

Two scope conditions bound the results of §2. First, Theorem 10.1 and Corollary 10.2 are stated and proved within the decidable fragment of §1.2; an $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ instance whose satisfaction predicate falls outside that fragment is not covered, and is routed to the open-problems treatment of Chapter 17. Second, Corollary 10.2 presupposes a preserved artifact--specification pair; the discipline by which such preservation is achieved over long horizons is Chapter 12's subject, and the analysis of settings in which preservation fails is Chapter 21's.

## §3 Per-axiom application and the cryptographic-transition contrast

### §3.0 The shape of §3

Section 2 proved Theorem 10.1 in the form quantified over the axioms. Section 3 discharges the theorem's content axiom by axiom, citing for each the Chapter 9 classification it consumes, and then develops the practical contrast that the theorem draws between $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ verification and the public-key-dependent attestation tooling of the software supply chain. As in §2, no axiom's primitive-class membership is re-derived here; Chapter 9 §§3.1--3.4 settled those memberships, and §3 applies Theorem 10.1 to each.

### §3.1 A1: append-only provenance

By Chapter 9 §3.1, the verification procedure $V_{A1}$ for append-only provenance places in its critical path a class-(a) primitive: the hash function that chains successive version records, by which each record commits to its predecessor. No public-key primitive appears; the chaining is a symmetric construction. Applying Theorem 10.1, $V_{A1}$ is quantum-survivable, and by Lemma 10.1a the survival is at a bounded, one-time parameter increase: the provenance chain that hashed with, say, SHA-256 moves to SHA-512, after which the append-only property is verified under the quantum adversary at full pre-quantum security. The provenance structure itself is unchanged; only the size parameter of its hash is doubled, once.

### §3.2 A2: surface--substrate consistency

By Chapter 9 §3.2, the verification procedure $V_{A2}$ for surface--substrate consistency consults no cryptographic primitive of any class: it checks behavioral equivalence between the surface presentation and the substrate, a class-(b) computation. Applying Theorem 10.1, $V_{A2}$ is quantum-survivable, and by Lemma 10.1b the survival is unconditional --- no parameter increase, no mitigation. The consistency check computes the same verdict under a quantum adversary as without one, because its soundness rests on no hardness assumption.

### §3.3 A3: caller-side exhaustiveness over $R_{\mathrm{may}}$

By Chapter 9 §3.3, the verification procedure $V_{A3}$ for caller-side exhaustiveness consults no cryptographic primitive: it checks coverage of the may-set $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ by the caller's discharge specifications, together with decidable invariant-verification for the proven-unreachable cases --- all class-(b) computation. Applying Theorem 10.1, $V_{A3}$ is quantum-survivable, and by Lemma 10.1b unconditionally so.

### §3.4 A4: substrate-parameterized projection consistency

By Chapter 9 §3.4, the verification procedure $V_{A4}$ for substrate-parameterized projection consistency consults no cryptographic primitive: it checks the consistency relation $\sim_X$ over the projection families $\Pi_X$ on their joint domains, the algebraic local-section and restriction-map checking that §3.4's symmetry conclusion identified as non-cryptographic. Applying Theorem 10.1, $V_{A4}$ is quantum-survivable, and by Lemma 10.1b unconditionally so.

Taken together, the four applications give the chapter's result in concrete form: $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ verification is quantum-survivable across all four axioms --- A1 at a bounded one-time parameter increase, A2 through A4 unconditionally --- because not one of the four verification procedures places a public-key primitive in its critical path.

### §3.5 The cryptographic-transition contrast and the SI4 instantiation

The theorem's practical force is sharpest where it is contrasted with tooling that does depend on the broken class. On the SI4 software-supply-chain stack of Chapter 16, structural-honesty verification coexists with an attestation fabric built from sigstore signatures, in-toto attestations, and SLSA provenance. Every one of those attestation mechanisms depends on public-key signatures --- class (c) --- and each therefore carries a genuine cryptographic-transition obligation: over the coming years, each must migrate to a post-quantum public-key scheme, on pain of its signatures becoming forgeable once a large quantum computer exists.

The contrast Theorem 10.1 draws is that this obligation is confined to the attestation fabric and does not reach the verification it attests. By Chapter 9 Proposition 9.4, the cryptographic fragility of the supply chain is localized to the transmission layer; the truth layer, where $\Pi_{A_i}(S)$ lives, and the verification layer, where each $V_i$ runs without any public-key primitive, are untouched. Concretely, on SI4: when a sigstore key scheme is retired, the signatures that conveyed past verification verdicts cease to be trustworthy, but the verdicts themselves can be regenerated by re-running the $V_i$ on the preserved artifacts and specifications, exactly as Corollary 10.2 provides. The signature was, as §1.7 put it, an efficiency optimization on a verification that never depended on it; its cryptographic-transition obligation is real but is the transmission layer's to bear, and bearing it changes nothing about whether the underlying structural-honesty claims are true or re-verifiable. The supply chain has post-quantum work to do, and that work leaves the structural honesty of its artifacts exactly where it found it.
