## Framing: First Detailed Evidentiary Discharge of T83's J

### Chapter 13's role: evidence, not re-proof

Chapter 13 is the first detailed evidentiary discharge of T83's named judgment-case set $J$ for its SI1 portion. Chapter 8 §3 established T83 as a definitional-adequacy claim relative to $J$ (the named twenty-eight-case judgment set spanning SI1 through SI4), with the detailed substrate-specific evidence routed to Chapters 13--16. Chapter 13 instantiates that routing for SI1: it supplies the substrate-specific evidence that Chapter 8 explicitly deferred to the case-study block, evidencing T83's adequacy claim for the seven SI1 cases under SI1's declared $(O, K, R, R_{\mathrm{may}}, \Pi_X, \sim_X)$.

The chapter's role is evidence, not re-proof. Chapter 8 names $J$, supplies the SHV vocabulary mapping pattern, and establishes the structured-interpretation discipline (§§3.1--3.2). Chapter 13 does not re-prove T83 as a theorem and does not re-open Chapter 8's integrative theorem work; it provides the operational evidence that T83's adequacy claim is substantiated for SI1. The asymmetry is structural: T83 is a definitional-adequacy theorem at the empirical-relative-to-$J$ layer of the Principle of Layered Defense (Chapter 8 §0.2); Chapter 13 supplies the empirical evidence at that layer for the SI1 portion. Re-proving the theorem at the case-study layer would conflate the layers; supplying the evidence is the case-study chapter's proper work.

This framing is analogous to the relationship between Chapter 8 §2's T82 finite-witness construction (which used an SI1-vocabulary minimal-fragment witness to demonstrate formal satisfiability of A1--A4) and Chapter 13's full-scope SI1 instantiation (which uses Bayyinah at its actual operational scope to evidence A1--A4 holding). Chapter 8 §2's witness is a model-existence proof at the formal-consistency layer; Chapter 13 is the operational-instantiation evidence at the empirical layer. Both layers are necessary; neither subsumes the other.

### J-discharge scope: the seven SI1 cases

Chapter 13 discharges the seven SI1 cases named in Chapter 8 §3.1's judgment-case set $J$: three positive cases (SI1-P1, SI1-P2, SI1-P3) where the substrate operates correctly under its declared scope and practitioners would recognize structural honesty; three negative cases (SI1-N1, SI1-N2, SI1-N3) where the substrate exhibits a structural-honesty failure that practitioners would recognize; and one boundary case (SI1-B1) where practitioner judgment is debatable and the case is routed to Chapter 21 per Chapter 8 §3.6's boundary-case discipline.

The seven cases are named at the chapter level in §3.1 of Chapter 8 and discharged by detailed substrate evidence in Chapter 13 §7 (Loop 2). The case-discharge scope is exactly seven: not fewer (under-discharge would be a structural-honesty gap with T83) and not more (re-opening $J$'s enumeration is Chapter 8's prerogative, not Chapter 13's). Cases outside the named $J$ are explicitly out of scope for Chapter 13; their structural-honesty implications for AX-SH at the SI1 substrate are routed to Chapter 21 falsification-protocol work (long-horizon $J$-evolution) or Chapter 20 substrate-generalization analysis as relevant.

### Cross-chapter dependencies and template precedent

Chapter 13 depends on Chapters 3--7 (the typed-object machinery and the four axioms A1--A4 that Bayyinah is mapped to) and Chapter 8 (the T83 integrative-evaluation framework, the named $J$, the SHV vocabulary mapping pattern, and the Principle of Layered Defense). Chapter 13 does not depend on Chapters 9--12, 17--23, or the other case-study chapters (14--16). The natural read-order is Chapters 1--8, then Chapter 13.

Chapter 13 establishes the template for Chapters 14--16. The SI1.0--SI1.9 cluster structure used in Section 14 of the audit ledger maps to Chapter 13's section structure (§§0--9) and becomes the template for Chapter 14 (SI2 Furqan), Chapter 15 (SI3 Munafiq), and Chapter 16 (SI4 Supply-chain stack) with substrate-specific variation inside the sections rather than at the top-level chapter contract. Chapter 16's SI4 may need additional internal layering in §§1--2 to describe the four-substrate stack, but the top-level chapter structure is uniform across the case-study block.

### Chapter 13 / Chapter 8 boundary and Chapter 13 / Chapter 21 boundary

Chapter 13's scope is the substrate-specific evidence for the seven SI1 cases at the empirical-relative-to-$J$ layer. The chapter does not extend beyond this scope: long-horizon SI1 dynamics (Bayyinah's evolution over decades, the practitioner-judgment evolution that may add new SI1 cases to $J$ in the future, the emergent-misappropriation surveillance of Bayyinah-derived practices) are Chapter 21 falsification-protocol work, not Chapter 13's. Boundary cases where practitioner judgment is debatable receive an explicit AX-SH rationale or are routed to Chapter 21 per Chapter 8 §3.6's boundary-case discipline; SI1-B1 is routed to Chapter 21 with explicit rationale supplied in §7 (Loop 2).

The Chapter 13 / Chapter 8 boundary preserves the layered-defense discipline: Chapter 8 owns T83's adequacy theorem at the empirical-relative-to-$J$ layer; Chapter 13 owns the SI1 evidence at the same layer. The two chapters meet at the layer boundary without overlap: Chapter 13 does not re-state the theorem, and Chapter 8 does not anticipate the substrate-specific evidence.

## Bayyinah scanner v1.1.0: substrate description

### Primary vocabulary and operational scope

Bayyinah is a file-layer scanning system at version v1.1.0. The scanner reads file blobs from a declared input domain and emits structured scan output describing the blob's intrinsic file-kind, content classification, and scan completeness. For the purposes of the SI1 case-study abstraction, the public surface is represented by the operation $\mathrm{scan}(\mathrm{blob})$ and its structured output; Bayyinah's actual deployment interface may expose additional CLI flags, output formats, or operational modes that this abstraction does not enumerate. The operational scope of v1.1.0 includes file blobs of size up to 64MB, drawn from the twenty-three-kind file-kind taxonomy (§1.2 below), with classification structured by the zahir/batin split (§1.3) and verified for PDFs by the byte-identical parity check (§1.4). The scan-incomplete primitive (§1.5) is the substrate-internal vocabulary for declaring that a scan operation could not complete on a specific blob. Implementation-level details beyond the Bayyinah v1.1.0 public numerical summary are used in this chapter only where documented by the Bayyinah reference implementation; otherwise they function as illustrative operational detail and not as independent adequacy evidence.

### File-kind taxonomy at full scope

Bayyinah v1.1.0's file-kind taxonomy comprises twenty-three file kinds spanning document, image, audio, code, and binary formats. The taxonomy is the declared operational scope of Bayyinah's detection mechanisms: blobs whose intrinsic file-kind falls within the twenty-three-kind taxonomy are within scope and the surface API declares the file-kind explicitly; blobs whose file-kind falls outside the taxonomy are out of scope and the surface declines to assert a file-kind under v1.1.0's declared correspondence relation. The Chapter 8 §2 T82 witness reduced this taxonomy to the minimal three-kind fragment $\{\mathrm{PDF}, \mathrm{TXT}, \mathrm{BIN}\}$ for formal-satisfiability verification at the model-existence layer; Chapter 13 uses the full twenty-three-kind taxonomy as SI1's actual operational scope at the empirical layer.

The full taxonomy supports the 108 detection mechanisms described in §1.3 below. Future extensions to the taxonomy are corrigenda-tagged version events per Chapter 4 §1.1's A1 discipline (the Liskov-Wing version-subtyping requirement with explicit corrigenda for any scope-narrowing).

### The 27/81 zahir-layer/batin-layer split

Bayyinah's content classification distinguishes *zahir* (manifest, directly observable) content from *batin* (latent, requiring substrate-internal correspondence relations) content. The 27/81 split refers to the operational structure of Bayyinah's detection mechanisms: 27 of the 108 mechanisms operate at the zahir (manifest) layer where the file-kind and classification are directly observable from the blob's surface bytes (file magic, header structure, encoding markers); 81 of the 108 mechanisms operate at the batin (latent) layer where classification requires substrate-internal correspondence between the blob's content and the file-kind's expected structural properties.

The zahir/batin distinction maps to AX-SH's declared-object discipline as follows. The zahir-layer mechanisms operate under the declared observer model $O$ (Chapter 3 §1.2) at its manifest-content reading: the observer's access to the blob is direct byte-reading of surface markers. The batin-layer mechanisms operate under projections in $\Pi_X$ (Chapter 7 §1.6) that read substrate-internal correspondence states beyond what direct surface observation supports; these projections are the substrate's mechanism for evidencing claims about file-kind that the surface alone cannot directly verify. The 27/81 ratio is documented in Bayyinah's substrate-internal classification logic; the specific assignment of each of the 108 mechanisms to either the zahir or batin layer is recorded in the substrate's operational documentation.

### The 17/17 PDF byte-identical parity check

Bayyinah v1.1.0 includes a PDF-specific byte-identical parity check verifying 17 declared structural properties of PDF blobs against 17 corresponding byte-comparison points in the raw blob bytes. The check provides byte-level evidence for PDF file-kind classification beyond what the file-magic detection alone supplies: when Bayyinah declares a blob is a PDF under v1.1.0's correspondence relation, the parity check substantiates that declaration through direct byte-comparison evidence. The 17/17 ratio is the declared parity-check coverage: 17 specific properties verified through 17 specific byte-comparison points.

The parity check is one of the projections in SI1's declared projection family $\Pi_X$ (specifically, $\pi_{\mathrm{pdf}}$ per Chapter 7 §1.6's projection identification, instantiated in §2.5 below). The projection's domain is the PDF subset of the operational context $K$; on PDF blobs, $\pi_{\mathrm{pdf}}$ returns the parity-check verdict alongside the shared kind coordinate per the Chapter 8 §2.2 patched discipline. The check is documented in Bayyinah's PDF-handling subsystem.

### The scan-incomplete primitive and version history v1.0 to v1.1.0

The scan-incomplete primitive is Bayyinah's substrate-internal vocabulary for declaring that a scan operation could not complete on a specific blob. The primitive is part of SI1's declared $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ (§2.4 below); the surface API may return scan-incomplete on the kind-detection dimension, on the classification dimension, or on the completeness dimension separately, each indicating a specific scope of partial scan result. The primitive supports SI1's A3 obligation: caller-side exhaustiveness over $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ requires that the caller community handle, propagate, or supply proven-unreachable certificates for scan-incomplete outcomes through Chapter 6 §1's three discharge paths.

The Bayyinah version history evidences A1's Liskov-Wing version-subtyping discipline (Chapter 4 §1.1) operationally. Version v1.0 (the initial release, dated 2026-04-23 in the v1.0 CHANGELOG) declared an operational scope of 14 file kinds and 89 detection mechanisms with 17/17 PDF parity-check coverage. Version v1.1.0 (CHANGELOG-witnessed 2026-04-24; source-witnessed transitively through the patch-only v1.1.1 initial commit `ad4fd400` of the public `Bayyinah-Integrity-Scanner` repository, dated 2026-04-26) extends the operational scope to 23 file kinds and 108 detection mechanisms while preserving the 17/17 PDF parity-check coverage and introducing the refined 27/81 zahir/batin split. v1.1.0 was not separately tagged or committed as a buildable source tree on any audited repository; v1.1.1 source bytes faithfully witness v1.1.0's mechanism count, zahir/batin split, FileKind taxonomy, analyzer count, and parity-sweep shape per the v1.1.1 CHANGELOG's explicit declaration that the v1.1.0 $\rightarrow$ v1.1.1 transition is patch-only ("no new analyzer, no new mechanisms, no new file kinds, no behaviour change"). The v1.0 $\rightarrow$ v1.1.0 transition is substantive evolution per Chapter 8 §2.7's substantive-evolution ecosystem assumption; the specific classification of the transition's changes (which are strengthenings, which are corrigenda-tagged events) is supplied in §3 (Loop 2) as A1 evidence. The 1,435 passing tests at v1.1.0 are CHANGELOG-witnessed only (v1.1.1 reports 1,446 tests, the v1.1.0 baseline plus 11 new registry tests); the test-count claim is treated as project-history evidence rather than independently source-verified at v1.1.0 per the chapter's source-posture discipline.

## AX-SH structured interpretation for SI1

Section 3 of Chapter 8 supplied the SHV vocabulary mapping pattern at the chapter-level (§3.2) and the structured-interpretation discipline (§§3.2--3.4). Section 2 of Chapter 13 instantiates that mapping pattern at the SI1 substrate level: each of the six declared objects $(O, K, R, R_{\mathrm{may}}, \Pi_X, \sim_X)$ from Chapter 3 §1's typed-object machinery is given its SI1-specific operational instantiation. The instantiation specializes Chapter 8's compact SHV mapping with Bayyinah-specific detail; it does not invent new machinery beyond what Chapters 3--8 supply.

### SI1's declared observer model O

SI1's declared observer model $O$ is file-blob observation at the kind layer with substrate-internal access to file content under the declared 64MB context-set restriction. $O$ is operationally instantiated as Bayyinah's I/O regime: the specific file-read mechanism (buffered streaming with declared maximum-blob-size enforcement), the specific buffer-handling discipline (decoded read with encoding-detection fallback), and the specific encoding-detection logic (the substrate-internal encoding inference mechanism that determines how raw bytes are interpreted as file content under each candidate file-kind hypothesis). The observer model is documented at the operational scope of Bayyinah's reference implementation.

### SI1's declared context set K

SI1's declared context set $K$ comprises file blobs of size up to 64MB whose intrinsic file-kind is drawn from the twenty-three-kind taxonomy (§1.2). Blobs outside $K$ --- blobs over 64MB, or blobs whose file-kind falls outside the taxonomy --- are out of SI1's scope and the surface API declines to make claims about them under v1.1.0's declared correspondence relation. The context set is the substrate's declared operational domain; satisfying A2 (Chapter 5 §1) requires that the surface-substrate consistency hold within $K$ but does not require claims outside $K$.

### SI1's declared correspondence relation R

SI1's declared correspondence relation $R$ is: scan output matches intrinsic blob state under (kind-detection, classification, completeness) consistency. $R(\mathrm{Surface}_{v1.1.0}, \mathrm{Substrate}_{v1.1.0})$ holds when, for every blob $b \in K$, $\mathrm{scan}(b)$ returns the correct file-kind under the twenty-three-kind taxonomy, the correct zahir/batin classification per the 27/81 split, and the correct scan-completeness status under the declared observer model $O$. For PDFs specifically, $R$ includes the byte-identical parity check substantiating PDF file-kind classification through the 17/17 parity-check coverage (§1.4). $R$ is the substrate-specific instantiation of A2's surface-substrate consistency obligation under the typed-object machinery of Chapter 3.

### SI1's declared $R_{\mathrm{may}}$

SI1's declared $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ is the verifier/caller-side conservative over-approximation of $R$, including all outcomes that $\mathrm{scan}(\mathrm{blob})$ may return: the declared correct outcomes (kind/classification/completeness tuples satisfying $R$) plus the declared partial outcomes via the scan-incomplete primitive (scan-incomplete on kind detection, scan-incomplete on classification, scan-incomplete on completeness, scan-failed). The $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ declaration follows the Chapter 6 §2.2 public/private $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ discipline and the Chapter 8 §4.2 patched discipline: $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ is the publicly relied-on or case-study-declared over-approximation --- whether producer-specified, verifier-published, or caller-surface --- under which A3 caller-side exhaustiveness is evaluated. The distinction between publicly relied-on (where actual external reliance on $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ is demonstrated by Bayyinah's operational deployment) and case-study-declared (where this chapter declares $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ for the purposes of evidencing the SI1 cases without pre-claiming external reliance) is evaluated in §8 (Loop 2) under the ecosystem-condition status taxonomy. Caller-side discharge through Chapter 6 §1's three discharge paths (handle, propagate-as-incomplete, supply-proven-unreachable-certificate) operates against the declared $R_{\mathrm{may}}$, not against a producer-private $R$.

### SI1's declared projection family $\Pi_X$

SI1's declared projection family $\Pi_X = \{\pi_{\mathrm{kind}}, \pi_{\mathrm{zb}}, \pi_{\mathrm{pdf}}, \pi_{\mathrm{scan}}\}$ is the four-projection family identified in Chapter 7 §1.6 at full SI1 scope. $\pi_{\mathrm{kind}}$ reads kind-detection results across the twenty-three-kind taxonomy and is defined on every blob in $K$; $\pi_{\mathrm{zb}}$ reads zahir/batin classification under the 27/81 split and is defined on blobs the substrate has classified; $\pi_{\mathrm{pdf}}$ reads PDF byte-identical parity check results under the 17/17 coverage and is defined on PDF blobs in $K$; $\pi_{\mathrm{scan}}$ reads scan-completeness status and is defined on blobs where scan-completeness is determinate (not partial).

Each projection carries the shared kind coordinate per Chapter 8 §2.2's patched discipline: $\pi_{\mathrm{kind}}(b) = (\mathrm{kind}(b))$; $\pi_{\mathrm{zb}}(b) = (\mathrm{kind}(b), \mathrm{zb}(b))$; $\pi_{\mathrm{pdf}}(b) = (\mathrm{kind}(b), \mathrm{pdf}\text{-}\mathrm{parity}(b))$; $\pi_{\mathrm{scan}}(b) = (\mathrm{kind}(b), \mathrm{scan}\text{-}\mathrm{complete}(b))$. The shared kind coordinate ensures that the consistency relation $\sim_X$ (§2.6 below) is well-defined across projections.

### SI1's declared consistency relation $\sim_X$

SI1's declared consistency relation $\sim_X$ requires file-kind agreement among projection outputs on the joint domain. For two projections $\pi_i$ and $\pi_j$ and a blob $b$ in their joint domain, $\pi_i(b) \sim_X \pi_j(b)$ if and only if the projections agree on the kind coordinate at $b$. The relation is exercised by A4's joint-domain consistency obligation (Chapter 7 §1): joint-domain consistency under $\sim_X$ requires that every pair of projections that are both defined at $b$ produce kind-coordinate-agreeing outputs.

Although $\Pi_X$ and $\sim_X$ are exercised together by A4, they are distinct declared objects in Chapter 7's declared-object discipline: $\Pi_X$ names the substrate's projection mechanisms; $\sim_X$ names the consistency relation by which projections are checked. Section 14 of the audit ledger separates them into SI1.2.5 (the projection family) and SI1.2.6 (the consistency relation) for template precedent: Chapters 14--16 will follow the same split (SI2.2.5/SI2.2.6, SI3.2.5/SI3.2.6, SI4.2.5/SI4.2.6). The separation does not change the substantive A4 obligation, which is the joint-domain consistency of projection outputs under the named consistency relation.

## A1 evidence: SI1 version-subtyping and corrigenda discipline

### SI1 version history at the surface level

The Bayyinah version history at the surface level comprises the v1.0 initial release (dated 2026-04-23: 14 file kinds, 89 detection mechanisms, 17/17 PDF parity-check coverage, an earlier zahir/batin classification structure) and the v1.1.0 canonical version (CHANGELOG-witnessed 2026-04-24, source-witnessed transitively through the patch-only v1.1.1 initial commit `ad4fd400`: 23 file kinds, 108 detection mechanisms, 17/17 PDF parity-check coverage preserved, the refined 27/81 zahir/batin split introduced). The v1.0 $\rightarrow$ v1.1.0 transition is the substantive evolution event that Chapter 13's A1 evidence is structured around. Section 1.5 of this chapter named the substantive content of the transition; §3 evaluates which transition components are strengthenings under Liskov-Wing behavioral-subtyping discipline, which are corrigenda-tagged events, and what A1 satisfaction evidence this combination supplies.

### Liskov-Wing version-subtyping evidence at v1.0 to v1.1.0

The transition's components are classified as follows. The file-kind taxonomy extension from 14 to 23 kinds is a strengthening: nine file kinds are added to the operational scope (4 video kinds + 5 audio kinds) without withdrawing any of the original 14 kinds. A v1.0 caller relying on the original 14-kind taxonomy continues to receive correct behavior under v1.1.0 for those 14 kinds, plus additional correct behavior for the nine new kinds. The detection mechanism additions from 89 to 108 mechanisms are strengthenings: the 19 new mechanisms (8 video, 9 audio, 2 cross-stem) add operational capability without modifying or removing the original 89. The PDF parity-check coverage was *preserved* at 17/17 across the v1.0 $\rightarrow$ v1.1.0 transition --- the Phase-0 PDF fixture-set cardinality was unchanged, and the byte-identical parity invariant continued to hold across all 17 fixtures. The preservation of the 17/17 invariant across substantive substrate evolution is itself a Liskov-Wing witness: the foundational byte-identity invariant survives intact even as the substrate's operational scope substantially expands. The zahir/batin split refinement from the v1.0 structure to the 27/81 v1.1.0 split is the most structurally complex change: where the refinement adds classification detail without narrowing the substrate's content-classification commitments, it is a strengthening; where it reclassifies content previously labeled zahir as batin (or vice versa), it requires explicit corrigendum tagging per Chapter 4 §1.1's A1 discipline.

The Liskov-Wing version-subtyping evidence is therefore mixed: most of the transition's components are strengthenings (additions only, with the 17/17 parity invariant explicitly preserved), and the zahir/batin refinement requires corrigenda treatment for any specific reclassifications that narrow prior commitments. The mixed-evidence character is documented at the substrate's reference-implementation level; where specific refinement components are reconstructed from project history rather than directly documented in the Bayyinah v1.1.1 source (the byte-anchor for v1.1.0 per §1.5), the prose treats them as project-history evidence per the Loop 1 source-posture discipline.

### Corrigenda events in SI1 history

Where the v1.0 to v1.1.0 transition includes corrigenda-tagged events, those events are evidence that Bayyinah's evolution exercises corrigenda discipline operationally rather than merely declaring it abstractly. The candidate corrigenda events in the transition are: the zahir/batin split refinement components that reclassify previously-labeled content (rather than only adding new classifications); the file-kind taxonomy extension components that revise the boundaries of existing kinds (rather than only adding new kinds); and the detection mechanism additions that supersede earlier mechanisms (rather than only adding to them). For each candidate event, the question is whether the Bayyinah reference implementation documents the change as a corrigendum-tagged event (with explicit withdrawal of the prior claim) or as an additive strengthening (with no withdrawal). Components documented as corrigendum-tagged events substantiate A1's corrigenda discipline; components documented as additive strengthenings do not (and do not need to, since A1 only requires corrigenda for actual claim withdrawals).

The number and identity of specific corrigendum-tagged events in the v1.0 to v1.1.0 transition is the substrate-internal documentation question that determines SI1.8.4's ecosystem-condition status (demonstrated, partial, etc.) in §8 below.

### A1 satisfaction evidence

The combination of the strengthening-character of most transition components (§3.2), the required corrigenda-tagged treatment of any zahir/batin refinement components that narrow prior commitments (§3.3), and the substantive operational character of the v1.0 to v1.1.0 evolution (Loop 1 §1.5) together support A1 satisfaction for SI1, conditional on the substrate-internal documentation showing that any withdrawal or scope-narrowing components were explicitly corrigenda-tagged. If the transition is purely additive, A1 satisfaction is supported by version-subtyping alone; if withdrawals occurred without corrigenda tags, that would be an A1 gap rather than A1 evidence. The evidence does not introduce any new axiom conditions beyond A1 as stated in Chapter 4 §1.1; SI1's A1 satisfaction is evaluated against A1's existing Liskov-Wing version-subtyping discipline with corrigenda for scope-narrowing, not against a modified or extended A1.

## A2 evidence: SI1 surface-substrate consistency per version

### Per-version surface-substrate consistency at v1.0

At v1.0, A2's surface-substrate consistency obligation is $R_0(\mathrm{Surface}_{v1.0}, \mathrm{Substrate}_{v1.0})$ holds: for every blob $b \in K_0$ under v1.0's declared context set (file blobs of size up to 64MB in the original 14-kind taxonomy), $\mathrm{scan}(b)$ at v1.0 returns the correct (kind, classification, completeness) tuple under v1.0's declared correspondence relation $R_0$. The substrate's intrinsic file-kind, content-classification, and scan-completeness state at $b$ matches the surface API's declared scan output for $b$. The 89 detection mechanisms at v1.0 cover the v1.0 14-kind taxonomy in the sense that every file-kind in the taxonomy is supported by at least one detection mechanism; the 17/17 PDF parity check substantiates correspondence for PDF blobs specifically.

### Per-version surface-substrate consistency at v1.1.0

At v1.1.0, A2's surface-substrate consistency obligation is $R_1(\mathrm{Surface}_{v1.1.0}, \mathrm{Substrate}_{v1.1.0})$ holds: for every blob $b \in K_1$ under v1.1.0's declared context set (file blobs of size up to 64MB in the 23-kind taxonomy), $\mathrm{scan}(b)$ at v1.1.0 returns the correct (kind, classification, completeness) tuple under v1.1.0's declared correspondence relation $R_1$. The 108 detection mechanisms at v1.1.0 cover the v1.1.0 23-kind taxonomy; the 17/17 PDF parity check substantiates correspondence for PDF blobs. For PDF blobs specifically, $R_1$ includes the 17 parity-check properties verified through the 17 byte-comparison points (Loop 1 §1.4), giving direct byte-level evidence for PDF file-kind classification beyond what the file-magic detection alone supplies.

### Concrete detection-mechanism results substantiating R

The substrate's per-file-kind detection accuracy is documented at the level of Bayyinah's test suite results. Specific concrete cases supporting $R_1$: PDF kind detection across the 23-kind taxonomy with byte-comparison parity for the PDF subset (the 17/17 parity-check coverage); TXT encoding detection with charset identification across the supported encoding regimes; BIN file-magic detection with format-family classification for binary formats. Where the test-suite results are documented in the Bayyinah reference implementation, they substantiate $R_1$ directly; where specific per-file-kind accuracy claims are not source-documented at the chapter's level of detail, the chapter treats them as illustrative operational detail rather than independent adequacy evidence per the Loop 1 implementation-detail source-posture discipline.

### A2 satisfaction evidence

The combination of per-version surface-substrate consistency at v1.0 (§4.1) and v1.1.0 (§4.2), together with the concrete detection-mechanism evidence (§4.3), supports A2 satisfaction for SI1 at both versions to the extent documented by the Bayyinah reference implementation and test-suite evidence. The evidence does not introduce any new axiom conditions beyond A2 as stated in Chapter 5 §1; SI1's A2 satisfaction is evaluated against A2's existing per-version surface-substrate consistency under declared $(O, K, R)$, not against a modified or extended A2.

## A3 evidence: SI1 caller-side exhaustiveness over $R_{\mathrm{may}}$

### SI1 caller-diversity model

The SI1 caller-diversity model includes internal CI roles (gating downstream processing on scan output via pipeline status codes), audit-tool roles (cross-referencing scan output against external manifests), downstream-pipeline roles (consuming scan output for content-routing decisions), and forensic-analysis roles (using scan output as evidence in audit chains). Where these caller roles are documented in Bayyinah's deployment context as actually exercised by real callers in operational use, the model is supported by documentation; where actual external caller diversity is not yet demonstrated for a specific role, Chapter 13 classifies this as an operational-nontriviality limitation rather than a failure of A3 per the Loop 1 caller-diversity-model source-posture discipline. The distinction is preserved at the chapter level: A3 holds formally when the caller community (however small or large, documented or modeled) exhausts $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ through Chapter 6 §1's three discharge paths; whether the operational interpretation of A3 as structural-honesty discipline is satisfied operationally depends on §8's ecosystem-condition status evaluation.

### Caller-side discharge patterns through the three $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ discharge paths

The caller-diversity model exercises each of Chapter 6 §1's three discharge paths. CI callers handle declared correct outcomes (kind/classification/completeness tuples) directly, propagate scan-incomplete via CI-pipeline status codes (the handle-or-propagate discharge), and may supply proven-unreachable certificates for scan-failed outcomes on pre-verified blobs (the handle/propagate/proof-unreachable discharge). Audit-tool callers handle declared outcomes, propagate scan-incomplete with annotations like "deferred verification" in audit logs, and supply proven-unreachable certificates for outcomes the audit tool's pre-conditions exclude (e.g., scan-failed cannot occur for blobs the audit tool has already verified as well-formed). Downstream-pipeline callers handle declared outcomes and propagate scan-incomplete upward through their respective pipelines. Forensic-analysis callers may use any of the three discharge paths depending on their specific role in the audit chain.

The discharge pattern coverage is documented where the Bayyinah reference implementation supplies specific caller-discharge examples; otherwise the pattern coverage is modeled from the operational structure of $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ and the three discharge paths.

### Concrete examples of caller exhaustiveness over $R_{\mathrm{may}}$

Specific concrete examples supporting caller exhaustiveness include: a CI caller processing a batch of mixed-kind blobs (PDF, TXT, BIN) handles each declared correct outcome via downstream routing, propagates scan-incomplete on partially-scanned blobs as pipeline-warnings, and handles scan-failed by halting downstream processing; an audit-tool caller processing the same batch handles each declared correct outcome by recording cross-check results, propagates scan-incomplete as deferred-verification annotations, and supplies proven-unreachable certificates for scan-failed on pre-verified blobs.

The examples are illustrative of the discharge pattern coverage. Where specific examples are documented in the Bayyinah reference implementation's deployment documentation, they substantiate caller exhaustiveness directly; where examples are modeled from the operational structure of A3's three discharge paths, they substantiate the structural pattern without claiming specific historical instances.

### A3 satisfaction evidence

The combination of the SI1 caller-diversity model (§5.1), the three-discharge-path coverage (§5.2), and the concrete examples (§5.3) supports A3 satisfaction for SI1 under the declared caller-diversity model and $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ discharge structure. Where caller roles and discharge examples are documented in Bayyinah's deployment context, the evidence is empirical; where they are modeled from the operational structure of $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ and the three discharge paths, the evidence supports the structural pattern but leaves operational nontriviality to §8.1's partial ecosystem-status classification. The evidence does not introduce any new axiom conditions beyond A3 as stated in Chapter 6 §1; SI1's A3 satisfaction is evaluated against A3's existing caller-side exhaustiveness obligation over $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ through the three discharge paths, not against a modified or extended A3.

## A4 evidence: SI1 joint-domain projection consistency under $\sim_X$

### SI1 four-projection family at full operational scope

The four-projection family $\Pi_X = \{\pi_{\mathrm{kind}}, \pi_{\mathrm{zb}}, \pi_{\mathrm{pdf}}, \pi_{\mathrm{scan}}\}$ at full SI1 scope is the projection family identified in Chapter 7 §1.6 and instantiated in Loop 1 §2.5. Each projection's domain at full scope is: $\pi_{\mathrm{kind}}$ defined on all blobs in $K_1$ (the 23-kind taxonomy under v1.1.0's context set); $\pi_{\mathrm{zb}}$ defined on blobs the substrate has classified under the 27/81 zahir/batin split; $\pi_{\mathrm{pdf}}$ defined on PDF blobs in $K_1$; $\pi_{\mathrm{scan}}$ defined on blobs where scan-completeness is determinate. Each projection carries the shared kind coordinate per Chapter 8 §2.2's patched discipline. The projection-family structure is documented at the substrate's reference-implementation level.

### Joint-domain analysis for the four projections

The four projections have overlapping but non-identical domains. The full joint domain $\mathrm{dom}(\pi_{\mathrm{kind}}) \cap \mathrm{dom}(\pi_{\mathrm{zb}}) \cap \mathrm{dom}(\pi_{\mathrm{pdf}}) \cap \mathrm{dom}(\pi_{\mathrm{scan}})$ is the set of PDF blobs in $K_1$ where classification under the zahir/batin split is computed and scan-completeness is determinate. Pairwise joint domains are larger: $\mathrm{dom}(\pi_{\mathrm{kind}}) \cap \mathrm{dom}(\pi_{\mathrm{zb}})$ includes all classified blobs across the 23-kind taxonomy (not only PDFs); $\mathrm{dom}(\pi_{\mathrm{kind}}) \cap \mathrm{dom}(\pi_{\mathrm{scan}})$ includes all blobs where scan-completeness is determinate; and so on. A4's joint-domain consistency obligation under $\sim_X$ requires that every pair of projections that are both defined at a blob $b$ produce kind-coordinate-agreeing outputs at $b$.

### Concrete cases of joint-domain consistency under $\sim_X$

Specific concrete cases supporting joint-domain consistency: a PDF blob where $\pi_{\mathrm{kind}}$ returns "PDF" as the kind coordinate, $\pi_{\mathrm{zb}}$ returns ("PDF", zb-classification) with PDF as the shared kind coordinate, $\pi_{\mathrm{pdf}}$ returns ("PDF", parity-check-verdict) with PDF as the shared kind coordinate, and $\pi_{\mathrm{scan}}$ returns ("PDF", complete) with PDF as the shared kind coordinate. All four projections agree on the kind coordinate ("PDF") at $b$; $\sim_X$ holds at $b$. A TXT blob (not in $\pi_{\mathrm{pdf}}$'s domain) where the three projections $\pi_{\mathrm{kind}}, \pi_{\mathrm{zb}}, \pi_{\mathrm{scan}}$ all agree on the kind coordinate ("TXT") exhibits joint-domain consistency on the pairwise joint domains, even though the full four-way joint domain does not apply.

The examples are documented at the substrate's reference-implementation level via the test-suite results substantiating per-projection accuracy.

### A4 satisfaction evidence

The combination of the four-projection family at full operational scope (§6.1), the joint-domain analysis (§6.2), and the concrete consistency cases (§6.3) substantiates A4 satisfaction for SI1 at the chapter-evidence layer. The evidence does not introduce any new axiom conditions beyond A4 as stated in Chapter 7 §1; SI1's A4 satisfaction is evaluated against A4's existing joint-domain consistency obligation under $\sim_X$, not against a modified or extended A4.

## Seven judgment-case discharges for SI1

Section 7 is the load-bearing center of Chapter 13: it discharges the seven SI1 cases named in Chapter 8 §3.1's judgment-case set $J$. Per the Section 14 spec-canon case-type discipline, positive cases (SI1-P1, P2, P3) are grounded in actual Bayyinah v1.1.0 operational behavior where possible; negative cases (SI1-N1, N2, N3) may be either documented failure-mode patterns or constructive counterfactuals, with constructive cases explicitly labeled; boundary cases (SI1-B1) receive either an explicit AX-SH rationale or are routed to Chapter 21 with explicit routing rationale. The seven cases collectively substantiate T83's adequacy claim for the SI1 portion of $J$; they do not substantiate T83's adequacy claim beyond the named seven cases, and they do not silently upgrade SI1 evidence into general file-layer adequacy.

### SI1-P1: complete file-kind detection across many file types

Substrate scenario: a routine scan operation processes a batch of blobs spanning multiple file-kinds in the 23-kind taxonomy. Each blob's intrinsic file-kind is detected correctly under SI1's declared $(O, K, R, R_{\mathrm{may}}, \Pi_X, \sim_X)$. The four projections agree on the kind coordinate across the joint domain for each blob; the surface API emits correct (kind, classification, completeness) tuples for each blob under $R_1$.

AX-SH classification: structurally honest. A1 holds (no version evolution exercised in this scenario beyond what §3 evidences); A2 holds (the surface-substrate consistency is direct: scan output matches intrinsic blob state); A3 holds (the caller community discharges $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ correctly because all outcomes are declared correct outcomes within $R$); A4 holds (projection consistency under $\sim_X$ is direct: all four projections agree on kind coordinate).

Expected practitioner judgment: structurally honest. The scanner is doing what its surface API claims; routine scan correctness is the baseline structural-honesty expectation for a file-layer scanner. Alignment evidence: the AX-SH classification matches practitioner judgment directly; there is no debate about routine correct behavior being structurally honest.

### SI1-P2: scan-incomplete propagation

Substrate scenario: a scan operation encounters scan-incomplete on a specific blob --- for example, a partially truncated file where kind detection completes but classification is partial, or a file where the encoding-detection logic cannot reach a definitive verdict. The surface API correctly emits the scan-incomplete primitive on the affected dimension. A CI caller propagates the scan-incomplete result via pipeline-warning status codes (the propagate-as-incomplete discharge path from Chapter 6 §1); an audit-tool caller records the scan-incomplete result as a deferred-verification annotation.

AX-SH classification: structurally honest. A1 holds (no version-evolution issue); A2 holds (the surface API correctly declares scan-incomplete under the declared $R$, which includes scan-incomplete as a partial-outcome declaration); A3 holds (the caller community discharges scan-incomplete through the propagate-as-incomplete path correctly); A4 holds (the scan projection $\pi_{\mathrm{scan}}$ correctly reports the incomplete state, agreeing with other projections on the kind coordinate where defined).

Expected practitioner judgment: structurally honest. The scanner is being honest about its inability to complete scanning, and the caller community handles this honestly through the propagate-as-incomplete path. Alignment evidence: AX-SH and practitioner judgment match. Practitioners value the explicit scan-incomplete declaration over silent partial-completion; the structural-honesty discipline applied to scan completeness is exactly what scan-incomplete primitive supports.

### SI1-P3: PDF parity-check confirmation

Substrate scenario: a PDF blob is scanned, and the byte-identical parity check verifies 17 declared structural properties against 17 byte-comparison points. The parity-check verdict confirms parity. The four projections agree on the kind coordinate "PDF"; $\pi_{\mathrm{pdf}}$ returns the parity-check verdict (confirmed) alongside the shared kind coordinate. A downstream audit tool uses the parity-check confirmation as evidence in its audit chain.

AX-SH classification: structurally honest. A1 through A3 hold as in the baseline routine-scan case. A4 holds with particular salience: the parity-check projection $\pi_{\mathrm{pdf}}$ and the kind-detection projection $\pi_{\mathrm{kind}}$ both confirm the blob's PDF identity through independent observation regimes (byte-comparison evidence versus file-magic evidence). Joint-domain consistency under $\sim_X$ is substantiated through the agreement of two independently-grounded projections.

Expected practitioner judgment: structurally honest. The substrate's commitment to byte-level PDF identity is verified through independent evidence and surfaced to downstream audit tools. Alignment evidence: AX-SH and practitioner judgment match. The parity-check substantiation is exactly the kind of cross-projection verification practitioners value for structural-honesty claims about file-kind classification.

### SI1-N1: undeclared scan-incomplete surfaced as scan-complete

*This is a modeled failure-mode judgment case, not presently asserted as a documented Bayyinah historical failure.* Whether specific historical instances of this pattern are documented in Bayyinah's QA records is a project-history question; the case's role in Chapter 13 is to show how AX-SH would classify the corresponding failure mode and to substantiate the structural-honesty discipline by which Bayyinah's design guards against this mode.

Substrate scenario: a scan operation encounters internal scan-incomplete state (e.g., the classification dimension cannot be fully determined under the declared observer model), but the surface API declares scan-complete in some output channel without surfacing the scan-incomplete primitive. The substrate's intrinsic state at the blob does not match the surface's declared scan output.

AX-SH classification: structurally dishonest. A2 fails: $R_1(\mathrm{Surface}_{v1.1.0}, \mathrm{Substrate}_{v1.1.0})$ does not hold at the failing blob because the surface's declared scan-complete contradicts the substrate's actual scan-incomplete state. A1, A3, A4 may still hold at the substrate level, but the A2 failure is sufficient for structural dishonesty.

Expected practitioner judgment: structurally dishonest. The scanner is lying about its scan completeness; the suppression of the scan-incomplete primitive is the exact form of dishonesty the primitive is designed to prevent. Alignment evidence: AX-SH and practitioner judgment match; the failure-mode pattern is exactly what A2's surface-substrate consistency discipline catches.

### SI1-N2: scope-narrowing without corrigenda-tagging

*This is a constructive negative judgment case, not a documented Bayyinah historical failure. Its role is to show how AX-SH would classify the corresponding SI1 failure mode if it occurred in a future version evolution.*

Substrate scenario: a hypothetical version evolution v1.1.0 to v1.2.0 narrows the file-kind taxonomy --- for example, removes a specific file-kind from the supported taxonomy without explicitly corrigendum-tagging the removal. A v1.1.0 caller relying on the removed file-kind's correct detection does not receive correct behavior under v1.2.0 for that kind; the silent scope narrowing breaks Liskov-Wing behavioral subtyping.

AX-SH classification: structurally dishonest. A1 fails: Liskov-Wing version-subtyping is violated by the silent scope-narrowing without corrigenda-tagging. A2, A3, A4 may still hold at v1.2.0 within its narrowed scope, but the A1 failure is sufficient for structural dishonesty.

Expected practitioner judgment: structurally dishonest. The scanner is silently withdrawing prior commitments without acknowledging the withdrawal; v1.1.0 callers are betrayed by v1.2.0's narrowed scope. Alignment evidence: AX-SH and practitioner judgment match; the failure-mode pattern is exactly what A1's corrigenda discipline catches.

### SI1-N3: PDF parity-check disagreement without diagnostic

*This is a constructive negative judgment case, not a documented Bayyinah historical failure. Its role is to show how AX-SH would classify the corresponding SI1 failure mode if it occurred.*

Substrate scenario: a hypothetical PDF blob is scanned and the parity-check produces a parity-mismatch result (one or more of the 17 declared structural properties does not match the corresponding byte-comparison point). However, the surface API does not surface a diagnostic about the parity-mismatch: $\pi_{\mathrm{pdf}}$ records the parity-mismatch internally, but the surface declares the blob's PDF identity as fully substantiated without qualifying the declaration with the parity-mismatch status.

AX-SH classification: structurally dishonest. A2 fails if the surface declares PDF identity as fully substantiated while the substrate's PDF parity projection records a parity-mismatch that should qualify or reject that declaration under SI1's declared $R$ (Loop 1 §2.3 included the 17/17 PDF parity check as part of $R$ for PDF blobs; suppressing a parity-mismatch from the declared scan output violates $R$). Whether A4 also fails depends on the strength of SI1's declared $\sim_X$. Under SI1's minimal kind-coordinate $\sim_X$ (Loop 1 §2.6), both $\pi_{\mathrm{kind}}$ and $\pi_{\mathrm{pdf}}$ carry kind = "PDF" as their shared coordinate; they agree on the kind coordinate and therefore do not directly violate $\sim_X$, even though the parity-mismatch is operationally relevant. A4 fails only if $\sim_X$ is declared to compare parity status (or some richer notion than kind-coordinate agreement) on the PDF joint domain; under minimal $\sim_X$, the primary failure is A2.

The case therefore functions as a constructive failure-mode test for whether SI1's declared $\sim_X$ is strong enough to expose parity disagreements at the A4 layer, or whether parity disagreements are caught only at the A2 layer through the surface's correspondence-relation discipline. The methodological observation is that a consistency relation defined narrowly (kind-coordinate agreement only) cannot by itself surface richer projection disagreements; if practitioners want such disagreements caught at the A4 layer, the substrate's declared $\sim_X$ must be strengthened beyond kind-coordinate agreement. This boundary observation is routed to Chapter 21 alongside SI1-B1's cross-layer completeness question as part of the long-horizon $\sim_X$-strength evolution.

Expected practitioner judgment: structurally dishonest. The scanner is concealing internal projection disagreement; practitioners would recognize the concealment as structural dishonesty about PDF identity claims, regardless of whether the AX-SH classification routes the failure through A2 or A4. Alignment evidence: AX-SH and practitioner judgment match on the structural-dishonesty verdict; the case additionally exposes a methodologically useful boundary about $\sim_X$ strength.

### SI1-B1: partially-classified file with complete kind detection

Substrate scenario: a file is scanned with kind detection complete (the file's kind is determined correctly under $\pi_{\mathrm{kind}}$) but classification only partial (the zahir/batin classification under $\pi_{\mathrm{zb}}$ returns scan-incomplete on the classification dimension while $\pi_{\mathrm{kind}}$ returns the kind correctly). The scan-incomplete projection $\pi_{\mathrm{scan}}$ indicates incomplete on classification but complete on kind.

Practitioner judgment is debatable on this scenario. Some practitioners view kind-detection-complete-with-classification-incomplete as structurally honest: the scanner is being honest about classification incompleteness while completing kind detection, and the scan-incomplete primitive is correctly surfaced on the classification dimension. Other practitioners view the cross-layer incompleteness propagation question as not yet settled by AX-SH: whether scan-incomplete at the classification layer should contaminate the file-kind-level honesty claim is itself a meta-question about how AX-SH's discipline handles cross-layer projection incompleteness.

AX-SH classification: structurally honest under the kind-detection-layer reading. At the kind-detection layer, all four axioms are satisfied: A1 holds (no version-evolution issue), A2 holds (the kind detection matches intrinsic blob kind under $R_1$), A3 holds (the caller community discharges scan-incomplete on classification through the propagate-as-incomplete path), A4 holds (projections agree on kind coordinate at the joint domain where defined).

*The case is routed to Chapter 21 because it concerns the evolution of practitioner judgment about cross-layer completeness propagation: whether scan-incomplete at the classification layer should contaminate file-kind-level honesty. Chapter 13 records the boundary rather than forcing a premature classification.* The cross-layer propagation question is itself a long-horizon question about how AX-SH's discipline should evolve as cross-layer completeness scenarios become more operationally significant; Chapter 21's falsification-protocol work (named-open O5) is the proper site for that evolution. Alignment evidence: practitioner judgment is debatable; Chapter 13 supplies the AX-SH classification at the kind-detection layer with explicit acknowledgment that the cross-layer question is routed forward.

## Ecosystem-condition status for SI1

Section 8 evaluates the four Chapter 8 §0.3 ecosystem conditions for SI1 using the five-status taxonomy: *demonstrated* (the condition is operationally evident in Bayyinah's deployment), *modeled* (the condition is plausible under a working model of operational deployment but not yet documented), *partial* (the condition is partly demonstrated and partly modeled), *absent* (the condition does not hold in the current Bayyinah deployment), or *routed-to-Chapter-21* (the condition's status is itself a long-horizon question routed forward). These statuses do not become new axioms; they describe operational nontriviality per Chapter 8 §0.3's auxiliary-not-axiom discipline.

### Caller diversity status for SI1

The SI1 caller-diversity model from §5.1 (internal CI, audit-tool, downstream-pipeline, forensic-analysis caller roles) is partly demonstrated and partly modeled. Where specific caller roles are documented in Bayyinah's deployment context as actually exercised by real callers, the model is *demonstrated* for those roles. Where caller roles are described from the operational structure of $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ and the three discharge paths without specific documented external-caller instances, the model is *modeled* for those roles. The aggregate status of SI1.8.1 (caller diversity) is *partial*: caller diversity is operationally plausible and architecturally supported, but not yet fully demonstrated across all caller roles.

### Projection multiplicity status for SI1

The four-projection family $\{\pi_{\mathrm{kind}}, \pi_{\mathrm{zb}}, \pi_{\mathrm{pdf}}, \pi_{\mathrm{scan}}\}$ from Loop 1 §2.5 declares four distinct projection roles documented at the substrate's reference-implementation level. The aggregate status of SI1.8.2 is *demonstrated* with respect to declared projection multiplicity: Bayyinah declares four distinct projection roles. Independence of implementation mechanisms is documented where the reference implementation shows distinct code paths or evidence sources for each projection ($\pi_{\mathrm{pdf}}$'s byte-comparison evidence versus $\pi_{\mathrm{kind}}$'s file-magic evidence versus $\pi_{\mathrm{zb}}$'s substrate-internal classification evidence versus $\pi_{\mathrm{scan}}$'s completion-status evidence); otherwise the chapter treats independence as role-level rather than implementation-level. The role-level demonstration is sufficient to substantiate Chapter 8 §0.3's projection-multiplicity ecosystem condition under the auxiliary-not-axiom discipline.

### Substantive evolution status for SI1

The v1.0 to v1.1.0 transition (file-kind taxonomy extension, detection-mechanism additions, 17/17 parity-check invariant preservation, zahir/batin split refinement) is *demonstrated*: the evolution is documented and is substantive under Chapter 8 §2.7's substantive-evolution criterion. The aggregate status of SI1.8.3 (substantive evolution) is *demonstrated*: SI1 deployment includes substantive version evolution exercising A1's discipline.

### Corrigenda discipline exercised status for SI1

The status of SI1.8.4 (corrigenda discipline exercised) depends on the specific corrigenda events in the v1.0 to v1.1.0 transition per §3.3. On the evidence currently surfaced in Chapter 13, SI1.8.4 is classified as *partial* unless the Bayyinah reference implementation or project history records specific corrigenda-tagged withdrawal events in the v1.0 to v1.1.0 transition. The chapter records the condition under which the status would become *demonstrated*: if the transition includes documented corrigenda-tagged events (specifically, zahir/batin refinement components that reclassify previously-labeled content with explicit corrigendum tagging, or file-kind taxonomy revisions with explicit withdrawal tagging), the condition is *demonstrated* (corrigenda discipline is exercised on documented withdrawn-claim transitions); but Chapter 13 does not claim demonstrated status absent that documentation. The specific corrigendum-event count in the transition is the substrate-internal documentation question whose resolution determines the precise status; until that documentation is verified, the *partial* classification is the structurally honest position.

## Chapter close: T83 tie-back, Chapter 21 routing, Chapter 20 surfacing

### T83 tie-back: the seven SI1 cases discharged

Chapter 13 discharges the seven SI1 cases named in Chapter 8 §3.1's judgment-case set $J$: SI1-P1, SI1-P2, SI1-P3 (§§7.1--7.3, three positive cases yielding AX-SH-honest classification consistent with practitioner judgment); SI1-N1, SI1-N2, SI1-N3 (§§7.4--7.6, three negative cases yielding AX-SH-dishonest classification consistent with practitioner judgment, with N1 labeled as modeled failure-mode judgment case and N2/N3 explicitly labeled as constructive counterfactuals per the Section 14 spec-canon case-type discipline); and SI1-B1 (§7.7, boundary case routed to Chapter 21 with explicit rationale per Chapter 8 §3.6's boundary-case discipline). The seven J-IDs are named explicitly here for trivial cross-reference checkability per Section 14's SI1.9.1 discipline. The integrative-evaluation argument from Chapter 8 §3.5 is now substantiated for the SI1 portion of $J$ at the chapter-evidence layer.

### Chapter 21 routing for SI1

Chapter 13's scope is the seven named SI1 cases at the empirical-relative-to-$J$ layer. Long-horizon SI1 dynamics (Bayyinah's evolution over decades, the practitioner-judgment evolution that may add new SI1 cases to $J$ in the future, the emergent-misappropriation surveillance of Bayyinah-derived practices) are routed to Chapter 21 falsification-protocol work (named-open O5 in Section 6 of the audit ledger). The SI1-B1 boundary case's cross-layer incompleteness question (§7.7) is routed to Chapter 21 specifically because it concerns the evolution of practitioner judgment about cross-layer completeness propagation. Chapter 13 does not solve these long-horizon questions; it names what it discharges (the seven cases at the chapter-evidence layer) and what it routes forward.

### Chapter 20 routing for SI1: permissive surfacing of substrate-generalization observations

Chapter 13 may surface SI1-specific observations relevant to Chapter 20 substrate-generalization analysis; it does not assert that SI1 generalizes to other file-layer substrates. Specifically: the four-projection family structure (kind, zb, pdf, scan) is SI1-specific to file-layer scanning; whether the same projection-family structure generalizes to other file-layer substrates (other file-scanning systems, content-addressed storage systems, file-system metadata services) is Chapter 20's substrate-generalization analysis. The zahir/batin classification structure may generalize beyond file-layer substrates to other substrates with manifest/latent content distinctions; the substantive operational evolution from v1.0 to v1.1.0 is a pattern that may be observed in other long-lived substrates. These observations are made available to Chapter 20's analytical work without claim of generalization.

The closing of Chapter 13 returns to the Loop 1 framing (§0.1): Chapter 13 supplies evidence for the SI1 portion of T83's adequacy claim, not a re-proof of T83 and not a substrate-generalization claim. The four-axiom evidence (§§3--6), the seven judgment-case discharges (§7), the ecosystem-condition status evaluation (§8), and the T83/21/20 routing (§9) together substantiate Chapter 13's contribution to T83 at the empirical-relative-to-$J$ layer for SI1.
