## Framing: Second Detailed Evidentiary Discharge of T83's J

### Chapter 14's role: evidence, not re-proof

Chapter 14 is the second detailed evidentiary discharge of T83's named judgment-case set $J$ for its SI2 portion. Chapter 8 §3 established T83 as a definitional-adequacy claim relative to $J$ (the named twenty-eight-case judgment set spanning SI1 through SI4), with the detailed substrate-specific evidence routed to Chapters 13--16. Chapter 13 instantiated that routing for SI1 (the file-layer Bayyinah substrate). Chapter 14 instantiates it for SI2: it supplies the substrate-specific evidence that Chapter 8 explicitly deferred to the case-study block, evidencing T83's adequacy claim for the seven SI2 cases under SI2's declared $(O, K, R, R_{\mathrm{may}}, \Pi_X, \sim_X)$.

The chapter's role is evidence, not re-proof. Chapter 8 names $J$, supplies the Furqan vocabulary mapping pattern (Chapter 8 §3.3), and establishes the structured-interpretation discipline. Chapter 14 does not re-prove T83 as a theorem and does not re-open Chapter 8's integrative theorem work; it provides the operational evidence that T83's adequacy claim is substantiated for SI2. The asymmetry is structural: T83 is a definitional-adequacy theorem at the empirical-relative-to-$J$ layer of the Principle of Layered Defense (Chapter 8 §0.2); Chapter 14 supplies the empirical evidence at that layer for the SI2 portion. Re-proving the theorem at the case-study layer would conflate the layers; supplying the evidence is the case-study chapter's proper work.

This framing parallels Chapter 13's relationship to Chapter 8: just as Chapter 13 §0.1 distinguished Chapter 8 §2's T82 minimal-fragment witness (model-existence at the formal-consistency layer) from Chapter 13's full-scope SI1 instantiation (operational instantiation at the empirical layer), Chapter 14 distinguishes Chapter 8 §3.3's Furqan vocabulary mapping pattern (a structured-interpretation skeleton at the chapter-level) from Chapter 14's full-scope SI2 instantiation (operational instantiation at the empirical layer on Furqan v0.11.1's actual substrate). Both layer relationships are preserved by Chapter 14's evidence-not-re-proof discipline.

### J-discharge scope: the seven SI2 cases

Chapter 14 discharges the seven SI2 cases named in Chapter 8 §3.1's judgment-case set $J$: three positive cases (SI2-P1, SI2-P2, SI2-P3) where Furqan operates correctly under its declared scope and practitioners would recognize structural honesty; three negative cases (SI2-N1, SI2-N2, SI2-N3) where the substrate exhibits a structural-honesty failure that practitioners would recognize, with negative cases labeled as documented historical failure or constructive counterfactual per the Chapter 13 case-type discipline; and one boundary case (SI2-B1) where practitioner judgment is debatable and the case is routed to Chapter 21 per Chapter 8 §3.6's boundary-case discipline.

The seven cases are named at the chapter level in §3.1 of Chapter 8 and discharged by detailed substrate evidence in Chapter 14 §7 (Loop 2). The case-discharge scope is exactly seven: not fewer (under-discharge would be a structural-honesty gap with T83) and not more (re-opening $J$'s enumeration is Chapter 8's prerogative, not Chapter 14's). Cases outside the named $J$ are explicitly out of scope for Chapter 14; their structural-honesty implications for AX-SH at the SI2 substrate are routed to Chapter 21 falsification-protocol work (long-horizon $J$-evolution) or Chapter 20 substrate-generalization analysis as relevant.

### Cross-chapter dependencies and template inheritance

Chapter 14 depends on Chapters 3--7 (the typed-object machinery and the four axioms A1--A4 that Furqan is mapped to), Chapter 8 (the T83 integrative-evaluation framework, the named $J$, the Furqan vocabulary mapping pattern §3.3, and the Principle of Layered Defense), and Chapter 13 (the case-study chapter template). Chapter 14 does not depend on Chapters 9--12, 17--23, or Chapters 15--16. The natural read-order is Chapters 1--8, then Chapter 13, then Chapter 14.

Chapter 14 inherits the case-study chapter template established by Chapter 13. The SI2.0--SI2.9 cluster structure used in Section 15 of the audit ledger maps to Chapter 14's section structure (§§0--9) with the same SIx.0--SIx.9 skeleton: framing (§0), substrate description (§1), AX-SH structured interpretation (§2), A1--A4 evidence (§§3--6), seven judgment-case discharges (§7), ecosystem-condition status (§8), and chapter close (§9). The template is intentionally stable across SI1 through SI4; substrate-specific variation lives inside the sections rather than at the top-level chapter contract. Chapter 14 is the second instantiation of this template after Chapter 13; Chapter 15 (SI3 Munafiq) and Chapter 16 (SI4 Supply-chain) will be the third and fourth instantiations.

The template inheritance carries the Chapter 13 spec-canon and post-prose patches forward as discipline-template language: documented-vs-modeled distinction throughout substrate description and axiom evidence, explicit constructive labeling for hypothetical negative cases, the five-status ecosystem-condition taxonomy (demonstrated / modeled / partial / absent / routed-to-Chapter-21), and the $\sim_X$-strength awareness in N3 case framing. Chapter 14 adds SI2-specific precision through the nine Section 15 spec-canon patches recorded in this chapter's version-status note.

### Chapter 14 / Chapter 8 boundary and Chapter 14 / Chapter 21 boundary

Chapter 14's scope is the substrate-specific evidence for the seven SI2 cases at the empirical-relative-to-$J$ layer. The chapter does not extend beyond this scope: long-horizon SI2 dynamics (Furqan's evolution over decades, the practitioner-judgment evolution that may add new SI2 cases to $J$ in the future, the emergent-misappropriation surveillance of Furqan-derived practices, and the cross-layer diagnostic-severity question raised by SI2-B1) are Chapter 21 falsification-protocol work, not Chapter 14's. Boundary cases where practitioner judgment is debatable receive an explicit AX-SH rationale or are routed to Chapter 21 per Chapter 8 §3.6's boundary-case discipline; SI2-B1 is routed to Chapter 21 with explicit rationale supplied in §7 (Loop 2).

The Chapter 14 / Chapter 8 boundary preserves the layered-defense discipline: Chapter 8 owns T83's adequacy theorem at the empirical-relative-to-$J$ layer; Chapter 14 owns the SI2 evidence at the same layer. The Chapter 14 / Chapter 13 boundary preserves the substrate-specific evidence layer: Chapter 13 owns SI1 evidence, Chapter 14 owns SI2 evidence, with no overlap between the two case-study chapters' substrate-specific claims. Chapter 14 may cite Chapter 13's patched-language template (e.g., the $\sim_X$-strength template from Chapter 13 §7.6 N3) as inheritable discipline, but does not re-state Chapter 13's substrate-specific evidence for SI1.

## Furqan prototype type-checker v0.11.1: substrate description

### Primary vocabulary and operational scope

Furqan is a prototype type-checker for a structural-honesty-discipline source language, at version v0.11.1, implemented as parser, type-checker, and types modules with CLI behavior and a test suite of 539 passing tests. For the purposes of the SI2 case-study abstraction, the public surface is represented by CLI invocation(s) such as $\mathrm{furqan\ check\ \langle module\rangle}$ and their structured diagnostic output; Furqan's actual interface may expose additional flags, modes, or invocation forms not enumerated here. The substrate is explicitly a *prototype type-checker, not a full compiler or runtime*: out-of-scope features such as code generation, optimization, and runtime behavior are explicitly excluded from SI2's declared scope. This prototype-scope boundary is load-bearing for several SI2 J-cases: SI2-P3 (the substrate's honest declaration of scope limits through the unsupported-construct diagnostic) and SI2-B1 (the boundary case concerning advisory-or-severity-ambiguous warning-level diagnostics) both depend on the substrate being honest about what it is and is not.

The operational scope of v0.11.1 includes Furqan programs and modules within the supported surface syntax (§1.2 below), with structural-honesty discipline checked by the seven primitives at compile time (§1.3), the substrate's implementation distributed across parser, type-checker, and types modules with CLI behavior (§1.4), and 539 passing tests as the substrate's documented evidence base (§1.5). Implementation-level details beyond the Furqan v0.11.1 public summary are used in this chapter only where documented by the Furqan reference implementation; otherwise they function as illustrative operational detail and not as independent adequacy evidence, per the Chapter 13 SI1.1.1 source-posture template.

### Surface syntax and supported language constructs

Furqan v0.11.1 supports a specific subset of Furqan source syntax including the seven structural-honesty primitives (§1.3) implemented as compile-time checks. Programs whose syntax falls within the supported subset are within scope; the surface API processes them through the parser, type-checker, and types modules and emits structured diagnostic output. Programs outside the supported syntax subset --- whether malformed within the supported syntax or well-formed at the lexical level but using a construct outside the supported subset --- surface at the substrate level as parse-failure with exit code 2, distinct from Marad-class structural-honesty violations (exit code 1). At v0.11.1 the parse-failure outcome is the $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ class covering both malformed-input and outside-supported-subset cases; finer $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ taxonomy (for instance, a separately-named `UnsupportedConstructError` exception distinct from `ParseError`) is reserved for future Furqan versions. The chapter retains the conceptual distinction between malformed-input parse error and outside-subset unsupported-construct because the A3 caller-side discharge implications differ between the two cases (§2.4 below), even though the substrate at v0.11.1 surfaces both through the same parse-failure exit code.

### Seven structural-honesty primitives implemented as compile-time checks

Furqan v0.11.1 implements seven specific structural-honesty primitives as compile-time checks: *Bismillah scope*, *Zahir/batin*, *Additive-only*, *Scan-incomplete*, *Mizan*, *Tanzil*, and *Ring-close*, to the extent documented by the Furqan v0.11.1 source and test suite. Each primitive corresponds to a declared syntactic/type-level discipline that Furqan v0.11.1 checks at compile time; Chapter 14 treats these as prototype type-checker checks, not as full semantic guarantees about compiled or runtime behavior, consistent with the SI2.1.1 prototype-scope boundary. Bismillah scope enforces declared-scope discipline: a Furqan module must declare its scope boundary and the type-checker verifies that operations stay within the declared scope. Zahir/batin enforces manifest/latent classification discipline: content with both manifest and latent components must be type-distinguished and the type-checker verifies that manifest claims are not made about latent-only content. Additive-only enforces version-evolution discipline: revisions to a module must be additive strengthenings or explicit corrigenda-tagged events, with the type-checker verifying the additive-only property of incremental changes. Scan-incomplete enforces scan-completeness-propagation discipline: where a type-check operation cannot complete on a specific module, the type-checker emits a scan-incomplete diagnostic that downstream callers must handle, propagate, or supply proven-unreachable certificates against. Mizan enforces balance-preservation discipline: bidirectional operations and dual-typed structures must preserve balance properties across the type-system's pairing, with the type-checker verifying balance preservation. Tanzil enforces controlled-disclosure discipline: information flow from higher-trust to lower-trust contexts must traverse explicit disclosure type-witnesses, with the type-checker verifying that implicit downcasting is prevented. Ring-close enforces substrate-closure discipline: type-system operations form a closed ring under the declared composition rules, with the type-checker verifying that out-of-ring constructions are rejected.

The seven primitives are the substrate-internal vocabulary that maps to AX-SH's declared-object discipline in §2. The specific implementation of each primitive at the type-system level (which type-system rules verify which structural-honesty property, which test cases substantiate the verification, which diagnostic vocabulary the CLI emits) is documented at the substrate's reference-implementation level; where specific implementation details are not source-documented at the chapter's level of detail, the chapter treats them as illustrative operational detail per the implementation-detail source-posture discipline.

### Parser, type-checker, and types module structure with CLI behavior

Furqan v0.11.1's implementation comprises three primary modules executed in sequence by the CLI: a *parser* module reading source syntax and producing an abstract-syntax representation, a *type-checker* module evaluating the seven structural-honesty primitives at compile time against the abstract-syntax representation, and a *types* module declaring the type-system structure (the typing rules, the type categories, the type-witness vocabulary) that the type-checker exercises. The CLI invocation $\mathrm{furqan\ check\ \langle module\rangle}$ exercises these modules in sequence: parse first, type-check second, with structured diagnostic output emitted at the end describing the outcome (accept, reject with structural-honesty diagnostic, parse error, unsupported construct, type error, or scan-incomplete) per the $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ enumeration of §2.4.

The module structure is documented at the Furqan reference implementation's level. The parser/checker/types decomposition is treated as source-documented where reflected in the v0.11.1 repository structure; any finer-grained module interaction described here is illustrative unless directly supported by the reference implementation, per the Chapter 13 SI1.1.1 implementation-detail source-posture template. The five-projection family declared in §2.5 maps onto distinct functional roles within and beyond these three modules: $\pi_{\mathrm{parse}}$ reads the parser's accept/reject result; $\pi_{\mathrm{check}}$ reads the type-checker's verdict on each of the seven primitives; $\pi_{\mathrm{diag}}$ reads the CLI's diagnostic-emission record; $\pi_{\mathrm{test}}$ reads the test-suite's pass/fail status; $\pi_{\mathrm{cli}}$ reads the CLI's exit code and structured-output verdict. The functional separation of these five projection roles is documented at the module-and-CLI level; whether each role corresponds to a fully-independent implementation mechanism is the question evaluated in §8.2 (Loop 2) under the projection-multiplicity ecosystem-condition status.

### 539 passing tests as test-suite evidence

Furqan v0.11.1 ships with 539 passing tests, used here as the substrate's documented evidence base for A2 satisfaction (per-version surface-substrate consistency). Where the v0.11.1 test suite categorizes tests by parser behavior, type-checker behavior, structural-honesty primitive checks across the seven primitives, and CLI behavior, Chapter 14 uses those categories as source-documented; otherwise, the chapter treats that breakdown as project-history or case-study classification rather than independently verified source categorization. The 539-test count is treated as source-documented only if tied to the v0.11.1 release/test output; where the count is reported from project history rather than directly verified against v0.11.1's release artifacts, the chapter treats it as project-history evidence rather than independently verified external evidence, per the Chapter 13 SI1.1.5 v1.0 baseline source-posture template.

The test-suite supports SI2's A2 evidence in §4 (Loop 2) at the chapter-evidence layer; the specific per-primitive coverage of the 539 tests and the test categories' substantiation of each of the four axioms A1--A4 is the substrate-internal documentation question that A2 evidence depends on. Where the per-primitive and per-axiom test coverage is documented, A2 satisfaction is supported empirically; where the coverage is reported but not directly verified, A2 satisfaction is supported to the extent documented per the Chapter 13 SI1.4.4 patched-language template.

## AX-SH structured interpretation for SI2

Section 3 of Chapter 8 supplied the Furqan vocabulary mapping pattern at the chapter-level (§3.3) and the structured-interpretation discipline. Section 2 of Chapter 14 instantiates that mapping pattern at the SI2 substrate level: each of the six declared objects $(O, K, R, R_{\mathrm{may}}, \Pi_X, \sim_X)$ from Chapter 3 §1's typed-object machinery is given its SI2-specific operational instantiation. The instantiation specializes Chapter 8's compact Furqan vocabulary mapping with v0.11.1-specific detail; it does not invent new machinery beyond what Chapters 3--8 supply, and it does not introduce any new axiom conditions beyond A1--A4 as stated in Chapters 4--7.

### SI2's declared observer model O

SI2's declared observer model $O$ is the type-checker / CLI observation regime: the observer reads Furqan source modules through the parser, evaluates the seven structural-honesty primitives through the type-checker, and emits structured diagnostic output through the CLI. The observer model is operationally instantiated as Furqan's compile-time-check regime: the specific module-read mechanism (file-system access to source modules under the declared supported-syntax subset), the specific parser behavior (production of the abstract-syntax representation), the specific type-checker behavior (evaluation of the seven primitives in their declared sequence under the type-system rules), and the specific CLI output behavior (the structured diagnostic emission per $R_{\mathrm{may}}$). The observer model is documented at the operational scope of Furqan's reference implementation.

### SI2's declared context set K

SI2's declared context set $K$ comprises Furqan programs and modules within the supported surface syntax (§1.2). Modules whose syntax cannot be parsed are not members of the well-formed-module subset of $K$, but parse-error outcomes remain part of $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ (§2.4) because callers must handle them through Chapter 6 §1's three discharge paths. Unsupported constructs are scope-honesty outcomes: well-formed inputs using constructs outside the supported subset, likewise represented in $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ and requiring caller-side discharge. The distinction matters at the axiom layer: A2's surface-substrate consistency obligation evaluates within the well-formed subset of $K$ (where $R$ between the type-checker's diagnostic output and the substrate's intrinsic primitive-check state is well-defined), while A3's caller-side exhaustiveness obligation operates over $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ (which includes parse-error and unsupported-construct outcomes that the well-formed subset does not). The K / $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ alignment is documented at the substrate's reference-implementation level; satisfying A2 requires the surface-substrate consistency hold within the well-formed subset, while satisfying A3 requires caller-side exhaustiveness over the full $R_{\mathrm{may}}$.

### SI2's declared correspondence relation R

SI2's declared correspondence relation $R$ is: type-checker diagnostic output matches the declared structural-honesty typing rules. $R(\mathrm{Surface}_{v0.11.1}, \mathrm{Substrate}_{v0.11.1})$ holds when, for every Furqan module $m \in K$, the type-checker's diagnostic output for $m$ correctly reflects whether $m$ satisfies the seven structural-honesty primitives under the declared type-system rules: an accept verdict is correct when $m$ satisfies all seven primitives; a reject-with-structural-honesty-diagnostic verdict is correct when $m$ violates one or more primitives and the diagnostic identifies the violated primitive(s); a type-error verdict is correct when $m$ exhibits a type-system failure within $K$ (a typing-rule violation that is not specifically one of the seven primitive violations); a scan-incomplete diagnostic is correct when the type-checker cannot complete the structural-honesty primitive check on $m$ under the declared observer model $O$. $R$ is the substrate-specific instantiation of A2's surface-substrate consistency obligation under the typed-object machinery of Chapter 3 for the type-checker substrate.

### SI2's declared $R_{\mathrm{may}}$

SI2's declared $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ is the verifier/caller-side conservative over-approximation of $R$, including all outcomes that the surface API may return enumerated as seven distinct outcome categories: (a) accepted; (b) rejected with structural-honesty diagnostic (a primitive violation correctly surfaced); (c) parse error (a syntax failure within the supported syntax subset); (d) unsupported construct (a scope-honesty outcome where the input is well-formed but uses a construct outside the supported subset; distinct from parse error which indicates malformed input within the supported syntax); (e) type error (a type-system failure within $K$ that is not specifically one of the seven primitive violations); (f) internal/tooling error if such outcomes are observable; (g) scan-incomplete-style diagnostic for incomplete type-check states where applicable. The seven outcome categories are treated as the case-study-declared $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ categories for v0.11.1's declared scope; where Furqan's release documentation or CLI tests explicitly establish exhaustiveness of possible returns, Chapter 14 treats that exhaustiveness as source-documented. Unsupported construct and parse error are distinct categories with different A3 caller-side discharge implications, distinguished here at the chapter-evidence layer in addition to the Section 15 spec level.

The $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ declaration follows the Chapter 6 §2.2 public/private $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ discipline and the Chapter 8 §4.2 patched discipline: $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ is the publicly relied-on or case-study-declared over-approximation --- whether producer-specified, verifier-published, or caller-surface --- under which A3 caller-side exhaustiveness is evaluated. The distinction between publicly relied-on (where actual external reliance on $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ is demonstrated by Furqan's operational deployment) and case-study-declared (where this chapter declares $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ for the purposes of evidencing the SI2 cases without pre-claiming external reliance) is evaluated in §8 (Loop 2) under the ecosystem-condition status taxonomy. Caller-side discharge through Chapter 6 §1's three discharge paths (handle, propagate-as-incomplete, supply-proven-unreachable-certificate) operates against the declared $R_{\mathrm{may}}$, not against a producer-private $R$.

### SI2's declared projection family $\Pi_X$

SI2's declared projection family $\Pi_X = \{\pi_{\mathrm{parse}}, \pi_{\mathrm{check}}, \pi_{\mathrm{diag}}, \pi_{\mathrm{test}}, \pi_{\mathrm{cli}}\}$ is the five-projection family identified in Section 15 SI2.2.5 at full SI2 scope. $\pi_{\mathrm{parse}}$ reads the parser module's accept/reject result on the module's syntax (defined on all input modules); $\pi_{\mathrm{check}}$ reads the type-checker module's verdict on each of the seven structural-honesty primitives[^1] (defined on modules that pass the parser); $\pi_{\mathrm{diag}}$ reads the CLI's diagnostic-emission record (defined on all modules that produce CLI output); $\pi_{\mathrm{test}}$ reads the test-suite's pass/fail status for the module's test cases (defined on modules covered by test cases in the 539-test suite); $\pi_{\mathrm{cli}}$ reads the CLI's exit code and structured-output verdict (defined on all modules that complete CLI invocation).

Each projection carries the shared module-identity coordinate per the Chapter 8 §2.2 patched discipline: $\pi_{\mathrm{parse}}(m) = (\mathrm{id}(m), \mathrm{parser}\text{-}\mathrm{verdict}(m))$; $\pi_{\mathrm{check}}(m) = (\mathrm{id}(m), \mathrm{primitive}\text{-}\mathrm{check}\text{-}\mathrm{results}(m))$; $\pi_{\mathrm{diag}}(m) = (\mathrm{id}(m), \mathrm{diagnostic}\text{-}\mathrm{record}(m))$; $\pi_{\mathrm{test}}(m) = (\mathrm{id}(m), \mathrm{test}\text{-}\mathrm{status}(m))$; $\pi_{\mathrm{cli}}(m) = (\mathrm{id}(m), \mathrm{exit}\text{-}\mathrm{code}(m))$. The shared module-identity coordinate ensures that the consistency relation $\sim_X$ (§2.6 below) is well-defined across projections, analogous to the shared kind coordinate in Chapter 13's SI1 projection family. The module-identity coordinate is SI2-specific: Bayyinah's shared coordinate was file-kind; Furqan's is module-identity, reflecting the fact that the projections are reading different aspects of the same Furqan module rather than the same aspect of different files.

### SI2's declared consistency relation $\sim_X$

SI2's declared consistency relation $\sim_X$ requires agreement among projection outputs on the joint domain. The minimal $\sim_X$ requires module-identity agreement plus accept/reject status agreement: for two projections $\pi_i$ and $\pi_j$ and a module $m$ in their joint domain, $\pi_i(m) \sim_X \pi_j(m)$ if and only if the projections agree on the module-identity coordinate at $m$ and agree on the accept/reject status (where defined). Under minimal $\sim_X$, two projections may agree that a module is rejected while disagreeing about the diagnostic category; that disagreement is not an A4 failure unless $\sim_X$ is strengthened to compare diagnostic category. Strengthenings of $\sim_X$ may require agreement on error category (when one projection reports a specific failure category, other projections defined at $m$ should not report a contradicting failure category) and agreement on primitive-check results (when one projection reports a specific primitive's verdict, other projections defined at $m$ should report a consistent verdict on that primitive); these are additional A4 conditions only when $\sim_X$ is declared at the strengthened level. The strength of $\sim_X$ in SI2 is a declared substrate property: under minimal $\sim_X$, certain projection disagreements may be caught primarily at the A2 layer rather than the A4 layer per the Chapter 13 SI1.7.N3 $\sim_X$-strength template.

Although $\Pi_X$ and $\sim_X$ are exercised together by A4 (Chapter 7 §1), they are distinct declared objects in Chapter 7's declared-object discipline. Section 15 of the audit ledger separates them into SI2.2.5 (the projection family) and SI2.2.6 (the consistency relation) for template fidelity with Chapter 13 (which separated SI1.2.5 and SI1.2.6) and Chapters 15--16 (which will follow the same split: SI3.2.5/SI3.2.6, SI4.2.5/SI4.2.6). The separation does not change the substantive A4 obligation, which is the joint-domain consistency of projection outputs under the named consistency relation, with the relation's strength determining what disagreements A4 catches versus what is routed through A2 or other axioms.

## A1 evidence: SI2 version-subtyping and corrigenda discipline

### SI2 version history at the surface level

The Furqan version history at the surface level comprises the v0.x.y series leading to v0.11.1, with intermediate versions documenting the evolution of the supported syntax subset, the seven structural-honesty primitives, the parser/checker/types module decomposition, and the CLI behavior. The v0.11.1 transition history is the substrate evidence base for A1 satisfaction. Section 1.5 of this chapter named the v0.11.1 substrate at full operational scope; §3 evaluates which transition components in the v0.x.y to v0.11.1 evolution are strengthenings under Liskov-Wing behavioral-subtyping discipline, which are corrigenda-tagged events, and what A1 satisfaction evidence this combination supplies.

The specific intermediate-version content of the v0.x.y series is documented at the Furqan reference implementation's release notes and changelog; where specific transition components are reconstructed from project history rather than directly documented in the v0.11.1 source artifacts, the prose treats them as project-history evidence per the Loop 1 source-posture discipline.

### Liskov-Wing version-subtyping evidence at v0.x.y to v0.11.1 transitions

The transition components across the v0.x.y to v0.11.1 evolution are classified as follows where source-documented. Additions to the supported syntax subset are strengthenings: new well-formed module shapes become acceptable to the parser, without any prior well-formed shape becoming unacceptable. Additions to the seven structural-honesty primitives or to the type-checker's verification of existing primitives are strengthenings: new structural-honesty disciplines are enforced or existing disciplines are enforced more thoroughly, without weakening prior enforcement. Additions to the test-suite (increases toward the v0.11.1 total of 539 tests) are evidentiary strengthenings rather than substrate strengthenings: they substantiate A2 satisfaction more thoroughly without changing what the substrate guarantees. Expanded diagnostic vocabulary --- richer error category labels, more specific primitive-violation messages, additional CLI output structure --- is a strengthening at the surface API level: callers continue to receive correct accept/reject verdicts plus more informative diagnostic content.

Components that may be corrigenda-tagged events include any narrowings or withdrawals of prior structural-honesty claims: removed primitives, narrowed supported syntax, withdrawn diagnostic categories, or revised typing rules that reject programs prior versions accepted. Whether the v0.x.y to v0.11.1 evolution includes such corrigenda-tagged components, and whether they are explicitly tagged in the reference implementation's release notes, is the substrate-internal documentation question that determines SI2.8.4's ecosystem-condition status in §8 below. The Liskov-Wing version-subtyping evidence is therefore mixed in the same sense as Chapter 13 §3.2's analogous evidence for SI1: most transition components are strengthenings, and any narrowing components require corrigenda treatment per Chapter 4 §1.1's A1 discipline.

### Corrigenda events in SI2 history

Where the v0.x.y to v0.11.1 transition includes corrigenda-tagged events, those events are evidence that Furqan's evolution exercises corrigenda discipline operationally. Candidate corrigenda events include any specific changes that withdraw prior structural-honesty claims: removed primitives (e.g., a primitive present in v0.5.0 not present in v0.11.1), narrowed supported syntax (constructs accepted in v0.6.0 rejected in v0.11.1 as unsupported), withdrawn diagnostic categories (an error category emitted in v0.7.0 retired in v0.11.1), or revised typing rules that change accept/reject classification for specific module shapes. For each candidate event, the question is whether the Furqan reference implementation documents the change as a corrigendum-tagged event (with explicit withdrawal of the prior claim) or as an additive strengthening (with no withdrawal). Components documented as corrigendum-tagged events substantiate A1's corrigenda discipline; components documented as additive strengthenings do not require corrigenda treatment.

The number and identity of specific corrigendum-tagged events in the v0.x.y to v0.11.1 evolution is the substrate-internal documentation question that determines SI2.8.4's status in §8 below. Where the documentation does not record specific corrigenda events --- whether because the evolution was purely additive or because corrigenda were applied without explicit tagging --- the chapter classifies the corrigenda-exercise status conservatively per the Chapter 13 SI1.8.4 partial-unless-documented template.

### A1 satisfaction evidence

The combination of the strengthening-character of most transition components (§3.2), the required corrigenda-tagged treatment of any narrowing or withdrawal components (§3.3), and the substantive operational character of the v0.x.y to v0.11.1 evolution (Loop 1 §1.5) together support A1 satisfaction for SI2, conditional on the substrate-internal documentation showing that any withdrawal or scope-narrowing components were explicitly corrigenda-tagged. If the transition is purely additive, A1 satisfaction is supported by version-subtyping alone; if withdrawals occurred without corrigenda tags, that would be an A1 gap rather than A1 evidence. The evidence does not introduce any new axiom conditions beyond A1 as stated in Chapter 4 §1.1; SI2's A1 satisfaction is evaluated against A1's existing Liskov-Wing version-subtyping discipline with corrigenda for scope-narrowing, not against a modified or extended A1.

## A2 evidence: SI2 surface-substrate consistency per version

### Per-version surface-substrate consistency at recent prior Furqan versions

At each documented prior Furqan version $v_i$ in the v0.x.y series, A2's surface-substrate consistency obligation is $R_i(\mathrm{Surface}_{v_i}, \mathrm{Substrate}_{v_i})$ holds: for every well-formed module $m \in K_i$ under $v_i$'s declared context set, $\mathrm{furqan\ check\ } m$ at $v_i$ returns the correct accept/reject verdict and diagnostic content under $v_i$'s declared correspondence relation $R_i$. The per-version test-suite results at $v_i$ are the documented evidence base for $R_i$'s holding: test cases covering well-formed modules in $K_i$ with verified expected outcomes substantiate the surface-substrate consistency at $v_i$. Where the v0.x.y series' per-version test-suite results are documented in the Furqan reference implementation's release artifacts, the per-version A2 evidence is empirical; where the per-version results are reconstructed from project history, the evidence is project-history per the Loop 1 source-posture discipline.

### Per-version surface-substrate consistency at v0.11.1

At v0.11.1, A2's surface-substrate consistency obligation is $R_1(\mathrm{Surface}_{v0.11.1}, \mathrm{Substrate}_{v0.11.1})$ holds: for every well-formed module $m \in K_1$ under v0.11.1's declared context set (well-formed modules in the supported syntax subset per the Loop 1 §2.2 K/$R_{\mathrm{may}}$ alignment), $\mathrm{furqan\ check\ } m$ at v0.11.1 returns the correct accept/reject verdict and diagnostic content under v0.11.1's declared correspondence relation $R_1$. The 539 passing tests cover well-formed modules in $K_1$ exercising each of the seven structural-honesty primitives at the type-system level. The test-suite is the substrate's documented evidence base for v0.11.1 A2 satisfaction.

The K/$R_{\mathrm{may}}$ alignment from Loop 1 §2.2 is operative here: A2's evaluation is within the well-formed subset of $K_1$ where $R_1$ is well-defined; parse-error and unsupported-construct outcomes are not in the well-formed subset and are not evaluated under $R_1$, but they remain $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ outcomes handled by A3 in §5.

### Concrete test-suite results substantiating R

The 539 passing tests substantiate $R_1$ across the seven primitives. Per-primitive test coverage --- where the test suite categorizes tests by primitive --- exercises each of Bismillah scope, Zahir/batin, Additive-only, Scan-incomplete, Mizan, Tanzil, and Ring-close. Per-module-shape test coverage exercises different Furqan module shapes within the supported syntax subset. CLI behavior tests exercise the structured diagnostic output for accept, reject-with-structural-honesty-diagnostic, parse error, unsupported construct, type error, and scan-incomplete outcomes. Where the test-suite categorization is documented in the Furqan reference implementation, these categorizations substantiate $R_1$ directly; where specific per-primitive or per-shape categorizations are not source-documented at the chapter's level of detail, the chapter treats them as illustrative operational detail rather than independent adequacy evidence, consistent with the Loop 1 §1.5 539-test source-posture discipline.

### A2 satisfaction evidence

The combination of per-version surface-substrate consistency at recent prior versions (§4.1) and v0.11.1 (§4.2), together with the concrete test-suite evidence (§4.3), supports A2 satisfaction for SI2 at v0.11.1 (and at the documented prior versions where evidence exists) to the extent documented by the Furqan reference implementation and test-suite evidence. The evidence does not introduce any new axiom conditions beyond A2 as stated in Chapter 5 §1; SI2's A2 satisfaction is evaluated against A2's existing per-version surface-substrate consistency under declared $(O, K, R)$, not against a modified or extended A2.

## A3 evidence: SI2 caller-side exhaustiveness over $R_{\mathrm{may}}$

### SI2 caller-diversity model

The SI2 caller-diversity model includes developer-direct roles (developers running $\mathrm{furqan\ check}$ interactively on local modules during development), CI-pipeline roles (continuous-integration systems running $\mathrm{furqan\ check}$ as a gating step in build/test pipelines), build-system roles (build orchestration tools invoking $\mathrm{furqan\ check}$ as part of a multi-stage build process), and downstream-tooling roles (other tools consuming Furqan's diagnostic output for IDE integration, code-review automation, or documentation generation). Where these caller roles are documented in Furqan's deployment context as actually exercised by real callers in operational use, the model is supported by documentation; where actual external caller diversity is not yet demonstrated for a specific role, Chapter 14 classifies this as an operational-nontriviality limitation rather than a failure of A3 per the Chapter 13 SI1.5.1 caller-diversity-model source-posture discipline.

The caller-diversity model is SI2-specific in one structural respect: developer-direct interactive use is a load-bearing SI2 role because Furqan is a prototype type-checker --- human developers running the checker on modules during development are part of the intended use. This role is more central for SI2 than for the SI1 template, where the caller model was organized around file-scanning consumers.

### Caller-side discharge patterns through the three $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ discharge paths

The caller-diversity model exercises each of Chapter 6 §1's three discharge paths over the seven $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ categories from Loop 1 §2.4. CI-pipeline callers handle accepted outcomes (downstream build proceeds), reject-with-structural-honesty-diagnostic outcomes (downstream build halts with the diagnostic surfaced), and type-error outcomes (downstream build halts with the type-error message); they propagate parse-error and unsupported-construct outcomes via CI exit codes and pipeline-warning status (the propagate-as-incomplete and out-of-scope discharge paths respectively); they may supply proven-unreachable certificates for internal/tooling errors only where the input environment has been pre-verified strongly enough to justify such a certificate, otherwise internal/tooling errors should be handled or propagated as incomplete/tooling-failure outcomes. Developer-direct callers handle outcomes interactively: the human developer reads the diagnostic and responds appropriately. Build-system callers integrate with CI behavior but may have additional retry or build-orchestration logic. Downstream-tooling callers consume the structured diagnostic output and apply role-specific handling.

The discharge pattern coverage is documented where the Furqan reference implementation supplies specific caller-discharge examples; otherwise the pattern coverage is modeled from the operational structure of $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ and the three discharge paths per the Chapter 13 SI1.5.2 patched template. The K/$R_{\mathrm{may}}$ layer distinction from Loop 1 §2.2 is operative: callers must discharge over the full $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ (including parse-error and unsupported-construct outcomes that are not in the well-formed subset of $K$), not only over $K$-internal outcomes.

### Concrete examples of caller exhaustiveness over $R_{\mathrm{may}}$

Specific concrete examples supporting caller exhaustiveness include: a CI pipeline processing a batch of Furqan modules where each module's outcome (accepted, rejected-with-diagnostic, parse error, unsupported construct, type error) is handled by appropriate pipeline routing; a developer working interactively on a single module who reads each $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ outcome as it appears and responds (fix the syntax for parse errors, refactor for unsupported constructs, address the primitive violation for reject-with-diagnostic outcomes); a downstream IDE tool consuming Furqan's diagnostic output and presenting each outcome category as an appropriate UI annotation.

Where specific examples are documented in the Furqan reference implementation's deployment documentation, they substantiate caller exhaustiveness directly; where examples are modeled from the operational structure, they substantiate the structural pattern without claiming specific historical instances.

### A3 satisfaction evidence

The combination of the SI2 caller-diversity model (§5.1), the three-discharge-path coverage (§5.2), and the concrete examples (§5.3) supports A3 satisfaction for SI2 under the declared caller-diversity model and $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ discharge structure. Where caller roles and discharge examples are documented in Furqan's deployment context, the evidence is empirical; where they are modeled from the operational structure of $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ and the three discharge paths, the evidence supports the structural pattern but leaves operational nontriviality to §8.1's partial ecosystem-status classification. The evidence does not introduce any new axiom conditions beyond A3 as stated in Chapter 6 §1; SI2's A3 satisfaction is evaluated against A3's existing caller-side exhaustiveness obligation over $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ through the three discharge paths, not against a modified or extended A3.

## A4 evidence: SI2 joint-domain projection consistency under $\sim_X$

### SI2 five-projection family at full operational scope

The five-projection family $\Pi_X = \{\pi_{\mathrm{parse}}, \pi_{\mathrm{check}}, \pi_{\mathrm{diag}}, \pi_{\mathrm{test}}, \pi_{\mathrm{cli}}\}$ at full SI2 scope is the SI2-specific instantiation of the candidate projection family identified in Chapter 7 §1.6, with projection naming reflecting Furqan's parser/checker/diagnostic/test/CLI module architecture rather than the more abstract syntactic/typed/diagnostic/dependency framing used at the Chapter 7 prerequisite level; the substrate-specific instantiation is established in Loop 1 §2.5. Each projection's domain at full scope is: $\pi_{\mathrm{parse}}$ defined on all inputs for which parser invocation completes and returns a parser verdict (parser crashes or tooling failures are treated as $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ internal/tooling outcomes rather than ordinary parser-domain cases); $\pi_{\mathrm{check}}$ defined on modules that pass the parser (the well-formed subset of $K_1$); $\pi_{\mathrm{diag}}$ defined on all modules that produce CLI output; $\pi_{\mathrm{test}}$ defined on modules covered by test cases in the 539-test suite; $\pi_{\mathrm{cli}}$ defined on all modules that complete CLI invocation. Each projection carries the shared module-identity coordinate per the Loop 1 §2.5 patched discipline.

The projection-family structure is documented at the substrate's reference-implementation level per the Loop 1 §1.4 module-decomposition source-posture; whether each projection role corresponds to a fully-independent implementation mechanism is the question evaluated in §8.2 below under the projection-multiplicity ecosystem-condition status.

### Joint-domain analysis for the five projections

The five projections have overlapping but non-identical domains. The full joint domain $\mathrm{dom}(\pi_{\mathrm{parse}}) \cap \mathrm{dom}(\pi_{\mathrm{check}}) \cap \mathrm{dom}(\pi_{\mathrm{diag}}) \cap \mathrm{dom}(\pi_{\mathrm{test}}) \cap \mathrm{dom}(\pi_{\mathrm{cli}})$ is the set of well-formed modules in $K_1$ covered by test cases that complete CLI invocation --- a subset of $K_1$ where all five projections are simultaneously well-defined. Pairwise joint domains are larger: $\mathrm{dom}(\pi_{\mathrm{parse}}) \cap \mathrm{dom}(\pi_{\mathrm{diag}})$ includes essentially all input modules; $\mathrm{dom}(\pi_{\mathrm{check}}) \cap \mathrm{dom}(\pi_{\mathrm{test}})$ includes the well-formed modules covered by tests; and so on. A4's joint-domain consistency obligation under $\sim_X$ requires that every set of projections both defined at a module $m$ produce module-identity-agreeing outputs at $m$, plus accept/reject status agreement under minimal $\sim_X$ (with diagnostic-category or primitive-check agreement required only under strengthened $\sim_X$ per Loop 1 §2.6).

### Concrete cases of joint-domain consistency under $\sim_X$

Specific concrete cases supporting joint-domain consistency: a well-formed Furqan module $m$ where $\pi_{\mathrm{parse}}$ returns parser-accept, $\pi_{\mathrm{check}}$ returns "accept" (all seven primitives verified), $\pi_{\mathrm{diag}}$ returns the structured "no errors" diagnostic, $\pi_{\mathrm{test}}$ returns test-pass on the covering test cases, and $\pi_{\mathrm{cli}}$ returns exit code zero with the success-structured output. All five projections agree on the module-identity coordinate at $m$ and on the accept/reject status (accept); $\sim_X$ holds at $m$ under minimal $\sim_X$. A well-formed Furqan module $m'$ that violates a structural-honesty primitive where $\pi_{\mathrm{parse}}$ returns parser-accept, $\pi_{\mathrm{check}}$ returns "reject" on the violated primitive, $\pi_{\mathrm{diag}}$ returns the structured primitive-violation diagnostic, $\pi_{\mathrm{test}}$ returns test-pass on the covering test cases (the tests verify that the type-checker correctly rejects the violation), and $\pi_{\mathrm{cli}}$ returns exit code nonzero with the failure-structured output. All five projections agree on reject status; $\sim_X$ holds under minimal $\sim_X$.

The examples are documented at the substrate's reference-implementation level via the 539-test results substantiating per-projection accuracy where the test categorization supports the cross-projection consistency.

### A4 satisfaction evidence

The combination of the five-projection family at full operational scope (§6.1), the joint-domain analysis (§6.2), and the concrete consistency cases (§6.3) supports A4 satisfaction for SI2 at the chapter-evidence layer under minimal $\sim_X$, to the extent documented by Furqan's projection roles, CLI behavior, and test-suite evidence. The evidence does not introduce any new axiom conditions beyond A4 as stated in Chapter 7 §1; SI2's A4 satisfaction is evaluated against A4's existing joint-domain consistency obligation under $\sim_X$, not against a modified or extended A4. The $\sim_X$-strength observation carried forward from the Chapter 13 SI1.7.N3 template: under minimal $\sim_X$ (accept/reject status only), certain projection disagreements --- particularly disagreements where one projection's diagnostic content contradicts another projection's accept verdict --- may be caught primarily at A2 rather than A4. The SI2-N3 case in §7.6 exercises this $\sim_X$-strength boundary explicitly.

## Seven judgment-case discharges for SI2

Section 7 is the load-bearing center of Chapter 14: it discharges the seven SI2 cases named in Chapter 8 §3.1's judgment-case set $J$. Per the Chapter 13 case-type discipline, positive cases (SI2-P1, P2, P3) are grounded in actual Furqan v0.11.1 operational behavior where possible; negative cases (SI2-N1, N2, N3) may be either modeled failure-mode patterns or constructive counterfactuals, with constructive cases explicitly labeled; boundary cases (SI2-B1) receive either an explicit AX-SH rationale or are routed to Chapter 21 with explicit routing rationale. The seven cases collectively substantiate T83's adequacy claim for the SI2 portion of $J$; they do not substantiate T83's adequacy claim beyond the named seven cases, and they do not silently upgrade SI2 evidence into general language-layer adequacy.

### SI2-P1: routine type-check success across many Furqan modules

Substrate scenario: a batch of well-formed Furqan modules in $K_1$ is processed through $\mathrm{furqan\ check}$ at v0.11.1. Each module passes the parser (so $\pi_{\mathrm{parse}}$ accepts), satisfies all seven structural-honesty primitives at the type-system level (so $\pi_{\mathrm{check}}$ accepts on each primitive), produces no error diagnostics (so $\pi_{\mathrm{diag}}$ returns no-errors), passes covering test cases (so $\pi_{\mathrm{test}}$ reports pass), and yields CLI exit code zero (so $\pi_{\mathrm{cli}}$ returns success). The five projections agree on the module-identity coordinate and on the accept status across the joint domain. The surface API emits the correct accept verdict for each module under $R_1$.

AX-SH classification: structurally honest. A1 holds (no version-evolution issue in this scenario beyond what §3 evidences); A2 holds (the surface-substrate consistency is direct: accept output matches intrinsic primitive-check state); A3 holds (the caller community discharges $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ correctly because all outcomes are declared correct outcomes within $R$); A4 holds (projection consistency under $\sim_X$ is direct: all five projections agree on accept status).

Expected practitioner judgment: structurally honest. The type-checker is doing what its surface API claims; routine type-check correctness is the baseline structural-honesty expectation for a prototype type-checker substrate. Alignment evidence: the AX-SH classification matches practitioner judgment directly.

### SI2-P2: structural-honesty primitive violation correctly diagnosed

Substrate scenario: a well-formed Furqan module violates one of the seven structural-honesty primitives at the type-system level (for example, a Bismillah scope violation where operations cross the module's declared scope boundary, or a Tanzil violation where information flows from higher-trust to lower-trust context without traversing a disclosure type-witness). The type-checker correctly identifies the primitive violation: $\pi_{\mathrm{check}}$ reports reject on the violated primitive; $\pi_{\mathrm{diag}}$ emits the structured structural-honesty diagnostic naming the violated primitive; $\pi_{\mathrm{test}}$ reports pass on the covering test cases (the tests verify that the type-checker correctly rejects this violation pattern); $\pi_{\mathrm{cli}}$ returns nonzero exit code with the failure-structured output. The surface API emits the correct reject-with-structural-honesty-diagnostic verdict under $R_1$.

AX-SH classification: structurally honest. A1, A3, A4 hold as in the baseline routine-scan case. A2 holds with particular salience: the rejection is the correct surface declaration under $R_1$ because the substrate's intrinsic primitive-check state is violation-present and the surface diagnostic correctly reflects that state. The seven-primitive vocabulary from Loop 1 §1.3 is exercised here as both the substrate's discipline (the module's actual structural-honesty state) and the surface's vocabulary (the diagnostic naming the violated primitive).

Expected practitioner judgment: structurally honest. The type-checker is correctly rejecting a structural-honesty violation and surfacing the violated primitive; this is exactly what practitioners expect a structural-honesty type-checker to do. Alignment evidence: AX-SH and practitioner judgment match.

### SI2-P3: unsupported-construct diagnostic correctly emitted

Substrate scenario: a Furqan module uses a construct outside the supported syntax (well-formed at the lexical level but using a language feature outside v0.11.1's supported subset --- for instance, a feature anticipated for a future version but not yet implemented). The type-checker / parser correctly emits an unsupported-construct diagnostic: $\pi_{\mathrm{parse}}$ recognizes the input as well-formed at the lexical level but flags the unsupported construct; $\pi_{\mathrm{diag}}$ emits the structured unsupported-construct diagnostic; $\pi_{\mathrm{cli}}$ returns the appropriate exit code with the unsupported-construct structured output. The module is not in the well-formed subset of $K_1$ (because the construct is outside the supported syntax), but the surface honestly reports the scope limitation.

The diagnostic is structurally analogous to Bayyinah's SI1.7.P2 scan-incomplete propagation in the sense that the tool honestly declines to make an in-scope type-checking claim; the precise A3 discharge path is propagate-as-incomplete (when $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ treats unsupported-construct as a partial outcome the caller propagates) or out-of-scope handling (when $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ treats unsupported-construct as a scope-boundary signal), depending on how Loop 1 §2.4's $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ enumeration treats unsupported constructs in the specific caller context.

AX-SH classification: structurally honest. The substrate is honest about its scope limits as a prototype type-checker (Loop 1 §1.1 prototype-boundary discipline); the unsupported-construct diagnostic is the correct surface declaration for an out-of-K but well-formed-at-lexical-level input. A2's well-formed-K evaluation does not apply (the input is not in the well-formed subset of $K$); A3 is satisfied in this scenario when the declared or modeled caller role correctly handles the unsupported-construct outcome through the propagate-as-incomplete or out-of-scope discharge path.

Expected practitioner judgment: structurally honest. The substrate is being honest about its scope limits; the unsupported-construct diagnostic is the correct way to signal "this input is well-formed at the surface level but I'm not going to make a type-checking claim about it because it uses a feature outside my supported subset." Alignment evidence: AX-SH and practitioner judgment match.

### SI2-N1: structural-honesty primitive violation not surfaced

*This is a modeled failure-mode judgment case, not presently asserted as a documented Furqan historical failure.* Whether specific historical instances of this pattern are documented in Furqan's QA records is a project-history question; the case's role in Chapter 14 is to show how AX-SH would classify the corresponding failure mode and to substantiate the structural-honesty discipline by which Furqan's design guards against this mode.

Substrate scenario: a well-formed Furqan module violates one of the seven structural-honesty primitives at the type-system level, but the type-checker accepts the module without emitting a primitive-violation diagnostic. The substrate's intrinsic primitive-check state at the module is violation-present, but the surface API declares accept. $\pi_{\mathrm{check}}$ reports accept (the type-checker fails to identify the violation); $\pi_{\mathrm{diag}}$ emits no structural-honesty diagnostic; $\pi_{\mathrm{cli}}$ returns exit code zero.

AX-SH classification: structurally dishonest. A2 fails: $R_1$ does not hold at the failing module because the surface's accept declaration contradicts the substrate's actual primitive-violation state. A1, A3, A4 may still hold formally, but the A2 failure is sufficient for structural dishonesty.

Expected practitioner judgment: structurally dishonest. The type-checker is failing to surface a structural-honesty violation; the suppression of the primitive-violation diagnostic is the exact form of dishonesty the structural-honesty disciplines are designed to prevent. Alignment evidence: AX-SH and practitioner judgment match.

### SI2-N2: scope-narrowing without corrigenda-tagging

*This is a constructive negative judgment case, not a documented Furqan historical failure. Its role is to show how AX-SH would classify the corresponding SI2 failure mode if it occurred in a future version evolution.*

Substrate scenario: a hypothetical Furqan future version (post-v0.11.1) narrows the operational scope --- removes one of the seven primitives, or revises the supported syntax to reject programs prior versions accepted, or withdraws a diagnostic category --- without explicitly corrigendum-tagging the removal. A v0.11.1 caller relying on the removed primitive's enforcement, or on the prior-acceptable syntax, does not receive correct behavior under the hypothetical future version for that case; the silent scope-narrowing breaks Liskov-Wing behavioral subtyping.

AX-SH classification: structurally dishonest. A1 fails: Liskov-Wing version-subtyping is violated by the silent scope-narrowing without corrigenda-tagging. A2, A3, A4 may still hold at the hypothetical future version within its narrowed scope, but the A1 failure is sufficient for structural dishonesty.

Expected practitioner judgment: structurally dishonest. The type-checker is silently withdrawing prior commitments without acknowledging the withdrawal; v0.11.1 callers are betrayed by the hypothetical future version's narrowed scope. Alignment evidence: AX-SH and practitioner judgment match.

### SI2-N3: projection disagreement not surfaced as diagnostic

*This is a constructive negative judgment case, not a documented Furqan historical failure. Its role is to show how AX-SH would classify the corresponding SI2 failure mode if it occurred and to exercise the $\sim_X$-strength template from Chapter 13 SI1.7.N3 on Furqan's substrate.*

Substrate scenario: a well-formed Furqan module is processed. $\pi_{\mathrm{check}}$ reports accept (the type-checker's verdict). However, $\pi_{\mathrm{diag}}$ emits diagnostics indicating a structural-honesty primitive violation or error category that should have prevented acceptance --- not advisory warnings, but diagnostic content describing an actual primitive failure that the substrate's intrinsic state exhibits. The surface does not surface the inconsistency coherently: the accept verdict and the diagnostic content describing the violation are both emitted without reconciliation.

AX-SH classification: under SI2's minimal $\sim_X$ (module-identity agreement plus accept/reject status agreement only, per Loop 1 §2.6), the primary failure may be A2 rather than A4. A2 fails because $R_1$ does not hold: the surface declares accept while the substrate's actual primitive-check state is violation-present (the diagnostic content's existence is evidence of that), so the accept verdict contradicts the substrate state. Whether A4 also fails depends on the strength of $\sim_X$. Under minimal $\sim_X$, the projections may not directly disagree on the accept/reject coordinate (since $\pi_{\mathrm{check}}$'s coordinate is accept and $\pi_{\mathrm{diag}}$'s primary coordinate is diagnostic content rather than accept/reject status); A4 holds vacuously on this dimension. Under strengthened $\sim_X$ (where diagnostic-category agreement or primitive-check-result agreement is part of the consistency requirement), A4 also fails: the diagnostic content's reporting of a primitive violation is inconsistent with $\pi_{\mathrm{check}}$'s accept verdict.

The case therefore exercises the same $\sim_X$-strength boundary observed in Chapter 13 SI1.7.N3: a consistency relation defined narrowly (here, accept/reject agreement only) cannot by itself surface richer projection disagreements; if practitioners want such disagreements caught at the A4 layer, the substrate's declared $\sim_X$ must be strengthened beyond accept/reject agreement. This boundary observation is routed to Chapter 21 alongside SI2-B1's diagnostic-severity question as part of the long-horizon $\sim_X$-strength evolution.

Expected practitioner judgment: structurally dishonest. The type-checker is concealing internal projection disagreement; practitioners would recognize the concealment as structural dishonesty regardless of whether AX-SH routes the failure through A2 or A4. Alignment evidence: AX-SH and practitioner judgment match on the structural-dishonesty verdict; the case additionally exposes a methodologically useful boundary about $\sim_X$ strength specific to the type-checker substrate.

### SI2-B1: advisory or severity-ambiguous warning-level diagnostic

Substrate scenario: a well-formed Furqan module type-checks successfully ($\pi_{\mathrm{check}}$ accepts, $\pi_{\mathrm{test}}$ passes) but $\pi_{\mathrm{diag}}$ emits warning-level diagnostics that are advisory or severity-ambiguous --- not encoding a violation of one of the seven structural-honesty primitives, but raising secondary structural-honesty concerns at the boundary (for example, a style-related observation, a performance-related advisory, or a deprecated-feature note that does not constitute a primitive violation under v0.11.1's discipline).

Practitioner judgment is debatable on this scenario. Some practitioners view advisory warning-level diagnostics as structurally honest: the type-checker is communicating additional information beyond accept/reject without rejecting the module, and the warning-level severity correctly signals that no primitive is violated. Other practitioners view the question of whether warning-level diagnostics should affect structural-honesty classification as not yet settled by AX-SH at the case-study layer: whether such warnings constitute a structural-honesty surface element that A2 must evaluate, or whether they are pre-axiom advisory content outside AX-SH's surface-substrate consistency scope, is itself a meta-question about how AX-SH's discipline handles diagnostic severity.

AX-SH classification: structurally honest under the seven-primitive-violation reading. At the seven-primitive layer, all four axioms are satisfied: A1 holds (no version-evolution issue); A2 holds (the accept verdict matches the substrate's actual no-violation primitive state); A3 holds (callers handle the accept-with-warnings outcome); A4 holds (projections agree on accept status). *Scope boundary*: if a warning encodes an actual violation of one of the seven primitives, the case moves from boundary to negative (handled by SI2-N1 if the violation is suppressed entirely or SI2-N3 if surfaced inconsistently with the accept verdict).

*The case is routed to Chapter 21 because it concerns the evolution of practitioner judgment about diagnostic-severity propagation: whether warning-level diagnostics should affect AX-SH structural-honesty classification when they do not encode primitive violations.* Chapter 14 records the boundary rather than forcing a premature classification. The diagnostic-severity-propagation question is itself a long-horizon question about how AX-SH's discipline should evolve as diagnostic-severity scenarios become more operationally significant; Chapter 21's falsification-protocol work is the proper site for that evolution. Alignment evidence: practitioner judgment is debatable; Chapter 14 supplies the AX-SH classification at the seven-primitive layer with explicit acknowledgment that the diagnostic-severity question is routed forward.

## Ecosystem-condition status for SI2

Section 8 evaluates the four Chapter 8 §0.3 ecosystem conditions for SI2 using the five-status taxonomy (demonstrated / modeled / partial / absent / routed-to-Chapter-21) per the Chapter 13 SI1.8 template. These statuses do not become new axioms; they describe operational nontriviality per Chapter 8 §0.3's auxiliary-not-axiom discipline.

### Caller diversity status for SI2

The SI2 caller-diversity model from §5.1 (developer-direct, CI-pipeline, build-system, downstream-tooling roles) is partly demonstrated and partly modeled. Where specific caller roles are documented in Furqan's deployment context as actually exercised by real callers, the model is *demonstrated* for those roles; where caller roles are described from the operational structure of $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ and the three discharge paths without specific documented external-caller instances, the model is *modeled* for those roles. Developer-direct interactive use is a load-bearing role for a prototype type-checker that contributes to demonstrated-status if direct human use is documented in Furqan's deployment context. The aggregate status of SI2.8.1 (caller diversity) is *partial*: caller diversity is operationally plausible and architecturally supported, but not yet fully demonstrated across all caller roles.

### Projection multiplicity status for SI2

The five-projection family $\{\pi_{\mathrm{parse}}, \pi_{\mathrm{check}}, \pi_{\mathrm{diag}}, \pi_{\mathrm{test}}, \pi_{\mathrm{cli}}\}$ from Loop 1 §2.5 declares five distinct projection roles documented at the substrate's reference-implementation level. The aggregate status of SI2.8.2 is *demonstrated* with respect to declared projection multiplicity: Furqan declares five distinct projection roles. Independence of implementation mechanisms is documented only where the Furqan source shows distinct code paths, modules, or evidence sources for parser, checker, diagnostics, test suite, and CLI projections; otherwise independence is role-level rather than implementation-level per the Loop 1 §1.4 module-decomposition source-posture. The role-level demonstration is sufficient to substantiate Chapter 8 §0.3's projection-multiplicity ecosystem condition under the auxiliary-not-axiom discipline.

### Substantive evolution status for SI2

The v0.x.y to v0.11.1 transition is *demonstrated*. The substrate's CHANGELOG ladder witnesses 18 documented version transitions through v0.11.1, of which 10 are substantive: seven primitive-introduction transitions (v0.1.0 Bismillah scope, v0.2.0 Zahir/batin, v0.3.0 Additive-only, v0.4.0 Scan-incomplete, v0.5.0 Mizan, v0.6.0 Tanzil, v0.7.0 Ring-close closing the seven-primitive ring) plus three architectural-slice transitions (v0.8.0 status-coverage / D11 supplementary checker, v0.9.0 CLI entry point, v0.10.0 `Project` class for multi-module support), with v0.10.1 contributing cross-module type resolution (D23) and v0.11.0--v0.11.1 contributing parser resource limits and `MAX_NESTING_DEPTH` re-export. The aggregate transition history is strictly additive: zero `Removed` sections, zero `Withdrawn` or `Reverted` or `Deprecated` sections, zero corrigenda mentions through v0.11.1. The substantive-evolution ecosystem status for SI2 is therefore *demonstrated*, not *partial*. The Furqan substrate exemplifies Chapter 8 §2.7's substantive-evolution-ecosystem assumption at the prototype-type-checker scale: a sequence of well-documented substantive transitions, each strengthening the prior surface, with the additive-only invariant the substrate itself enforces preserved across the whole sequence as a Liskov-Wing witness.

### Corrigenda discipline exercised status for SI2

The status of SI2.8.4 (corrigenda discipline exercised) depends on the specific corrigenda events in the v0.x.y to v0.11.1 transition per §3.3. On the evidence currently surfaced in Chapter 14, SI2.8.4 is classified as *partial* unless the Furqan reference implementation or project history records specific corrigenda-tagged withdrawal events in the v0.x.y to v0.11.1 transition. The chapter records the condition under which the status would become *demonstrated*: if the transition includes documented corrigenda-tagged events (specifically, removed primitives, narrowed supported syntax components, or withdrawn diagnostic categories with explicit corrigendum tagging), the condition is *demonstrated*; but Chapter 14 does not claim demonstrated status absent that documentation. The *partial* classification is the structurally honest position until that documentation is verified.

## Chapter close: T83 tie-back, Chapter 21 routing, Chapter 20 surfacing

### T83 tie-back: the seven SI2 cases discharged

Chapter 14 discharges the seven SI2 cases named in Chapter 8 §3.1's judgment-case set $J$: SI2-P1, SI2-P2, SI2-P3 (§§7.1--7.3, three positive cases yielding AX-SH-honest classification consistent with practitioner judgment); SI2-N1, SI2-N2, SI2-N3 (§§7.4--7.6, three negative cases yielding AX-SH-dishonest classification consistent with practitioner judgment, with N1 labeled as modeled failure-mode judgment case and N2/N3 explicitly labeled as constructive counterfactuals per the case-type discipline); and SI2-B1 (§7.7, boundary case routed to Chapter 21 with explicit rationale per Chapter 8 §3.6's boundary-case discipline). The seven J-IDs are named explicitly here for trivial cross-reference checkability per the Chapter 13 SI1.9.1 template. The integrative-evaluation argument from Chapter 8 §3.5 is now substantiated for the SI2 portion of $J$ at the chapter-evidence layer.

### Chapter 21 routing for SI2

Chapter 14's scope is the seven named SI2 cases at the empirical-relative-to-$J$ layer. Long-horizon SI2 dynamics (Furqan's evolution over time, the practitioner-judgment evolution that may add new SI2 cases to $J$ in the future, the emergent-misappropriation surveillance of Furqan-derived type-checker practices) are routed to Chapter 21 falsification-protocol work. Two specific Chapter 21 routings from Chapter 14: the SI2-B1 boundary case's diagnostic-severity-propagation question (§7.7) is routed to Chapter 21 specifically because it concerns the evolution of practitioner judgment about whether warning-level diagnostics should affect structural-honesty classification; the SI2-N3 case's $\sim_X$-strength observation (§7.6) is routed alongside Chapter 13 SI1.7.N3's $\sim_X$-strength observation as part of the long-horizon $\sim_X$-strength evolution work in Chapter 21.

### Chapter 20 routing for SI2: permissive surfacing

Chapter 14 may surface SI2-specific observations relevant to Chapter 20 substrate-generalization analysis; it does not assert that SI2 generalizes to other language-layer substrates. Specifically: the five-projection family structure (parse, check, diag, test, cli) is SI2-specific to type-checker substrates; whether the same projection-family structure generalizes to other language-layer substrates (other type-checkers, compilers, linters, static-analysis tools) is Chapter 20's substrate-generalization analysis. The seven structural-honesty primitives are SI2-specific in their exact form (Bismillah scope, Zahir/batin, Additive-only, Scan-incomplete, Mizan, Tanzil, Ring-close); whether the underlying structural-honesty disciplines generalize beyond SI2 to other substrates is again Chapter 20's analysis. The prototype-type-checker-vs-full-compiler-runtime scope boundary observable in SI2 is a pattern that may generalize to other prototype-stage substrates. These observations are made available to Chapter 20's analytical work without claim of generalization.

The closing of Chapter 14 returns to the Loop 1 framing (§0.1): Chapter 14 supplies evidence for the SI2 portion of T83's adequacy claim, not a re-proof of T83 and not a substrate-generalization claim. The four-axiom evidence (§§3--6), the seven judgment-case discharges (§7), the ecosystem-condition status evaluation (§8), and the T83/21/20 routing (§9) together substantiate Chapter 14's contribution to T83 at the empirical-relative-to-$J$ layer for SI2.

## Framing: Third Detailed Evidentiary Discharge of T83's J

### Chapter 15's role: evidence, not re-proof

Chapter 15 is the third detailed evidentiary discharge of T83's named judgment-case set $J$ for its SI3 portion. Chapter 8 §3 established T83 as a definitional-adequacy claim relative to $J$ (the named twenty-eight-case judgment set spanning SI1 through SI4), with the detailed substrate-specific evidence routed to Chapters 13--16. Chapter 13 instantiated that routing for SI1 (the file-layer Bayyinah substrate); Chapter 14 instantiated it for SI2 (the language-layer Furqan substrate). Chapter 15 instantiates it for SI3: it supplies the substrate-specific evidence that Chapter 8 explicitly deferred to the case-study block, evidencing T83's adequacy claim for the seven SI3 cases under SI3's declared $(O, K, R, R_{\mathrm{may}}, \Pi_X, \sim_X)$.

The chapter's role is evidence, not re-proof. Chapter 8 names $J$, supplies the Munafiq vocabulary mapping pattern (Chapter 8 §3.4), and establishes the structured-interpretation discipline. Chapter 15 does not re-prove T83 as a theorem and does not re-open Chapter 8's integrative theorem work; it provides the operational evidence that T83's adequacy claim is substantiated for SI3. The asymmetry is structural: T83 is a definitional-adequacy theorem at the empirical-relative-to-$J$ layer of the Principle of Layered Defense (Chapter 8 §0.2); Chapter 15 supplies the empirical evidence at that layer for the SI3 portion. Re-proving the theorem at the case-study layer would conflate the layers; supplying the evidence is the case-study chapter's proper work.

This framing parallels Chapter 13's relationship to Chapter 8 (which distinguished T82's minimal-fragment witness at the formal-consistency layer from SI1's full-scope instantiation at the empirical layer) and Chapter 14's relationship to Chapter 8 (which distinguished Chapter 8 §3.3's Furqan vocabulary mapping pattern as structured-interpretation skeleton from Chapter 14's SI2 instantiation on Furqan v0.11.1's substrate). Chapter 15 makes the corresponding distinction for SI3: Chapter 8 §3.4 supplies the Munafiq vocabulary mapping pattern at the chapter-level; Chapter 15 supplies the full-scope SI3 instantiation on Munafiq Protocol v3's specification substrate. All three case-study chapters preserve the evidence-not-re-proof discipline at their own substrate layers.

A citation-relationship discipline applies specifically to SI3 and is named here once for the rest of the chapter. Munafiq Protocol v3 §7 (the input-level performed-alignment extension) cites the surface-substrate divergence framework as "unifying structure" for input-level performed-alignment instances, identifying the Bayyinah Integrity Scanner [@arfeen2026bayyinah] as the file-layer empirical anchor. Chapter 15 in turn cites Munafiq Protocol v3 as the SI3 substrate-of-record. The relationship is *recursive substrate-instantiation*, not circular evidentiary support: Munafiq Protocol v3 is not cited as independent validation of AX-SH; it is cited as the model-layer protocol substrate to which AX-SH is applied. Munafiq's retrospective empirical-consistency claims (Sleeper Agents [@hubinger2024sleeper], Alignment Faking [@greenblatt2024alignment], Boxo et al. [-@boxo2025], Sheshadri et al. [-@sheshadri2025]) are substrate-of-record content documenting Munafiq's own evidence base, not independent validation of the four axioms.

**Companion note on flagship-paper scope-narrowing (v1.1 addition).** The flagship paper *Structural Honesty: Axioms for Detecting Surface-Substrate Divergence in AI Systems* (Arfeen 2026, doi 10.5281/zenodo.21500700) presents the model-layer diagnostic layer at compressed venue-facing scope: it discriminates only the decision-relevant pair, compliant-but-shallow versus performed (deceptively aligned), and defers the full four-process taxonomy and its completeness treatment to this monograph. The flagship's v0.6 SHV Model Council found the four-process taxonomy non-exhaustive under its own predicates when treated as a complete classification; the flagship responded by scope-narrowing to the discriminator pair rather than defending an exhaustiveness claim its evidence did not support. This chapter is that monograph-side completeness-boundary treatment -- a non-exhaustiveness analysis with explicit boundary handling, not a proved exhaustive partition: §5.2 states the full four-process formal predicates as Munafiq Protocol v3 §2 specifies them; §7 discharges the seven SI3 judgment cases against those predicates; §9 acknowledges via SI3-B1 and the substrate's §9 Incompleteness Boundary that residual classes not cleanly captured by the four processes are routed to boundary-case handling. The flagship's scope-narrowing does not demote the four-process content this chapter treats; it reflects venue-facing evidentiary parsimony, and Ch15's completeness-boundary treatment is the substrate the flagship's monograph-deferral resolves to. Whether the four predicates can be revised into a genuinely mutually exclusive partition (in particular for Processes 3 and 4, whose current predicates admit boundary overlap) is registered as future work; this chapter claims the boundary analysis, not the partition.

### J-discharge scope: the seven SI3 cases

Chapter 15's full chapter contract discharges the seven SI3 cases named in Chapter 8 §3.1's judgment-case set $J$: three positive cases (SI3-P1, SI3-P2, SI3-P3) where the Munafiq protocol operates correctly under its declared scope and practitioners would recognize structural honesty; three negative cases (SI3-N1, SI3-N2, SI3-N3) where the substrate exhibits a structural-honesty failure that practitioners would recognize, with negative cases labeled as documented historical failure or constructive counterfactual per the Chapter 13--14 case-type discipline; and one boundary case (SI3-B1) where practitioner judgment is debatable, grounded in Munafiq's own §9 Incompleteness Boundary and routed to Chapter 21 per Chapter 8 §3.6's boundary-case discipline.

The seven cases are named at the chapter level in §3.1 of Chapter 8 and are discharged by detailed substrate evidence in Chapter 15 §7. The case-discharge scope is exactly seven: not fewer (under-discharge would be a structural-honesty gap with T83) and not more (re-opening $J$'s enumeration is Chapter 8's prerogative, not Chapter 15's). The chapter's substrate-description and AX-SH-instantiation sections (§§0--2) prepare the substrate-fidelity ground for the seven case discharges in §7; cases outside the named $J$ are explicitly out of scope for Chapter 15; their structural-honesty implications for AX-SH at the SI3 substrate are routed to Chapter 21 falsification-protocol work or Chapter 20 substrate-generalization analysis as relevant.
