## furqan-lint v0.8.5: substrate description

### Primary vocabulary and substrate identity

SI4's substrate-of-record is the supply-chain four-substrate verification stack composing sigstore (identity), in-toto (process), SLSA (institutional maturity), and SHV (semantic) layers, per audit-ledger Section 5 and the canonical Chapter 4 §1.6 enumeration. Chapter 16's empirical evidence base is the operational furqan-lint tool at v0.8.5 (May 3, 2026) [@arfeen2026furqanlint], which instantiates the SI4 stack in practice at its SHV-semantic + artifact-validation + gate-enforcement + audit-of-self operational layers, as documented in `furqan_lint_thesis_paper_v1_1.pdf` (Arfeen 2026, May 9; 40 pages including Appendix A). Per the thesis §1.2 self-description, furqan-lint *is* a structural-honesty linter, a static-analysis tool, a continuous-integration gate, and a translator of Furqan programming-language semantics into static-analysis findings on Python, Rust, and Go. furqan-lint *is not* a complete type checker (mypy, rustc, and the Go compiler are); a style checker (ruff, rustfmt, gofmt are); a security scanner (Snyk, Veracode, and similar are); or a replacement for any of these. It is the operational SHV-semantic-layer instantiation that catches what those existing supply-chain-stack layers structurally cannot catch.

The substrate is operational code distributed under Apache 2.0 license on PyPI with source at `github.com/BayyinahEnterprise/furqan-lint`, plus the thesis paper as substrate-of-record documentation. The combination is analogous to the SI1 substrate (Bayyinah source tree plus thesis paper) and the SI2 substrate (Furqan compiler plus thesis paper), and is distinct from the SI3 substrate (Munafiq Protocol v3 paper as both substrate-of-record and substrate). SI4 is operational software with runnable code, tagged versions, and a 347-test test suite at v0.8.5; substrate-source verification was correspondingly higher-cost than SI3's unitary 7-page protocol-paper verification and structurally similar to the SI1/SI2 verification cycles.

The substrate type for SI4 is *operational static-analysis / continuous-integration / audit-of-self*, distinct from SI1 (file-layer integrity scanner), SI2 (language-layer type system and compiler), and SI3 (model-layer protocol substrate). furqan-lint operates as a static-analysis tool, a continuous-integration gate, and a recursive audit-of-self system: checking source artifacts (Python, Rust, Go code) for structural-honesty defects; enforcing release-pipeline gates that block non-conforming commits; and applying its own checks to its own substrate via the audit-of-self pattern.

### Four shapes of structural-honesty defects

The substrate's thesis paper §3 identifies four shapes of structural-honesty defects that the substrate's five checks (next subsection) collectively target. Each shape is a class of latent defects falling outside the coverage of existing style, type, and security tooling.

*Shape 1 --- Optional collapse through propagation* (substrate §3.1): a Python function declares a return type of `Optional[X]` but its caller's signature drops the `Optional`, narrowing incompleteness silently. The upstream Optional source returns None for the failure case; a local handler narrows the None away (often by returning a default value or by failing silently); downstream consumers treat the resulting value as if the Optional incompleteness never existed. The defect is structural because it produces no test failure under typical unit-test patterns (the happy path passes); ruff does not flag it (the syntax is well-formed); mypy in default mode does not flag it (the caller's signature is internally consistent with its own statements).

*Shape 2 --- Silently removed public name* (substrate §3.2): a library author renames a public function under a minor-version bump without explicit retirement procedure. Downstream consumers' code fails on the next dependency upgrade; the structural defect is that the surface (the version string `1.1.0` suggesting backward compatibility) does not match the substrate (the rename is structurally a deletion plus an addition). Liskov substitution [@liskov1994behavioral] is violated under the structural-honesty surface-substrate frame.

*Shape 3 --- Zero-return ring-close on unannotated code* (substrate §3.3): a function declares it returns an integer with zero return statements anywhere in its body. The Python interpreter accepts the shape; rustc and the Go compiler reject it. The defect is operational in Python-only contexts (where rustc-level enforcement is absent) and structurally honest only where the declared return type is consistent with the executed control flow.

*Shape 4 --- Return-None mismatch on unannotated or dynamic code* (substrate §3.4): a Python function expected to return `str` has explicit `return None` on at least one path; the annotation completeness fails to surface the contradiction at the declared-type vs returned-value interface. The defect is Python-only by design; Rust and Go compilers reject the firing condition before furqan-lint is invoked.

These four shapes are not exhaustive of all latent defects; they are a falsifiable class identified by the substrate as targetable by static analysis through Furqan programming-language semantics.

### Five checks across two subcommands

The substrate ships five static checks across two subcommands (substrate §5). The `check` subcommand runs four: *D24* (all-paths-return) fires when a function with a non-None return type has at least one control-flow path that does not reach a return statement; *D11* (status-coverage) fires when a function with a non-may-fail return type invokes a may-fail producer without handling the failure case --- may-fail producers are `Optional[X]` in Python, `Option<T>` / `Result<T,E>` in Rust, and `(T, error)` in Go; *R3* (zero-return / ring-close) fires when a function with non-None return type contains zero return statements anywhere, the disjoint complement of D24; *return-None mismatch* fires when a Python function with non-Optional return type has an explicit `return None` on at least one path, Python-only by compiler-rejection design. The `diff` subcommand runs one: *additive-only* fires on any public name present in old that is absent in new; renaming is structurally a deletion plus an addition and is therefore a finding.

### Three language adapters and the unified-pipeline architecture

Three language adapters ship in v0.8.5 with a common intermediate representation: a unified runner pipeline produces Furqan-semantic findings from Python, Rust, and Go source. The Python adapter ships in the standard wheel (no extras) and runs all four `check`-subcommand checks plus `diff`. The Rust adapter ships behind the `[rust]` optional-dependency extra (tree-sitter and tree-sitter-rust runtime dependencies) and runs D24, D11, R3, and additive-only (no return-None mismatch because rustc rejects the firing condition at compile time). The Go adapter ships behind the `[go]` optional-dependency extra (compiles a `goast` binary at install time via a PEP 517 build hook; requires Go 1.21+ on `PATH` at install time but not at runtime) and runs D24, D11, and additive-only (no R3 or return-None mismatch because the Go compiler rejects the firing conditions). Coverage asymmetry is documented and intentional, not adapter omission.

Separately, ten further languages are theorized as *future* adapters by structural-fit category in substrate §6.5 and Table 3 (Strong-fit: TypeScript/JavaScript, Kotlin, Swift, Scala, C#, C++23, OCaml/F#, Zig; Partial-fit: Java and Elixir; Compiler-enforced: Haskell; Weak-fit/Not-recommended: Ruby); none are committed to a release schedule and none ship in v0.8.5. The future-adapter theorization is distinct from the v0.8.5 shipping coverage evidence: Tables 1 and 2 of the thesis document the shipping coverage matrix (the three adapters and per-check coverage); Table 3 documents the theoretical-fit projection (the ten future-adapter candidates).

### Thirteen quality gates

The substrate enforces thirteen continuous-integration quality gates against every pull request, each a falsifiable assertion about the project's substrate enforced mechanically rather than relied upon as author vigilance. The substrate's §9 enumerates the gates across eight subsections: §9.1 names five tool-on-itself gates (`furqan-lint check src/` enforces D24, D11, R3, and return-None mismatch on the project's own Python source; additive-only enforces public-surface stability on `src/furqan_lint/__init__.py`); §9.2 names the CHANGELOG-math gate (parses CHANGELOG entries for documented test-count deltas and verifies actual pytest collection count matches); §9.3 names the four-place completeness gate (every documented limit must have all four surfaces --- fixture, pinning test, README entry, CHANGELOG entry); §9.4 names the release-sweep gate (version-string consistency across `pyproject.toml`, `__init__.py`, and the latest CHANGELOG header); §9.5 names the extras-matrix gate (every optional-dependency configuration in `pyproject.toml` exercised by at least one CI job); §9.6 names the README-drift gate (public commands documented in README match argument-parser registration in `cli.py`); §9.7 names the origin-tag-presence smoke gate (origin remote has a tag matching current substrate version, runs only when `CHECK_ORIGIN_TAGS=1`); §9.8 names the Go-specific gates (Go documented-limits four-place mirror; `goast` qualified-method-name behavior; Go public-surface additive-only on Go fixtures --- three gates running only when the `[go]` extra is installed). The substrate's count is thirteen, consistent with the enumeration 5 (§9.1) + 1 (§9.2) + 1 (§9.3) + 1 (§9.4) + 1 (§9.5) + 1 (§9.6) + 1 (§9.7) + 3 (§9.8) = 13 when §9.1's five tool-on-itself gates count as five individual gates and §9.8's Go-specific gates count as three.

The thirteen-gate enforcement framework is qualitatively distinct from the five checks of §2.3. The checks operate on *target source code* (Python, Rust, or Go projects that furqan-lint is invoked against); the gates operate on *furqan-lint's own source code and release artifacts* (the project's own CI workflow enforces the gates against every pull request to the project itself). The substrate operationalizes its own structural-honesty discipline through this dual-layer organization: external checks plus internal gates.

### Audit-of-self pattern, reciprocal contract, and substrate evidence base

The project operationalizes the recursive structural-honesty discipline through the *audit-of-self pattern* (substrate §7) instantiating the reciprocal contract specified in the Bayyinah Audit Framework v3.0 [@arfeen2026baf] (substrate §11.1). Three operational mechanisms instantiate the pattern: (a) a pre-commit hook runs `furqan-lint check src/` on every commit, with a finding blocking the commit at the local machine before the substrate diverges into a non-clean state; (b) a continuous-integration matrix --- the round-21 audit finding surfaced the matrix-coverage gap in the v0.8.3 cycle (pre-v0.8.3 CI exercised only Python no-extras configuration), and v0.8.4 operationalized the expanded 14-job matrix (Python 3.10--3.13 $\times$ no-extras / `[rust]` / `[go]` plus a Python 3.12 full-combination job) per the v0.8.4 CHANGELOG entry --- re-runs the same check on every supported Python version with adapter coverage, catching local-hook bypass attempts; (c) three documented audit-of-self findings examples surface in the substrate's evidence record --- the v0.4.1 CRITICAL pre-commit-hook installation finding (v0.4.0 hook shipped with a `pyproject.toml` `furqan>=0.11.0` version-spec that resolved against PyPI which only hosted `furqan==0.10.1`, causing pip dependency resolution to fail; v0.4.1 corrected it by declaring furqan as a dependency via canonical GitHub URL), the v0.7.2 prompt-grounding self-check finding (round-15 prompt specified planned Rust return-None mismatch checker; round-16 empirically demonstrated rustc rejects firing condition before furqan-lint sees the file; planned work dropped before shipping infrastructure-for-no-job), and the v0.8.5 attribution-discipline corrective (audit-chain's historical record violated the four-place pattern via auditor-name inline comments; corrective release fixed the substrate without rewriting history).

The reciprocal contract per substrate §11.1: a linter for structural honesty whose own code is structurally dishonest is a contradiction; in the substrate's own phrasing, "there is no path by which a finding ships to PyPI." The substrate's evidence base is grounded in the operational substrate: 347 tests at v0.8.5 (105 of which are gate tests, approximately 30% of the total), 27 documented releases over May 2--3, 2026, the audit-of-self findings record, and the CHANGELOG immutability discipline. The substrate-source verification cycle (analogous to the Chapter 13 verification against the Bayyinah source tree and the Chapter 14 verification against the Furqan source tree) was discharged in Cycle 8 (May 15, 2026) against the v0.8.5 source tree at the tagged commit (commit `a65db25812d30661a4031247fa6f8504b68d5b85`) at the operational-evidence-base layer; supply-chain-stack-layer substrate-source verification against sigstore, in-toto, SLSA, and SHV canonical sources is referenced via the corresponding bibliography entries per the SI4 substrate-of-record discipline established in canonical Chapter 4 §1.

## AX-SH structured interpretation for SI4

### Declared observer model $O$

SI4's declared observer model $O$ is the pipeline-embedded checker plus human maintainers, observing both code snapshots and transitions across three invocation points: the furqan-lint CLI (`furqan-lint check src/` and `furqan-lint diff old new`); the pre-commit hook (running on `git commit` at the local machine); and the GitHub Actions CI workflow (running on pull-request push and on release-tag push across the 14-job matrix). The observer model includes both the static-analysis checker invocations (the five checks of §1.3) and the audit-of-self gate enforcement (the thirteen quality gates of §1.5). Caller-side diversity per the A3 obligation is exercised at §5; the present §2.1 names the observer model only as the spec-canon-declared object.

### Declared applicability context set $K$ and the $K$ vs $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ layer distinction

$K$ is the set of supply-chain configurations (branches, environments, CI stages, deployment paths) where furqan-lint is declared in scope. A target system is in $K$ if and only if three conditions are met: the target source is Python 3.10--3.13, Rust (any 2018 / 2021 / 2024 edition), or Go (compatible with the `goast` binary built at install time); the adapter is installed (the standard wheel for Python; the `[rust]` extra for Rust; the `[go]` extra for Go with Go 1.21+ on `PATH` at install time); and the project has integrated furqan-lint via at least one of the three invocation points (manual CLI, pre-commit hook, or CI workflow).

Target source outside $K$ does not disappear from the SI4 frame; it appears as $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ outcomes (out-of-language-adapter-scope, out-of-Python-version-scope, or lint-unconfigured per the §2.4 enumeration below) requiring A3 discharge per the Chapter 14 K/$R_{\mathrm{may}}$ patched template, not as silently dropped cases. The $K / R_{\mathrm{may}}$ layer distinction is load-bearing: A2 / $R$ evaluates correspondence only on target systems inside $K$, while A3 / $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ enumerates the observable outcomes that arise across the full target-system universe including out-of-$K$ cases.

### Declared correspondence relation $R$

$R(\mathrm{Surface}_{v0.8.5}, \mathrm{Substrate}_{v0.8.5})$ holds when the declared supply-chain policies --- the thirteen quality gates as stated in the CHANGELOG, README, and CI configuration --- match the actual behavior of the stack as exercised by furqan-lint. Specifically: declared-policy claims about which checks fire, which gates block, and which findings the audit chain has surfaced must match the substrate-actual code, tests, CI workflow definitions, and audit-chain CHANGELOG record. Per-version $R$ is evaluated against each version's declared scope: v0.1.0 had 41 tests and 2 Python checkers; v0.8.5 has 347 tests, 3 language adapters, and 13 quality gates. The 27-version per-version $R$ ladder is the operational A2 evidence base.

Full per-version $R$ verification across all 27 versions is a substrate-source verification obligation (post-canon); Chapter 21 routing per §0.4 applies to the falsification-protocol dimension of this claim. The present §2.3 names $R$ as the spec-canon-declared correspondence relation; concrete per-version evidence and case-illustrated $R$ examples are presented at §4.

### Declared $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ observable-outcome categories

$R_{\mathrm{may}}$ enumerates the observable outcomes that arise when the observer model $O$ is exercised across the full target-system universe (inside and outside $K$); it is an enumeration of observable outcomes, not a correctness verdict. Correctness in any category routes to $R$, A2, or A4 per the Chapter 14 $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ patched template. SI4's $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ has eight observable-outcome categories:

1.  *Check-pass per family*: D24, D11, R3, return-None, and additive-only each emits pass per file or per project.

2.  *Check-fail per family*: the same five categories each emit fail with a documented diagnostic and suggested fix.

3.  *Check-not-applicable*: documented per-language-per-check (R3 not applicable on Go; return-None not applicable on Rust and Go).

4.  *Lint-unconfigured*: project source where furqan-lint is not invoked (no pre-commit hook, no CI integration, no CLI invocation).

5.  *Pipeline-bypassed*: a finding lands on origin via manual hook override or force-push; CI re-runs catch the bypass and fail the PR.

6.  *Alarm-unconsumed*: a CI failure that produces output the maintainer does not act on; out-of-scope for the tool itself but in-scope for the audit-of-self framework.

7.  *Out-of-language-adapter-scope*: target source is in an unsupported language (TypeScript, Java, and so on) and furqan-lint emits no finding.

8.  *Documented-limit-acknowledged*: target source exhibits a shape that triggers one of the v0.8.5 documented limits (aliased imports, generics with type parameters, and similar), and the checker emits "documented limit" rather than a finding.

Caller-side discharge patterns through the three $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ discharge paths (Chapter 6 §1) are described in §5.

### Declared projection family $\Pi_X$

SI4's declared projection family at full operational scope is the five-projection family
$$\Pi_X = \{\pi_{\mathrm{source}},\ \pi_{\mathrm{build}},\ \pi_{\mathrm{test}},\ \pi_{\mathrm{release}},\ \pi_{\mathrm{audit}}\},$$
mirroring the substrate's five-layer supply-chain-stack organization. $\pi_{\mathrm{source}}$ projects to declared source-code claims (function signatures, public-name surfaces). $\pi_{\mathrm{build}}$ projects to declared build claims (`pyproject.toml` dependencies, the extras-matrix, the PEP 517 build hook). $\pi_{\mathrm{test}}$ projects to declared test-suite claims (unit / integration / gate test markers, fixture-as-SUI organization). $\pi_{\mathrm{release}}$ projects to declared release claims (CHANGELOG entries, version-string consistency, PyPI Trusted Publishing OIDC). $\pi_{\mathrm{audit}}$ projects to declared audit-chain claims (rounds, severity-classified findings, the four-place pattern, audit-of-self findings).

Each projection's domain is determined by whether the corresponding stack layer is configured for the target project: $\pi_{\mathrm{source}}$ is defined where source code is in scope for at least one adapter; $\pi_{\mathrm{build}}$ where `pyproject.toml` or `Cargo.toml` or `go.mod` is parsable; $\pi_{\mathrm{test}}$ where a `tests/` directory exists with pytest markers; $\pi_{\mathrm{release}}$ where a CHANGELOG and version-string are maintained; $\pi_{\mathrm{audit}}$ where the audit-of-self framework is operative (rounds documented, four-place pattern applied). Each carries the shared substrate-identity coordinate per the Chapter 8 §2.2 patched discipline.

### Declared cross-projection consistency relation $\sim_X$: minimal vs strengthened

As in Chapters 13--15, SI4's cross-projection consistency relation $\sim_X$ is parameterized by strength. *Minimal* $\sim_X$ requires target-substrate-identity agreement plus layer-verdict-status agreement: each projection produces a verdict on whether the projected layer is structurally honest at the target, and the verdicts agree on the target's identity and on the layer-verdict-status disposition. *Strengthened* $\sim_X$ adds two further coherence requirements: *cross-layer-claim coherence* requires that source-layer claims and release-layer claims agree on public-surface contents, test-layer claims and gate-layer claims agree on which gates are enforced, and audit-chain claims and CHANGELOG claims agree on which findings closed in which release; *audit-discipline coherence* requires that the four-place pattern is satisfied uniformly across documented limits (every limit has its fixture, pinning test, README entry, and CHANGELOG entry consistently).

The minimal-versus-strengthened distinction is load-bearing for SI4-N3 case framing at §7.6 and joins the cross-chapter $\sim_X$-strength pattern (SI1-N3 / SI2-N3 / SI3-N3 / SI4-N3, four-instance pattern). Concrete joint-domain analysis under $\sim_X$ is presented at §6.

## A1 evidence: SI4 version-subtyping and corrigenda discipline

### SI4 version-history at the operational layer

The substrate documents twenty-seven releases between May 2 and May 3, 2026 (v0.1.0 through v0.8.5; v0.7.4 absorbed into v0.8.0 per the substrate's own immutability discipline). Each release has a CHANGELOG entry naming the audit-chain round, the severity-classified findings closed, and the test-count delta. The 27-version trajectory is the operational A1 ladder, analogous to the SI1 v1.0 $\rightarrow$ v1.1.0 $\rightarrow$ v1.1.1 ladder of Chapter 13 and the SI2 v0.x.y ladder of Chapter 14. On the narrow A1 version-history / release-count dimension, SI4's 27-version trajectory is the densest version-history evidence in the case-study block: SI1 documented 2 versions; SI2 documented 18 across multiple weeks per Chapter 14 §3.1; SI3 documented 3 protocol-document versions over weeks; SI4 documents 27 operational versions across May 2--3, 2026. This is a dimensional comparative observation about version-count density, not a claim about overall SI4 adequacy or strongest-in-block evidence; the corrigenda-discipline comparative claim is scoped separately at §3.3. The comparative claim is scoped exactly as in Section 17 sub-rows SI4.3.1--SI4.3.3: version-count density and corrigenda-discipline only, not on any other dimension.

### Liskov-Wing version-subtyping across 27 versions

Each v0.x.y $\rightarrow$ v0.x.(y+1) transition classifies as strengthening per the Chapter 4 §1.1 criterion (Liskov-Wing behavioral subtyping [@liskov1994behavioral]). The substrate's §8 documents six phase groupings across the 27 releases. The *Genesis* phase (v0.1.0 through v0.3.5) added foundational Python implementation, thread-safety, and diagnostic refinement. The *CI integration pivot* (v0.4.0 through v0.4.1) added the GitHub Action and pre-commit hook and closed the CRITICAL hook-installation finding. The *R3 round* (v0.6.0 through v0.6.1) added the zero-return / ring-close checker and closed two earlier documented limits; substrate-source-actual: no v0.5.x versions exist; numbering advances directly from v0.4.1 to v0.6.0 per the CHANGELOG trajectory. The *Rust adapter phases* (v0.7.0 through v0.7.4) added the Rust adapter as the largest single source addition, landed the prompt-grounding self-check at v0.7.2, added the dead-code retirement pin at v0.7.3, and absorbed v0.7.4 into v0.8.0. The *Go adapter and CI matrix expansion* (v0.8.0 through v0.8.4) added the Go adapter, surfaced the round-21 CI-matrix-coverage finding at v0.8.3, expanded the matrix from 5 to 14 jobs at v0.8.4 per the v0.8.4 CHANGELOG entry, and landed PyPI Trusted Publishing OIDC. The *Attribution corrective* (v0.8.5) was a documentation-only release closing the round-23 attribution-discipline finding. Each transition is structurally additive or scope-narrowing; none is silent withdrawal.

### Substrate-internal corrigenda discipline as A1-equivalent

SI4 exercises corrigenda discipline through three operational mechanisms that together make the A1 evidence comparatively stronger than SI1, SI2, and SI3 on the corrigenda-discipline dimension specifically. First, the substrate operates under *CHANGELOG immutability* (convention-enforced with CI-audit support per the Bayyinah Audit Framework v3.0 [@arfeen2026baf]): historical CHANGELOG sections are preserved verbatim; corrections are added as new entries rather than as rewrites of older ones. The v0.8.5 attribution corrective is the documented example: rather than rewriting prior CHANGELOG sections that had named auditors inline, v0.8.5 added a new entry codifying the going-forward convention and left the historical sections intact. Second, the *four-place pattern* is *mechanically enforced* via the four-place completeness gate at §9.3 of the thesis: every documented limit must have all four surfaces (fixture + pinning test + README entry + CHANGELOG entry); the gate fails the CI run if any of the four surfaces is missing. This is the strongest of the three mechanisms: enforcement is mechanically-gated, not author-vigilance-dependent. Third, *dead-code retirement pinning* (convention-enforced with CI-audit support): removed code is pinned with forward-compatibility tests asserting non-existence; v0.7.3 added the pin for code removed in v0.6.1, ensuring the absence is structurally tracked rather than merely undocumented. The combination makes SI4's corrigenda-discipline evidence stronger than SI1 and SI2 on this dimension (which evidence corrigenda discipline through CHANGELOG and tagging conventions only, without the four-place gate's mechanical enforcement) and stronger than SI3 on this dimension (which is protocol-document-only without operational-software substrate, so no CI-gate enforcement is available at all).

### A1 satisfaction evidence at the chapter-evidence layer

A1 is satisfied at SI4 conditional on the documented 27-version trajectory, the CHANGELOG immutability discipline, the four-place pattern mechanical enforcement, and the dead-code retirement pinning practice. The chapter inherits A1 from Chapter 4 §1.1 unmodified and instantiates it on the furqan-lint v0.8.5 substrate; no new axiom conditions are introduced. Full per-version A1 verification across all 27 versions is a substrate-source verification obligation (post-canon); Chapter 21 routing per §0.4 applies to the falsification-protocol dimension of this claim.

## A3 evidence: SI4 caller-side exhaustiveness over $R_{\mathrm{may}}$

### SI4 caller-diversity model: three-role separation aligned to three invocation points

SI4's caller-diversity model exercises three roles aligned to the substrate's three invocation points. The *CLI-invoker role*: human developer or AI assistant running `furqan-lint check src/` or `furqan-lint diff old new` directly. The *pre-commit-hook role*: the pre-commit framework invoking `furqan-lint check src/` on every commit before push. The *CI-workflow role*: GitHub Actions workflow invoking the same checks across the 14-job matrix on pull-request push and on release-tag push. The three roles encounter $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ differently: CLI-invokers see all eight categories of §2.4 directly; pre-commit-hook roles see check-pass / check-fail / not-applicable / documented-limit-acknowledged synchronously, with the commit blocking on fail; CI-workflow roles see the same plus pipeline-bypassed (when a pre-commit override is detected by CI) and alarm-unconsumed (when CI failure produces output the maintainer does not act on, surfaced via the audit-of-self framework not by furqan-lint itself). All three roles are *demonstrated* at the substrate level via the substrate's own integration-test layer per thesis §10.2 (whether organized as a `tests/integration/` filesystem subdirectory or as pytest-marker-tagged tests in the broader `tests/` tree is a substrate-source organizational detail not load-bearing for the caller-diversity claim) and the CI matrix definition; this is substrate-documented evidence, not modeled-from-substrate-structure inference. SI4's caller-diversity status is operationally stronger than SI1 (single-role file-scanner) and SI2 (single-role compiler) and SI3 (two-role protocol-applier + protocol-output-consumer with applier demonstrated and consumer modeled) on the caller-diversity-count dimension specifically.

### Caller-side discharge patterns through the three $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ discharge paths

The three caller roles cover the eight $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ categories of §2.4 exhaustively through the three discharge paths of Chapter 6 §1. CLI-invokers handle check-pass / check-fail outcomes via direct emission and standard exit codes (0 on clean, 1 on findings, 2 on argument errors); they propagate not-applicable and documented-limit-acknowledged outcomes through diagnostic prose without forcing a verdict. Pre-commit-hook roles handle check-fail via commit-block (the strongest discharge --- the substrate cannot ship the failing commit); they propagate not-applicable as commit-pass and documented-limit-acknowledged as commit-pass with diagnostic. CI-workflow roles handle pipeline-bypassed via cross-version re-runs (the 14-job matrix catches bypass attempts where pre-commit was skipped); they handle alarm-unconsumed via the audit-of-self framework's round-by-round review pattern documented in §11.2 of the substrate. The three discharge paths cover the eight $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ categories exhaustively per the Chapter 14 SI2.5.2 patched template.

### Concrete examples of caller exhaustiveness over $R_{\mathrm{may}}$

*CLI-invoker scenario* per substrate §7.3: a developer runs `furqan-lint check src/` locally, encounters a check-fail on D11 status-coverage, fixes the issue, and reruns to clean.

*Pre-commit-hook scenario* per substrate §11.1: a developer commits; pre-commit invokes `furqan-lint check src/`; the hook encounters a check-fail; the commit is blocked; the developer fixes and re-commits.

*CI-workflow scenario*: the 14-job CI matrix at v0.8.5 exercises checks across one lint / repo-hygiene job; Python-only, Rust-extra, and Go-extra test jobs across Python 3.10--3.13 (twelve matrix jobs); plus one Python 3.12 full `[rust,go]` coexistence job --- totaling fourteen. The substrate's round-21 audit finding surfaced the matrix-coverage gap in the v0.8.3 cycle (the pre-v0.8.3 matrix exercised only the Python adapter under the no-extras configuration; the Rust and Go adapters compiled in dev-loop but were not exercised under CI's partial-extras configurations); v0.8.3 landed the round-21 corrective gates including `test_ci_workflow.py` and `test_extras_matrix_gate.py`; v0.8.4 operationalized the matrix expansion from five jobs to fourteen per the v0.8.4 CHANGELOG entry, closing the round-21 HIGH-severity finding ("a CI matrix that does not exercise every adapter is structurally equivalent to having no CI for the unexercised adapters"). Modeled-from-substrate-structure scenarios that the expanded matrix can catch include pipeline-bypassed cases where a developer overrides pre-commit locally and force-pushes: the CI matrix re-runs the checks on every supported Python version and adapter configuration, so a bypass attempt would surface as a CI failure on the pull request. This pipeline-bypassed scenario is modeled from the substrate's CI self-check architecture (thesis §7.2) rather than documented as a specific historical event in the audit chain.

*Out-of-scope scenarios*: a project written in TypeScript (no adapter) appears under out-of-language-adapter-scope; a Python 3.9 codebase appears under out-of-Python-version-scope; a project without furqan-lint integration appears under lint-unconfigured.

All scenarios are documented at the substrate level (§§7--11) or modeled from the substrate's operational structure per the documented-vs-modeled discipline.

### A3 satisfaction evidence at the chapter-evidence layer

A3 is satisfied at SI4 with the three-role caller-diversity model (CLI-invoker, pre-commit-hook, CI-workflow), all three roles demonstrated at the substrate level. Operational nontriviality routes to §8.1 per the Chapter 13--14--15 patched template. The eight-category $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ enumeration of §2.4 is exhaustively covered by the three discharge paths per §5.2. The chapter inherits A3 from Chapter 6 unmodified and instantiates it on the furqan-lint v0.8.5 substrate; no new axiom conditions are introduced.

## A4 evidence: SI4 projection consistency under $\sim_X$

### SI4 projection family at full operational scope

The five-projection family $\Pi_X = \{\pi_{\mathrm{source}}, \pi_{\mathrm{build}}, \pi_{\mathrm{test}}, \pi_{\mathrm{release}}, \pi_{\mathrm{audit}}\}$ specified in §2.5 instantiates Chapter 7's $\Pi_X$ machinery on the SI4 substrate, mirroring the substrate's five-layer supply-chain-stack organization. Each projection's domain is determined by which stack layer is exercised at the target project: $\pi_{\mathrm{source}}$ is defined where source code is in scope for at least one adapter; $\pi_{\mathrm{build}}$ where `pyproject.toml` / `Cargo.toml` / `go.mod` is parsable; $\pi_{\mathrm{test}}$ where a `tests/` directory exists with pytest markers; $\pi_{\mathrm{release}}$ where a CHANGELOG and version-string are maintained; $\pi_{\mathrm{audit}}$ where the audit-of-self framework is operative. Not every projection is defined on every target; projection coverage is layer-dependent per the substrate's modular discipline.

### Joint-domain analysis for the five projections

The full joint domain is the set of target projects where all five projections are defined: source code in scope, build configuration parsable, test suite present with markers, CHANGELOG maintained, audit framework operative. furqan-lint itself at v0.8.5 is the canonical joint-domain example: all five projections are exercised on the project's own substrate per the audit-of-self pattern. A4's joint-domain consistency under minimal $\sim_X$ requires target-identity agreement plus layer-verdict-status agreement on joint-domain targets. Strengthened $\sim_X$ additionally requires cross-layer-claim coherence (source-layer and release-layer claims agree on public-surface contents; test-layer and gate-layer claims agree on which gates are enforced; audit-chain and CHANGELOG claims agree on which findings closed in which release) and audit-discipline coherence (the four-place pattern is satisfied uniformly across documented limits). Joint-domain depth varies by target-project maturity: a target project may have $\pi_{\mathrm{source}}$ and $\pi_{\mathrm{build}}$ defined but lack $\pi_{\mathrm{audit}}$. A4 evaluates consistency among the projections actually defined on each target.

### Concrete cases of joint-domain consistency under $\sim_X$

The canonical joint-domain example is furqan-lint at v0.8.5 itself, evaluated *at the case-study-instantiation layer rather than as independent validation of the four axioms*: all five projections produce consistency-verdict-positive on the project's own substrate. $\pi_{\mathrm{source}}$ is positive (the five tool-on-itself gates of substrate §9.1 clean on the project's own Python source). $\pi_{\mathrm{build}}$ is positive (the release-sweep gate of §9.4 clean; the extras-matrix gate of §9.5 clean). $\pi_{\mathrm{test}}$ is positive (the CHANGELOG-math gate of §9.2 clean: 347 tests as documented). $\pi_{\mathrm{release}}$ is positive (the origin-tag-presence gate of §9.7 clean; the PyPI Trusted Publishing OIDC operational since v0.8.4). $\pi_{\mathrm{audit}}$ is positive (the four-place completeness gate of §9.3 clean; the CHANGELOG immutability discipline operative; the 27-version trajectory documented). All five projections agree on target-identity and on the joint Project-Structurally-Honest verdict.

A partial-domain example: a target project with $\pi_{\mathrm{source}}$ and $\pi_{\mathrm{build}}$ defined but no $\pi_{\mathrm{audit}}$ (because the project has not adopted the Bayyinah Audit Framework discipline). A4 evaluates only the defined projections; the joint verdict is conditional on the projection coverage achieved.

### A4 satisfaction evidence at the chapter-evidence layer

A4 satisfaction holds at SI4 under minimal $\sim_X$, to the extent documented by furqan-lint v0.8.5's five-projection structure, the canonical joint-domain example of the project's own substrate, and the partial-domain handling per the substrate's modular discipline. The $\sim_X$-strength observation from Chapters 13--15 (SI1-N3, SI2-N3, SI3-N3) carries forward to SI4-N3 framing in §7.6 below as the fourth instance in the cross-chapter $\sim_X$-strength pattern. The substrate's §10.6 empirical-gap claim is relevant: under strengthened $\sim_X$ (cross-layer-claim coherence including comparator-analysis claims), certain consistency questions await the proposed successor study and are Chapter 21 routing rather than chapter-evidence claims.

## Seven SI4 judgment-case discharges

### SI4-P1: correct check-fail emission on D11 status-coverage

SI4-P1 is a positive case. Substrate scenario: target Python source contains `def f(x: int) -> int: y = g(x); return y + 1` where `g(x) -> Optional[int]`. furqan-lint's `check` fires a D11 status-coverage finding: the caller `f` does not handle the None arm of `g`'s Optional return type before reading the integer arm. Diagnostic prose names the specific call site and suggests handling the None case. Practitioners --- Python developers familiar with Optional and None semantics --- would recognize this as a structural-honesty defect that the existing tooling (ruff, mypy in default mode) does not catch. AX-SH classification: structurally honest; the check-fail verdict matches the substrate-actual structural-honesty defect type. Substrate evidence is grounded in thesis §3.1 (Optional collapse through propagation), §5.2 (D11 semantics), and the failing fixtures in `tests/fixtures/python/failing/`.

### SI4-P2: correct additive-only finding on silent public-name removal

SI4-P2 is a positive case. Substrate scenario: a library author renames a public function `def process_data` to `def process_dataset` in a minor-version bump from v1.0.0 to v1.1.0. furqan-lint's `diff old.py new.py` fires an additive-only finding: the public name `process_data` is present in old and absent in new; renaming is structurally a deletion plus an addition. Practitioners --- library maintainers familiar with semantic versioning conventions --- would recognize this as a Liskov-substitution-principle violation that the version-string alone of semantic versioning does not enforce. AX-SH classification: structurally honest; the additive-only-finding verdict matches the substrate-actual silent-removal defect type. Substrate evidence is grounded in thesis §3.2 (silently removed public name), §5.5 (additive-only diff), and the Liskov substitution principle [@liskov1994behavioral].

### SI4-P3: correct documented-limit-acknowledged emission on aliased Optional import

SI4-P3 is a positive case. Substrate scenario: target Python source contains an aliased Optional import passed through an intermediate module --- the substrate's documented-limit case. Concretely: module `a.py` contains `from typing import Optional as Opt`; module `b.py` contains `from a import Opt`; module `c.py` contains `from b import Opt` followed by `def f(x: int) -> Opt[int]: ...`. furqan-lint's `check` on `c.py` emits the documented-limit-acknowledged outcome: per the v0.8.5 documented limit (thesis §12.2), aliased Optional imports are recognized for the simple direct-import case but not when the alias is imported through one or more intermediate modules. The simple direct-import case (`from typing import Optional as Opt` used in the same file) is by contrast *recognized* and produces the normal D11 / D24 check path. The applier correctly emits documented-limit-acknowledged on the intermediate-module case rather than forcing a finding on inconclusive evidence. AX-SH classification: structurally honest; the substrate's §10.4 fixture-as-SUI discipline and §12.2 language-coverage limitations together prescribe acknowledging the limit rather than over-claiming. The A3 discharge path is propagate-as-incomplete with documented-limit-acknowledged tag, per the Chapter 14 SI2.7.P3 patched template.

### SI4-N1: documented operational failure --- the v0.4.1 CRITICAL pre-commit-hook installation finding

SI4-N1 is a negative case, framed as a documented operational shipped-and-broken failure. Substrate scenario: v0.4.0 shipped `.pre-commit-hooks.yaml` declaring `furqan` as a dependency via the `pyproject.toml` version specification `furqan>=0.11.0`; PyPI at the time only hosted `furqan==0.10.1`, so pip's dependency-resolution step failed and the hook shipped in a non-functional installation state. The structural test (YAML schema validation) passed in v0.4.0; functional install tests would have caught the failure but had not yet been added. Round-8 audit surfaced the finding; v0.4.1 closed it by declaring furqan as a dependency via canonical GitHub URL and adding functional install tests as four-place-pattern pinning. AX-SH classification: structurally dishonest at the level of A2 satisfaction in v0.4.0 (the surface-claim "the pre-commit hook works" did not match the substrate-actual "hook fails at install"); structurally honest at the level of A1 satisfaction in v0.4.1 (corrigendum tagged as version-update, four-place pattern applied). The case-discipline is documented-not-constructive per the Chapter 13--14 SI1.7.N1 / SI2.7.N1 patched template, contrasting with the SI3-N1 case in Chapter 15 which was constructive because Munafiq has no operational anchor.

### SI4-N2: documented prevented failure --- the v0.7.2 prompt-grounding self-check

SI4-N2 is a negative case, framed as a documented *prevented* failure --- pre-shipment catch, distinct in failure-class from SI4-N1's shipped-and-broken pattern. Substrate scenario: the round-15 prompt specified a planned Rust analogue of the return-None mismatch as the third Rust checker for v0.7.2. The round-16 pre-implementation critique constructed a battery of test cases attempting to write Rust source that would trigger the firing condition; the critique empirically demonstrated that rustc rejects all such shapes at compile time before furqan-lint sees the file. `fn f() -> i32 { None }` does not parse; rustc rejects it as a type mismatch before AST processing. The translator delta and `check_return_none` wiring would have shipped infrastructure for a check with no job. v0.7.2 dropped the planned analogue and shipped Result-aware D11 instead.

AX-SH classification: the audit-of-self pattern *prevented* an A2 failure pre-shipment. Had the planned shape shipped (counterfactual), the surface-claim "return-None mismatch checker fires on Rust" would not have matched the substrate-actual "rustc rejects the firing condition before checker invocation," constituting A2 dishonesty. Because the audit caught the drift before execution, the v0.7.2 substrate as-shipped maintained A2 satisfaction; the case demonstrates that audit-of-self functioned as designed. **As shipped at v0.7.2, A2 remained satisfied; the prevented A2 failure is counterfactual, not realized.** The case is the substrate's own §11.2 "prompt-execution drift" failure mode caught operationally. The case is documented (a real substrate-event, not constructive), but distinct from SI4-N1's shipped-and-broken pattern: SI4-N1 is post-shipment corrective, SI4-N2 is pre-shipment catch.

### SI4-N3: cross-layer claim disagreement in the v0.8.5 attribution corrective

SI4-N3 is a negative case framing a documented audit-chain-claim versus source-code-claim divergence. Substrate scenario: the audit framework's going-forward convention attributes findings to "round-N audit" without naming the auditor inline; pre-v0.8.5 CHANGELOG entries and source-code inline comments attributed findings to a specific named auditor ("Fraz"). The audit-chain claim and source-code claim diverged on the same attribution: $\pi_{\mathrm{audit}}$ produced one verdict (the going-forward convention), $\pi_{\mathrm{source}}$ produced a contradictory verdict (the named-auditor inline comments). Under minimal $\sim_X$ (target-identity plus layer-verdict-status agreement only), the primary failure is A2: the source-code attribution claim contradicts the audit-chain attribution claim. Under strengthened $\sim_X$ (cross-layer-claim coherence required), A4 may also fail because $\pi_{\mathrm{audit}}$ and $\pi_{\mathrm{source}}$ on the joint-domain target (the audit chain's own historical record) produce projection-classification disagreement.

The case functions as a constructive failure-mode test for $\sim_X$-strength per the Chapter 13--14--15 SI1.7.N3 / SI2.7.N3 / SI3.7.N3 cross-chapter pattern. **SI4-N3 is the fourth instance in the cross-chapter $\sim_X$-strength pattern (SI1-N3 / SI2-N3 / SI3-N3 / SI4-N3); the four-instance pattern is evaluated for substrate-generalization at the Chapter 21 layer per §9.2 routing (e).** The $\sim_X$-strength split is load-bearing for SI4-N3: **A2 is the primary failure under minimal $\sim_X$; A4 is a failure only under strengthened $\sim_X$ (when cross-layer-claim coherence is required).** Whether the four-instance cross-chapter pattern supports a strengthened $\sim_X$ as the default theoretical posture is the long-horizon question that the Chapter 21 evaluation will address; Chapter 16 itself does not resolve the pattern, it contributes the fourth datapoint. v0.8.5 closed the divergence via the four-part discipline: going-forward convention codification + source-code inline-comment sweep + Attribution-discipline note in CHANGELOG.md + immutability-preserved historical sections.

### SI4-B1: audit-of-self trust gradient ceiling

SI4-B1 is a boundary case. The substrate's §11.3 audit-of-self trust gradient ceiling is the *primary* framing anchor, with §12.3 methodological limitations as secondary anchor. The audit-of-self pattern surfaces small structural deficits early and continuously, before they compound; the substrate empirically generated the 27-version trajectory under this discipline. The framework explicitly names "audit-of-self has an inherent ceiling on adversarial rigor" as one of three documented limitations (§11.3 trust gradient). The substrate's §12.3 methodological limitations extend the boundary to procedural-framework dimensions (single-practitioner, two-day window, generalizability not yet demonstrated). Whether the audit-of-self pattern's reliability generalizes beyond the single-practitioner / two-day window of v0.8.5 to other practitioners, other teams, longer feedback loops, or adversarial-rigor contexts is a Tier 1 empirical question the chapter cannot resolve at the chapter-evidence layer.

The boundary is real: practitioners agree that audit-of-self at SI4 produced the documented trajectory; practitioners may reasonably disagree on whether it would produce comparable trajectories in adversarial-rigor contexts. AX-SH classification depends on disposition: if the substrate honestly acknowledges the trust-gradient ceiling (§11.3) and the methodological-limitations boundary (§12.3), the substrate is structurally honest at the boundary. **If the substrate over-claims audit-of-self as a universal substitute for adversarial-rigor audit, the case would move from boundary to negative.** The substrate's actual §11.3 and §12.3 acknowledge the ceiling explicitly, keeping the case at the boundary.

*Resolution direction* (distinct from B1 framing anchor): the substrate's §10.6 empirical-gap claim names the comparator-analysis successor study as the substrate's own proposed resolution direction. This is methodologically distinct from the §11.3 / §12.3 framing anchors --- §10.6 names what would resolve the boundary, not what grounds it. §9.2 routing (a) handles the §10.6 comparator-analysis successor study as a separately-tracked Chapter 21 routing class. The boundary case itself routes to Chapter 21 procedural-commitment falsification research per PMD v1.2 §0.1; the methodological-limitations questions are also routed there.

## Ecosystem-condition status

### Caller diversity

Aggregate status: *demonstrated* per the substrate's three-role caller-diversity model (§5.1). All three caller roles (CLI-invoker, pre-commit-hook, CI-workflow) are demonstrated at the substrate level via integration tests, pre-commit configuration, and CI workflow definition. SI4's caller-diversity status is stronger than SI1 (single-role file-scanner), SI2 (single-role compiler), and SI3 (two-role protocol-applier + protocol-output-consumer with applier demonstrated and consumer modeled) on the caller-diversity-count dimension specifically, because all three SI4 caller roles are substrate-documented and operationally-exercised.

### Projection multiplicity

Aggregate status: *demonstrated* with respect to declared projection roles and evidence-source diversity. The five projections (§2.5) correspond to genuinely different stack layers with distinct evidence sources: $\pi_{\mathrm{source}}$ draws on static-analysis tooling (mypy, rustc, the Go compiler); $\pi_{\mathrm{build}}$ on packaging conventions (PEP 517, Cargo, `go.mod`); $\pi_{\mathrm{test}}$ on pytest marker discipline; $\pi_{\mathrm{release}}$ on PyPI Trusted Publishing OIDC and semantic-versioning conventions; $\pi_{\mathrm{audit}}$ on the Bayyinah Audit Framework v3.0 four-place pattern and round-by-round review. Implementation independence holds at SI4 (unlike SI3 where it did not) because each projection's evidence base is a separately-implementable software discipline.

### Substantive evolution

Aggregate status: *demonstrated* per the 27-version trajectory at v0.1.0 $\rightarrow$ v0.8.5 (§3.1). The v0.x.y transitions add substantive content: foundational implementation (v0.1.0), thread-safety and diagnostic refinement (v0.3.x), CI integration (v0.4.x), the zero-return checker (v0.6.x), the Rust adapter (v0.7.x), the Go adapter and CI matrix expansion (v0.8.x), and the attribution corrective (v0.8.5). Each phase is substrate-source-documented and constitutes substantive evolution.

The thesis paper's Appendix A extends the substantive-evolution observation to post-v0.8.5: v0.9.0 added the ONNX adapter as a parallel diagnostic family; v0.10.0 and v0.11.0 added the Sigstore-CASM Gate 11 verifier; v0.11.6 reports 599 tests. The Appendix A continuation is acknowledged as research-program evolution but is *not load-bearing for SI4 evidence at the chapter-evidence layer*: SI4's analytic depth is pinned at v0.8.5, and Appendix A material is research-program-continuation context only. Later versions may enter via post-canon corrigenda cycles or via a separately-anchored substrate-of-record paper if and when one is published; the Chapter 16 SI4 evidence contract is closed at v0.8.5.

### Corrigenda discipline exercised

Aggregate status: *demonstrated*, with three distinct evidence sources stronger than SI1, SI2, and SI3 on the narrow corrigenda-discipline dimension only (not on overall adequacy) (§3.3). The CHANGELOG immutability mechanism is convention-enforced with CI-audit support; the four-place completeness gate at §9.3 is the strongest mechanism (mechanically enforced, not author-vigilance-dependent); dead-code retirement pinning is convention-enforced with CI-audit support. The mechanically-gated component is the discriminating feature relative to SI1 and SI2 (which evidence corrigenda discipline through CHANGELOG and tagging conventions only without the mechanical gate); SI3 (protocol-document-only without operational-software substrate) lacks CI-gate enforcement at all.

## §17.0 Role and scope

This chapter names two boundaries of the dissertation's central results, and it names them as open problems rather than closing them. The first is a boundary of decidability: the verification of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ is decidable only within a specific fragment, characterized in Chapter 10, and outside that fragment the question of axiom satisfaction is undecidable. The second is a boundary of preservation: the long-horizon guarantees of Chapters 11 and 12 hold for artifacts, specifications, and implementations that are in fact preserved, and they fall silent where preservation has not occurred. Four earlier passages route these two matters here explicitly --- Chapter 10 §1.3 ("systems falling outside it are routed to Chapter 17, not silently assumed away"), Chapter 11 §1.0, Chapter 12's scope statement, and Chapter 21 §21.3 --- and the present chapter exists to receive them.

The discipline of the chapter is inherited, not invented. The scan-incomplete primitive of the Furqan structural-honesty discipline (Chapter 14), instantiated operationally in the Bayyinah file scanner (Chapter 13) and the Munafiq protocol (Chapter 15), prescribes that a verifier which cannot fully extract the substrate it is meant to judge clamps its confidence and names the gap, rather than asserting a consistency claim it has not earned. Chapter 17 applies that same primitive reflexively, to the dissertation's own theorems. Where the theory cannot decide, it says so; where it cannot reach a preserved substrate, it says so. Naming the boundary is not a concession appended to the framework; it is the framework behaving as it requires its objects to behave.

Two limits on the chapter's ambition should be stated at the outset. First, it does not re-derive the apparatus it works from: the decidable-fragment framework is Chapter 10's, the preservation-adequacy result is Chapter 12's, and both are consumed here as cited boundaries, not reproved. Second, it does not solve the problems it names. In the manner the outline sets for the open-problems part, it states each problem precisely, locates it against the established results, and identifies the preliminary work that would constitute progress, leaving the problems open for future researchers. The claim ledger records the decidability limit as E1, a scope-exclusion held to be bounded-complete by design; this chapter is the prose discharge of that exclusion's forward-reference, not its resolution.

## §17.1 The undecidable fragments

### §17.1.1 Where decidability ends

Chapter 10 §1.3 fixes, axiom by axiom, the conditions under which the satisfaction predicate of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ is decidable. For Axiom 1 (append-only provenance), decidability holds under finite version histories, a finite set of truth-status tags, and decidable behavioral subtyping. For Axiom 2 (surface--substrate consistency), it holds under a finite observer-model and context-set $(O, K)$, a finite-state correspondence relation $R$ drawn from the Chapter 5 family, and a finite-state substrate. For Axiom 3 (caller-side exhaustiveness over $R_{\mathrm{may}}$), it holds under a finite $R_{\mathrm{may}}$, finite caller-discharge specifications, and decidable invariant-verification for the proven-unreachable cases. For Axiom 4 (substrate-parameterized projection consistency), it holds under finite projection families $\Pi_X$, finite joint domains, and a decidable consistency relation $\sim_X$. The decidable fragment is precisely the conjunction of these four finiteness conditions.

A fragment that violates them lies outside. Unbounded version histories, infinite-state substrates, an undecidable correspondence or consistency relation, an infinite $R_{\mathrm{may}}$ or projection family --- any of these places the corresponding satisfaction predicate beyond the reach of a decision procedure. This is not a defect in the proofs of Part III. Those proofs are stated relative to the fragment, and within it they are sound; Theorem 10.1, Theorem 11.1, and Theorem 12.1 each carry the decidable-fragment scope as a stated hypothesis. The undecidability is a limit on the *reach* of those results, marked here so that no reader mistakes a fragment-relative theorem for an unconditional one.

The undecidability is also not exotic. It is inherited from the underlying relations once their finiteness is dropped, and those relations are classically understood. The bisimulation relation that underwrites Axiom 2 is decidable on finite-state systems in $O(m \log n)$ time but undecidable on general Turing machines; the refinement relation that underwrites the Axiom 3 typing direction is decidable on finite algebraic types but undecidable on infinite types in general. The dissertation's introductory matter already names this in its statement of what the work does not do. Chapter 17 simply takes the statement seriously as a research boundary: the fragment is exactly as large as decidable bisimulation and decidable refinement allow it to be, and the interesting question is what happens at its edge.

### §17.1.2 The open problem

Inside the decidable fragment, a verifier can answer the question "does this system satisfy the axiom?" with a terminating procedure. Outside it, no such procedure exists, and the dissertation's downstream guarantees inherit the conditionality directly: the $n$-fold independence of Chapter 11, the quantum survivability of Chapter 10, and the preservation adequacy of Chapter 12 are all stated over the decidable fragment and say nothing beyond it. The open problem is therefore not the satisfaction question itself, which is settled to be undecidable, but its honest successor: what verifier behavior is available, and what can be claimed, when the satisfaction question cannot be decided?

The survivability question of Chapter 10 illustrates how the problem changes character at the boundary, a point Chapter 21 §21.3 makes precisely. Within the fragment, Theorem 10.1 shows that verification survives the quantum transition because no public-key primitive sits in its critical path; the procedure exists, and the theorem shows it endures. In the undecidable fragment there is no terminating verification procedure to begin with, so the question "does the procedure survive the transition?" is replaced by the prior question "is there a procedure at all?" --- and the answer is no. A guarantee about the durability of a verification capability is vacuous where the capability does not exist. The open problem inherits this: it asks not how to preserve a decision procedure beyond the fragment, but what honest partial capability can stand in for one.

### §17.1.3 Preliminary directions

Three directions would constitute progress, and the chapter names them without claiming any of them is reached.

The first is sound one-sided semi-decision. Several of the underlying relations, while undecidable, are semi-decidable in the direction of violation: a counterexample to consistency, once exhibited, is checkable even when the search for it may not terminate. A verifier built on this asymmetry returns "violation found" soundly, returns "no violation found within the bound" honestly, and never returns "consistent" without a proof; on non-termination it clamps its confidence rather than defaulting to a positive claim. This is the scan-incomplete primitive lifted from the file substrate to the undecidable fragment. Progress would consist of characterizing, per axiom, which satisfaction predicates admit sound semi-decision in the violation direction, and stating the resulting honest-verifier contract as a theorem rather than a design preference.

The second is sound finite abstraction. An infinite system can be replaced by a finite abstraction whose satisfaction is decidable, after which the honesty question becomes whether the abstraction is sound: does satisfaction on the abstraction imply satisfaction on the concrete system, or only the converse, and which one-sidedness does each axiom require? Progress would consist of abstraction families, one per axiom, with a proven direction of soundness and a calibration that ties the verifier's reported confidence to the abstraction's precision, so that a coarse abstraction yields a correspondingly clamped claim.

The third treats the fragment boundary as a design constraint rather than only an analysis result. A system can be engineered to remain inside the decidable fragment --- bounded histories, finite-state correspondence relations, finite projection families --- and the Furqan type-checker of Chapter 14 already does exactly this, declaring its scope as a decidable fragment of $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ and type-checking only within it. Progress here is a characterization of the expressiveness cost: how much of the operationally interesting structural-honesty discipline can be kept inside the fragment by construction, and which properties genuinely require the undecidable reach and so can only ever be approached by the first two directions. This is named as a dissertation-scale problem for future researchers; the present work establishes only that the boundary is real, located, and not silently crossed.

## §17.2 The non-preserved settings

### §17.2.1 Where preservation's guarantee ends

Theorem 12.1 proves that a system observing the six elements of the preservation discipline --- multi-substrate replication, cryptographic agility, format stability, institutional anchoring, translation discipline, and the designated-continuation protocol --- secures retrievability, integrity-checkability, and re-executability across the long horizon. The theorem is an adequacy result conditioned on observance. It does not speak to the settings it explicitly hands onward: those in which the discipline was not observed, and those in which it was observed but preservation failed nonetheless, through catastrophic loss exceeding the replication redundancy, institutional collapse outlasting the anchoring, or format obsolescence outrunning the migration cadence. In each of these the artifact, specification, or implementations have not been preserved, and Theorem 12.1 is silent by construction.

The forgery-resistance guarantee of Chapter 11 meets the same boundary from a different side. Theorem 11.1 makes undetected forgery require the coordinated corruption of all $n$ independent re-implementations, and Proposition 11.2 fixes the effective strength of the guarantee as the count of surviving independent fault sources. A setting in which implementations have been lost is a setting in which $n$ has fallen, and the guarantee falls with it: below the threshold at which enough independent witnesses survive, the resistance the theorem promises is no longer present. Non-preservation is thus not a single failure mode but a continuum along which the Part III and Part IV guarantees lose their hypotheses.

### §17.2.2 The open problem

The open problem is what structural-honesty guarantee, if any, survives when the substrate is not preserved, and it has two faces. The first is reconstruction: from what partial remains can a verification capability be recovered, and with what residual confidence? The second is graceful degradation: as preservation is progressively lost --- implementations dropping below $n$, fixture corpora decaying, reference parity eroding --- how does the guarantee degrade, is the degradation monotone, and, the structurally decisive question, does the system know that it has degraded? A guarantee that silently continues to assert full strength while its substrate erodes is precisely the surface--substrate divergence that Axiom 2 exists to detect; the honest requirement is that reported confidence track surviving redundancy.

### §17.2.3 Preliminary directions

Three directions again mark what progress would look like.

The first is degradation as a clamp rather than a cliff. The honest response to partial preservation loss is the scan-incomplete clamp once more: a verifier that has lost some of its independent re-implementations should report the reduced effective strength of Proposition 11.2, not a maintained guarantee. Progress would be a formal degradation curve for each Part III and Part IV guarantee as a function of surviving preservation, carrying the honesty constraint that the system's reported confidence is a sound lower bound on its actual surviving redundancy --- never an over-claim.

The second is reconstruction bounds. Because the specification is itself a preserved artifact under the discipline, a lost implementation can in principle be re-implemented from it. But a reconstructed implementation is an independent witness only if the re-implementer does not consult the survivors; otherwise reconstruction restores count without restoring independence, and the effective strength of Proposition 11.2 does not rise. Progress would be a characterization of the conditions under which reconstruction restores genuine independence, connecting directly to the independence assumption that Chapter 21 §21.2 names as the empirically falsifiable hinge of the whole forgery-resistance guarantee.

The third observes that the non-preserved setting is the dual of the undecidable fragment, and names the duality as itself a research direction. In the undecidable fragment the verifier lacks a terminating procedure; in the non-preserved setting it lacks the substrate on which to run a procedure it has. Both are settings in which the verifier cannot obtain what a positive consistency claim would require, and in both the honest response is the same primitive: name the gap, clamp the claim. A unified account of partial verification under missing capability and missing substrate --- one theory covering both faces --- is named here as a multi-decade target, of a piece with the substrate-generalization program that Chapter 20 takes up.

## §17.3 The unifying principle

The two boundaries are not independent caveats. They are one discipline applied in two places, and the discipline is the scan-incomplete primitive turned upon the dissertation itself. In every operational instance the framework already insists on it: the Bayyinah scanner clamps confidence when it cannot extract the bytes (Chapter 13); the Furqan type-checker confines itself to a declared decidable fragment (Chapter 14); the Munafiq protocol operates under bounded observability and reports accordingly (Chapter 15). The structurally honest move, whenever a verifier cannot fully see, is to name the limit and clamp the claim rather than assert a guarantee it has not earned.

Chapter 17 makes that move for the theory. $\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ does not claim to decide structural honesty on arbitrary systems; to claim it would be to assert a decision for an undecidable question, which is the very species of surface--substrate divergence the framework is built to catch. It does not claim to preserve what has not been preserved. Stating these two boundaries is therefore not an apology for the theory's reach but an exercise of the theory: a surface claim --- "$\mathsf{AX\text{-}SH}$ verification is decidable," "the preservation guarantee holds" --- is held to exactly its substrate warrant, the decidable fragment and the observed discipline, and not extended past it. The recursive Incompleteness Boundary that Chapter 22 develops applies here in its simplest form: no framework certifies its own complete reach from the inside, and the honest response is the append-only naming of the boundary, left open to future work, in place of a claim of completeness.

## §17.4 Synthesis and routing

This chapter discharges the forward-references that Chapter 10 (§1.0, §1.3, §1.8), Chapter 11 (§1.0), Chapter 12 (scope), and Chapter 21 (§21.3) route to Chapter 17. The undecidable fragments and the non-preserved settings are named-open here, each located precisely against the established result it bounds --- the decidable fragment of Chapter 10, the preservation adequacy of Chapter 12, the effective-strength count of Proposition 11.2 --- and each accompanied by the preliminary directions whose completion would constitute progress. Consistent with claim-ledger E1, the decidability limit is recorded as a scope-exclusion, bounded-complete by design; naming it here is the discharge of its forward-reference obligation, not its solution.

Three forward routings remain. The empirical falsification of the independence assumption, on which the non-preservation degradation of §17.2 depends, is Chapter 21's (§21.2). The self-application of the naming discipline this chapter uses --- the framework holding its own surface claims to their substrate --- is Chapter 22's. The designated-continuation protocol on which the reconstruction question of §17.2.3 ultimately leans, since reconstruction presupposes a preserved specification and an institution to maintain it, is Chapter 23's.

The chapter solves neither problem, and that is its function. It marks, as exactly as the established results allow, where the dissertation's guarantees stop: at the edge of the decidable fragment, and at the edge of what has been preserved. A reader who carries that boundary forward will not mistake the conditional theorems of Part III and Part IV for unconditional ones, which is the whole of what an honest open-problems chapter is asked to secure.
