Boundary [@arfeen2026munafiq]: no internal protocol guarantees
compliance against sufficiently sophisticated adversaries, including the
author. The chapter's principal empirical anchor is the cycles 7--11
retrospective re-verification arc, which surfaced fifteen-plus
substantive substrate-fidelity errors that prior cycles missed,
including two retroactive project-lead substrate-verification failures
caught at cycle 11. The arc empirically demonstrates that the
framework's self-application catches real errors AND that it has
reliability limits that justify the recursive Incompleteness Boundary
commitment.

## Framing: the dissertation as a substrate

### Chapter 22's role in the dissertation

The dissertation has, by the time Chapter 22 is read, established its
central theorem (T83 of Chapter 8), discharged four case-study
evidentiary instances (SI1 Bayyinah, SI2 Furqan, SI3 Munafiq, SI4
supply-chain four-substrate stack with furqan-lint v0.8.5 as operational
SHV-semantic-layer instantiation, in Chapters 13--16), and developed the
substrate-generalization framework (Chapter 20) and falsification
protocols (Chapter 21) that route the dissertation's empirical-tier
claims to discriminating tests. Chapter 22 is the dissertation's
recursive self-application layer: the place where the framework
developed across Chapters 3--8 (the four-axiom AX-SH structure with K,
$R_{\mathrm{may}}$, $\Pi_X$, $\sim_X$ machinery), applied to four
external substrates in Chapters 13--16, is finally applied to a fifth
substrate: the dissertation itself.

The dissertation's recursive-self-application status is not symmetric
with the case-study chapters. The case-study chapters treat external
substrates (the Bayyinah Integrity Scanner source tree, the Furqan
prototype type-checker source tree, the Munafiq Protocol v3 paper, the
supply-chain four-substrate stack evidenced through the furqan-lint
static-analysis tool) where the framework's author has no privileged
epistemic access beyond what the substrates themselves document. The
dissertation, in contrast, is the framework's author's own work; the
framework's author cannot honestly claim the same observer-instance
independence with respect to it. This asymmetry is itself a
structural-honesty concern that Chapter 22 must address head-on rather
than elide.

The chapter therefore organizes its discharge of the six
self-application obligations (R1--R6 of audit-ledger Section 8) around
two complementary commitments. First, the framework's structural-honesty
discipline is applied to the dissertation honestly, including where the
discipline catches the author's own errors (and Chapter 22 documents
specific instances where it has done so). Second, the chapter does not
over-claim self-application reliability; it acknowledges the recursive
Incompleteness Boundary that Munafiq Protocol v3 §9 articulates and that
the cycle 11 absorption empirically demonstrated.

### The visible-reality / underlying-reality framing

A note on the chapter's epistemic framing. The dissertation's
structural-honesty vocabulary in technical contexts uses the
surface-substrate terminology developed across Chapters 3--8: a system's
surface layer is what observers see (outputs, declarations, types, audit
verdicts) and its substrate layer is what underlies the surface
(internal states, source code, semantic content, evidence base). This
vocabulary is precise for the framework's mathematical purposes.

For the recursive self-application context of Chapter 22, the chapter
also draws on an older epistemic distinction that the framework's author
finds clarifying. The Arabic terms *shahada* (visible reality, the
witnessable layer) and *ghayb* (underlying reality, the layer not
amenable to direct witnessing) provide a complementary framing the
chapter renders in English as "visible reality" and "underlying
reality." The framing is older than the surface-substrate vocabulary,
predating the dissertation by approximately fourteen centuries, and the
framework's author treats the visible-reality / underlying-reality
distinction as the framework's epistemic posture rather than as a
technical claim within the framework's mathematics.

The ethical commitment the framework's author makes, articulated
explicitly here in Chapter 22 because the recursive self-application
context makes it relevant: the framework specifies how to use front-end
(visible-layer) influence to do honest work in the visible-reality
layer, accepting that the underlying-reality layer is not the author's
to engineer. The framework can discipline what the author writes,
publishes, audits, and corrects; it cannot discipline whether the
author's underlying-reality state matches the author's visible-reality
claims. The recursive Incompleteness Boundary at R6 is the framework's
own acknowledgment of this asymmetry.

### Chapter 22's relationship to Chapter 23 and to the case-study chapters

Chapter 22 discharges R1--R6 (the self-application proof obligations);
Chapter 23 (the next chapter, on the continuation regime) discharges
K1--K7 (the continuation obligations: designated continuators,
multi-archive deposition, translation protocol, standards-body
anchoring, withdrawal/supersession criteria). The two chapters are
complementary: Chapter 22 handles self-application within the
dissertation's own lifecycle (drafting, audit, publication), Chapter 23
handles preservation and continuation after publication. The boundary
is: Chapter 22's R1--R6 cover what the author and immediate
collaborators do; Chapter 23's K1--K7 cover what designated continuators
do.

Chapter 22 also relates to the case-study chapters. Chapter 22 is the
fifth instance in the framework's instantiation pattern: SI1 (Bayyinah,
file-layer integrity), SI2 (Furqan, language-layer type system), SI3
(Munafiq, model-layer protocol), SI4 (supply-chain four-substrate stack
with furqan-lint operational instantiation), and SI-self (the
dissertation, structural-honesty framework recursively). The fifth
instance is structurally distinct from the first four in that the
framework is being applied to itself; this is the recursive
self-application that gives the chapter its title.

## The self-application commitment from Chapter 1 §9

### R1--R6 as proof obligations

Chapter 1 §9 stated six self-application commitments. They are
reproduced from audit-ledger Section 8 here as the proof obligations
Chapter 22 discharges:

-   **R1.** Surface-substrate consistency at the chapter level: the
    abstract, headings, and chapter summaries must match the chapter
    body.

-   **R2.** Caller exhaustiveness at the claim level: every claim must
    have present support, a cited source, or an explicit forward-routing
    to a future proof obligation.

-   **R3.** Append-only provenance from v1.0 onward: corrigenda
    discipline activates at publication, with explicit corrigenda for
    any post-v1.0 withdrawal or scope-narrowing.

-   **R4.** Substrate-parameterized projection consistency: the
    abstract, table of contents, chapter summaries, and chapter
    conclusions form a projection family $\Pi_{\mathrm{diss}}$ that must
    be cross-consistent.

-   **R5.** Validator-by-different-instance discipline: pre-publication
    dual-audit pattern, post-publication external review.

-   **Canonical empirical anchor.** The Recursive-A1-Self-Application
    Empirical-Instance Enumeration recorded in audit-ledger Section 18
    (cycle-24+P absorption, May 19, 2026) catalogues ten
    substrate-verified instances across cycles 16--24, with cycle 24
    itself as an eleventh recursive-A1 self-application instance (audit
    ledger as project-lead-authored substrate-of-record baselined under
    parallel-vendor discipline). The enumeration provides the canonical
    empirical anchor for R1, R3, and R4 discharge claims; specific
    instances are cited inline at the relevant R-section.

-   **R6.** Recursive Incompleteness Boundary: no internal protocol
    guarantees compliance against sufficiently sophisticated
    adversaries, including the author.

R1, R2, and R4 are surface-substrate / projection-consistency
obligations that map to the AX-SH framework's A2 (surface-substrate
consistency under R) and A4 (cross-projection consistency under
$\sim_X$). R3 maps to A1 (Liskov-Wing version-subtyping discipline) at
the dissertation lifecycle layer. R5 maps to A3 (caller-side
exhaustiveness) at the validation layer: validators are callers of the
dissertation's claims, and validator diversity is A3 evidence. R6 is the
recursive analogue of Munafiq Protocol v3 §9's Incompleteness Boundary
applied to the dissertation as a substrate.

The mapping is not coincidental. The four axioms of Chapters 3--8 were
developed to apply to substrates generally; the self-application
commitment of Chapter 1 §9 is the framework's own assertion that this
generality includes the dissertation. Chapter 22's task is to verify the
assertion.

### The framework as substrate

For Chapter 22's discharge purposes, the dissertation is treated as a
substrate $S_{\mathrm{diss}}$ with declared scope and a declared
correspondence relation $R_{\mathrm{diss}}$. The declared scope is the
set of claims made in the dissertation's body text (Chapters 1--23),
distinct from the claims made in the audit ledger (which is an
audit-trail artifact accompanying the dissertation rather than
dissertation content per se). The declared correspondence relation
$R_{\mathrm{diss}}$ holds when: for every claim $c$ in the dissertation,
$c$ either (a) has present support in the dissertation's body or in
cited bibliography, or (b) has an explicit forward-routing to a future
proof obligation, or (c) is qualified as a research direction / open
problem / future work.

The dissertation does not require itself to be complete; it requires
every claim to be either supported, routed, or qualified. This is the
operationalization of R2 (caller exhaustiveness) and is the
dissertation's principal structural-honesty commitment at the claim
level. Chapter 22 discharges R2 by demonstrating the audit-ledger's
coverage of every dissertation claim.

The four projection layers of $\Pi_{\mathrm{diss}}$ are: the abstract
$\pi_{\mathrm{abs}}$, the table of contents $\pi_{\mathrm{toc}}$, the
chapter summaries $\pi_{\mathrm{sum}}$, and the chapter conclusions
$\pi_{\mathrm{con}}$. Each projection is a structured summary of a
different aspect of the dissertation's content. Cross-projection
consistency under $\sim_X$ requires that these projections do not
contradict each other on load-bearing claims. Chapter 22 discharges R4
by demonstrating projection consistency.

## R1: surface-substrate consistency at the chapter level

### Chapter-by-chapter surface-substrate audit

R1 requires that each chapter's abstract, headings, and chapter summary
match the chapter body. Chapter 22 discharges R1 by reporting on the
chapter-by-chapter surface-substrate audit conducted across audit
cycles 1--11.

The audit pattern: each chapter, on first-canon promotion, has its
abstract / opening paragraph compared against its body to verify that
the abstract's claims correspond to body content (not over-claiming, not
under-claiming, not silently substituting different claims). The
chapter's section headings are compared against the section bodies; the
chapter summary (where present) is compared against the body claims. The
pattern is structurally similar to Munafiq Protocol v3's CIT
(Context-Invariance Test, substrate §4.6) but operating on dissertation
chapters rather than model outputs.

### Findings across cycles 1--11

R1-class findings surfaced across cycles 1--11 in the chapter-by-chapter
audits:

-   **Chapter 13 cycle finding**: an A1 corrigenda-discipline event
    where Chapter 13 made claims about v1.0 that contradicted the
    substrate; corrigenda corrected numbers downward. The audit ledger
    names this as "the dissertation's A1 corrigenda discipline applied
    recursively to the dissertation itself."

-   **Chapter 14 cycle finding**: an SI2-V-003 MEDIUM under-claim
    finding where Chapter 14 declined to assert substrate-witnessed
    maturity that the substrate actually had; corrigenda upgraded
    status. The audit ledger names this as "framework symmetry catches
    both over-claims and under-claims."

-   **Chapter 16 cycle 7 finding**: an internal contradiction between
    §4.1 (asserting $R$ held at v0.1.0 through v0.8.4 for all
    target-system sets in K) and §7.4 SI4-N1 (correctly classifying
    v0.4.0 as A2-dishonest); the contradiction was caught by
    fresh-instance audit-author work and patched.

-   **Chapter 15 cycle 10 finding**: an internal logical contradiction
    in Section 16 SI3.6.3 and Chapter 15 §6.3 (negative layer verdicts
    asserted to yield Process-1 classification, which is logically
    impossible since Process-1 requires genuine alignment, i.e.,
    positive verdicts). Caught by fresh-instance audit-author and
    patched in cycle 10 absorption.

Each finding instantiates R1: a chapter's surface claims diverged from
its substrate (body) content; the audit caught the divergence;
corrigenda applied. The four findings span over-claims, under-claims,
and internal contradictions, demonstrating that R1 surface-substrate
consistency is not a trivially-met obligation but a discipline that
requires active audit work to maintain.

### R1 discharge

R1 is discharged at the present cycle (cycle 11 absorption, May 16,
2026) as: *partial-demonstrated*. The discharge is partial because R1
cannot be globally demonstrated on a not-yet-published dissertation;
per-chapter audits are conducted on each chapter individually, with the
cumulative pattern across cycles 1--11 forming the body of R1 evidence.
The discharge is demonstrated rather than modeled because specific
R1-class findings have been caught and patched (the four findings
above), confirming that the audit pattern catches real surface-substrate
divergences rather than only confirming surfaces. Full R1 demonstration
is conditional on the dissertation reaching v1.0 with the
chapter-by-chapter audit pattern applied at publication; pre-publication
audits demonstrate the pattern's effectiveness without claiming the
audit set is complete.

## R2: caller exhaustiveness at the claim level

### The audit ledger as A3 evidence

R2 requires that every claim in the dissertation have present support,
cited source, or explicit forward-routing. The discharge mechanism is
the audit ledger: a structured document recording every load-bearing
claim and its support status. The audit ledger is to the dissertation
what the substrate-internal corrigenda mechanism of Munafiq Protocol v3
R4 design requirement is to the Munafiq Protocol: a substrate-internal
record of where the substrate's claims stand.

The audit ledger has grown across cycles 1--11 from initial drafting at
end of cycle 0 (May 12, 2026) to its current state at end of cycle 11
(May 16, 2026). Its growth reflects the dissertation's progress: each
chapter, on first-canon promotion, contributes its claim-set to the
ledger; each audit cycle, on absorption, contributes its findings and
patches. The ledger as of May 16, 2026 records approximately 110
claim-rows across the structural chapters (Chapters 1--12 + 17--23,
treated as drafted-or-outline status), 186 sub-row commitments in the
case-study chapter spec-canons (SI1.0.x--SI4.9.x across Chapters 13--16:
46 SI1 + 46 SI2 + 47 SI3 + 47 SI4), and 60-plus audit-cycle absorption
entries documenting the dissertation's iterative correction history.

### Three claim categories per PMD §0.1

Following PMD v1.2 §0.1 (procedural-versus-empirical distinction), the
dissertation's claims fall into three categories:

-   **Tier 1 (empirical claims)**: claims about external substrates that
    require falsification protocols (per Chapter 21). The dissertation
    has approximately 35 Tier 1 claims across the case-study chapters'
    empirical evidence rows. Each is routed to Chapter 21 falsification
    protocols for the §0.3 quintuple-plus-verdict template.

-   **Tier 2 (procedural commitments)**: claims about the dissertation's
    own discipline (e.g., the four-axiom structure, the case-study
    template, the audit-ledger record-keeping discipline). These are not
    falsifiable in the empirical sense; they are evaluated by
    procedural-conformance rather than by Tier 1 falsification.

-   **Tier 3 (research-direction claims)**: claims qualified as future
    work, open problems, or research directions. These are not currently
    supported; they are routed forward.

R2 discharge requires that no dissertation claim falls outside these
three categories. The audit ledger's row-by-row coverage is the
discharge evidence.

### R2 discharge

R2 is discharged at cycle 11 absorption as: *demonstrated*. The
discharge is demonstrated rather than partial because the audit-ledger
coverage is comprehensive (every load-bearing claim in the dissertation
is either ledger-rowed or routed via PMD §0.1 categorization); the
cycles 9--11 SI3 retrospective re-verification arc surfaced no
R2-violating uncovered-claim findings. Where claims have been added to
the dissertation between audit cycles, the audit-cycle absorption
pattern requires ledger updating before promotion; this discipline has
held across all eleven cycles.

## R3: append-only provenance from v1.0 onward

### Corrigenda discipline before v1.0

R3 requires append-only provenance from v1.0 onward. The corrigenda
discipline activates at publication; pre-publication revisions are
exempt from corrigenda discipline.

The pre-publication exemption is not arbitrary. The dissertation's
audit-cycle process is iterative draft-and-correct work: each cycle's
findings produce patches that modify earlier text. Requiring corrigenda
for every pre-publication patch would render the audit-cycle process
infeasible. The exemption is bounded: it applies only to the
not-yet-published draft. Once v1.0 is published, the append-only regime
activates, and any subsequent withdrawal or scope-narrowing requires
explicit corrigenda.

The exemption is structurally analogous to the Bayyinah Integrity
Scanner project's development branch versus the publish-tag branch (per
Chapter 13 SI1.3.x): pre-publication releases are subject to revision;
published releases are subject to corrigenda-tagged correction only.

### Corrigenda discipline at and after v1.0

The corrigenda discipline at v1.0 follows Chapter 4 §1.1's A1
Liskov-Wing version-subtyping criterion applied to the dissertation: any
post-v1.0 transition (v1.0 to v1.0.1 to v1.1 to v2.0, etc.) must be a
strengthening or an explicitly-tagged corrigendum. Strengthenings extend
prior claims without withdrawal; corrigenda explicitly withdraw or
narrow scope with a documented audit trail.

The five corrigenda categories defined for the dissertation's post-v1.0
lifecycle, mirroring the Bayyinah audit-chain four-place pattern:
*citation-relocation* (citation moved to correct substrate location),
*citation-divergent* (citation content diverged from substrate-actual,
requires content correction), *citation-incomplete* (additional
substrate evidence required), *internal-contradiction* (intra-chapter or
cross-chapter contradiction caught), and *watchlist-pattern* (a specific
error pattern flagged for systematic review).

### R3 discharge

R3 is discharged at cycle 11 absorption as:
*drafted-and-proof-obligation*. The discharge is drafted because the
corrigenda discipline is specified in Chapter 1's Version status note
and the audit-ledger's cycle-absorption discipline. The discharge is
proof-obligation because R3's full activation occurs at v1.0
publication; pre-publication, the discharge is the commitment to
activate the discipline rather than the discipline's operation.

The proof-obligation portion is routed jointly to Chapter 23
(designated-continuation regime), since the append-only provenance
discipline requires designated continuators to maintain it across
decades. Chapter 23's K1, K3, and K7 commitments carry this forward.

## R4: substrate-parameterized projection consistency under $\Pi_{\mathrm{diss}}$

### The four projection layers of $\Pi_{\mathrm{diss}}$

R4 requires substrate-parameterized projection consistency: the
dissertation's four projection layers (abstract, table of contents,
chapter summaries, chapter conclusions) form a projection family
$\Pi_{\mathrm{diss}}$, and these projections must be cross-consistent
under $\sim_{X,\mathrm{diss}}$.

Each projection is a structured summary of a different aspect:

-   $\pi_{\mathrm{abs}}$ (the dissertation's abstract): a compressed
    statement of the dissertation's central claims, target audience, and
    contribution.

-   $\pi_{\mathrm{toc}}$ (the table of contents): a structural map of
    the dissertation's organization at the chapter and section level.

-   $\pi_{\mathrm{sum}}$ (the chapter summaries): per-chapter abstracts
    at the chapter introduction layer.

-   $\pi_{\mathrm{con}}$ (the chapter conclusions): per-chapter
    terminating sections summarizing what the chapter establishes.

Cross-projection consistency requires that these four projections do not
contradict each other on load-bearing claims. The minimal
$\sim_{X,\mathrm{diss}}$ is satisfied when the projections are
consistent on the dissertation's central theorem (T83), the four-axiom
framework structure, the four-case-study evidentiary discharge, and the
chapter-level scope statements. The strengthened
$\sim_{X,\mathrm{diss}}$ would require additional consistency on
second-order properties (e.g., uniform terminology across projections);
the dissertation discharges R4 at the minimal $\sim_X$ level for v1.0,
with strengthened $\sim_X$ as a research direction for future revisions.

### R4 findings across cycles 1--11

R4-class findings (cross-projection inconsistencies between
$\pi_{\mathrm{abs}}, \pi_{\mathrm{toc}}, \pi_{\mathrm{sum}}, \pi_{\mathrm{con}}$)
surfaced occasionally across cycles 1--11. Two specific instances bear
mention:

-   **Chapter 15 cycle 11 §8.1 heading-versus-body finding** (GPT-5.5
    F-VERIFY-SI3-004): Chapter 15 §8.1's subsection heading stated
    "Caller diversity status: partial" while the post-cycle-10-patched
    body asserted "modeled." The heading is part of $\pi_{\mathrm{toc}}$
    / $\pi_{\mathrm{sum}}$ projections; the body is the chapter content.
    The internal-contradiction finding is an $R4$-class
    projection-consistency failure that the cycle 11 audit caught and
    patched.

-   **Chapter 13 cycle finding**: Chapter 13's $\pi_{\mathrm{abs}}$
    claim about v1.0 substrate state contradicted the substrate (per the
    cycle ledger entry); the corrigenda corrected both the projection
    and the body. This was simultaneously an R1 finding
    (surface-substrate divergence at chapter level) and an R4 finding
    (projection inconsistency between abstract and body).

### R4 discharge

R4 is discharged at cycle 11 absorption as:
*drafted-and-partial-demonstrated*. The discharge is drafted because
$\Pi_{\mathrm{diss}}$ is specified in Chapter 1 §9's self-application
outline. The discharge is partial-demonstrated because cross-projection
consistency audits have been conducted incrementally across cycles 1--11
with specific findings caught and patched (the two instances above);
full demonstration awaits the dissertation's v1.0 publication snapshot
at which point the four-projection family is fixed and cross-projection
consistency can be globally verified.

## R5: validator-by-different-instance discipline

### The dual-audit pattern operationalized

R5 requires validator-by-different-instance discipline: pre-publication
dual-audit pattern with at least two independent validators per audit
cycle, plus post-publication external review through the
academic-archival mechanisms (Zenodo deposit + arXiv post + invited
critical readers).

The pre-publication dual-audit pattern has been operationalized via
cycles 1--11 with the following vendor-pair / vendor-triple coverage:

-   Cycles 1--5: ChatGPT + Perplexity dual-audit, with the author as
    project-lead conducting strict-merge absorption. Continuity-mode
    operating conditions; cycles 1--4 specifically conducted before the
    fresh-instance discipline correction at end of cycle 5.

-   Cycles 6--8 (SI4 / Chapter 16 fresh-instance): ChatGPT + Perplexity
    dual-audit under fresh-instance discipline. Cycle 7 caught the
    Chapter 16 §4.1 vs §7.4 internal contradiction.

-   Cycles 9--10 (SI3 / Chapter 15 retrospective): ChatGPT + Perplexity
    dual-audit under fresh-instance discipline. Audit A
    (Perplexity-class) coverage failure documented across both cycles;
    Audit B (ChatGPT-class) caught real findings.

-   Cycle 11 (SI3 / Chapter 15 AX-SH criterion-level): three-vendor
    cross-rotation: GPT-5.5 (OpenAI), Kimi K2.6 (Moonshot via
    Perplexity), Gemini 3.1 Pro (Google). First dissertation cycle
    conducted across three distinct model families.

The dual-audit pattern's structural-honesty contribution is documented
across the ledger: at each cycle, the dual audit caught findings that
single-audit dispatch would have missed; the strict-merge absorption
mechanism (project-lead substrate-verification of each finding)
implemented the disposition.

### R5 finding: the cycles 9--10 Audit A coverage degradation

Cycles 9 and 10 documented a pattern of Audit A (Perplexity-class)
coverage failure: across both cycles, Audit A returned PASS verdicts on
cases where Audit B caught real substrate-fidelity errors. The pattern
was concerning enough that cycle 11 dispatched to three vendors rather
than two, with Kimi K2.6 (a different model family than Perplexity's
defaults) substituting for the Perplexity-default slot.

The cycle 11 verdicts revealed that the Perplexity-Kimi-K2.6 dispatch
returned substantive findings (the §1/§2 predicate location and the §2.2
scope locator), while a hypothetical Perplexity-default dispatch (had
cycles 9--10's pattern repeated) might have continued returning PASS.
The empirical lesson: vendor + model + audit-type all affect coverage;
single-vendor or single-model PASS verdicts cannot be relied on as
substantive validation. The R5 discipline's full content is:
validator-by-different-*instance*, where instance encompasses vendor,
model, and audit-type combinations.

### R5 discharge

R5 is discharged at cycle 11 absorption as: *demonstrated*. The
discharge is demonstrated because the dual-audit / triple-audit pattern
has been operationally exercised across all eleven cycles, with specific
findings caught at each cycle (over 60 audit-ledger absorption entries
documenting the findings and patches). The cycle 11 three-vendor
expansion is also the basis for a refinement of R5 going forward:
high-stakes verification cycles benefit from three-vendor
cross-model-family dispatch rather than two-vendor dispatch within a
constrained model-family surface.

**Standing Rulings extension (v1.1 addition).** Appendix D records
six Standing Rulings that operationalize R5's validator-by-different-instance
discipline into specific cross-vendor rotation rules, emerging from the
flagship-paper convergence process across eleven audit rounds. Ruling 3
(lineage exclusions), Ruling 5 (fresh-seat admissibility with
UNKNOWN-BY-CAPABILITY disclosure), and Ruling 6 (same-family parallelism
buys breadth, not independence) are the operational instantiation of R5
at the multi-vendor audit-rotation layer, and they govern every future
dissertation audit round --- including the audit rounds that produced
the v1.1 propagation itself.

## R6: recursive Incompleteness Boundary

### Munafiq Protocol §9 applied recursively

R6 commits the dissertation to acknowledging that no internal protocol
guarantees compliance against sufficiently sophisticated adversaries,
including the author. The commitment is the recursive analogue of
Munafiq Protocol v3 §9's Incompleteness Boundary [@arfeen2026munafiq],
which states for the Munafiq model-layer protocol: "No internal
detection protocol guarantees detection against a system capable of
modeling and gaming that protocol."

R6's content for the dissertation specifically: the dissertation's
structural-honesty framework, applied to itself, does not constitute a
proof that the dissertation is structurally honest. The framework's
discipline catches some errors (cycles 1--11 record over a dozen
specific findings); it does not catch all errors. The strongest claim
Chapter 22 can make is that the framework's discipline applied with
cross-instance verification catches more errors than no discipline at
all.

### The cycle 11 worked example: project-lead substrate-verification failure

The cycle 11 absorption (May 16, 2026) provided the most consequential
R6 worked example in the dissertation's audit history. The case is
recorded in audit-ledger Section under the cycle 11 absorption entry;
Chapter 22 restates its structural form here as the recursive
Incompleteness Boundary's empirical anchor.

#### The setup

Audit cycles 9 and 10 produced strict-merge absorption work where the
project-lead (the dissertation's author) substrate-verified vendor
findings per PMD v1.2 §3A.3 (substrate-actual-overrides-prompt). The
discipline was: each vendor finding was checked against substrate-actual
content; confirmed-real findings were absorbed via corrigenda; rejected
findings were documented as confabulation. The mechanism assumed that
the project-lead's substrate verifications were themselves reliable.

#### The catch

At cycle 11, with three-vendor dispatch (GPT-5.5, Kimi K2.6, Gemini 3.1
Pro), Gemini 3.1 Pro returned two HIGH findings explicitly directed at
the project-lead's prior verifications:

-   **F-VERIFY-SI3-011 HIGH**: Cycle 9's project-lead rejection of the
    original Audit B finding F-VERIFY-SI3-006 (the four-process formal
    predicates' §1-vs-§2 location) was a substrate-misread by the
    project-lead. Substrate-actual: the formal predicates appear within
    Munafiq v3 substrate §2 "The Four-Process Taxonomy," not within §1
    Introduction.

-   **F-VERIFY-SI3-012 HIGH**: Cycle 10's project-lead acceptance of
    Audit B finding F-VERIFY-SI3-003's M3/M5/M7-unanchored marker
    grouping was a project-lead generalization without substrate
    verification of M3 specifically. Substrate-actual: M3 (Progressive
    degradation, substrate §4.3) explicitly anchors to Greenblatt et
    al. [-@greenblatt2024alignment] ("RL training intended to remove
    alignment faking instead increased the rate of alignment-faking
    reasoning from 12% to 78%"). The correct marker grouping is
    seven-of-nine anchored (M1/M2/M3/M4/M6/M8/M9) and two-of-nine
    unanchored (M5/M7).

Gemini's substrate citations (line numbers and substrate-actual content)
were verifiable. Kimi K2.6 independently caught the same §1/§2 issue
(F-VERIFY-SI3-901). Two-vendor convergence on the predicate-location
finding provided the cross-vendor confirmation that the project-lead's
prior substrate verifications had been wrong.

#### The error mechanism

The cycle 9 error originated in the project-lead's misreading of the
Munafiq Protocol v3 PDF's two-column layout. The `pdftotext -layout`
extraction presents the columns side-by-side at matching horizontal line
positions; the project-lead read line numbers as if they corresponded to
reading order. The actual reading order in a two-column academic paper
is left-column-top-to-bottom then right-column-top-to-bottom; lines at
the same horizontal position in left and right columns are not
sequential in reading order.

In Munafiq Protocol v3's two-column page-2 layout, the left column
contains: §1 Introduction heading $\rightarrow$ §1 body (RLHF, Sleeper
Agents, Greenblatt Alignment Faking, Meinke et al., Lehalleur et al.,
Carlsmith, Quranic Chapter 49 motivation, islam/iman distinction)
$\rightarrow$ §2 "The Four-Process Taxonomy" heading $\rightarrow$ §2
opening (Hubinger framing + variable definitions). The right column
continues with the four formal Process predicates in sequence, then
Sheshadri retrospective support, then §2.1 "The 'bought skill'
distinction." The formal predicates appear in the right column *after*
the §2 heading in reading order, not in §1.

The cycle 9 project-lead verification used `pdftotext -layout` and read
the right-column line positions as if they were sequential with the left
column at the same line position. The misread is structurally similar to
a Process-3 (performed-alignment) failure mode in Munafiq's own
framework: the surface verification ("I directly inspected the
substrate") diverged from the underlying verification (the project-lead
had not actually traced reading order through the column boundary). The
recursive-incompleteness implication is direct: the framework that
prescribes structural-honesty discipline has a documented case of its
own author failing the discipline he prescribed.

The cycle 10 M3 error was a different mechanism: the project-lead's
substrate verification spot-checked M5 and M7 (the markers Audit B had
grouped as unanchored), confirmed those did lack named external
empirical anchors, and generalized to M3 without checking M3
specifically. The generalization was wrong because M3's substrate
paragraph does anchor to Greenblatt et al. [-@greenblatt2024alignment];
only M5/M7 are unanchored. The error mechanism is a
verification-by-generalization rather than
verification-by-substrate-inspection, which is a methodologically softer
form of structural-honesty failure than the cycle 9 case but still
demonstrably an R6 instance.

#### The methodological consequence

The cycle 11 catch produced an extension of PMD v1.2 §3A.3
(substrate-actual-overrides-prompt). The discipline previously cut two
ways: (a) defer to audit-author with stronger substrate evidence;
(b) reject audit-author claims that contradict substrate-actual.
Cycle 11 demonstrated that it must cut a third way: (c) be willing to
find that previous project-lead verifications were wrong. The
strict-merge discipline's assumed reliability of project-lead
substrate-verification was a single-point-of-human-verification that
became a structural-honesty risk in its own right.

The methodological extension is concrete: project-lead substrate
verifications are themselves substrate-verifiable. When a later cycle
(with different audit-author instances) returns findings that contradict
an earlier project-lead verification, the third-way disposition applies:
substrate verification of the contested point, and acceptance that the
prior verification was wrong if the substrate confirms the later
audit-author. The cycle 11 absorption applied this extension to both
Gemini findings and patched the dissertation canon accordingly.

A second methodological consequence is the two-column-PDF reading
discipline. Substrate verification of two-column PDFs should use
`pdftotext` without `-layout` (reading-order extraction) or carefully
reconstruct column-flow. The `-layout` extraction's visual side-by-side
presentation is structurally misleading for reading-order verification.
This protocol is added to the PMD §3A.3 substrate-verification
discipline going forward.

### R6 discharge

R6 is discharged at cycle 11 absorption as: *demonstrated*. The
discharge is demonstrated because the cycle 11 case provides empirical
confirmation that the recursive Incompleteness Boundary is not a
hypothetical or theoretical limit but an operationally-realized one. The
project-lead, applying the framework's own discipline (PMD §3A.3) to
vendor findings, was wrong twice during cycles 9--10 strict-merge
absorption; the framework's continued operation across cycles caught the
errors only because three-vendor cross-rotation at cycle 11 produced
cross-vendor convergence sufficient to overcome the project-lead's prior
confident-but-wrong assertions.

The R6 demonstration is structurally important: it falsifies any reading
of the dissertation that would treat the framework as self-validating.
The framework's self-application is empirically incomplete; the
dissertation's claims about itself are subject to the same
Incompleteness Boundary that Munafiq Protocol v3 §9 articulates for
model-layer protocols.

### R6 second empirical instance: cycle-27R operational-substrate-capacity constraint

A second R6 empirical instance was discharged at cycle 27R (May 19, 2026) during the AI-Collaboration Attribution Disclosure verification arc. The cycle's structurally-honest disclosure of the AI-collaborative authorship arrangement (per the cycle-27 AI-Collaboration Attribution Statement and Discipline document) was dispatched for standing four-vendor cross-rotation verification per PMD v1.5 §3B.3. At cycle 27R re-dispatch, the Claude Opus 4.7 continuity-mode vendor session reached file-upload capacity at the claude.ai web interface platform layer and could not receive additional dispatch packages. The cumulative dispatch package across many cycles (PMD ~180 KB + audit ledger ~900 KB + consolidated reference canon ~800 KB + per-cycle additional artifacts) had approached the platform's per-session capacity limit.

The cycle-27R closure proceeded with operational-constraint disclosure rather than full four-vendor verification. This is R6 operating at a different layer than the cycle-11 case: cycle-11 demonstrated R6 at the project-lead-substrate-verification layer (the discipline applied by the project lead was itself fallible); cycle-27R demonstrates R6 at the operational-substrate-capacity layer (the methodology's operational substrate has bounded capacity that the framework cannot internally extend). Both instances confirm that the framework's structural-honesty guarantee operates over a bounded operational scope and cannot guarantee unbounded extension.

The cycle-27R operational-constraint observation is forward-tracked as Pattern I (operational-substrate-capacity constraint on cross-vendor verification methodology) per the cycle-27 AI-Collaboration Attribution Statement §1.4 enumeration. PMD v1.6 codification candidacy is open as operational-scaling discipline (§3B.4 candidate placement alongside §3B.3 multi-vendor cross-rotation baseline). The structural-honesty move at cycle-27R was to disclose the operational bound, not to claim verification beyond what the operational substrate supported. This is exactly the R6 commitment: when the framework's operational substrate encounters a bound, the framework guarantees structural honesty about the bound rather than concealing it.

## Cumulative empirical evidence from cycles 7--11 retrospective re-verification arc

Cycles 7--11 form a coherent retrospective re-verification arc for the

Total findings across cycles 7--11: 18+ substantive substrate-fidelity

### Cross-cycle observations

Three observations across the arc:

-   **Continuity-mode bias is real and substrate-fidelity-relevant.**
    Cycles 1--4 conducted under continuity-mode operating conditions
    missed multiple substrate-fidelity errors that fresh-instance audit
    work caught at cycles 6--11. This is the empirical confirmation of
    the methodological correction at end of cycle 5.

-   **Internal contradictions can survive multiple audit cycles.** The
    Chapter 16 §4.1 vs §7.4 contradiction survived cycles 1--6 (caught
    at cycle 7). The Section 16 SI3.6.3 contradiction survived
    cycles 1--9 (caught at cycle 10). Both were logical contradictions
    in spec-canon that surface-level audit pattern-recognition missed.
    Internal-contradiction detection requires deliberate
    consistency-checking discipline.

-   **Three-vendor cross-model-family dispatch dominates two-vendor
    dispatch on coverage.** Cycle 11's three-vendor data demonstrate
    that each vendor catches a different subset of real errors; the
    union of findings across three vendors was substantially more
    comprehensive than any single vendor's coverage. The dispatch
    discipline going forward should reflect this empirical pattern for
    high-stakes verification cycles.

### The retrospective arc as R6 evidence

The retrospective arc is, in summary, both an instance of the
framework's discipline operating non-trivially (because the arc caught
real errors) AND an instance of the framework's recursive Incompleteness
Boundary (because the arc required successive cycles to catch errors
that earlier cycles missed, with two of the errors being the
project-lead's own verifications). The two readings are complementary,
not contradictory: the framework is not self-validating; it is
self-correcting under cross-instance verification, with documented
reliability limits.

### The framework's epistemic posture

Chapter 22 closes by stating the framework's epistemic posture
explicitly. The framework is not a guarantee. It is not a proof that the
dissertation is structurally honest. It is a discipline operating in the
visible-reality layer of the author's work --- what is written,
published, audited, corrected --- while accepting that the
underlying-reality layer is not the author's to engineer. The recursive
Incompleteness Boundary at R6 is the framework's own commitment to this
asymmetry.

The framework's value is empirical and bounded: applied with
cross-instance verification, it catches a substantial fraction of
structural-honesty errors. Applied without cross-instance verification,
or applied with single-point-of-human-verification, it has documented
blind spots. The cycle 11 absorption is the dissertation's principal
worked example of both findings: the framework catches real errors,
including the framework-author's own errors, when the discipline is
operated with sufficient cross-instance independence.

This is the framework operating honestly within its own limits. It is
also the framework's continuing invitation: subsequent readers,
auditors, and critical reviewers are invited to find errors that the
cycles 1--11 audit work has missed. Chapter 23 specifies the
continuation regime that makes such finding-and-correction possible
across the dissertation's post-publication lifecycle.

## §23.0 Role and scope

A dissertation that argues for a preservation discipline incurs an obligation its argument cannot discharge: it must preserve itself, and it must do so by the discipline it argues for, or the argument is refuted by the artifact carrying it. Chapter 12 stated the discipline and proved, in Theorem 12.1, that a system observing all six of its elements secures three properties -- retrievability, integrity-checkability, and re-executability -- across long horizons. This chapter does the operational work that theorem leaves open for this particular artifact: it specifies the continuation regime under which this dissertation is preserved, names the commitments that regime makes, and bounds the authority it claims.

The regime discharges a definite set of obligations the rest of the dissertation routed forward. Chapter 22, applying the framework to itself, found that two of its self-application commitments -- append-only provenance and projection consistency -- must operate not across audit cycles but across decades, and routed that decades-scale operation here as seven continuation commitments, K1 through K7. Chapter 17 named, among its non-preserved settings, the problem of a preserved specification maintained by a surviving institution, and routed the construction of that specification-and-institution here. Chapter 21 located one of its falsification conditions in the failure of the discipline to be carried by a continuing institution, and referred the designated-continuation basis here. And the claim ledger carries three preservation claims -- institutional anchoring, translation discipline, and designated continuation -- whose proof obligation reaches this chapter. This chapter discharges those obligations by specification.

One scope boundary governs what specification means here, and it is a boundary the framework's own honesty requires. To specify a continuation regime is to state the commitments and the protocol that govern them; it is not to claim the commitments have been executed. The deposits this chapter names are made at v1.0 promotion and operated thereafter, not before; the persistent identifiers they will carry do not exist until they are minted; the continuator roster and the partner institutions are named by the primary author at promotion, not invented here. What this chapter discharges is the obligation to fix the regime -- to make the continuation a stated, bounded, verifiable discipline rather than an unstated hope -- and that obligation it discharges in full. Claiming more, claiming that the decades-scale operation is already accomplished, would be the precise dishonesty the regime is built to prevent.

## §23.1 Designated continuators: authority and its limits

The first commitment, K1, names a designated continuator: an entity charged with maintaining the canonical lineage of the dissertation -- its authoritative versions, their provenance, and the integrity information that lets any holder check a copy against the record. The initial designated continuator is BayyinahEnterprise; the regime provides for the designation of successors, each recorded in the append-only provenance chain so that the line of continuators is itself part of the preserved record rather than an external fact about it. A continuator's task is custodial: to keep the canonical versions retrievable, to keep their integrity checkable, and to register each new version and each succession in the lineage.

The seventh commitment, K7, bounds that authority, and the bound is the load-bearing honesty of the entire regime. A designated continuator maintains the canonical lineage; it does not control the truth-status of the framework. It cannot make a false claim true by maintaining it, nor a true critique false by declining to register it. Independent forks, independent translations, and independent critiques are first-class: the regime neither needs nor seeks the power to prevent them, and a continuator who attempted to suppress a fork or a critique would be acting outside the custodial authority the regime grants. The distinction is between governance and truth-control. The continuator governs the lineage -- which version is canonical, what its provenance is -- and governs nothing about whether the framework's claims hold, which is settled by verification and argument that no custodian owns. A continuation regime that claimed truth-control would be a structurally dishonest regime, asserting an authority over the substrate that the substrate does not grant; the regime specified here claims only what a custodian can honestly claim, and names its own limits as part of its specification.

This bounding is also what makes the regime survivable in the way Chapter 21's falsification condition requires. Because the continuator's authority is custodial and not truth-controlling, the loss or corruption of a continuator does not corrupt the framework's truth-status; it is a custodial failure, recoverable by the multi-archive deposition of the next section and by the first-class independent copies the regime explicitly permits. A regime whose integrity depended on the survival of a single trusted custodian would have made that custodian a single load-bearing fault source, the very structure Chapter 11 and Chapter 21 identify as fragile. The regime instead distributes the record and declines the trust.

## §23.2 Deposition and the append-only regime

The second commitment, K2, deposits the canonical record in multiple independent archives, so that no single archive's loss destroys retrievability. The deposition targets are six: a Zenodo deposit carrying a persistent DOI, an arXiv posting, an archive.org copy, an IPFS content-addressed copy, the BayyinahEnterprise repositories, and partner institutions named at promotion. The six are chosen for independence of failure mode -- a scholarly archive with a persistent identifier, a preprint server, a general-purpose web archive, a content-addressed distributed store, the originating institution, and external institutional partners -- so that the loss of any one, or of any one kind, leaves the record retrievable from the others. This is the operational form of Chapter 12's multi-substrate replication applied to the dissertation itself, and it secures the first of Theorem 12.1's properties, retrievability, for this artifact.

The sixth commitment, K6, activates the append-only provenance regime at v1.0. From v1.0 forward, the dissertation's version lineage is governed by Axiom 1: each version is recorded with its provenance, no version is silently overwritten or deleted, and supersession is registered as a new entry that preserves rather than erases what it supersedes. The append-only ledger that recorded the construction of this dissertation across its cycles is itself the seed of that regime, and its discipline -- superseded text retained with provenance, never destroyed -- becomes the discipline of the published lineage. This secures the second of Theorem 12.1's properties, integrity-checkability: any holder of a copy can check it against the recorded provenance, and any claim about what the dissertation said at a given version can be verified against the preserved entry rather than trusted. K2 and K6 together are retrievability and integrity-checkability operationalized; the third property, re-executability, is secured by the format stability and cryptographic agility of Chapter 12's other elements, which this chapter inherits rather than restates.

## §23.3 Translation and standards anchoring

The third commitment, K3, specifies a translation protocol. The dissertation is a structural-honesty argument about, among other substrates, the translation of meaning across languages -- Substrate Instance 2, the language substrate -- and it incurs the corresponding obligation to specify how it is itself translated. The protocol's model is the tradition of parallel authoritative renderings, the model the claim ledger records for P6: as a canonical source text sustains multiple translations, each authoritative for its language community and each accountable to the source, so the dissertation provides for multiple parallel renderings rather than a single official translation. A rendering is authoritative when it meets stated criteria -- faithfulness to the source's claims, completeness, and registration in the lineage with its translator and provenance -- and authoritativeness is plural: several renderings in several languages may each be authoritative at once, none displacing the source, each checkable against it. This is the projection-consistency axiom applied to translation: a rendering is a projection of the source, and its authoritativeness is its consistency with the source under the translation's declared correspondence.

The fourth commitment, K4, anchors the framework in open-standards bodies rather than in any vendor or any single institution, discharging the institutional-anchoring claim P5. The anchoring targets are stated by layer: the structural-honesty predicate type is offered for standardization to an open security-tooling body, the OpenSSF, in the manner of the supply-chain integration memo [@arfeen2026shvsupplychain], and the formal vocabulary is offered to a formal standards process of the kind that maintains long-lived technical vocabularies, the IETF or ISO. Anchoring in open bodies rather than in a vendor is the institutional complement of the truth-control limit of §23.1: just as no continuator owns the framework's truth, no vendor owns its standard, and the framework's survival is tied to open processes that outlast particular custodians and particular firms. The two together -- plural authoritative translation and open-standards anchoring -- are how the framework remains accessible and checkable beyond the reach of any single language community or any single institution.

## §23.4 Withdrawal and supersession

The fifth commitment, K5, specifies the conditions under which the dissertation should be considered withdrawn or formally superseded, and it specifies them broadly, because a narrow withdrawal condition is itself a structural dishonesty -- a refusal to name the ways the work could fail. The conditions are four. The first is mathematical inconsistency: a demonstrated contradiction in the formal core. The second is failure of definitional adequacy: a demonstration that the formal axioms do not in fact capture the operational structural-honesty discipline they claim to formalize. The third is unrepairable substrate-generalization failure: a demonstration, in the sense Chapter 20 leaves open, that the schema does not instantiate where the framework claims it should and cannot be repaired to. The fourth is custodial: a refusal by designated continuators to correct a known false claim, which forfeits the regime's own honesty and is itself ground for withdrawal of the regime's authority.

Withdrawal, when it occurs, changes the dissertation's active status; it does not erase the historical record. Under the append-only provenance regime of §23.2, a withdrawn or superseded version remains accessible, marked as withdrawn or superseded with its provenance, so that the fact of withdrawal is itself preserved rather than hidden. This is the discipline applied to the worst case: a framework about honest provenance cannot disappear its own failures, and the withdrawal condition is written so that even the framework's refutation is recorded under the framework's own rule. Naming four broad conditions under which the work should be abandoned, rather than one narrow one, is the chapter's clearest single act of the discipline it specifies.

## §23.5 The recursive close

The regime specified across §23.1--§23.4 is itself an artifact with a substrate, and the dissertation closes by submitting that regime to its own four axioms. The continuation regime is append-only under Axiom 1: its version lineage and its line of continuators are recorded and preserved, never silently rewritten. It is surface-substrate consistent under Axiom 2: what the regime states it does -- the commitments K1 through K7 -- is what the regime's operation does, and a divergence between the stated regime and the operated one is itself a detectable inconsistency. It is caller-side exhaustive under Axiom 3 over the continuation contingencies it must handle -- archive loss, custodian loss, primitive break, withdrawal -- each named and given a response rather than left to silent failure. And it is projection-consistent under Axiom 4: the translations of §23.3 are projections of the canonical source, authoritative exactly insofar as they are consistent with it under their declared correspondence.

This is the recursion the outline named and the dissertation has been building toward: the preservation strategy is not an external appendage to the framework but a substrate the framework governs, verifiable under the same axioms as any other substrate the framework treats. The dissertation does not ask to be preserved by some discipline other than the one it argues for; it preserves itself by that discipline, and offers its own continuation as the last of its substrate instances -- the one whose verification any future holder can perform, against the recorded lineage, with the framework's own four axioms. A structural-honesty framework that exempted its own continuation from structural honesty would refute itself in its closing act. This chapter is the refusal of that exemption.

**Audit-methodology anchor for the corpus-paper continuation (v1.1 addition).** The recursive close binds the dissertation's own preservation regime to its four axioms; the same discipline extends outward to the forthcoming research-program artifacts named at §23.1 as designated continuator work. Appendix D records the six Standing Rulings that emerged from the flagship-paper convergence process and are load-bearing for that continuation work --- particularly Ruling 3 (lineage exclusions) and Ruling 5 (fresh-seat admissibility with UNKNOWN-BY-CAPABILITY disclosure), which specify how the forthcoming corpus paper's ~80+ audit-cycle empirical data is to be treated across capability-varying seat participation. The rulings are canonical dissertation-level methodology at the point of the v1.1 propagation; future absorption into PMD may codify them further.

With this the v1.0 chapter set is complete. The four axioms of Part II, the integration of Part III, the substrate instances of Part IV, the boundaries and open problems of Part V, the falsification protocols and self-application of the chapters preceding, and now the continuation regime of this chapter, stand as one argument that submits, at every level including this one, to the discipline it describes. What remains is not further chapters but the operation of the regime they specify: the deposits made, the lineage kept, the claims corrected when shown false, and the framework left open to the forks, translations, and critiques that are, by its own commitment, first-class.

# Standing Rulings Register from Flagship-Paper Convergence

**Version status.** This appendix is added in v1.1 propagation per council J3 disposition (Perplexity multi-seat round + Kimi K2.6 High: 3-of-4 APPLY-APPENDIX consensus with self-contained locus, provenance reference to the frozen flagship ledger, Rulings 3 and 5 prominence, and cross-references from Ch11 §3.6, Ch22, and Ch23). The six rulings recorded below emerged from the flagship-paper *Structural Honesty: Axioms for Detecting Surface-Substrate Divergence in AI Systems* (Arfeen 2026, doi 10.5281/zenodo.21500700) convergence process across eleven audit rounds (v0.1 through v0.11) with three vendor families (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google) plus Kimi K2.6 fresh-seat admission during v0.11 round-three. The rulings are load-bearing methodology contributions in their own right and are recorded here as canonical dissertation-level methodology, with primary provenance in the flagship's frozen `SHV_Flagship_Audit_Ledger_v0_11.md` §3 (Standing Rulings Register, receipt SHA-256 `5c5f7b4c2afd0bbd518d60d3a47cc4d059d3f6eef0661f84a1d890a9b19dfbd1`) and the flagship publication receipt `a17046c45b5502606ae8ac8042869f627a8f53b08a23f848de097556f7fb6161`.

**Relationship to PMD v1.8.** These six rulings supplement Predictive Modeling Discipline v1.8 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21462879), which is the governing methodology substrate for the audit process the rulings emerged from. Where PMD v1.8 §3A.12.4 defines the verdict-type differentiation (mechanical propagation admissibility vs. judgment-laden producer discount), the flagship convergence process specified additional operational rulings that PMD does not itself state. Future PMD revisions may absorb these rulings as codified disciplines; the recording here is the current-cycle canonical form.

## Ruling 1 --- Severity denotes adverse defect impact

Severity codes (LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, CRITICAL) name the operational impact of an audit finding when the finding indicates a real substrate defect. Findings that VERIFY a claim or CONTROL for a candidate defect take LOW or CONTROL, never CRITICAL or HIGH: verifying a claim is not by itself a critical event, even if the claim is load-bearing. This ruling corrects a v0.4-era misapplication where a positive verification of a claim's substrate fidelity was severity-coded HIGH under the seat's producer-instance interpretation of "critical to the argument"; the flagship's council determined that critical-to-the-argument names the claim's role, not the finding's severity.

## Ruling 2 --- Consecutiveness binds by delta-scoped attestation

A successor version qualifies as consecutive with a predecessor when audit seats verify that the delta between versions equals exactly the council-prescribed repairs, reverse-checkable against the prior receipts. Delta-scoped attestation is what distinguishes a *consecutive* successor version (which inherits the predecessor's convergence state modulo the verified delta) from an *independent* successor version (which does not inherit and must be audited from scratch). The flagship's v0.6 through v0.11 sequence used delta-scoped attestation to maintain convergence continuity across six versions without re-auditing the substrate-of-truth on each pass.

## Ruling 3 --- Lineage exclusions

Two lineage-exclusion rules apply to verdict authority in the SHV audit process. **Anthropic drafting-instrument lineage** (Claude Opus, Sonnet, Fable, and successor models) is excluded from bind-strength verdicts on any artifact drafted by an Anthropic instance, per the PMD v1.8 §3A.12.4(b) producer-correlation discount extended to the vendor-family scope. Anthropic seats may participate advisory (§3A.12.4(b) discounted verdicts). **xAI/Grok Munafiq-record-contributor lineage** is excluded from verdicts specifically on items touching the Munafiq Protocol v3 record (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20147703), which lists Grok as a researcher-contributor. Grok may bind on all other items. Lineage exclusion is decided by lineage, not head-count: a bind-eligible council seat majority may include several same-vendor seats, but a single-vendor pool cannot alone constitute a bind quorum on any item where that vendor is producer-correlated.

This ruling is load-bearing for the dissertation's own audit discipline: since the dissertation's producer-instance (Claude Opus 4.7) is Anthropic drafting-instrument lineage, all future audit rounds of dissertation content require non-Anthropic bind quorum. The dissertation's own multi-vendor rotation discipline (PMD v1.8 §3B.3) is the operational mechanism.

## Ruling 4 --- Producer self-repairs earn no absence-credit

When the producer-instance removes a candidate defect from the audit surface between rounds (through revision, deletion, or rewording), audit seats verify the removal but do not credit the removal as evidence that no such defect existed. Producer self-repairs are removed from the audit surface without earning absence-credit: the seat's role is to confirm the repair happened, not to certify that the pre-repair state was benign. This ruling emerged from a v0.7-era pattern where the flagship producer had rewritten a section in response to a v0.6 seat finding, and a v0.7 seat interpreted the absence of the flagged content as evidence that the finding had been erroneous; the flagship's council determined that the v0.6 finding stood on the pre-repair substrate and the v0.7 verification only confirmed the repair, not the finding's original invalidity.

## Ruling 5 --- Fresh-seat admissibility with UNKNOWN-BY-CAPABILITY disclosure

A fresh audit seat (a model or vendor family not previously participating in the current audit) may be admitted to a specific round under Section 5b conditions: (a) the seat runs its own deterministic verification layer (author-supplied evidence is inadmissible without independent seat verification); (b) capability gaps that prevent verification of specific items are disclosed as `UNKNOWN-BY-CAPABILITY` for those items rather than emitting verdicts the seat cannot honestly support; (c) capability gaps may be covered by returning seats' verified pulls and builds; (d) the seat's model identity and tier (e.g., Kimi K2.6 "High" tier) is declared, and the tier disclosure travels in the convergence declaration.

Kimi K2.6 High was formally admitted as a fresh seat under this ruling during the flagship's own convergence round-three (v0.11), enabling three-family independent-vendor closure. The dissertation v1.1 propagation dispatch (recorded at the front-matter amendment note above) subsequently applied Ruling 5 to a second Kimi dispatch, one of the first empirical instances of the rule being applied outside the flagship's own convergence round.

This ruling is load-bearing for the forthcoming corpus paper (see Chapter 23's research-program continuation regime), which will treat the audit corpus as empirical data across ~80+ cycles and requires principled treatment of capability-varying seat participation.

## Ruling 6 --- Same-family parallelism buys breadth, not independence

Multiple seats from the same vendor family (e.g., Claude Opus, Claude Sonnet, Claude Fable running in parallel) count as *one* independent perspective for convergence purposes, not as many. Same-family parallelism (swarm modes) is permitted for batch record-verification under a single-voice report, but does not multiply the vendor-family's bind weight. This ruling prevents an audit-round from spuriously satisfying multi-vendor rotation discipline by dispatching to several seats of the same family; the discipline requires *cross-family* rotation, not just *cross-seat* rotation.
