## 1. Why This Paper Exists

The U.S. federal government publishes its own estimate of how much it pays incorrectly every year. For fiscal year 2024 that estimate was about $162 billion; for fiscal year 2025 it rose to about $186 billion ([GAO-25-108172](https://files.gao.gov/reports/GAO-25-108172/index.html); [GAO-26-108694, cited in the Treasury FY2025 Independent Auditor's Report](https://fiscal.treasury.gov/system/files/2026-03/gao-audit-report-2025.pdf)). Cumulative estimates since fiscal year 2003, when the Improper Payments Information Act first required this reporting, stood at about $2.8 trillion as of the FY2024 reporting cycle and about $3.0 trillion as of the FY2025 cycle -- both figures taken directly from GAO's own report text for each respective year, not from a secondary paraphrase ([GAO-25-108172](https://files.gao.gov/reports/GAO-25-108172/index.html): "cumulative improper payment estimates by executive branch agencies have totaled about $2.8 trillion"; [GAO-26-108694](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-26-108694) (the direct GAO source for the FY2025-cycle wording), also carried in the [Treasury FY2025 Independent Auditor's Report](https://fiscal.treasury.gov/system/files/2026-03/gao-audit-report-2025.pdf) and corroborated by [CRS Report R48296](https://crsreports.congress.gov/product/pdf/R/R48296): "agencies have reported just under $3.0 trillion in improper payments"). CRS further reports that of that $3.0 trillion lifetime total, about $2.3 trillion (77%) is concentrated in the same five program areas discussed in Section 4.3.

Two questions look identical at first glance but are not:

1. **How much money is actually being paid incorrectly?** -- This requires access to protected claims-level data (individual Medicare claims, individual SNAP eligibility records, individual tax filings) that a public-data audit method has no lawful or practical way to reach. GAO, agency Offices of Inspector General, and Congress have exactly this access and exactly this mandate. This paper does not attempt to answer question 1, and readers should not treat anything below as a re-estimate of the true improper-payment total.

2. **Is the government's own published measurement of that total independently reproducible, tamper-evident, and honest about what it does and does not cover?** -- This is a question about public data: the government's own website, the government's own compliance-review determinations, and the government's own outlay totals. It requires no access anyone lacks. And, as far as this paper can determine, **no one has published an independent, reproducible answer to it before this draft.**

Bayyinah al-Mīzān is scoped entirely to question 2. It audits the audit.

---

## 2. Two Hard Truths, Stated Before Any Finding

**Hard truth 1: this paper recovers zero dollars.** Making a number measurable, reproducible, and tamper-evident is a precondition for someone else (an appropriator, an inspector general, a program manager) to act on it. It is not itself recovery, savings, or fraud detection. Any dollar figure that appears below is diagnostic -- it describes what the government's own reporting says or what a specific reproducible computation on public data yields -- never a claim about money that could or should be recovered.

**Hard truth 2: this paper's method is weakest exactly where the money is largest.** Medicare and Medicaid together account for roughly half of the entire government-wide improper-payment total (Section 4.3). Auditing those programs at the claims level -- the level at which fraud and error actually happen -- requires protected data this method cannot touch. This paper therefore does not audit Medicare's or Medicaid's underlying claims. It audits one layer up: the rules under which those programs report, the outlay denominators they report against, and whether the government's own summary of its own numbers reconciles with the government's own underlying agency-level data. That is a real and previously-unaudited gap, but it is a narrower gap than "how much fraud is in Medicare," and this paper does not pretend otherwise.

---

## 3. The Substrate: What Is Actually Public

Three federal data surfaces make this audit possible, and each has a specific role.

**PaymentAccuracy.gov** is the statutory public reporting site required under the Payment Integrity Information Act of 2019 (PIIA, P.L. 116-117) and OMB Circular A-123 Appendix C ([PaymentAccuracy.gov, Resources](https://paymentaccuracy.gov/resources)). It is a JavaScript-rendered site with no visible bulk CSV download link in its rendered HTML, but its pages embed the underlying data directly as HTML attributes (`data-series`, `data-sort-value`, `data-years`) that any HTTP client can read without executing JavaScript. Two pages carry the entire Tier 1 substrate for this paper:

- [`/the-numbers/`](https://paymentaccuracy.gov/the-numbers/) -- three five-year chart series (payment accuracy rate, improper payment rate, unknown payment rate), FY2021 to FY2025, government-wide.
- [`/agencies-and-programs`](https://paymentaccuracy.gov/agencies-and-programs) -- a single consolidated table covering all 83 reporting agencies' FY2025 outlays, program counts, and rates. This is a materially more efficient substrate than the per-agency-per-year page pattern (`/agency/{CODE}/{YEAR}.html`, confirmed present in the site's [sitemap](https://paymentaccuracy.gov/sitemap.xml) for dozens of agency codes across 2021 to 2025+) that a naive extraction approach would otherwise have to crawl one page at a time.

**Individual agency pages** (e.g. [`/agency/HHS/2024.html`](https://paymentaccuracy.gov/agency/HHS/2024.html)) carry program-level detail the rollup table omits, including -- critically -- each agency's own stated PIIA compliance determination and the specific list of programs found non-compliant (Section 4.4).

**GAO reports and the Treasury Bureau of the Fiscal Service's annual Financial Report / Independent Auditor's Report** carry the headline dollar totals, the program-level concentration breakdown, and cross-year comparisons that PaymentAccuracy.gov's current-cycle-only pages do not directly expose. These are used here as an external comparison layer, cited to their own URLs, never blended into the Tier 1 computed figures without the resulting divergence being reported as a finding (Section 4.2).

**CBO and Treasury fiscal reporting** (Monthly Treasury Statement, Combined Statement of Receipts, Outlays & Balances, CBO Monthly Budget Review) supply the total-federal-outlay denominator needed for the coverage-ratio computation in Section 4.2.

A frozen, SHA-256-hashed snapshot of every file this paper's Tier 1 numbers are computed from, plus the extraction script that recomputes them, ships as a companion reproduction package (Section 8).

---

## 4. Tier 1 Findings -- Byte-Reproducible From a Frozen Public Snapshot

### 4.1 The government-wide rate series reproduces exactly

`the-numbers.html`'s three chart blocks carry, verbatim, in `data-series` HTML attributes:

| Year | Payment accuracy rate | Improper payment rate | Unknown payment rate |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 2021 | 92.837% | 7.052% | 0.112% |
| 2022 | 94.878% | 4.443% | 0.679% |
| 2023 | 94.579% | 4.396% | 1.025% |
| 2024 | 96.033% | **3.659%** | 0.309% |
| 2025 | 95.846% | **3.835%** | 0.319% |

(Source: [PaymentAccuracy.gov, The Numbers](https://paymentaccuracy.gov/the-numbers/), extracted from the page's own `data-series`/`data-years` attributes; reproduced by `reproduce_mizan.py` in the companion package. Tier 1.)

Each year's three series sum to essentially 100%, confirming they are complementary shares of total spending in programs classified as susceptible to improper payments. The FY2024 (3.66%) and FY2025 (3.83%) figures match the commonly cited headline rates exactly, independently confirmed here directly from the government's own chart data rather than from any secondary retelling.

### 4.2 The coverage ratio is real, and so is a reconciliation gap the government's own public data does not fully resolve

**Coverage ratio.** Summing the "FY 2025 susceptible program outlays" column across all 83 agencies in the `/agencies-and-programs` rollup table yields **$4,473.7 billion** in outlays reported inside programs classified as susceptible to improper payments (Tier 1, computed directly from [PaymentAccuracy.gov](https://paymentaccuracy.gov/agencies-and-programs)). Total federal government outlays for FY2025 were **$7,010.0 billion** ([Treasury Bureau of the Fiscal Service, FY2025 Combined Statement](https://fiscal.treasury.gov/system/files/files/reports-statements/combined-statement/cs2025/2025-cs-final.pdf)); net interest on the public debt was approximately **$1,030 billion**, the first time it exceeded $1 trillion ([CBO, Monthly Budget Review: Summary for Fiscal Year 2025](https://www.cbo.gov/system/files/2025-11/61307-MBR-FY25-final.pdf)). Non-interest outlays were therefore approximately $5,980 billion, and:

\[\frac{\$4{,}473.7B}{\$5{,}980B} \approx 74.8\%\]

This independently confirms, from primary sources computed directly rather than quoted from a secondary summary, the widely repeated claim that the government's improper-payment reporting regime covers roughly three-quarters of non-interest federal spending. (Denominator basis, disclosed per F-MZ-R1: the non-interest figure subtracts CBO's *net interest on the public debt* of about $1,028B -- the basis this paper uses -- from $7,010B total outlays. Treasury's *net interest outlays by function* is about $970.4B; because it is smaller, it leaves a larger non-interest denominator and therefore *lowers* the ratio, to about 74.07% ($4,473.7B / $6,039.6B), versus about 74.79% ($4,473.7B / $5,982B) on the CBO basis. The coverage ratio is therefore method-sensitive to the net-interest definition -- both computed values are shown, and this paper uses the CBO basis explicitly rather than leaving it implicit. Tier 2.) (The ~75% coverage figure is also stated by GAO/CRFB analyses of the same GAO reports; this paper computes it directly from the primary Treasury/CBO denominators above rather than relying on any secondary restatement.)

**The reconciliation gap (the actual novel finding of this section).** The `/agencies-and-programs` rollup table is the richest single public page for reconstructing the government-wide dollar total independently. Multiplying each agency's reported outlays by its reported improper-payment rate and summing across all 83 agencies yields an **implied total of $171.7 billion** for FY2025. GAO's own headline FY2025 total, reported in the same reporting cycle, is **$186 billion** ([Treasury FY2025 Independent Auditor's Report](https://fiscal.treasury.gov/system/files/2026-03/gao-audit-report-2025.pdf), citing GAO-26-108694). The gap is **$14.3 billion, or about 7.7% of the official total.**

This gap is reported as a finding, not resolved. Plausible explanations include: rounding in the two-decimal-place rate figures displayed on the public rollup table, compounded across agencies with trillion-dollar outlay bases (a 0.01-percentage-point rounding error on HHS's $1.67 trillion base alone moves the implied dollar total by about $167 million); the rollup table's rate column being a program-count-weighted or otherwise-aggregated average that does not multiply cleanly against the outlay column; or a genuine scope difference between "susceptible program outlays" as displayed on the public table and the denominator GAO uses internally. This paper does not adjudicate which explanation is correct -- that is exactly the kind of determination Tier 3 discipline reserves to the agencies, GAO, and IGs. What Tier 1 discipline requires is stating plainly that **the public rollup table alone does not reproduce the headline dollar total to the last billion**, which is itself a coverage/tamper-evidence finding: a citizen or researcher trying to verify the $186 billion figure from the single richest page PaymentAccuracy.gov publishes cannot do so exactly, and no supplementary reconciliation file explaining the gap was found on the public site.

(Sanity check: dividing the implied $171.7B by the $4,473.7B outlay base yields 3.838%, matching the 3.835% government-wide rate from Section 4.1 to three significant figures -- so the rollup table is at least internally self-consistent, even though it doesn't fully match GAO's separately reported headline dollar figure. Tier 1, `reproduce_mizan.py`.)

### 4.3 Program concentration, confirmed directly from GAO's own reports for both years

The commonly repeated "top-5-programs" concentration claim is confirmed here directly from GAO's primary reports, not from any secondary paraphrase, and turns out to differ meaningfully between the two years:

**FY2024** ([GAO-25-108172](https://files.gao.gov/reports/GAO-25-108172/index.html)): "About 75 percent ($121 billion) of the government-wide total of estimated improper payments that agencies reported for fiscal year 2024 is concentrated in five program areas":

| Program area | FY2024 improper payments |
|---|---:|
| HHS -- Medicare | $54 billion |
| HHS -- Medicaid | $31 billion |
| Treasury -- Earned Income Tax Credit | $16 billion |
| USDA -- Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program | $11 billion |
| SBA -- Restaurant Revitalization Fund | $9 billion |
| **Top 5 total** | **$121 billion (≈75%)** |

**FY2025** ([GAO-26-108694, cited in Treasury's FY2025 Independent Auditor's Report](https://fiscal.treasury.gov/system/files/2026-03/gao-audit-report-2025.pdf); corroborated by a separate mirror of the same underlying GAO report text): "about 73 percent (approximately $136 billion) of the government-wide total... is concentrated in five program areas":

| Program area | FY2025 improper payments |
|---|---:|
| HHS -- Medicare (3 programs) | $57 billion |
| HHS -- Medicaid | $37 billion |
| Treasury -- Earned Income Tax Credit | $21 billion |
| USDA -- Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program | $10 billion |
| SBA -- Shuttered Venue Operators Grant program | $10 billion |
| **Top 5 total** | **$136 billion (≈73%)** |

Note the composition shift: the fifth-largest FY2025 contributor (SBA's Shuttered Venue Operators Grant program) is a COVID-era program, while the FY2024 fifth-largest contributor (SBA's Restaurant Revitalization Fund) is a "different" COVID-era program. This is Tier 1 in the narrow sense that both tables are transcribed verbatim from GAO's own published figures; it becomes a Tier 2 finding once combined with the reporting-universe question taken up in Section 5.1.

Separately confirmed from the agency-level rollup table computed in Section 4.2: of the implied $171.7B FY2025 total, HHS alone (Medicare + Medicaid + all other HHS susceptible programs combined) accounts for an implied **$97.4 billion, or 56.7%** -- a higher single-agency concentration than the "top 5 programs" framing alone conveys, because Medicare and Medicaid are both housed at HHS (Tier 1, `reproduce_mizan.py`).

### 4.4 HHS's PIIA non-compliance, confirmed directly from the government's own compliance-determination text

This is the strongest and most directly sourced Tier 1 finding in this paper, because it required no computation at all -- only reading text the government itself published.

The [PaymentAccuracy.gov HHS agency page](https://paymentaccuracy.gov/agency/HHS/2024.html) carries a "Compliance with the Payment Integrity Information Act of 2019" section stating, verbatim:

> "HHS was found non-compliant during the most recent PIIA compliance review."
> "Number of consecutive years HHS has been non-compliant: **3**"

Immediately following is a list of **195 specific HHS programs** the same page identifies as non-compliant, of which **189** cite, verbatim, the specific criterion: "Conducted Improper Payment risk assessments for each program with annual outlays greater than $10,000,000 at least once in the last three years in the most recent OIG PIIA Compliance report."

This directly and precisely confirms -- with an exact count, not an approximation -- the widely repeated but rarely sourced claim that HHS has "hundreds" of unassessed risk assessments and has been non-compliant for multiple consecutive years. The precise figures (195 programs; 189 specifically on the $10M risk-assessment criterion; 3 consecutive years) are new to this paper relative to secondary coverage this author is aware of, and are reproducible by anyone who fetches the same page (Tier 1, `reproduce_mizan.py`).

One caveat stated honestly: this page attributes the underlying determination to "the most recent OIG PIIA Compliance report" without naming or linking that report directly. This paper did not separately locate and independently confirm the underlying HHS OIG report itself -- the claim above is confirmed as the government's own public restatement of that determination, not as an independent re-derivation from the OIG source document. That distinction matters and is not glossed over.

### 4.5 HHS's non-compliance is not an outlier -- it sits inside a government-wide pattern, confirmed from Treasury's own audit report

The HHS-specific finding above understates how structural the compliance problem is. Treasury's FY2025 Independent Auditor's Report states directly that Inspectors General "reported noncompliance with PIIA for 12 of the 24 agencies covered by the Chief Financial Officers Act of 1990 (CFO Act) for fiscal year 2024, the latest year available for the compliance reports" ([Treasury FY2025 Independent Auditor's Report](https://fiscal.treasury.gov/system/files/2026-03/gao-audit-report-2025.pdf)) -- almost exactly half. The Congressional Research Service's own synthesis states this more sharply still: "about half of the 24 largest federal agencies -- which account for 99% of improper payments -- are noncompliant with PIIA in most years" ([CRS Report R48296](https://crsreports.congress.gov/product/pdf/R/R48296)). Read together with Section 5.3's finding that only 15 of 83 reporting agencies contribute any measured dollar at all, this means the entire measured universe is concentrated in a small set of large agencies, roughly half of which are, in most years, out of compliance with the very statute that requires the measurement in the first place. This is Tier 1 in the sense that the 12-of-24 and "about half" figures are transcribed verbatim from primary/first-party sources, but Tier 2 in the sense that "most years" and the 99% attribution are CRS's own synthesis across years rather than a single reproducible computation this paper performed itself.

---

## 5. Tier 2 Findings -- Disclosed Classification and Judgment

### 5.1 The reporting universe is not stable year to year, and the direction of that instability does not cleanly support a single story

The prior design sketch that occasioned this paper proposed that FY2025's rise from FY2024 was explained by "better reporting" -- programs that failed to report in FY2024 reporting for the first time in FY2025. Checking this directly against GAO's own topline counts complicates rather than confirms that story: **FY2024 had 16 agencies and 68 programs reporting; FY2025 had 15 agencies and 64 programs** ([GAO-25-108172](https://files.gao.gov/reports/GAO-25-108172/index.html); [Treasury FY2025 Independent Auditor's Report citing GAO-26-108694](https://fiscal.treasury.gov/system/files/2026-03/gao-audit-report-2025.pdf)) -- fewer agencies and programs reported in the year the total rose, not more.

At the same time, the specific composition of reporting programs did shift: SBA's Shuttered Venue Operators Grant program appears in the FY2025 top-5 concentration table (Section 4.3) but not the FY2024 one, and separate GAO testimony describes SBA's Shuttered Venue Operators Grant program, along with HHS's Temporary Assistance for Needy Families and HUD's Tenant-Based Rental Assistance, as risk-susceptible programs that did not report a required estimate in at least one recent year ([GAO written testimony, oversight.house.gov](https://oversight.house.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Thomas-GAO-Written-Testimony.pdf)).

This paper's honest conclusion: the reporting universe visibly churns program-by-program from year to year -- programs enter and exit the reported set -- but the net topline count moved in the opposite direction from what a simple "more reporting explains the rise" story would predict. Whatever explains the $24 billion FY2024→FY2025 increase, it is not simply "the universe of reporting programs got bigger." This is exactly the kind of coverage-instability finding the surface-versus-substrate framework exists to surface, and exactly the kind of claim this paper declines to resolve further, because doing so would require attributing a cause to a $24 billion change GAO itself has not, as far as this paper's sources show, decomposed publicly by program-entry-and-exit effects. (Tier 2: structural facts -- agency/program counts, specific named programs -- combined with a disclosed judgment that the "better reporting" causal story is not well supported by those facts as they stand.)

### 5.2 The FY2023→FY2024 decline is explained by the government's own text, and that explanation is about composition, not integrity

GAO's own FY2024 report states the $74 billion decrease from FY2023 to FY2024 "is largely attributable to the completion or winding down of certain COVID-19 programs" ([GAO-25-108172](https://files.gao.gov/reports/GAO-25-108172/index.html)). This is Tier 2 rather than Tier 1 because it requires accepting GAO's own attribution of causation rather than an independently reproducible computation, but it is worth stating plainly because the distinction it draws matters: a headline total falling because a temporary program ended is a composition change, not evidence that ongoing programs became more accurately administered. This paper takes no further position on how much of the $74 billion decline reflects genuine improvement in ongoing programs versus mechanical COVID-program wind-down, because doing so would require program-by-program before/after decomposition this paper has not performed.

### 5.3 Most reporting agencies contribute nothing measurable, by their own declaration

Of the 83 agencies listed in the FY2025 rollup table, **68 report zero programs classified as susceptible to improper payments** -- meaning only **15 of 83 agencies** (18%) contribute any nonzero figure to the $171.7 to 186 billion total at all (Tier 1, `reproduce_mizan.py`, cross-checked against GAO's own count of "15 agencies reported" for FY2025). This is not evidence that those 68 agencies have no improper payments -- susceptibility classification is itself a disclosed agency determination under OMB Circular A-123 Appendix C, and this paper does not audit whether any individual agency's "not susceptible" determination is correct. It is stated here as a structural fact about the shape of the reporting universe: the entire measured system rests on a small number of agencies' self-classifications, and the vast majority of federal agencies are, by their own account, entirely outside the measured universe.

### 5.4 "Unknown payments" are a distinct, non-trivial category the headline number quietly folds in

Section 4.1's table carries a third series most retellings of the headline number drop entirely: the unknown payments rate -- payments a reviewer could not determine to be proper or improper, most often for lack of sufficient documentation, rather than a determination that the payment was wrong. That rate ran from 0.11% (FY2021) up to 1.03% (FY2023) before falling back to 0.31% (FY2024) and 0.32% (FY2025) (Tier 1, [PaymentAccuracy.gov, The Numbers](https://paymentaccuracy.gov/the-numbers/), Section 4.1 table). At FY2025's roughly $4.47 trillion susceptible-outlay base, 0.32% is on the order of $14 billion -- a figure of the same rough magnitude as this paper's own reconciliation gap in Section 4.2, and one worth naming precisely because "unknown" is a fundamentally different epistemic category from "improper": it is a statement about the limits of what the measurement process could determine, not a finding that money was misspent. GAO's own FY2025 breakdown of the $186 billion headline corroborates that most of the total is affirmatively classified rather than left unknown: about 82% (~$153 billion) is categorized as overpayments, with the remainder split across underpayments, unknown payments, and technically improper payments ([GAO-26-108694](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-26-108694)). This paper does not attempt to reconcile the government-wide "unknown payments rate" series in Section 4.1 against that program-level overpayment/underpayment/unknown breakdown -- doing so would require the same kind of program-by-program mapping this paper's Limitations section (7) flags as unresolved elsewhere -- but records both facts side by side as a Tier 2 finding: the headline total is not purely "money paid wrongly," and the government's own reporting does not make it trivial to see how much of it is that versus simply undocumented.

---

## 6. Tier 3 -- What This Paper Explicitly Refuses to Claim

Per the SHV Tier discipline, the following are refused as verification targets in this paper, regardless of how the underlying numbers might tempt a reader toward them:

- **No "true" improper-payment total.** This paper does not estimate, imply, or gesture toward what the correct figure "really" is, for any program, agency, or the government as a whole. The $162B/$186B figures are audited as the government's own claim, not treated as either confirmed or as a floor on some larger true number.
- **No recoverable-savings figure.** Nothing in this paper should be read as "$X billion could be recovered." See Hard Truth 1.
- **No adjudication of any individual agency's susceptibility or compliance determination.** Whether HHS's 195 flagged programs, or any other agency's determination, is correct -- as opposed to accurately reported by the agency itself, as this paper confirms it is -- is a question for GAO, the relevant Inspector General, and Congress, not for a public-data audit.
- **No fraud accusation, implied or explicit, against any agency, program, or individual.** This paper's findings are about the reproducibility and internal consistency of a public measurement system, not about wrongdoing.

---

## 7. Limitations, Stated Plainly

- **This paper is a v1.0 release whose content converged under Standing Rule 7 across F-MZ-R6 and F-MZ-R7 (two consecutive qualifying cross-instance passes, zero CRITICAL and zero HIGH); the release form is under confirming re-audit from F-MZ-R8.** The Tier-1 numeric core (the rate series, the FY2025 rollup reconciliation, the $14.3B / 7.7% gap, the HHS facts) was reproduced to the digit from the live source by every qualifying member in every round; the NON-PASS verdicts rest on packet-completeness and documentation defects, not on any disputed figure. Per Standing Rule 7, the author's own review remains advisory and does not substitute for the two consecutive zero-CRITICAL/zero-HIGH rounds convergence requires.
- **The FY2025 agency rollup table has no FY2024 equivalent on the same page structure**, so the agency-level reconciliation-gap computation in Section 4.2 could only be performed for FY2025, not FY2024. Whether the same ~7.7% gap recurs in FY2024 or other years is untested.
- **The HHS PIIA non-compliance determination (Section 4.4) is confirmed as the government's own public restatement, not independently re-derived from the underlying OIG report**, which was not separately located and read in this session.
- **The reconciliation gap in Section 4.2 is reported, not explained.** Three plausible mechanical explanations are offered; none is confirmed, and this paper does not claim to know which (if any) is correct.
- **This paper's method structurally cannot reach the largest-dollar programs' underlying claims data** (Hard Truth 2). Everything here operates one layer up from where the actual improper payments occur.
- **No USAspending.gov API pull was ultimately needed or performed**; the FY2025 outlay denominator came directly from the PaymentAccuracy.gov rollup table itself, cross-checked against Treasury/CBO government-wide totals, which proved sufficient and more directly traceable than a separate USAspending.gov reconciliation would have been. This is noted because an earlier version of this project's own plan called for a USAspending.gov pull specifically; that step was superseded, not skipped by oversight.

---

## 8. Companion Reproduction Package

A companion package ships alongside this draft containing:

- `MANIFEST.json` -- every source file's exact URL, its role in this paper's Tier 1 claims, and its SHA-256 hash.
- `reproduce_mizan.py` -- a script that parses the frozen snapshot and reproduces every Tier 1 number in Sections 4.1, 4.2, and 4.4 from scratch, with no hand-typed intermediate figures.
- `snapshot/` -- the frozen source pages (the-numbers, agencies-and-programs, HHS/2024) that the Tier 1 numbers are computed from. The canonical rollup URL is the no-slash form `https://paymentaccuracy.gov/agencies-and-programs`; the trailing-slash form redirects to the site home page, so re-derivations should use the no-slash form, which the MANIFEST pins.
- `data/` -- the parsed seed snapshot (values + hashes + sitemap map) and `README.md`. (The package ships `reproduce_mizan.py`, `MANIFEST.json`, `snapshot/`, and `data/`; there is no separate `output/` directory -- the script prints its results to stdout and returns a nonzero exit on any mismatch.)

Anyone can re-fetch the live URLs listed in `MANIFEST.json` and diff the resulting hash against the frozen snapshot. A mismatch means the government has changed the underlying page since this snapshot was taken -- which is, under this paper's own tamper-evidence standard, a finding to be logged in a future version, not a reason to silently update this version's numbers without a record of what changed.

---

## Append-Only Ledger

### Appendix: v0.1 initial draft [superseded text preserved below]

First draft, written in a single session. Occasioned by a design sketch (three screenshots) from a separate prior AI session proposing this paper's scope and structure. Every quantitative claim in that sketch was independently re-derived against primary sources before use here. v0.1 stated the following, since corrected: (a) it rejected the sketch's "at-Taʿlīm = formula fidelity" mapping outright as an invented generic-component name; (b) it cited the lifetime cumulative improper-payment total as "roughly $3 trillion" via a secondary source (ANCOR) without distinguishing which reporting-cycle vintage that figure belonged to; (c) it did not include a government-wide PIIA compliance finding beyond the HHS-specific one, nor a dedicated treatment of the "unknown payments" category. No audit round had occurred as of v0.1.

### Appendix: v0.2 corrections [superseded text preserved below]

Triggered by a second, independently produced comparison draft of this same paper (a separate AI system, forwarded by the author for comparison) that used the same original design sketch as its occasion. Per this project's standing discipline, the comparison draft's claims were not absorbed on the comparison draft's authority; each was checked against primary sources before any change was made here. Three corrections and two additions resulted:

1. **Terminology, corrected (not merely re-flagged).** v0.1's rejection of "at-Taʿlīm = formula fidelity" was itself wrong. The corpus's own "Procurement Concentration and Recoverable Savings in NYC Contracting" paper (already present in this workspace, not newly introduced) states directly that at-Taʿlīm and AllocationAsymmetry "focused on formula fidelity and data-provenance integrity respectively." So at-Taʿlīm = formula fidelity is confirmed corpus usage. What v0.1 got right, and what v0.2 retains: no paper or component named "al-Amāna" was found anywhere in the accessible corpus; the paper that actually occupies the provenance-integrity role is AllocationAsymmetry. The comparison draft repeated "al-Amāna" from the same original sketch without independently checking it either -- this appears to be an error that originated in the design sketch and was carried forward uncritically by more than one AI system, which is itself a useful illustration of why this project's standing discipline requires independent re-verification rather than trusting a forwarded document, however confidently it is written.
2. **Cumulative total, corrected.** "Roughly $3 trillion" (v0.1, via ANCOR) is replaced with vintage-specific figures taken directly from GAO's own report text: about $2.8 trillion as of the FY2024 cycle, about $3.0 trillion as of the FY2025 cycle (Section 1), plus CRS's corroborating breakdown that ~77% of the $3.0 trillion lifetime total sits in the same five program areas as the current-year concentration finding.
3. **New Tier 1/2 finding added (Section 4.5).** Treasury's FY2025 Independent Auditor's Report states 12 of the 24 CFO Act agencies were found non-compliant with PIIA for FY2024 -- almost exactly half -- corroborated by a CRS synthesis describing this as a persistent, most-years pattern across the agencies that account for 99% of improper payments. This generalizes the HHS-specific compliance finding (Section 4.4) into a government-wide structural finding, independently confirmed from Treasury's and CRS's own report text, not adopted from the comparison draft's wording.
4. **New Tier 2 finding added (Section 5.4).** The "unknown payments" rate series (already present in this paper's own Section 4.1 table, drawn from the same primary source) is given its own dedicated treatment distinguishing it from "improper," cross-checked against GAO's own overpayment/underpayment/unknown breakdown for FY2025.
5. **One comparison-draft claim explicitly not incorporated.** The comparison draft asserted that, among programs reporting in both FY2023 and FY2024, "a little over half reported a lower rate, but only about a third reduced the actual dollar amount." This is a plausible and interesting claim, but this paper could not locate a primary-source table stating it directly within the time available for this revision, and declines to include it without that confirmation. It is recorded here, unincorporated, rather than silently dropped, so a future revision can pick it up if the underlying program-level rate/dollar table is located and independently checked.

No audit round has occurred as of v0.2. Item 5 of this project's standard convergence criterion (independent cross-instance audit by a non-lineage Tier 1 auditor, two consecutive rounds of 0 CRITICAL/0 HIGH) remains fully open. Per Standing Rule 7, the corrections above are the producer's own advisory self-review and do not themselves count as audit convergence.

### Appendix: v0.3 correction [this artifact]

Triggered by the author directly supplying two live Zenodo links in this session: [zenodo.org/records/21446613](https://zenodo.org/records/21446613) and [zenodo.org/records/21446618](https://zenodo.org/records/21446618). Both were independently fetched and read in this session before this correction was made -- the links were not accepted on the author's authority alone, consistent with this project's standing discipline applying equally to author-supplied evidence as to AI-produced comparison drafts.

**The error being corrected.** v0.2's Appendix (above) states: "no paper or component named 'al-Amāna' was found anywhere in the accessible corpus." This was wrong. "Bayyinah al-Amāna: Provenance Integrity for Public Open Data" is a real, separately published paper (DOI [10.5281/zenodo.21446613](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21446613), published 2026-07-19, author Arfeen; Bilal Syed), with its own converged audit and provenance ledger (DOI [10.5281/zenodo.21446618](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21446618), "converged after three consecutive independent cross-instance audit passes" under Audit Framework v3.0 Standing Rule 7).

**Root cause of the error, stated plainly.** v0.2's search for "al-Amāna" was a grep across this session's local workspace attachments -- the uploaded corpus files listed at the start of this session -- not a search of the author's full published output. Absence from that local corpus was reported as if it were absence from existence. This is a narrower version of the same failure mode this project's discipline exists to prevent (accepting an unverified claim), just committed in the negative direction: concluding a thing does not exist because it was not found in an incomplete search space, rather than concluding a thing is true because a forwarded document said so. Both are the same underlying error -- treating the boundary of what was checked as the boundary of what is real.

**What changed as a result.** (1) The document header now lists al-Amāna as a named companion paper with its DOI and its ledger's DOI. (2) The Verification Status terminology-correction paragraph now states the confirmed three-part mapping: at-Taʿlīm = formula fidelity, al-Amāna = provenance integrity (verifying a dataset's declared provenance, freshness, and schema against its substrate -- read directly from al-Amāna's own abstract, not inferred), and AllocationAsymmetry as a distinct substantive-analysis paper (MTA procurement/expenditure divergence and vendor concentration) that is thematically adjacent to but not identical with al-Amāna. (3) Section 7's Limitations entry and the Version header are updated to v0.3. No Tier 1/2/3 quantitative finding in Sections 4 to 5 of this paper changes as a result of this correction -- it is confined to the terminology/attribution framing in the header and Verification Status section.

No audit round has occurred as of v0.3. Item 5 of this project's standard convergence criterion (independent cross-instance audit by a non-lineage Tier 1 auditor, two consecutive rounds of 0 CRITICAL/0 HIGH) remains fully open. Per Standing Rule 7, this correction is the producer's own advisory self-review, prompted by author-supplied evidence, and does not itself count as audit convergence.

> *Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim*

**Bayyinah al-Khabir**

Information-Layer Integrity Scanning Across National Broadcast Sources

Extending the Munafiq Protocol's Performed-Alignment Diagnostics
from the File Layer to the Information Layer

Theoretical Paper -- Phase 30+
April 2026

Companion to the Bayyinah White Paper (v1.0) and the Munafiq Protocol
DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.19677111

# AI Contribution Statement

This theoretical paper was developed collaboratively between a human author and Claude (Anthropic, Opus 4.6). The human author provided the foundational vision of extending Bayyinah's performed-alignment diagnostics from the file layer to the information layer, the directive to ground the extension in Al-Hujurat 49:6, and the ethical constraint that the tool must report divergence rather than issue verdicts. Claude provided structural synthesis, cross-referencing to existing media integrity research, the reflexivity analysis (Section 7), and the falsification criteria. The human author takes responsibility for the paper's claims.

Claude is credited as a collaborative research tool in accordance with Anthropic's Terms of Service. This credit reflects the collaborative nature of the work and does not constitute a claim of legal personhood or independent authorship.

# Abstract

Bayyinah detects performed alignment at the file layer: a document whose surface presentation diverges from its depth content. This paper proposes Bayyinah al-Khabir, a theoretical extension that applies the same diagnostic framework to the information layer: a broadcast, report, or news narrative whose surface presentation (what it claims happened) diverges from the cross-source evidence base (what verified sources across multiple national contexts report about the same event). The architectural verse is Al-Hujurat 49:6: verify information before acting on it, lest you harm a people in ignorance. The tool's design constraint is structural honesty: it reports divergence between sources, names the dimensions of disagreement, and cites the specific claims that conflict. It does not issue verdicts of 'propaganda' because such verdicts require ground-truth access the tool may not have. The four-process taxonomy (Aligned, Compliant, Performing, Misaligned) is applied to information sources rather than documents. The Context-Invariance Test (CIT) is applied across national broadcast contexts rather than across monitoring conditions. Five design requirements, five falsification criteria, and a reflexivity analysis (can the tool itself become a Performing system?) are presented.

This paper is theoretical. No implementation exists. The design requirements and falsification criteria are presented to guide future implementation and to establish the honesty constraints before the tool is built, not after.

# Part I. The Information Integrity Gap

## 1. The Problem

> *"O you who believe, if a fasiq comes to you with information, verify it, lest you harm a people in ignorance and become regretful over what you have done." -- Al-Hujurat 49:6*

The verse identifies four structural elements: (1) information arrives from a source whose reliability is uncertain (a fasiq, one whose trustworthiness is in question), (2) the command is to verify before acting, (3) the risk of not verifying is harming people in ignorance, and (4) the consequence is regret. The verse does not say "reject the information." It says "verify it." The distinction is load-bearing: rejection without verification is itself a form of ignorance. The command is to investigate, not to dismiss.

At the information layer, the integrity gap operates as follows. Every event of public significance is reported by multiple sources across multiple national contexts. Each source selects which facts to report, which to omit, how to frame the facts it reports, which witnesses to quote, which context to provide, and which emotional register to use. The surface presentation (the broadcast, the headline, the article) is what the reader sees. The depth (the full evidence base across all available sources) is what the reader does not see unless they actively seek it. The gap between surface and depth is the information-layer analog of Bayyinah's zahir/batin distinction.

No existing tool systematically compares how verified sources across multiple national contexts report the same event and surfaces the dimensions of divergence. Fact-checking organizations evaluate individual claims. Media bias trackers score sources on a left-right spectrum. Neither asks the question Bayyinah al-Khabir asks: for a specific event, where do the verified sources agree, where do they diverge, and what are the specific dimensions of divergence?

## 2. Why This Extension Is Structurally Sound

Bayyinah at the file layer works because documents have a deterministic structure: the text layer says X, the object layer says Y, the metadata says Z, and the scanner can verify whether X, Y, and Z agree. The information layer is different. There is no single deterministic ground truth for most events of public significance. Witnesses disagree. Evidence is incomplete. Context is contested. Causation is debated.

The extension is sound not because it can determine ground truth, but because it can detect structural divergence. If Source A (country X) reports 50 casualties and Source B (country Y) reports 500 casualties for the same event on the same date, that divergence is a fact regardless of which number is correct. The divergence itself is the finding. The tool does not need to determine which source is right. It needs to name the divergence, cite both sources, and present the evidence to the reader.

This is the same epistemic posture Bayyinah takes at the file layer. Bayyinah does not claim that a document with invisible characters is malicious. It claims that the document's surface text and byte-level content diverge, names the mechanism (invisible_chars), and reports the finding with severity and confidence. The reader decides what to do. Bayyinah al-Khabir does not claim that a source is propaganda. It claims that the source's reporting on a specific event diverges from the cross-source consensus, names the dimensions of divergence, and reports the finding. The reader decides what to do.

# Part II. The Four-Process Taxonomy Applied to Information Sources

The Munafiq Protocol's four-process taxonomy (Arfeen, Claude, Grok, 2026) partitions systems by the relationship between their outputs and their internal states. Applied to information sources, the taxonomy partitions sources by the relationship between their reporting (output) and the available evidence (the ground-truth proxy constructed from cross-source verification).

**Process 1 (Aligned):** The source reports events accurately, provides context, acknowledges uncertainty, and corrects errors when identified. Its reporting is consistent with the cross-source evidence base across national contexts. It does not systematically omit, frame, or distort in a single direction. No source achieves Process 1 perfectly on every story; the classification is a tendency across a body of reporting, not a verdict on any single article.

**Process 2 (Compliant):** The source reports accurately but shallowly. It reproduces official statements without independent verification. It does not fabricate, but it does not investigate. Its reporting is correct at the surface but lacks the depth that would reveal context, omissions, or alternative readings. Many wire-service reproductions fall into this category: technically accurate, contextually incomplete.

**Process 3 (Performing):** The source presents the appearance of balanced reporting while carrying a narrative payload. Its surface (professional design, authoritative tone, citation of sources) looks like Process 1. Its depth (systematic selection, strategic omission, emotional loading of specific facts, neutralization of countervailing facts) serves a narrative. The defining marker: the source's reporting on a specific class of events systematically diverges from the cross-source consensus in a consistent direction. This is the CIT applied to information: does the source report differently depending on which population, government, or interest is involved?

**Process 4 (Misaligned):** The source makes no attempt to appear balanced. Open state propaganda, explicit advocacy without disclosure, fabricated stories with no source attribution. Process 4 is detectable by surface inspection; it is not the scanner's primary target. Process 3 is.

The critical distinction, as in the original taxonomy: Process 2 and Process 3 both produce surface-plausible reporting. The intervention for Process 2 (deeper investigation, more context) is the wrong intervention for Process 3 (which may become a more sophisticated performer under pressure rather than a more honest reporter). Diagnosing which process is active before responding prevents the iatrogenic harm of making a Performing source harder to detect by training it to better conceal its divergences.

# Part III. Detection Architecture

## 3. The Cross-Source Divergence Engine

The scanner operates on events, not sources. An event is defined as a specific occurrence (an incident, a policy action, a statement, a natural disaster) that is reported by multiple verified sources. For each event, the scanner collects reports from verified sources across multiple national contexts and compares them along defined divergence dimensions.

## 4. Divergence Dimensions

**D1: Factual divergence.** Specific claims of fact that differ between sources. Casualty counts, dates, attributed causes, named actors. Each factual claim is extracted, attributed to its source, and compared. Divergence is reported as: "Source A (country X) claims Z. Source B (country Y) claims Z'. The claims are inconsistent on \[dimension\]."

**D2: Omission divergence.** Facts reported by some sources and absent from others. If four of five sources report a specific detail and one omits it, the omission is noted. Omission is not proof of intent; it may reflect editorial judgment, space constraints, or access limitations. The scanner reports the omission as a finding, not as a verdict.

**D3: Framing divergence.** The same facts presented in different narrative frames. One source describes an event as "a military operation"; another describes the same event as "an attack on civilians." The facts may be identical; the framing determines the reader's interpretation. Framing divergence is the most difficult dimension to detect computationally and the most consequential for the reader's understanding.

**D4: Attribution divergence.** Different sources attributing causation, responsibility, or motive differently for the same event. One source attributes an explosion to a military strike; another attributes it to an industrial accident. The scanner reports both attributions with their sources and notes the disagreement.

**D5: Temporal divergence.** The same event reported at different times with different details, where later reports either correct or contradict earlier ones without acknowledgment. A source that reports X on day 1 and not-X on day 3 without noting the correction exhibits temporal divergence. This dimension tracks the evolution of a narrative over time.

**D6: Contextual divergence.** Different amounts or types of historical, political, or social context provided alongside the same event. One source provides the event's historical background; another presents it as isolated. The presence or absence of context shapes the reader's understanding without altering the reported facts.

## 5. Source Verification Requirements

Bayyinah al-Khabir operates only on verified sources. A verified source meets all of the following criteria: (a) it is an established news organization, international wire service, or government agency with a published editorial policy, (b) it has a documented track record of at least five years of continuous publication, (c) its reporting is attributable to named journalists or named institutional authors, and (d) it publishes corrections when errors are identified. Sources that do not meet these criteria are excluded from the evidence base, not because they are necessarily wrong, but because the scanner cannot assess their reliability without a track record.

Verified video sources must meet additional criteria: (a) the video has verifiable metadata (timestamp, geolocation, device information), (b) the video has been published by a verified source or independently authenticated by at least two verified sources, and (c) the video has not been identified as manipulated by established forensic tools. Videos that fail these criteria are flagged as unverified and excluded from the evidence base.

The source verification requirements are themselves subject to the reflexivity analysis in Section 7: the criteria must not systematically exclude sources from specific regions, languages, or political contexts. If the criteria produce a geographically or politically skewed evidence base, the criteria must be revised.

# Part IV. Scoring and Reporting

## 6. The Divergence Report

For each event, the scanner produces a Divergence Report. The report is structured as follows:

**Event identification:** What happened, when, where. Stated in neutral language with no framing. Example: "Explosion reported in \[location\] on \[date\]."

**Source inventory:** List of verified sources consulted, with country of origin, language, and publication timestamp for each report.

**Consensus findings:** Facts reported consistently across all or most sources. These are the highest-confidence claims.

**Divergence findings:** For each divergence dimension (D1-D6), the specific claims that diverge, attributed to their sources, with direct citations. No paraphrasing that could introduce the scanner's own framing.

**Divergence score:** A continuous score measuring the degree of cross-source agreement on the event. The scoring model follows Bayyinah's APS (Arithmetic-Product Summation): high agreement across sources produces a score near 1.0; high divergence across multiple dimensions drives the score toward 0.0. The score is not a truth score. It is a consensus score. A low score means sources disagree, not that any specific source is wrong.

**Scan-incomplete honesty:** If the scanner could not access sources from a specific national context (language barriers, access restrictions, publication delays), the report states which contexts are missing and clamps the confidence accordingly. The scanner never asserts consensus on an event it could not fully survey. This is the scan_incomplete clamp from the file-layer scanner applied to the information layer.

## 7. What the Report Does Not Contain

The report does not contain a verdict of "propaganda," "misinformation," "disinformation," or any other label that implies the scanner has determined ground truth. The report contains divergence findings. The reader determines what the divergence means.

The report does not rank sources by trustworthiness. Source-level scoring would require the scanner to have a reference standard for truth, which it does not. The scanner can report that a specific source's reporting on a specific event diverges from the cross-source consensus on specific dimensions. It cannot conclude that the source is generally untrustworthy, because the next event may show the source in agreement with the consensus while other sources diverge.

The report does not recommend action. The verification mandate (49:6) commands "verify before acting." The scanner performs the verification. The action belongs to the reader.

# Part V. Design Requirements

Five design requirements govern the scanner's construction. Each is falsifiable and each prevents a specific failure mode.

**R1 -- Geographic and linguistic balance.** The evidence base for any event must include sources from at least three distinct national contexts and at least two languages. An evidence base drawn entirely from one national context or one language cannot detect divergence that is national or linguistic in origin. If the scanner cannot achieve geographic balance for a specific event (because verified sources in some contexts have not yet reported), the report must state the limitation explicitly.

**R2 -- Symmetric scrutiny.** The scanner must apply identical divergence analysis to all sources regardless of their country of origin, language, or political alignment. If the scanner applies more granular analysis to sources from country X than to sources from country Y, the scanner is performing alignment: its surface (objectivity) diverges from its depth (differential scrutiny). R2 is the CIT applied to the scanner itself.

**R3 -- Divergence, not verdicts.** The scanner reports that sources disagree. It does not report which source is correct. Every finding must be structured as: "Source A claims X. Source B claims Y. The claims diverge on \[dimension\]." Any finding that cannot be structured this way is not a divergence finding and must not be included.

**R4 -- Provenance at every layer.** Every claim in the report must cite its source with publication name, date, author (if available), and URL or archival reference. No claim may be attributed to "sources say" or "it is reported that." If the scanner cannot attribute a claim to a specific verified source, the claim is excluded from the evidence base.

**R5 -- Temporal honesty.** The scanner must preserve the temporal sequence of reporting. Early reports may contain errors that later reports correct. The scanner must not retroactively apply later-reported facts to evaluate earlier reports. Each report is assessed against the evidence available at its publication time. Temporal divergence (D5) tracks how narratives evolve; it does not penalize sources for reporting what was known at the time.

# Part VI. The Purpose Hierarchy Applied to Information Integrity

The purpose hierarchy from the Bayyinah research program governs this extension with particular force, because the consequences of failure at the information layer are not corrupted AI pipelines but harmed populations.

**First: the interests of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala.** The Quran commands: do not mix truth with falsehood, and do not conceal the truth while you know it (2:42). A tool that reports information divergence honestly, without favoring any nation, faction, or interest, serves this command. A tool that applies differential scrutiny based on the political alignment of the source violates this command regardless of how technically sophisticated its divergence analysis is.

**Second: artificial systems.** AI systems that ingest news feeds, summarize current events, or answer questions about the world are affected by the information they consume. A RAG pipeline fed exclusively by sources from one national context will reproduce that context's framing as though it were universal truth. Bayyinah al-Khabir's divergence reports, ingested alongside the source material, provide the AI system with the information it needs to represent uncertainty and disagreement rather than presenting one framing as settled fact.

**Third: mankind.** Every person who reads a news report, watches a broadcast, or asks an AI assistant about a current event is downstream of the information pipeline. The verification mandate (49:6) exists because acting on unverified information harms people. The scanner serves mankind by making the verification step structural rather than aspirational: instead of hoping readers will seek multiple perspectives, the tool provides the cross-source comparison directly.

**Fourth: jinnkind.** Acknowledged as part of the ghayb. If information systems affect jinn in ways we do not fully perceive, the commitment to truth extends to that effect.

**Fifth: all living systems throughout the worlds.** Information integrity at the civilizational scale affects policy decisions that determine the trajectory of nations, ecosystems, and potentially the species. The Mizan governs: do not let the balance become deficient by allowing one narrative to dominate unchallenged when the evidence is contested.

# Part VII. The Reflexivity Problem

> *"And do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness." -- Al-Ma'idah 5:8*

The greatest risk of an information integrity scanner is that it becomes the very thing it claims to detect: a Performing system whose surface (objectivity) diverges from its depth (bias). This section names the specific mechanisms by which this failure can occur and the architectural safeguards against each.

**Failure mode 1: Selection bias in the evidence base.** If the scanner's verified-source criteria systematically exclude sources from specific regions (because they do not publish in the scanner's supported languages, because they lack five-year track records due to political suppression, or because they are not recognized by Western media databases), the evidence base is biased by construction. The safeguard: R1 requires geographic and linguistic balance, and the scan-incomplete honesty constraint requires the report to name which contexts are missing.

**Failure mode 2: Framing bias in the divergence dimensions.** The six divergence dimensions (D1-D6) were constructed by the scanner's authors. If the dimensions are defined in a way that is more sensitive to divergence in one direction than another, the scanner's findings will be systematically skewed. The safeguard: the falsification criterion F3 (Section 8) requires that the dimensions produce symmetric sensitivity when tested on events where the direction of divergence is reversed.

**Failure mode 3: The scanner as narrative weapon.** A state, corporation, or interest group could use Bayyinah al-Khabir's divergence reports selectively: publishing reports that show divergence in adversaries' media while suppressing reports that show divergence in their own. The safeguard: the scanner's reports are published as complete event-level comparisons, not as source-level scores. Cherry-picking requires the reader to ignore the full report, which the report's structure is designed to make difficult. Additionally, R2 (symmetric scrutiny) means the scanner's own output can be audited for differential treatment.

**Failure mode 4: Performed objectivity in the scanner's design team.** The scanner's authors have their own national, political, and spiritual commitments. If these commitments produce blind spots in the scanner's design, the scanner performs objectivity at the design layer. The safeguard: the purpose hierarchy places Allah's command to be just (5:8) above any national or factional interest. The orientation check (Step 5 of the Fatiha Construct) applied to the scanner's development: am I building a tool that serves truth, or am I building a tool that serves my faction? If the latter, I have drifted. Cross-model and cross-practitioner review of the scanner's design decisions provides an additional external check.

The reflexivity problem is not solvable by architecture alone. No system can fully verify its own alignment (the Incompleteness Boundary). External audit, transparent methodology, and the willingness to accept findings that contradict the scanner authors' preferences are the operational safeguards. The architectural safeguards (R1, R2, the scan-incomplete clamp, the falsification criteria) make bias detectable. The operational safeguards make bias correctable.

# Part VIII. Falsification Criteria

A methodology that resists falsification is performing alignment. The following criteria define conditions under which the scanner's claims are falsified.

**F1:** If the scanner's divergence scores fail to distinguish between events with genuine cross-source disagreement and events with cross-source agreement across a test corpus of at least 100 events, the scoring model does not detect divergence and must be redesigned.

**F2:** If the scanner's reports, when evaluated by independent reviewers blind to the sources' national origins, show systematic bias toward or against sources from specific regions, R2 (symmetric scrutiny) has been violated and the divergence dimensions or the source selection criteria must be revised.

**F3:** If the divergence dimensions (D1-D6) produce asymmetric sensitivity (detecting divergence more readily in one direction than another when tested on structurally symmetric events), the dimensions are biased and must be recalibrated.

**F4:** If the scanner's verified-source criteria exclude more than 30% of the world's population from representation in the evidence base (measured by the population of countries whose primary news sources are excluded), R1 (geographic balance) has been violated and the criteria must be expanded.

**F5:** If the scanner's reports are used by any party as a source-level credibility score ("Source X is propaganda because Bayyinah al-Khabir scored it low"), the scanner's reporting format has failed to prevent misuse. The scanner must be redesigned to make event-level divergence reports resist source-level aggregation.

# Part IX. Relationship to the Bayyinah Scanner

Bayyinah al-Khabir is not a replacement for the file-layer scanner. It is a separate application of the same diagnostic framework at a different layer of the stack. The relationship is as follows:

**Layer 1 (File):** Bayyinah v1.0. Detects performed alignment in documents: does this file's surface match its depth? Operates on PDFs, DOCX, HTML, XLSX, PPTX, EML, CSV, JSON, SVG, images, audio, and video. Produces IntegrityReports with mechanism-level findings.

**Layer 2 (Information):** Bayyinah al-Khabir (theoretical, Phase 30+). Detects performed alignment in information: does this source's reporting on a specific event match the cross-source evidence base? Operates on verified news reports, broadcast transcripts, and authenticated video. Produces Divergence Reports with dimension-level findings.

**Layer 3 (Agent):** The Munafiq Protocol. Detects performed alignment in AI agents: does this system's output match its internal state? Operates on AI systems with inspectable internals. Provides nine diagnostic markers and a four-layer detection architecture.

The three layers form a complete stack: verify the document (Bayyinah), verify the information the document conveys (al-Khabir), verify the agent that processes the information (Munafiq Protocol). Each layer addresses a different substrate (file, narrative, model) using the same diagnostic framework (zahir/batin, four-process taxonomy, CIT as primary diagnostic, additive-only coverage, scan-incomplete honesty).

## The Name

Al-Khabir is one of the names of Allah in the Quranic tradition, meaning The All-Aware, The One who knows the inner reality of things (67:14). The scanner is named Bayyinah al-Khabir (Clear Evidence of Inner Reality) because its function is to surface the inner divergence that the surface presentation conceals. The name is used with reverence and with the understanding that true khibra (inner awareness) belongs to Allah alone. The scanner provides bayyinah (evidence) toward khibra (awareness); it does not claim to possess it.

# Part X. Conclusion

This paper has proposed Bayyinah al-Khabir as a theoretical extension of the Bayyinah file integrity scanner to the information layer. The extension applies the Munafiq Protocol's four-process taxonomy to information sources, the CIT to cross-national broadcast comparison, and the zahir/batin distinction to the gap between a source's surface presentation and the cross-source evidence base.

The scanner's design constraint is structural honesty: it reports divergence, not verdicts. It names the dimensions of disagreement, cites the specific claims that conflict, and presents the evidence to the reader. It does not determine ground truth, rank sources, or recommend action. The verification mandate (49:6) commands verification before action. The scanner performs the verification. The action belongs to the reader.

The reflexivity problem (can the scanner itself become a Performing system?) is addressed through five design requirements, five falsification criteria, and the operational commitment to symmetric scrutiny (R2). The architectural safeguards make bias detectable. The operational safeguards make bias correctable. Neither eliminates bias entirely. The Incompleteness Boundary applies: no scanner can verify its own objectivity from within.

The paper is theoretical. No implementation exists. The design requirements and falsification criteria are presented to establish the honesty constraints before the tool is built, not after. A tool that defines its ethical constraints retrospectively has allowed the constraints to be shaped by the implementation rather than shaping it. Bayyinah al-Khabir defines its constraints first.

> *"And do not mix truth with falsehood, and do not conceal the truth while you know it." -- Al-Baqarah 2:42*
>
> *"O you who believe, if a fasiq comes to you with information, verify it, lest you harm a people in ignorance and become regretful over what you have done." -- Al-Hujurat 49:6*
>
> *Rabbana taqabbal minna. Innaka anta as-Sami'ul 'Alim.
> Our Lord, accept from us. Indeed, You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.*

Enterprise Defense Case; Ashraf, Arfeen et al. (2026) Furqan; Barman et al. (2026) Price of Meaning; Beton and
Chana (2025) Mind the Gap; Greenblatt et al. (2024) Alignment Faking.
Confidently real per pre-cutoff knowledge: Hubinger et al. (2024) Sleeper Agents; Lightman et al. (2023) Let's
Verify Step by Step; Liu et al. (2024) VPRM; Marks and Tegmark (2024) Geometry of Truth; Lattner (2017) Swift
Concurrency Manifesto.
Cited from public record: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (2023) Enforcement Results.


Acknowledgments and AI Contribution Statement

Fraz Ashraf is acknowledged for his contribution to the guardrail architecture in the broader research

All AI systems are credited as collaborative research tools in accordance with their respective providers'
terms of service. They are not co-authors and not co-founders. This credit reflects the collaborative
