Locus: Section 4.1 mechanism ED-K4, dosage-threshold and per-pupil-cost bullets; Verification
Status ED-K4 paragraphs.
Substance: The four ED-K4 figures F-ED-11 logged as cited-not-yet-individually-verified were
each re-read end-to-end against primary sources in this version. Two errors surfaced. (1) Version
mismatch: the Nickow, Oreopoulos & Quan pooled tutoring effect size was cited as ≈ 0.37 SD,
attributed to the linked 2024 peer-reviewed article (DOI 10.3102/00028312231208687). That
article's own abstract states an overall pooled ES of 0.288 SD (SE = 0.029, p < .001). The 0.37
SD figure is real, but belongs to the authors' earlier 2020 NBER working-paper draft of the same
study (w27476) -- a figure still repeated by several secondary sources (J-PAL, the U.S.
Department of Education) that cite the 2020 preprint rather than the 2024 published revision.
Citing 0.37 SD while linking the 2024 DOI conflated the two versions. (2) Mis-attribution: the
Saga Education tutoring-cost figure ("≈$1,900-$4,800/student") was cited to Mahmud (2025,
EdWorkingPaper 25-1352) -- a full-text check confirms that paper never mentions Saga
Education anywhere; it is a Mississippi-retention-policy paper with no tutoring-vendor content.
The correct source is Cook, Dodge, Farkas, Guryan, Ludwig et al., "Not Too Late" (NBER
w28531), specifically the University of Chicago Education Lab's hosted revision of that paper,
which states Saga's cost was $3,200-$4,800 per pupil during the 2013-2015 study period and has
since dropped to $1,800 per pupil via an AmeriCorps subsidy and a blended-learning 4:1 model
-- a $1,800-$4,800 range, not $1,900-$4,800; no source was located for a $1,900 figure
specifically. Two figures were confirmed rather than corrected: the Cook et al. pooled TOT
(≈0.28 SD) and one-year persistence (0.23 SD) figures matched the UChicago Ed Lab hosted
text verbatim (the NBER-hosted PDF draft shows 0.264/0.222 SD, an ordinary cross-revision
variance between working-paper drafts, not an error); and the Mississippi Literacy-Based
Promotion Act cost (≈$15 million/year), coaching-count (29 rising to 74), and effect-size (0.014
SD bare-mandate versus 0.322 SD funded-model by 2019) figures all matched Mahmud (2025)
verbatim. Separately, the "2-4x" ITT/TOT gap claim in the same section, previously coattributed to Nickow et al. (2024), was checked against that paper's accessible text and no
ITT/TOT discussion was found there; the claim is corroborated instead by a University of


Chicago Education Lab 2022-23 scale-up study (0.04 SD ITT versus 0.14 SD TOT, a 3.5x gap),
so the citation is narrowed to that source alone.
Disposition: RESOLVED-AND-RETAINED. Section 4.1's dosage-threshold bullet now cites
0.288 SD for Nickow, Oreopoulos & Quan (2024) with an explicit note distinguishing it from the
2020 preprint's 0.37 SD; the per-pupil-cost bullet now attributes the Saga Education range
($1,800-$4,800) to Cook et al./NBER w28531 rather than Mahmud (2025); the ITT/TOT gap
bullet now cites only the UChicago Ed Lab scale-up study. The Verification Status section and
the Section 4.1 citation-provenance paragraph are both updated to state that all four previouslyunverified ED-K4 figures are now individually verified end-to-end, with these two corrections
logged rather than silently applied. This finding does not, by itself, discharge Item 5 of the
paper's convergence criterion (independent cross-instance audit); it is the producing instance's
own follow-through on an action item it logged against itself in v1.0-rc2, and is subject to the
same non-lineage audit requirement as every other finding in this ledger.
Cross-reference: F-ED-11; ED-K4; Section 4.1; Verification Status.
F-ED-13 MEDIUM -- The recompute was an internal-consistency and cross-source check,
not a formula reconstruction; category-level reconstruction now performed [RESOLVEDAND-RETAINED in v1.0-rc5; provenance corrected v1.0-rc6; raised v1.0-rc4 from peer
review F-PR-2 and F-PR-4]
Locus: Verification Status "primary formula data" paragraph; Section 4.4.6 item 2; Section 4.4.2
(100.00 percent corroboration); Section 4.4.3 emit table; original Falsifiability item 2.
Substance: An independent peer-review pass reproduced the recompute from the archived
companion dataset and found that it sums the DOE Detail Report's own disclosed walkthrough
line items back to the DOE's own reported total (agreement within $2 to $18, rounding) and that
the total matches the Comptroller "FY2023 Initial" FSF column exactly for all five schools. Both
results are genuine and are retained. But this is an internal-consistency check of one DOE
document plus a cross-source match, not the formula reconstruction from weighted registers and
per-capita weights that the paper's original Falsifiability item 2 called for: the only formuladerived term is an aggregate prior-year register times a base rate, and the archived extract
contains no category-level weighted register. The Verification Status phrase "full category-level
weighted-register breakdowns" overstated what was captured, and the Section 4.4.2 "100.00
percent" base-allocation field is browser-viewed and absent from the archive.
Disposition: RESOLVED-AND-RETAINED (v1.0-rc5; provenance corrected v1.0-rc6). In
v1.0-rc4 this was absorbed only by downscoping, with the formula reconstruction left open
because the archive lacked the per-school category register. In v1.0-rc5 an independent nonlineage pass performed the reconstruction: a category-level Detail Report pull (Grade Weight,
Academic Intervention, ELL, Special Education, Portfolio) for all five schools shows the
category dollars sum to the register-times-rate base, and the full walkthrough is mechanistically
reconstructed as (FY2022 register times FY2022 rate) + teacher-salary-change (bridging to the
FY2023 rate; reviewer-verified to under $1, see Verification Status and F-ED-14) + registerchange adjustment (bridging FY2022 to FY2023 register) + foundation + collective-bargaining
terms. This is a genuine mechanistic explanation of the walkthrough (roll last year's register at
last year's rate forward through the salary-rate and register changes), not merely an internalconsistency check, and it discharges the F-PR-2 concern. Corrected in v1.0-rc6: v1.0-rc5


tagged the category-level Detail Report pull "user-performed, not reviewer-reproduced." The
reviewer has since reported that the pull was obtained by the reviewer's own live browser
automation and the reconstruction arithmetic was independently run by the reviewer, not merely
relayed; this is corrected to reviewer-obtained and reviewer-reproduced (see Verification Status).
Two honest residuals remain and are retained, not smoothed: (1) the register-change adjustment
uses a single blended base rate and carries a $1 to $60 residual because category-specific percapitas differ, so a fully category-exact reconstruction is a further refinement; (2) the categorylevel data is browser-obtained and is not yet in the companion dataset, so this specific
reconstruction is not yet independently reproducible by a third party from the archive itself.
Adding the category-level register (and the per-school base-allocation percentage) to the dataset
is carried to Next Audit Cycle as a reproducibility step, not a merits gap.
Cross-reference: F-PR-2; F-PR-4; F-ED-10; F-ED-11; F-ED-14; Section 4.4.6 falsifiability item
2; Al-Mutaffifin 19894724 Section 4.1a (per-case ratio pattern).
F-ED-14 MEDIUM -- Base-rate parameter ($4,223.00) is the rolled-forward FY2022 base
weight amount; resolved with a primary source [RESOLVED in v1.0-rc5; provenance
corrected v1.0-rc6; raised v1.0-rc4 from peer review F-PR-3]
Locus:
companion
dataset
five_school_fsf_fy2023_detail_report_extract.csv
(base_rate_per_pupil_usd = 4223.00) and fsf_recompute.py; F-ED-10 Substance ("$4,223.00
base rate"); companion dataset fsf_fy2023_weights_percapitas.xlsx (K-5 weight 1.0 per-capita =
$4,197.19).
Substance: The recompute's single largest term is the aggregate prior-year weighted register
times a base rate of $4,223.00 (roughly $3M of a roughly $4.1M total). The dataset's own
FY2023 per-capita reference table lists the base (K-5, weight 1.0) per-capita at $4,197.19. The
reviewer confirmed that $4,223.00 is the rate that makes the walkthrough reconcile to within $18
and that $4,197.19 does not (it would leave the recompute roughly $18k short on the base term),
so $4,223.00 is the rate the DOE actually applied. But its provenance and vintage are
undocumented: it is plausibly a prior-year (FY2022) or enrollment-blended system rate
consistent with the roll-forward method, which is not stated anywhere in the extract or the paper.
An undocumented load-bearing rate that disagrees with the paper's own included reference table
is a parameter-integrity gap.
Disposition: RESOLVED (v1.0-rc5; provenance corrected v1.0-rc6). Two independent lines
close this. (1) Reviewer-verified from the archived data: teacher-salary-change equals
fy22_register times ($4,197.19 minus $4,223.00) to under $1 (max deviation $0.78) for all five
schools, so the walkthrough uses the FY2022 rate ($4,223.00) on the FY2022 register and the
teacher-salary-change term bridges to the FY2023 rate ($4,197.19). The arithmetic only closes at
exactly those two values, so the identity itself pins both rates. (2) Primary source, reviewerfetched (corrected in v1.0-rc6; v1.0-rc5 tagged this user-supplied-cited-not-reviewer-fetched,
citing a robots block): the DOE FSF Working Group Meeting 3 deck publishes a year-by-year
Base Weight Amount table -- FY2021 $4,137.85, FY2022 $4,223.00, FY2023 $4,197.19 -- and
attributes the FY2023 decrease to average teacher salary falling for the first time in several years
due to increased retirements, which is why the rolled-forward FY2022 rate exceeds the current
FY2023 rate. The reviewer has since reported fetching this deck directly from its source URL in
the same session, with the full table returned and no robots block encountered by that fetch


method; the tag is corrected accordingly. The $4,223.00 versus $4,197.19 discrepancy flagged by
F-PR-3 is therefore not an error but the expected prior-year-versus-current-year distinction, now
documented from a source the reviewer directly confirmed. The remaining reproducibility step is
to cite the deck in the companion dataset alongside the weights table.
Cross-reference: F-PR-3; F-ED-10; F-ED-13; Verification Status (independent verification pass);
companion dataset fsf_fy2023_weights_percapitas.xlsx.

If any Tier 1 mechanism in Section 4 requires semantic disambiguation to fire, the label
is false (framework violation). Disambiguating report vintage (Initial versus Final budget
snapshot) is a disclosed-parameter choice, not a semantic one, so requiring it is not itself
a framework violation; but a result that depends on that disclosed choice to reproduce is
Tier 2, not Tier 1, by Section 3's own definition (corrected v1.0-rc2, F-RV-3; F-ED-10).
If ED-K2 gates are applied and reforms with subgroup regressions still report unqualified
aggregate improvement, the gate is not enforced as specified.
If ED-K4's remediation pathway is deployed and its logged attendance/uptake data shows
systematically lower uptake among the same subgroups the disaggregated regression gate
is meant to protect, coupling (a) has failed on its own terms and must be re-designed
before the gate may continue firing.
If ED-U2 cross-instance grading produces correlated errors across instances, the biasrelocation claim degrades to bias-preservation.
If ED-G1 reproduction passes correlate with committee merit judgments beyond chance,
the Tier 1 / Tier 3 separation in F-ED-3 is empirically wrong.
Added v1.0-rc2 (F-RV-2, F-ED-11). A structural or empirical result generated by a single
producing instance and presented as ship-grade must be independently reproducible by a
second party from archived source data, not merely re-describable by the same instance
re-running its own prior session. If the underlying data for a claim in this paper is not
archived in a form a second instance or human reviewer can retrieve and check, that
claim is tagged single-instance, not independently reproduced, and is not counted toward
this paper's convergence criterion until archived.
Worked-example falsifiability: Section 4.4.6 items 1 through 3.

## R0420 · Bayyinah at-Taʿlīm

- section: VI. Applied Audits & Public-Data Studies

Bayyinah at-Taʿlīm
Structural Honesty Verification for Educational Fairness Systems, from Primary Schooling
to Graduate Research

Claude (Anthropic).

and

New Frontier (Arfeen and Ashraf 2026, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20131072).
Audit trail, full version history, finding-by-finding provenance, and cross-vendor
verification discipline for this paper are published separately in the Audit and Provenance
Companion (see Provenance and Verification, Section 6). The FY2023 worked-example data and
recompute scripts are published as a Companion Dataset (see Data Availability, Section 8).
"And establish weight in justice and do not make the mizan deficient." (Ar-Rahman
55:9)


2
Abstract
Structural Honesty Verification (SHV) verifies the correspondence between a system's
surface (what it claims, reports, or certifies) and its substrate (what it actually distributes,
produces, or contains). This paper applies SHV to educational fairness across three tiers: primary
and secondary schooling, undergraduate admissions and assessment, and graduate research. The
central observation is that "fair" and "equitable" are surface claims that usually conceal which
mechanism is running, and that the algorithmic-fairness impossibility results make the choice of
fairness definition consequential rather than cosmetic. SHV does not choose the definition,
remove bias, or adjudicate merit; its contribution is to make an institution declare which fairness
definition its mechanism implements, to make resource and record divergences tamper-evident
and regression-gated, and to separate what is genuinely verifiable (funding, provenance, nondeletion, reproduction) from what is not (merit, equity, understanding). We organize the proposal
with a three-tier classification of what can and cannot be verified, present nine mechanisms
across the three educational tiers, and demonstrate the framework end-to-end on New York
City's Fair Student Funding formula, where a five-school FY2023 recompute reconstructs the
DOE's own allocation walkthrough from public data. The work is theoretical with one
operational worked example; it has undergone several independent cross-instance audit rounds
outside the authoring lineage, which passed with no critical or high-severity findings, including
one by a different model family; but not yet the two consecutive qualifying such rounds the
methodology requires for convergence, and its scope limits are stated explicitly.


3
1. Purpose and Scope
This paper applies Structural Honesty Verification (SHV) to educational fairness across
three tiers: primary and secondary schooling (K-12), undergraduate programs, and graduate and
masters research. SHV is the verification of correspondence between a system's surface (what it
claims, reports, certifies) and its substrate (what it actually distributes, produces, or contains),
across versions, contexts, and populations (Arfeen and Ashraf 2026). It composes with existing
accountability regimes; it does not replace them.
The central claim is deliberately narrow. SHV does not remove bias from education, does
not adjudicate which distribution of educational goods is just, and does not validate competence.
Its contribution is to make three things enforceable: (a) that an institution declare which
definition of fairness its mechanism implements, (b) that resource and record divergences
between surface and substrate be tamper-evident and regression-gated, and (c) that what is
genuinely verifiable (funding, provenance, non-deletion, reproduction) be separated from what is
not (merit, equity, understanding), with the second forbidden from borrowing the surface
language of the first.
2. The Governing Divergence: Declared Fairness versus Operative Fairness
"Fair" and "equitable" are surface claims that usually conceal which mechanism is
running. The algorithmic-fairness impossibility results establish that calibration and equalized
error rates cannot both hold once base rates differ across groups (Kleinberg, Mullainathan and
Raghavan 2016; Chouldechova 2017). Education inherits this as the equity-versus-equality split:
equal inputs and equal outcomes are different substrates and they conflict. An institution that
asserts "fair" without declaring its operative definition has already produced a surface-substrate
divergence.


4
SHV's first move is not to choose the definition -- that is a value judgment outside the
framework's authority -- but to make the declaration mandatory and machine-checkable, then to
verify that the substrate matches the declared definition rather than silently implementing a third
one.
3. Tier Discipline: What Can and Cannot Be Verified
The framework classifies every quantity it touches into one of three tiers, imported from
Al-Mutaffifīn (Arfeen 2026): Tier 1 (Verified) is a byte-deterministic structural address with
zero semantic interference; Tier 2 (Structural) is a bounded hybrid whose underlying data is
structural but whose aggregation introduces disclosed parameter choices; Tier 3 (Interpretive)
requires semantic adjudication and is refused as a verification target. The governing falsifiability
rule is that a mechanism labeled Tier 1 which requires the system to disambiguate semantic
meaning has leaked into Tier 3, and the framework is violated. Disambiguating a disclosed
parameter -- for example, which budget snapshot ("Initial" versus "Final") of a fiscal year is
being read -- is not a semantic disambiguation, but a result that depends on such a parameter to
reproduce is Tier 2, not Tier 1.

No Tier 3 mechanism is proposed. The recurring failure mode in educational applications
is a Tier 3 quantity presented in Tier 1 surface language.
4. Mechanisms
4.1 Primary and Secondary (K-12)
Surface claim audited: "equal opportunity." Substrate: funding tied to local property tax,
tracking, gifted and AP access, exclusionary discipline, and promotion/retention gating.


6
ED-K1 (Tier 1) -- Cross-section funding audit. Scan expenditure and allocation ledgers
by district or school against the declared fairness definition, and emit a divergence signal where
the funding structure applies short measure relative to the system's own need-weighted formula
(the asymmetric-measure signature of Al-Mutaffifīn). The novelty is not the scan -- equity
dashboards already disaggregate -- but its pairing with ED-K2. Demonstrated end-to-end in
Section 4.4.
ED-K2 (Tier 1 gate over Tier 2 aggregation) -- Disaggregated regression gate. A
reform may not report aggregate improvement if any protected subgroup regressed without a
logged, signed justification. Student records are append-only with correcting entries, never
immutable: silent deletion is prohibited, logged correction is permitted, so the right to
rectification is preserved.
ED-K3 (Tier 1) -- Scan-incomplete rating declaration. An accountability rating must
carry a typed declaration of what it did not measure: students removed pre-test through
disciplinary action, narrowed curriculum, untested domains.
ED-K4 (Tier 2) -- Remediation-coupled mastery gate. A phased-progression or
mastery gate may fire only when both couplings below are present, disclosed, and logged.
Absent either, the gate is refused as unfit to deploy. This is a hard precondition, because a bare
mastery gate is grade retention, which the empirical record ties to disproportionate pushout of
low-income and minority students.
(a) Resourced, automatically-triggered remediation. On a logged non-mastery
determination, a remediation pathway must activate automatically, with no principal-discretion,
referral, or parent-request gap, because discretionary triggering preserves exactly the disparity


7
the mechanism exists to close even where the remediation infrastructure is nominally universal
(Westall, Utter and Strunk 2023). The pathway must disclose at minimum: (1) a dosage threshold
grounded in the tutoring-RCT evidence -- at least three sessions per week, 30 to 50 minutes each,
delivered by trained teachers or well-trained paraprofessionals, sustained for a semester or year
(Nickow, Oreopoulos and Quan 2024 report an overall pooled effect of 0.288 SD across 96
RCTs; the often-cited 0.37 SD figure is from the 2020 working-paper draft; Guryan et al.
2021/2023 report a treatment-on-treated effect of about 0.28 SD, persisting near 0.23 SD one
year later); (2) an itemized funding source and per-pupil cost, so the "resourced" claim is
auditable rather than symbolic, comparable in disclosure to Mississippi's Literacy-Based
Promotion Act (about $15 million per year; 29 to 74 literacy coaches; Mahmud 2025) or the
Saga Education model (about $1,800 to $4,800 per pupil; Guryan et al. 2021/2023); (3) a defined
timeline with a re-assessment checkpoint; and (4) mandatory logging of actual attendance and
uptake, not mere eligibility, since intent-to-treat versus treatment-on-treated gaps of two- to
fourfold are common (a University of Chicago Education Lab scale-up reports 0.04 SD versus
0.14 SD, a 3.5-fold gap).
(b) Independent, non-substitutable disaggregated gate. Coupling (a) does not by itself
discharge the equality requirement. Michigan's Read by Grade Three law paired comparable
remediation and exemption infrastructure with its retention gate; that infrastructure equalized
retention by race once test scores were controlled, but the economic-disadvantage disparity
persisted -- economically disadvantaged students remained 2.4 to 3.3 percentage points more
likely to be retained, unexplained by performance, exemption eligibility, district characteristics,
or mobility, with the retention "bite" from scoring just below the cutoff falling almost entirely on
them (4.5 points versus a statistically insignificant 0.3 for others; Westall, Utter and Strunk


8
2023). The disaggregated subgroup regression gate must therefore run independently and
continuously, regardless of whether coupling (a) is nominally in place.
Honest caveats. The evidence base for ED-K4 is suggestive and triangulated, not a single
clean causal test. NYC's own best causal evidence on test-based retention (Geng and Rockoff
2017) finds large positive test-score effects but explicitly excludes English language learners and
special-education students, so it has no subgroup answer for two of the populations the gate
exists to protect. Response to Intervention, often assumed to be the default remediation vehicle,
is mixed-to-negative in the most rigorous national evaluation, with a statistically significant
negative effect of -0.17 SD for first graders (Balu et al. 2015); if RTI is the chosen vehicle, EDK4 requires the higher-dosage, higher-fidelity variant with independent outcome monitoring.
And no located study directly compares "gate plus mandated remediation" against "gate plus no
remediation" on subgroup-disaggregated outcomes; the supporting evidence is quasiexperimental and policy-comparison-based (Mahmud 2025; Jacob and Lefgren 2002). ED-K4 is
therefore evidence-informed, not evidence-guaranteed, which is why coupling (b) is retained as
the primary safeguard.
4.2 Undergraduate
Surface claim audited: "holistic, merit-based." Substrate: preference structures, testoptional policies that relocate bias, algorithmic screening.
ED-U1 (Tier 2) -- Declared-definition enforcement. The process must publish which
fairness definition it runs and be audited for substrate consistency with it. The framework does
not adjudicate which definition is just; it detects a "race-neutral" surface reintroducing the
variable through proxies, or a "holistic" surface operating substantively as a class filter.


9
ED-U2 (Tier 2, bounded) -- Validator-by-different-instance grading. Route
anonymized, rubric-gradeable outputs to an independent cross-institutional grader to reduce
localized grader effects. This is N-version programming and carries the Knight-Leveson (1986)
independence-failure caveat: it relocates bias to the validator surface rather than removing it, and
applies only to rubric-gradeable work; essay, studio, clinical, and research outputs resist it.
ED-U3 (Tier 2) -- Mizan-calibrated abstention. Three-valued assessment (pass / fail /
insufficient-evidence) that removes some arbitrary curving by permitting explicit abstention
rather than forcing a point estimate. It does not remove demographic bias: calibration and
equalized error rates are mutually exclusive once base rates differ, and bias also resides in the
rubric, the items, and any automated grader's training data. The mechanism buys honest
abstention, not bias removal.
4.3 Graduate and Masters
Surface claim audited: program prestige and marketed placement; mentorship.
ED-G1 (Tier 1 precondition, never sufficient) -- Thesis reproduction gate. Dataset,
code, and text must regenerate the stated results deterministically as a necessary precondition for
defense. This gates provenance (Tier 1), not merit (Tier 3); presenting reproduction as sufficient
for graduation would be a Tier 3 leak. Merit adjudication remains a human Tier 3 judgment the
framework does not perform.
ED-G2 (Tier 2) -- Disaggregated program-outcome disclosure. Completion, funding,
and placement broken out by group and cohort, with a scan-incomplete declaration of what the
marketing surface omits (revenue-driven admits, funded versus unfunded two-tier cohorts).


10
ED-G3 (Tier 1 record over Tier 3 target) -- Advising-obligation ledger. Append-onlywith-correcting-entries logging of committee obligations met or missed. The ledger entry is a
Tier 1 structural fact with a timestamp; any inference about mentorship quality is Tier 3 and is
not emitted. Advising variance falls hardest on first-generation and underrepresented students
who lack informal networks to route around a poor advisor, so making the obligation surfacecheckable is itself an equality intervention.
4.4 Worked Example: NYC Fair Student Funding
This is the paper's one fully worked example, in the spirit of Al-Mutaffifīn's Lehman
Repo 105 case. It does not accuse the NYC Department of Education (DOE) of misconduct; it
measures.
The surface claim. Fair Student Funding (FSF), introduced in 2007, is New York City's
stated equity mechanism: a weighted-pupil model in which dollars follow students, each carrying
a base weight plus additive need weights (grade, academic intervention, English Language
Learner, special education, portfolio; from FY2024 also temporary housing and concentration of
need). FSF is the largest single stream a school receives, historically 60 to 70 percent of a
school's budget and 57 percent on average in FY2024. If implemented as stated, every school's
allocation would equal 100 percent of its formula-generated amount.
The substrate, Layer 1 (allocation versus formula). The DOE publishes, per school,
both the FSF allocation received and the formula amount the weights generate; their ratio is a
Tier 1 structural address. Historically the two diverged system-wide in one direction. Per the
Independent Budget Office (IBO 2013), the FY2011 median school received 75.4 percent of its
formula amount, with about 98 percent of schools below formula; FY2012 rose to an 86.0


11
percent median with 94 percent still below. At the weight-category level, IBO's regression found
that the implied weight for middle-school students below academic standards was negative -schools serving more of those students received less funding, not more -- and that elementary
and high-school ELL students and high-school special-education Collaborative Team Teaching
students were funded below their formula weight across the years studied. This is the
asymmetric-measure signature located precisely in the regression. Separately and at the school
level, Voloch (2015) examined 451 high-school budgets for 2013-14, found FSF ranging from
81 to 134 percent of formula with only 8.5 percent of schools fully funded (median 86.19
percent), and reported a statistically significant inverse relationship between a school's percentof-formula funded and its enrollment size, its share of low-income students, and its share of ELL
students.
Layer 1 resolution. New York City committed to funding every school at no less than
100 percent of formula beginning in the 2021-22 school year (announced April 19, 2021), an
investment described as reaching 1,164 schools and over 700,000 students, corroborated by
IBO's 2025 report. The divergence was closed by adding money while over-formula schools
were held harmless, not by reallocation. A five-school FY2023 recompute (below) independently
confirms the 100-percent floor was still in effect two fiscal years later.
Layer 2 (formula versus need). Closing Layer 1 relocated the honest question to the
formula itself. A 2022 Working Group concluded the formula under-captured concentrated need;
FY2024 added a Students in Temporary Housing weight and a Concentration Need weight.
IBO's May 2025 analysis found their magnitude small: the temporary-housing weight raised
affected budgets by about $78 per pupil, and the concentration-need weight raised 304 schools'


12
budgets by about $95,000 on average, which IBO judged unlikely to produce an observable
system-wide outcome effect, with possible year-to-year budget instability.
What the framework emits, and what it refuses. At Tier 1 it emits the allocation-toformula ratio and its resolution. At Tier 2 it emits the weight-category regressivity, the schoollevel inverse relationship, and the magnitude of the FY2024 corrective weights. At Tier 3 it
refuses to judge whether 100 percent of formula is adequate or whether the weights are the
correct weights -- and, notably, IBO itself drew the same line, confining its 2013 analysis to how
closely the DOE implemented the formula rather than whether the formula distributes funds
appropriately.
Formula reconstruction (Tier 2). From the DOE's published FY2023 FSF Detail
Reports for five sample schools (28Q160, 10X085, 30Q258, 14K488, 30Q148), the allocation
walkthrough was reconstructed independently: for each school the category-level line items sum
to the reported weighted-register total within $2, and the full walkthrough -- prior-year weighted
register at the prior-year base rate ($4,223.00), a teacher-salary-change term bridging to the
current-year rate ($4,197.19), a register-change adjustment, the $225,000 foundation, and three
collective-bargaining terms -- reproduces the DOE's own reported total within $2 to $18
(rounding) for all five schools. The base rates are sourced to the DOE FSF Working Group's
published year-by-year Base Weight Amount table, which also explains why the current-year
rate is lower than the prior-year one (average teacher salary fell for the first time in several years
due to increased retirements). This is a genuine mechanistic account of the walkthrough, not
merely an internal-consistency check. Its result is Tier 2, not Tier 1, because reconciling to the
DOE's published figure requires disclosing which report vintage ("Initial" versus "Final") is
being matched. The reconstructed figure matches the Comptroller mastersheet's FY2023 "Initial"


13
column exactly; the divergence from the "Final" column is only partially explained by the
disclosed register-relief and enrollment columns, with a net-positive rate/collective-bargaining
residual remaining for three of the five schools that the Initial-vintage walkthrough does not
itemize.
Scope of this example. The five-school recompute is a demonstration of reproduction
mechanics on real public data, not a population-level audit, and should not be extrapolated to all
roughly 1,500 FSF-funded schools without further sampling. All figures and the recompute script
are published in the Companion Dataset (Section 8).
5. Limitations
SHV verifies claim-to-mechanism correspondence; it supplies no value judgment about
just distribution, and treating it as a justice oracle would be the exact surface-substrate inflation
the framework exists to catch. Fairness metrics are vulnerable to Goodhart's law -- once a
measure becomes an optimization target it ceases to be a good measure (Goodhart 1975;
Strathern 1997) -- so every fairness key performance indicator requires a calibration bound and a
stated valid range. Auditing carries its own equality cost -- whose data, whose classrooms, whose
behavior is surveilled -- so the audit apparatus itself owes a scan-incomplete declaration.
The ED-K4 evidence base, though pinned to primary sources, does not settle the
underlying causal question: no located study directly compares gated-with-remediation against
gated-without-remediation on subgroup-disaggregated outcomes. The worked example is a fiveschool Tier 2 demonstration, not a system-wide audit. Most consequentially for how this paper
should be read: it has undergone multiple independent cross-instance audit rounds outside the
authoring lineage, all passing at zero critical and zero high-severity findings. The first (an


14
OpenAI/GPT auditor) passed with six low-severity findings absorbed. A second (also GPT)
reproduced the results but its auditor attested it did not satisfy the required independence, being
the same model family as the first, so it does not count. A third, by a different model family
(Gemini) in a fresh context, passed cleanly and is the first fully-qualifying different-family
round. The convergence criterion the broader methodology imposes -- two consecutive
qualifying rounds by an auditor outside the authoring lineage, each finding no critical or highseverity defects -- has therefore not yet been met: one further qualifying round on the current
artifact is required, and no claim in this paper should be read as having cleared that bar.
6. Provenance and Verification
This paper is the version-of-record statement of what is claimed and at what confidence.
The complete audit trail -- the finding-by-finding provenance ledger, the full version history and
its corrections, the per-claim verification tags, and the cross-vendor and convergence discipline
under which the work was produced -- is published separately in the Bayyinah at-Taʿlīm Audit
and Provenance Companion (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21436486), so that a reader who wishes to
check how any claim was established, or how any earlier error was caught and corrected, can
trace it there. That companion is a load-bearing part of this research program: it is the
demonstration that the paper practices the structural honesty it proposes.
One provenance point is stated here because it governs how the framework may be used.
This research program draws its design vocabulary (the Tier discipline, the surface-substrate
frame, the asymmetric-measure signature) from structural readings of the Qur'an, but it does not
treat the Qur'an as a validated quantitative instrument for adjudicating educational outcomes, and
no mechanism in this paper requires it to be one. The program's own empirical work is explicit
and deflationary about the underlying textual-structure finding: roughly 82 percent of the


15
headline long-range autocorrelation gap it studies is attributable to an approximate length-sort,
the residual effect is small (about +0.10 to +0.15) and survives multiple-comparison correction at
only some lags, and an earlier claim of a Quran-specific Fibonacci growth pattern was falsified
and retracted. The Qur'an is a source of design primitives and diagnostic names, plus one small
candidate structural effect; any use of it as a truth-certifying oracle in another domain would
itself fail the verification the framework exists to perform.
7. AI Contribution Statement
The human author designed the research questions, the tier framework, and the
mechanism set, and takes responsibility for all claims. Claude (Anthropic) contributed analytical
synthesis, the worked-example verification and recompute, and drafting under the author's
direction, and is credited as a collaborative research tool, not a co-author. The verification,
correction, and audit history of this collaboration is documented in the Audit and Provenance
Companion.
8. Data Availability
The FY2023 five-school worked example is published as a Companion Dataset
(BayyinahEnterprise): per-school FSF Detail Report walkthrough extracts, category-level
weighted-register detail, the corresponding NYC Comptroller mastersheet rows, the FY2023
weight and per-capita reference table, and the recompute scripts, with a README stating
provenance and a CC-BY 4.0 license for the compilation. The underlying figures are public
records of the NYC DOE and the NYC Comptroller's Office.

## R0422 · Bayyinah al-Amāna: Provenance Integrity for Public Open Data

- section: VI. Applied Audits & Public-Data Studies
- source_file: Bayyinah_ProvenanceIntegrity_Paper_v1.0.pdf
- source_format: pdf
- text_sha256: eca7936b24727e7ddd252abb07b97756e9322bff2c26c7b300742332c436a97b

1

Bayyinah al-Amāna: Provenance Integrity for Public Open Data
Verifying Declared Provenance, Freshness, and Schema Against the Substrate, with a
Reproducible Worked Example on New York MTA Datasets
Bilal Syed Arfeen (BayyinahEnterprise), with collaborative analytical assistance from
Claude (Anthropic).
DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21446613. Audit and provenance ledger and dataset: DOI
10.5281/zenodo.21446618. Version 1.0, the canonical converged release (three consecutive
qualifying cross-instance audit passes; the two-consecutive-pass gate under Standing Rule 7 was
met and confirmed clean, with the rotation gap closed). Section 8 and the companion Current
State record the full round history and the honestly-recorded convergence caveats; the
reproduction package is deposited alongside the ledger at the second DOI.
Governed by: Bayyinah, Portable Structural Honesty Verification for Public-Service
Institutions (Arfeen 2026, the framework paper). Sibling notes: the Public-Ledger Allocation and
Asymmetric-Measure Audits (Arfeen 2026, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21445552), which surfaced
and deferred the provenance divergence this note takes up; and Bayyinah at-Taʿlīm (Arfeen
2026, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21436484).
Audit trail, full version history, and finding-by-finding provenance are published
separately in the Audit and Provenance Companion. The frozen captures and reproduction script
are published as a Companion Dataset (see Data Availability, Section 9).
"Render the trusts to those they belong to." (an-Nisa 4:58)


2
Abstract
Every civic-accountability analysis built on public open data silently assumes the data is
what the portal claims: official rather than derived, current rather than stale, and stable rather
than silently rewritten. This note applies Structural Honesty Verification to that assumption
itself. Structural Honesty Verification verifies the correspondence between a system's surface
(what it claims, reports, or certifies) and its substrate (what it actually is, produces, or contains).
Here the system is an open dataset, the surface is its declared provenance, freshness, and schema,
and the substrate is its actual provenance classification, row-level creation and update
timestamps, and served field inventory. The note defines three tiers of what can and cannot be
verified, and demonstrates the method end-to-end on two New York State datasets that report the
same underlying MTA procurement records: a community-created view (gpsc-qqsz) and the
first-party official dataset (twsw-2mqa). The worked example, reproducible from a single live
pull, establishes that the two diverge (identically in FY2023, by 70 records and about $58.1M in
FY2024, and by $0.75 in summed face value in FY2022 despite identical row counts); that both
datasets serve history whose currently-served rows were created hundreds to over a thousand
days after each fiscal year closed, in a single post-close batch (consistent with a wholesale
republish and equally with a first-time bulk load, which a single-pull timestamp cannot
distinguish); and that the community view exposes a different schema (23 fields versus 32). The
method detects and quantifies these divergences and refuses to judge whether any was legitimate,
authorized, or improper. It is a meta-layer: it makes the data-integrity assumption underlying
other accountability work checkable rather than inherited on faith.


3
1. Purpose and Scope
Structural Honesty Verification (SHV) is the verification of correspondence between a
system's surface and its substrate. Two sibling notes apply it to what public institutions distribute
(educational funding) and to what they report about procurement. Both, like nearly all open-data
analysis, rest on an unstated premise: that the portal serving the data is faithful, that a dataset
labeled official is first-party, that a "last updated" timestamp reflects the actual last change, and
that querying a closed historical period returns the same answer tomorrow as today. This note
verifies that premise directly.
The scope is deliberately narrow. The note measures provenance, freshness, and schema
fidelity as byte-level and structural facts. It does not assess data quality, accuracy, or fitness for
any purpose, and it does not adjudicate whether an observed divergence or post-close batch load
was a correction, a migration, an error, or a manipulation. That legitimacy question is reserved
for the publisher and for oversight; the method supplies the reproducible, tamper-evident
measurement those judgments would rest on, and stops there.
2. The Governing Divergence: Declared Provenance versus Actual Provenance
The surface of an open dataset is its self-presentation. A Socrata dataset declares a
provenance (official or community), a name, a schema, a row count, and a last-updated time, and
it implicitly presents any query against a closed reporting period as stable. The substrate is what
the bytes and system metadata actually show: whether the portal classifies the dataset as firstparty or as a derived view (the Socrata-declared provenance field, not an independent inquiry
into agency authorship), whether its currently-served historical rows were created at or long after
the period they describe, whether its served field inventory matches its declared schema, and
whether two datasets that claim to report the same records in fact agree.


4
Divergence between surface and substrate here is not rare or exotic. A communitycreated view can closely shadow an official dataset, close enough that a careful analyst
reproduces off the wrong one. A portal can republish an entire historical dataset years after the
fact while the "last updated" surface says little about how much of the past was regenerated. The
method names each such divergence precisely and quantifies it.
3. Tier Discipline: What Can and Cannot Be Verified
Consistent with the framework, the note sorts every claim into three tiers.
Tier 1 is verified and byte-deterministic: the SHA-256 of a frozen capture; a dataset's row
count and served field inventory; whether two datasets are byte-identical over a shared window;
and the row-level Socrata system timestamps :created_at and :updated_at for a fixed
historical window, including whether any historical row's timestamp postdates the close of its
own reporting period.
Tier 2 is structural and rests on disclosed parameters: the provenance classification read
from portal metadata (the Socrata-declared provenance field, official versus community view,
not an independent chain-of-custody inquiry); the declared last-updated time reconciled against
the actual row-timestamp distribution; and whether the served history is preserved-since-origin
or was instantiated in a single post-close batch, inferred from a uniform recent creation
timestamp across old rows (a batch that a single pull cannot resolve into a republish versus a
first-time bulk load).
Tier 3 is interpretive and is refused: whether a change was legitimate, authorized,
malicious, or intended to deceive; whether a divergence reflects error, correction, or
manipulation. The method detects and quantifies the divergence and hands the legitimacy


5
question to the publisher and to oversight. This refusal matters more here than in the sibling
notes, because the language of "silent edit" and "republished history" invites over-reading as an
accusation, and the substrate facts do not support one.
4. The Data-Interface Contract and the Socrata Adapter
The method depends on a small, portable interface. A Socrata portal exposes, for any
dataset, a metadata endpoint carrying provenance, schema, and last-updated fields, and a SODA
query endpoint that supports aggregate queries over the data and over the per-row system
columns :created_at and :updated_at. The dedicated revision endpoint
(/revisions.json) is not publicly served for these datasets, so a portal-native change log is
unavailable; the row-level system timestamps supply an available freshness signal (rowinstantiation timing) in its place, though not a full change log with prior values or edit
authorship. Because both New York City Open Data and data.ny.gov run Socrata, a single
adapter covers thousands of civic datasets. The MTA pair below is one worked instance of a
portable check, not an MTA-specific tool.
5. Worked Example: Two New York MTA Procurement Datasets
The datasets are gpsc-qqsz ("MTA Procurement Report (All)", declared provenance
community) and twsw-2mqa ("MTA Procurements: Beginning 2018", declared provenance
official), both on data.ny.gov, examined across the fiscal years ending December 31 of 2022,
2023, and 2024. Every figure below is reproducible from the accompanying package, offline
from a frozen capture and live against the endpoints.


6
5.1 Provenance classification and divergence
The metadata declares gpsc-qqsz a community-created view and twsw-2mqa official.
Comparing the two on the same reporting periods: FY2023 is identical (both 12,114 records,
$63,569,204,049.36); FY2024 diverges by 70 records and $58,072,427.23, a count divergence of
0.5103% and a face-value divergence of 0.0891%; and FY2022, despite identical row counts
(both 12,156), diverges by $0.75 in summed face value ($54,698,007,774.69 versus
$54,698,007,775.44). The last is the sharpest illustration of the method's resolution: a value-level
difference that a billion-rounded reading calls identical, surfaced only because the comparison is
exact.
5.2 Declared-versus-actual freshness
The primary freshness method reads the row-level :created_at system column for
each fixed historical window and asks whether the currently-served rows could have existed
when the period closed. They could not. In the community view, every FY2022, FY2023, and
FY2024 row carries a uniform :created_at of 2025-12-01, that is 1066, 701, and 335 days
respectively after each fiscal year closed. In the official dataset, every such row carries a uniform
:created_at of 2026-04-01, that is 1187, 822, and 456 days after close. A uniform creation

timestamp across an entire closed year indicates the window was instantiated in one batch after
the period closed, rather than through selective edits. That single-batch instantiation is consistent
with a wholesale republish of previously-served history and equally consistent with a first-time
bulk load of a dataset or view that had no prior served instance; a single live pull cannot
distinguish the two, and the note claims only the batch-after-close fact, not which of the two
produced it. Either way, none of the currently-served rows for that closed year predates a recent
bulk creation. The finding requires only a single live pull; no two-dated-pull time gap is needed.


7
5.3 Schema divergence
The community view serves 23 fields; the official dataset serves 32. Sixteen fields appear
in the official dataset but not the community view, and seven appear in the community view but
not the official dataset. Two datasets presenting as reports of the same records expose materially
different schemas, which a consumer selecting a source on name alone would not anticipate.
5.4 What the method emits, and what it refuses
At Tier 1 it emits the hashes, counts, exact divergences, and row timestamps. At Tier 2 it
emits the provenance classifications, the freshness reconciliation, and the post-close-batch
inference (a batch load after the period close, which a single pull does not resolve into a
republish versus a first-time bulk load). At Tier 3 it refuses: it does not conclude that the
community view is unauthorized, that any batch load was improper, that the FY2024 divergence
is an error in either dataset, or that any party intended to mislead. Batch loads, migrations, and
corrections routinely regenerate rows and their timestamps; detecting that a dataset's served
history was created recently is a substrate fact, not a charge.
6. Portability
The check generalizes to any Socrata-hosted dataset with a reporting-period field, and
degrades gracefully without one: the provenance, schema, snapshot-hash, and post-close-batch
checks need no period field, and only the "timestamp postdates period close" refinement does.
Across New York City Open Data and data.ny.gov alone this is thousands of datasets. The
value of the method is not the MTA finding but the portable capacity to verify, for any civic
dataset another analysis depends on, that its declared provenance, freshness, and schema match
its substrate.


8
7. Limitations
The method reads provenance, freshness, and schema; it says nothing about whether the
data values are correct, complete, or fit for a purpose. The freshness signal rests on Socrata's
:created_at/:updated_at semantics, which record when a row entered or last changed in

the served instance, not the full edit history; a portal that reloads a window wholesale erases finer
history, which the method reports as a post-close batch load (a republish or a first-time bulk load,
which a single pull cannot distinguish) rather than reconstructing what changed. The revision
endpoint being unavailable means the note cannot present a portal-native change log. The twodataset worked example is a demonstration of a portable method, not a survey; a systemwide
claim about the portal would require sampling many datasets. And, as everywhere in this
program, the note is producer-side and awaits the independent cross-instance audit described
next; no result here is convergence-verified.
8. Provenance and Verification
This is version 1.0, the canonical converged release. Under the framework's Standing
Rule 7, an artifact meets the convergence gate after two consecutive qualifying passes by
independent, non-producer-lineage auditors that execute the reproduction and return zero critical
and zero high findings. Three such passes have occurred (F-AM-R1, F-AM-R2, F-AM-R3), each
with at least two qualifying non-producer members returning zero critical and zero high; the
Claude producing lineage was quarantined throughout. The gate was met at F-AM-R2 and
confirmed clean at F-AM-R3 on the corrected artifact, and the F-AM-R3 pass-bearing set (GPT
5.5 and the rotated-in, successfully-isolated GPT 5.4) includes a qualifying member new relative
to the earlier clean pair, closing the rotation gap the earlier rounds could not. The remaining
caveat is honest and narrow: v1.0 is the thrice-passed substance with one LOW Section 1


9
wording fix absorbed (materially identical), and the convergence is met inside this producerdefined governance framework, while the externally-verifiable result -- every figure reproduces
exactly from live data.ny.gov under the exact fiscal-window filter, and the comparator is tamperevident under hash-gate defeat -- holds independently of the framework. The full round history
and finding-by-finding dispositions are in the Audit and Provenance Companion. The design
vocabulary (amāna as faithful safekeeping of a trust) is drawn from structural readings of the
Qur'an and is inspiration, not evidence: every figure in Section 5 is justified entirely by public
data, portal metadata, and arithmetic.
9. Data Availability and Reproduction
Every figure is reproducible from the New York State open-data portal without
authentication. The datasets are gpsc-qqsz and twsw-2mqa on data.ny.gov; provenance
and schema come from each dataset's metadata endpoint; freshness comes from the SODA
:created_at/:updated_at system columns filtered by fiscal_year_end_date; and the

divergence figures come from count(*) and sum(contract_amount) per fiscal year. A
frozen capture, its SHA-256 manifest, and a standard-library reproduction script that verifies the
hash, reproduces all four checks offline, re-pulls the live endpoints to detect drift, and self-tests
its own comparator accompany this note as a single reproduction package, deposited under an
immutable DOI alongside the audit and provenance ledger at DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21446618;
anyone can retrieve it there and re-run the full reproduction.
References

Zenodo. DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21445552. https://zenodo.org/records/21445552


10

Fairness Systems. Zenodo. DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21436484.

## R0424 · Independent Cross-Instance Audit — Round 1

- section: VI. Applied Audits & Public-Data Studies
- source_file: F-AA-R1_gpt_report.md
- source_format: md
- text_sha256: 72f36e7207b4ff425f2e56b18f71128f0dd824559a8da3f41b0b42efaa93a0fd

# Independent Cross-Instance Audit — Round 1

**Artifact:** *Bayyinah: Public-Ledger Allocation and Asymmetric-Measure Audits* (v0.1 corrected)
**Audit date:** 2026-07-19
**Auditor:** OpenAI GPT-5.6 Thinking
**Producing lineage stated by artifact:** Bilal Syed Arfeen / BayyinahEnterprise, with Claude (Anthropic) analytical assistance
**Round status:** **NON-PASS**
**Severity count:** **0 CRITICAL / 3 HIGH / 3 MEDIUM / 3 LOW / 0 INFO**

## 1. Independence attestation

I am an OpenAI model instance, not the Claude/Anthropic model lineage credited in the drafting of the note, and I had no role in producing the submitted artifact or reproduction package. The brief's cross-lineage independence condition therefore holds. The package does not provide the complete private rubric needed for me to certify a separate “Tier 1 auditor” designation; this report attests independence and competence of the work performed, not a framework label whose qualification rules were not supplied.

## 2. Verdict

**Round 1 does not pass.** The pass criterion is zero CRITICAL and zero HIGH findings. This round returns three HIGH findings, so it cannot count toward the two-round convergence gate.

**Direct answer to the requested controlling question:** **Yes. The note claims several things its data does not support in their current wording.** The exact arithmetic on `contract_amount` is reproducible, but:

1. it is presented as FY2024 spending/allocation even though `contract_amount` is the full value of a contract, including multi-year contracts awarded long before FY2024;
2. the 3.95% prime-vendor contract-value share is presented as the operative dollar substrate for New York MWBE utilization goals, although the governing framework concerns annual procurement, direct and indirect participation, contract-specific eligibility, and waivers; and
3. a competitive-process “pass” is declared without testing the MTA's operative procurement guidelines, waiver conditions, exception documentation, or coding accuracy.

These are surface-versus-substrate divergences, not arithmetic discrepancies.

## 3. Audit coverage and execution limits

Completed:

- inspected the brief, note, companion, snapshot, manifest, and reproduction script;
- verified the snapshot hash and row count;
- ran the supplied script offline;
- independently recomputed every Section 4 headline statistic from the frozen rows without importing the supplied calculation functions;
- recomputed the same measures using `amount_expended_for_fiscal_year`;
- tested award-year composition, conservative cross-year repeat fingerprints, missing/zero amounts, vendor aggregation, negative values, and Gini implementation;
- checked official field definitions, the governing procurement statute, MWBE goal structure, data-source provenance, PARIS reporting mechanics, and the capital-data schemas.

Not completed in this environment:

- the supplied `--live` request failed at DNS resolution, so a fresh live aggregate was not obtained through the script;
- the live row-level `project_number` join among the capital tables was not re-executed. The dataset schemas support the corrected claim, but functional join confirmation remains carried from the companion's EV-2 rather than independently reproduced here.

These uncompleted legs do not change the non-pass: the HIGH findings arise from the frozen rows, official field definitions, and governing legal structure. They must nevertheless be rerun in the corrected resubmission round.

## 4. Reproduction results

### 4.1 Package integrity

- Snapshot rows: **37,988**, matching the manifest.
- Snapshot SHA-256: **`9aefc01789854e79fa07d19484bc14be7a899ec7856b8c79fd4994629fdf0f09`**, matching the manifest.
- The snapshot bytes are canonical compact JSON under the manifest's stated convention.
- The supplied script reproduces its stated output exactly.

### 4.2 Exact reproduction on the selected `contract_amount` measure

| Quantity | Independent result | Note result | Status |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| FY2024 records | 13,718 | 13,718 | Match |
| Sum of `contract_amount` | $65,189,755,228.64 | $65.19B | Match |
| Positive-amount records | 12,322 | 12,322 | Match |
| Excluded missing/zero records | 1,396 (10.176%) | about 1,400 / roughly 10% | Rounded match |
| Competitive `contract_amount` share | 92.2197% | 92.2% | Match |
| MWBE count share | 18.7345% | 18.7% | Match |
| MWBE `contract_amount` share | 3.9532% | 3.95% | Match |
| Count/contract-value ratio | 4.7391x | 4.7x | Match |
| Top 5 / 10 / 20 shares | 22.143% / 30.415% / 41.777% | 22.1% / 30.4% / 41.8% | Match |
| Distinct vendor strings | 2,656 | 2,656 | Match |
| Gini | 0.9311677 | 0.931 | Match |

No negative `contract_amount` records were present. Basic case/whitespace vendor normalization does not materially alter the concentration result.

### 4.3 Measure-semantic recomputations

The official dataset defines `contract_amount` as the **total value of the contract**, while `amount_expended_for_fiscal_year` is the amount expended under the contract during that fiscal year.

On the same FY2024 rows:

- annual expenditures total **$8,170,228,558.54**, not $65.19B;
- prime-MWBE annual expenditures are **$576,915,678.94**, or **7.0612%**;
- the MWBE count-to-annual-expenditure ratio is **2.653x**, not 4.739x;
- competitive annual expenditures are **89.6533%**;
- state-contract and non-contract-purchase-order categories, which contribute no `contract_amount` in this extract, contribute **5.6175%** of annual expenditures combined.

The prime-MWBE annual-expenditure shares are **4.2468% (FY2022), 6.2714% (FY2023), and 7.0612% (FY2024)**. A count-versus-dollar asymmetry remains, but its magnitude and three-year trajectory are materially different.

### 4.4 Stock/flow and repeated-reporting diagnostics

Within the FY2024 report:

- **91.6876%** of the summed `contract_amount` belongs to records whose award date precedes 2024;
- only **8.3124%** belongs to records with a 2024 award date;
- award years extend back to **1984**;
- an exact full-field fingerprint finds **2,056 FY2024 rows (14.99%)**, carrying **$7.643B (11.72%)**, also present in the FY2022 or FY2023 snapshot. This is a conservative lower bound because the extract lacks a stable transaction identifier and field edits can hide repeats.

Thus $65.19B is not a clean annual flow of FY2024 awards or expenditures. It is the stock of total contract values reported in the FY2024 annual procurement file.

## 5. Findings

### F-AA-R1-01 — HIGH

**Identifier:** F-AA-R1-01
**Severity:** HIGH
**Locus:** Abstract; Sections 4 introductory paragraph, 4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 6, and 8; phrases including “FY2024 contract dollars,” “dollar volume in FY2024,” “largest awards,” and the three-year persistence interpretation.
**Substance — surface versus substrate:** The surface presents the $65.19B sum and its derived shares as FY2024 procurement spending/allocation. The substrate field is `contract_amount`, officially defined as the contract's total value, and 91.69% of the FY2024 sum comes from contracts awarded before 2024. Repeated multi-year contracts also recur across annual report vintages. The statistic is reproducible, but its annual-flow interpretation is not.
**Disposition:** **REQUIRES CORRECTION.** Choose and name the estimand. For annual spending, use `amount_expended_for_fiscal_year`. For awards made during 2024, filter on `award_date` and address missing dates. If retaining `contract_amount`, call it the total face value of contracts appearing in the FY2024 report, remove annual-spending/allocation language, and substantially narrow the persistence claim. Recompute all process, MWBE, concentration, and Gini figures on the chosen estimand. Add multi-year carryover and repeat-reporting limitations.
**Cross-reference:** Official MTA dataset data dictionary; ABO procurement-data limitations; independent recomputation §§4.3–4.4; F-AA-R1-02 and F-AA-R1-03.

### F-AA-R1-02 — HIGH

**Identifier:** F-AA-R1-02
**Severity:** HIGH
**Locus:** Abstract; Sections 2, 4.2, 4.4, and 6; especially the statements that 3.95% is “the relevant substrate,” “fewer than four cents on the dollar,” and that the count figure is the “short measure.”
**Substance — surface versus substrate:** The surface treats the `vendor_is_a_mwbe` share of total prime-contract face value as the operative measure against New York MWBE utilization goals. The governing substrate is more qualified: goals concern annual procurement and direct and indirect participation; contract-specific goals depend on available subcontract opportunities and disparity-study categories; participation may be credited through primes, subcontractors, and joint ventures; and waivers/exemptions matter. The dataset's binary prime-vendor flag cannot establish goal attainment or the full utilization denominator. On the closer annual-expenditure field, the prime-MWBE share is 7.06%, not 3.95%, but even 7.06% remains incomplete because indirect participation and goal-eligible spend are absent.
**Disposition:** **REQUIRES CORRECTION.** Recast 18.7% versus 3.95% as a descriptive prime-vendor count-versus-total-contract-value statistic, not the operative New York goal measure. To test declared-goal correspondence, obtain contract-specific or agency utilization data including annual eligible expenditures, certified prime and subcontract participation, industry/category goals, exemptions, and waivers. Until then, remove “honest measure,” “short measure,” “operative substrate,” and any implied goal-compliance inference. Add prime-only, eligibility, subcontracting, and waiver limitations.
**Cross-reference:** New York Executive Law §313 and related Article 15-A reporting provisions; independent recomputation §4.3; F-AA-R1-01.

### F-AA-R1-03 — HIGH

**Identifier:** F-AA-R1-03
**Severity:** HIGH
**Locus:** Sections 2, 4.1, and 4.4; the declared rule “contracts are competitively bid unless an exception is documented” and the conclusion that the process rule receives a “pass.”
**Substance — surface versus substrate:** The surface claims correspondence between a declared procurement rule and operative behavior. The substrate shows only the authority-supplied `award_process` category and value composition. New York Public Authorities Law §2879 requires each authority to adopt its own procurement guidelines, including competitive-selection provisions and circumstances for waiving competition. The note does not identify the operative MTA guideline, test whether each noncompetitive award fits a permitted exception, verify required documentation/approval, or validate the authority's coding. A high competitive share does not prove compliance with the declared rule and no universal pass threshold is established.
**Disposition:** **REQUIRES CORRECTION.** Report the competitive/noncompetitive composition as a descriptive Tier-2 statistic only. Withhold “pass,” “substrate matches surface,” and rule-compliance language unless the MTA's operative guidelines, thresholds, exception categories, waiver records, and approval/documentation requirements are elicited and tested transaction-by-transaction or through a defensible sample.
**Cross-reference:** New York Public Authorities Law §2879; official `award_process` data dictionary; F-AA-R1-01.

### F-AA-R1-04 — MEDIUM

**Identifier:** F-AA-R1-04
**Severity:** MEDIUM
**Locus:** Sections 3, 7, and 8; companion Verification Status; audit brief description of `gpsc-qqsz` as “the primary source itself.”
**Substance — surface versus substrate:** The surface identifies `gpsc-qqsz` as the primary MTA source. The portal identifies it as a community-created view based on the statewide authority procurement dataset and warns that New York State did not review or approve modifications. A first-party MTA-attributed dataset, `twsw-2mqa`, is separately published and more recently updated. The community view may accurately reflect official submitted data, but provenance is overstated.
**Disposition:** **REQUIRES CORRECTION.** Freeze and reproduce from the official MTA-attributed dataset or the official ABO statewide dataset filtered to MTA, then compare with `gpsc-qqsz`. Describe `gpsc-qqsz` accurately as a derived community view if retained. Record the source dataset ID, metadata version, query, retrieval time, and any row/schema divergence.
**Cross-reference:** Official Open Data metadata for `gpsc-qqsz`, `twsw-2mqa`, and the state-authority procurement dataset.

### F-AA-R1-05 — MEDIUM

**Identifier:** F-AA-R1-05
**Severity:** MEDIUM
**Locus:** Section 3, sentence stating that the report contains 111,879 contract records across fiscal years ending 2022 through 2024.
**Substance — surface versus substrate:** The surface states 111,879 records for the three-year interval. The frozen three-year substrate and manifest contain 37,988 records: 12,156 in FY2022, 12,114 in FY2023, and 13,718 in FY2024. The larger number appears to describe a broader historical view, not the stated three years.
**Disposition:** **REQUIRES CORRECTION.** Replace with 37,988 for the frozen FY2022–FY2024 extract, or state the broader date range and source for 111,879. Ensure all scope counts refer to the same dataset/version.
**Cross-reference:** Snapshot manifest; independent recomputation §4.1.

### F-AA-R1-06 — MEDIUM

**Identifier:** F-AA-R1-06
**Severity:** MEDIUM
**Locus:** Section 3 and Section 5; claim that state law requires public authorities to publish procurement reports to a common schema on the state open-data portal.
**Substance — surface versus substrate:** The surface attributes the entire standardized portal-publication mechanism directly to statute. The legal substrate requires annual authority reporting; PARIS supplies the common electronic reporting/template mechanism, and ABO in collaboration with Open Data NY publishes compiled data. The resulting common schema is real, but the legal/operational chain is compressed into an overstatement.
**Disposition:** **REQUIRES CORRECTION.** State that Public Authorities Law requires annual reporting; authorities submit through PARIS using standardized reporting structures; ABO/Open Data NY publishes compiled datasets. Avoid saying the statute itself directly mandates portal publication in the precise schema unless a specific provision establishes that mechanism.
**Cross-reference:** Public Authorities Law §2800; ABO public-authority data methodology; PARIS documentation.

### F-AA-R1-07 — LOW

**Identifier:** F-AA-R1-07
**Severity:** LOW
**Locus:** Sections 4 introductory paragraph, 4.4, and 6; “carry no dollar amount” / “no dollar amount” wording.
**Substance — surface versus substrate:** The surface merges missing and zero values. The substrate contains 1,348 missing `contract_amount` values and 48 explicit zeros, totaling 1,396 excluded records. Those conditions are analytically distinct.
**Disposition:** **REQUIRES CORRECTION.** Report missing and explicit-zero counts separately, explain why each is excluded, and bound sensitivity where feasible.
**Cross-reference:** Independent recomputation §4.2.

### F-AA-R1-08 — LOW

**Identifier:** F-AA-R1-08
**Severity:** LOW
**Locus:** `snapshot/MANIFEST.json`, field inventory.
**Substance — surface versus substrate:** The manifest lists 21 fields, while the snapshot contains 22. `vendor_province_region` is present in the rows but omitted from the manifest field list. The hash remains valid, so this is a metadata completeness defect rather than integrity failure.
**Disposition:** **REQUIRES CORRECTION.** Regenerate the manifest's field inventory programmatically from the frozen rows and add a validation that the listed set equals the actual set.
**Cross-reference:** Snapshot and manifest integrity check.

### F-AA-R1-09 — LOW

**Identifier:** F-AA-R1-09
**Severity:** LOW
**Locus:** Audit brief Materials item 4; companion Verification Status; `reproduce_paper2.py --live`.
**Substance — surface versus substrate:** The surface says `--live` checks drift against the current endpoint in connection with reproduction of every Section 4 figure. The script's live mode checks only FY2024 row count and summed `contract_amount`; it does not recompute or compare process shares, MWBE shares, prior-year persistence, vendor concentration, Gini, missingness composition, or source schema. Offseting or subgroup drift could therefore go undetected.
**Disposition:** **REQUIRES CORRECTION.** Make live mode run the complete calculation pipeline for all three years and compare every emitted statistic, source schema, and row/hash summary against the frozen baseline, with explicit tolerances and nonzero exit status on drift.
**Cross-reference:** Reproduction script; audit brief numerical-reproduction scope.

## 6. Checklist outcomes without findings

- **Arithmetic reproducibility:** PASS on the frozen snapshot for the selected `contract_amount` estimand.
- **Tier-3 leakage:** No accusation of intent, steering, discrimination, favoritism, or fraud was found. The explicit refusals are clear.
- **Concentration mechanism framing:** The non-culpable structural explanation is appropriately framed as a mechanism rather than an accusation. Its numerical basis must be recomputed on the corrected estimand.
- **Corrected capital-infrastructure claim F-AA-1:** Schema-level review supports that `kizb-nxtu` and `ehz8-ag3n` are tabular capital datasets and that project locations are separate, making a project-key join followed by spatial attribution necessary. No new contradiction was found. A fresh functional row-level join remains pending.
- **Portability scope:** The note properly says cross-jurisdiction portability is designed but not demonstrated.
- **Religious vocabulary/evidence separation:** The note explicitly treats the vocabulary as inspiration rather than empirical evidence; no finding.

## 7. Minimum correction package before re-audit

1. Select and define the dollar estimand: annual expenditure, new-award face value, or reported-contract stock.
2. Recompute all Section 4 figures consistently on that estimand and revise annual/persistence language.
3. Reframe the MWBE statistic as prime-vendor descriptive data unless full direct/indirect, eligible-spend, goal, waiver, and exemption data are added.
4. Remove the competitive-process “pass,” or execute a real declared-rule test against MTA guidelines and exceptions.
5. Rebase provenance on an official MTA/ABO source and reconcile the community view.
6. Correct the three-year record count, reporting-law phrasing, missing/zero split, manifest field list, and live-drift test.
7. Rerun the full live endpoint comparison and functional capital-location join.
8. Append these findings and dispositions to the companion ledger without silently replacing the superseded text.

## 8. Round disposition

**NON-PASS — revise and restart the two-consecutive-round count after absorption.**

The note retains a potentially publishable descriptive result: prime-MWBE vendors account for a substantially larger share of reported contract records than of either total reported contract face value or annual expenditures, and vendor contract values are highly concentrated. The present version does not yet establish the stronger declared-versus-operative conclusions it attaches to those numbers.
